docs.title: Spock AI Helper
docs.text:
Welcome to the Spock AI Helper documentation site. This guide serves as the primary reference for Spock-Onboarding, a local AI workstation management suite that helps users initialize, run, and query local large language model (LLM) environments from a clean starting point.

UI screenshots (captioned): Screenshot gallery · GitHub repo

docs.title: What is Spock-Onboarding?
docs.text:
Spock-Onboarding is a console-first initialization suite designed to provision and manage local LLM workstations from scratch. In this context, “greenfield” indicates that the system can be deployed on a new machine or fresh user profile without requiring prior AI tooling configuration. The suite automates setup by managing the following key aspects of the AI environment:

  • Hardware Detection — Scans GPU, VRAM, CPU, and RAM resources to identify system capabilities for local model deployment.
  • Model Management — Queries the Hugging Face Hub and downloads GGUF model files optimized for local inference with llama-server.
  • Server Lifecycle — Starts, stops, and monitors llama-server processes on port 8080 (embedding/semantic services) and port 8081 (chat).
  • RAG Search — Performs hybrid vector and FTS5 search over ingested documents to retrieve relevant context for prompts.
  • Document Ingestion — Uses the Wiki Agent to monitor directories and extract content from over 15 file formats into a searchable local knowledge base.
  • MCP Integration — Enables Model Context Protocol (MCP) integration, allowing the LLM to interact with external tools and data sources through compatible clients such as Cursor and OpenCode.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
• Local inference: The model runs on the user’s workstation rather than in a cloud service.
  • GGUF: A common file format for quantized large language models used by local inference engines.
  • RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation): A pattern where relevant documents are retrieved first and then included in the prompt to ground the model’s answer.
  • FTS5: SQLite’s full-text search extension, used here for fast keyword matching.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
To launch the Spock-Onboarding interface, run the following command in a terminal from the installation directory or an environment where Spock-Menu.bat is available:

Spock-Menu.bat

The menu provides entry points to hardware scanning, model management, server control, document ingestion, and AI chat features.

docs.title: AI Chat Helper
docs.text:
The Spock AI Helper (Spock-AI-Helper.bat) launches the underlying Python engine (helper_main.py) to provide a chat interface powered by the suite’s local chat LLM. The context used for the chat is pulled from curated files located in the AIHelperDocuments/ directory at the root of the Spock-Onboarding installation.

These curated files can include reference material, operational notes, or domain-specific guidance that helps the assistant answer questions consistently with the local workstation setup.

To launch the AI Chat Helper, run the following command in a terminal:

Spock-AI-Helper.bat

docs.title: Database Architecture: ship_computer.db
docs.text: The Spock application relies on a single, persistent SQLite 3 database named ship_computer.db to manage document storage, metadata, search indexes, and conversation history. This database acts as the central knowledge backbone for both the AI Chat Helper and the broader onboarding suite.

docs.title: Schema Overview
docs.text: The database is structured around several key tables and virtual tables: - documents: Stores raw file paths, ingestion timestamps, file types, and parsing status. - chunks: Contains text segments extracted during ingestion, along with parent document references and positional metadata. - fts5_index: A virtual table powered by SQLite’s FTS5 extension. It maintains an inverted index of all text chunks for rapid keyword and phrase matching. - embeddings: Stores high-dimensional vector representations of each text chunk. Vectors are typically stored as serialized binary blobs or fixed-length real arrays, depending on the SQLite extension in use. - chat_history: Logs user prompts, assistant responses, retrieval metadata, and session identifiers for context continuity and auditability. - query_logs: Tracks search parameters, retrieval scores, and execution times to optimize future RAG pipelines.

docs.title: Interaction with Spock Inquiries
docs.text: When a user submits a query, helper_main.py translates the request into structured SQL and vector similarity operations against ship_computer.db. The database handles transactional integrity, ensuring that document updates, embedding recalculations, and search results remain consistent across concurrent operations. All retrieval operations are cached at the application layer to reduce redundant disk I/O during rapid follow-up questions.

docs.title: Embedding LLM & Vector Database Workflow
docs.text: Spock uses a dedicated embedding LLM to convert unstructured text into numerical vectors that capture semantic meaning. This process enables the system to understand conceptual relationships between queries and documents, rather than relying solely on exact keyword matches.

docs.title: Embedding Generation
docs.text:
1. Text Chunking: During ingestion, documents are split into overlapping segments (typically 256–512 tokens) to preserve context while maintaining manageable vector dimensions.
  2. Local Inference: The embedding model runs on llama-server (port 8080). Each chunk is sent to the model, which outputs a fixed-length vector (e.g., 768 or 1536 dimensions).
  3. Storage: The resulting vectors are persisted in the embeddings table of ship_computer.db, linked to their corresponding chunks via foreign keys.

docs.title: Vector Search & Hybrid Retrieval
docs.text:
When a query is submitted, Spock performs a two-stage retrieval process: - Semantic Search: The user’s prompt is embedded using the same model. The system then executes a cosine similarity or inner-product search against the embeddings table to rank chunks by conceptual relevance. - Keyword Search: Simultaneously, FTS5 scans the fts5_index for exact term matches, handling technical identifiers, version numbers, and proper nouns that embeddings may dilute. - Re-Ranking & Fusion: Results from both pathways are merged using a weighted scoring algorithm. High-confidence matches are passed to the chat LLM as context, while low-scoring results are filtered out to prevent prompt bloat.

This hybrid approach ensures that Spock can accurately resolve both conceptual questions and precise technical lookups.

docs.title: How the Embedding LLM and Vector Database Work Together
docs.text:
The embedding LLM and the vector database serve different but complementary roles in Spock’s retrieval pipeline.

  • Embedding LLM: This model converts text into a dense numerical representation. It is used for both document chunks during ingestion and user prompts during search. Because the same model is used for both sides of the comparison, the resulting vectors live in the same semantic space.
  • Vector Database: In Spock, the vector database is implemented as part of ship_computer.db. The embeddings table stores the numerical vectors produced by the embedding LLM, while the chunks table stores the source text that each vector represents.
  • Search Behavior: When a user asks a question, Spock embeds the prompt and compares that vector against stored chunk vectors. Chunks with the highest similarity scores are considered semantically relevant.
  • Hybrid Strength: Embeddings are effective for conceptual matching, while FTS5 is effective for exact lexical matching. By combining both, Spock can answer questions such as “how do I configure retry behavior?” and “what is the exact flag name for timeout?” with comparable reliability.

docs.title: Ask AI vs. Deep Dive Inquiry Modes
docs.text: Spock distinguishes between two primary inquiry modes to balance response speed with retrieval depth. Both modes leverage ship_computer.db and the embedding pipeline, but they differ in scope and computational intensity.

docs.title: Ask AI
docs.text:
• Purpose: Rapid, conversational responses for straightforward questions.
  • Retrieval Strategy: Executes a lightweight FTS5 query combined with a shallow vector similarity scan (top-5 to top-10 chunks).
  • Database Interaction: Reads from cached indexes and avoids full table scans. Context window is kept minimal to reduce latency.
  • Use Case: Syntax help, quick definitions, status checks, and general navigation guidance.

docs.title: Deep Dive
docs.text:
• Purpose: Comprehensive, multi-source analysis for complex troubleshooting or architectural questions.
  • Retrieval Strategy: Triggers a full vector similarity sweep (top-20 to top-50 chunks), cross-references related documents via metadata joins, and applies recursive chunk expansion for context continuity.
  • Database Interaction: Performs deeper joins across documents, chunks, and embeddings tables. May initiate background embedding recalculations if source files have been modified since last ingestion.
  • Use Case: Multi-step debugging, policy analysis, cross-document synthesis, and detailed configuration guidance.

Users can explicitly select a mode via the chat interface, or Spock can auto-route queries based on prompt length, keyword triggers, and historical interaction patterns.

docs.title: SQLite 3 ship_computer.db Architecture
docs.text: ship_computer.db is the central SQLite 3 database used by the Spock application. It stores ingested content, derived chunks, embeddings, full-text search indexes, and metadata needed for both Ask AI and Deep Dive workflows.

docs.title: Core Tables
docs.text:
The following tables form the primary data model:

Table Purpose documents Tracks source files or records that have been ingested into Spock. chunks Stores the text segments created from each document. embeddings Stores the vector representations generated from each chunk. fts5_index Provides full-text search over chunk text using SQLite FTS5. metadata Stores document- or chunk-level attributes used for filtering and cross-referencing. ingestion_runs Records ingestion jobs, status, and timing information. query_logs Optionally records user queries, selected mode, and retrieval statistics.

A representative schema is:

CREATE TABLE documents (
    id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    source_path TEXT NOT NULL,
    title TEXT,
    content_type TEXT,
    file_hash TEXT,
    status TEXT NOT NULL,
    ingested_at TEXT NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE chunks (
    id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    document_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES documents(id),
    chunk_index INTEGER NOT NULL,
    text TEXT NOT NULL,
    token_count INTEGER,
    created_at TEXT NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE embeddings (
    id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    chunk_id INTEGER NOT NULL UNIQUE REFERENCES chunks(id),
    model_name TEXT NOT NULL,
    model_version TEXT,
    dimensions INTEGER NOT NULL,
    vector BLOB NOT NULL,
    normalized INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
    created_at TEXT NOT NULL
);

CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE fts5_index USING fts5(
    chunk_id,
    text,
    content='chunks',
    content_rowid='id'
);

docs.title: Relationships and Constraints
docs.text:
• chunks.document_id links each chunk to its parent document.
  • embeddings.chunk_id links each vector to the exact chunk it represents.
  • fts5_index maps search results back to chunks rows.
  • metadata can be associated with either documents or chunks, depending on the attribute being stored.
  • Indexes are typically maintained on documents.status, chunks.document_id, and embeddings.model_name to support fast retrieval and filtering.

docs.title: Ask AI Interaction
docs.text:
For Ask AI requests, Spock uses ship_computer.db in a read-optimized, low-latency manner.

  1. Prompt Embedding: The user prompt is sent to the embedding LLM and converted into a query vector.
  2. Lexical Search: Spock issues an FTS5 query against fts5_index to find chunks containing exact or near-exact terms.
  3. Semantic Search: Spock compares the query vector against stored vectors in embeddings and selects the highest-scoring chunks.
  4. Fusion and Truncation: The two result sets are merged, scored, and truncated to a small number of chunks.
  5. Context Assembly: The selected chunk text is passed to the chat LLM as context for a concise answer.

This mode is optimized for speed, so it typically avoids broad joins, large result sets, and background recomputation.

docs.title: Deep Dive Interaction
docs.text:
For Deep Dive requests, Spock uses ship_computer.db more extensively.

  1. Broader Retrieval: Spock retrieves a larger candidate set from both FTS5 and vector search.
  2. Metadata Joins: It joins across documents, chunks, embeddings, and metadata to identify related sources, tags, versions, or configuration scopes.
  3. Context Expansion: Spock may pull neighboring chunks from the same document to preserve continuity around a relevant passage.
  4. Cross-Document Synthesis: It can combine evidence from multiple documents when the question spans several sources.
  5. Staleness Checks: If a source file has changed since the last ingestion, Spock may flag the document for re-chunking and re-embedding.

This mode is optimized for completeness and accuracy rather than minimal latency.

docs.title: Concurrency and Performance Considerations
docs.text:
Because Spock is built on SQLite 3, the database is file-based and well suited to local or single-node deployment.

  • WAL Mode: Using write-ahead logging allows concurrent reads while writes are occurring, which is useful when ingestion and query traffic overlap.
  • Prepared Statements: Reusing prepared statements reduces parsing overhead and improves query consistency.
  • Vector Storage: Vectors are stored as BLOB values. Similarity scoring may be performed in Python or through a SQLite vector extension, depending on the deployment.
  • Hybrid Indexing: FTS5 handles lexical search efficiently, while vector search handles semantic similarity. Together, they reduce the need for a separate vector database service.

This design lets Spock maintain a single, inspectable SQLite database for both content storage and retrieval, while still supporting the two distinct inquiry modes used by the application.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
The following diagram illustrates the overall architecture of the Spock-Onboarding system:

graph TD
    U[User] --> O[Orchestrator Hub]
    O --> NS[Navigation Station]
    O --> ED[Engineering Deck]
    O --> LRS[Long Range Sensors]
    O --> SS[Science Station]

    NS --> HW[Hardware Scan]
    NS --> LS[Launch Servers]
    LS --> EM[llama-server :8080]
    LS --> CH[llama-server :8081]

    ED --> ASK[Ask AI / Deep Dive]
    ASK --> RAG[RAG API Server]
    RAG --> SC[(ship_computer.db)]

    SS --> WA[Wiki Agent]
    WA --> SC

docs.title: Explanation of Key Components
docs.text:
• Orchestrator Hub: Central management component that coordinates user requests, module interactions, and overall workflow state. It determines which subsystem should handle a request and maintains the session context for the user.
  • Navigation Station: Handles hardware detection, resource scanning, and server launch operations. It is responsible for identifying local inference resources and starting the required llama-server endpoints.
  • Engineering Deck: Provides AI chat interfaces and deep-dive analysis capabilities for the user. Ask AI requests are typically single-turn, context-grounded questions. Deep Dive requests use the RAG pipeline to gather more detailed local context before generating a response.
  • Long Range Sensors: Monitors system health, external data streams, and environmental metrics that may affect local inference performance or reliability.
  • Science Station: Manages document ingestion pipelines, knowledge-base maintenance, and content extraction workflows.
  • Wiki Agent: Extracts text from supported file formats, prepares it for indexing, and ingests it into the system’s database.
  • RAG API Server: Handles hybrid search over ingested documents by combining vector similarity with FTS5 keyword matching to return relevant context.
  • ship_computer.db: Central SQLite database that stores document chunks, embeddings, full-text indexes, metadata, and system state data used across the suite.

docs.title: SQLite Database Core (ship_computer.db)
docs.text: The ship_computer.db file is the foundational persistence layer for the Spock-Onboarding suite. It is built on SQLite 3, a lightweight, serverless, zero-configuration relational database engine that resides entirely on the local workstation. This design keeps knowledge retrieval and system-state operations offline, portable, and independent of external cloud services. SQLite's ACID compliance and Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) mode ensure data integrity and high concurrent read performance during active RAG queries.

docs.title: Data Storage Strategy
docs.text:
The database is structured to support high-performance Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) by separating semantic meaning from exact keyword matching:

  • Vector Embeddings Table: Stores high-dimensional vector representations of text chunks as binary large objects (BLOBs) or serialized JSON arrays. These vectors enable semantic similarity searches, retrieving context that matches the meaning of a user’s query rather than relying solely on literal keywords.
  • FTS5 Virtual Tables: Implements SQLite's Full-Text Search (FTS5) extension for rapid, tokenized keyword matching. This ensures that specific technical terms, identifiers, file paths, or error strings are retrieved efficiently without scanning the entire vector space.
  • Metadata & Provenance Tables: Track document sources, ingestion timestamps, original file paths, chunk boundaries, chunk sizes, and content types. This supports precise filtering, audit trails, and reliable context selection during retrieval.
  • System State & Configuration Tables: Store runtime parameters, embedding model identifiers, chunking strategies, and user preferences to maintain consistent behavior across sessions.

docs.title: Core Table Responsibilities
docs.text:
The following table responsibilities describe the practical role of each major data area inside ship_computer.db:

Area Purpose Documents Stores one row per ingested source file or logical document. This provides a stable parent record for chunks, metadata, and provenance. Chunks Stores the actual text fragments used for retrieval. Each chunk is a bounded piece of content that can be embedded, searched, and injected into an LLM prompt. Embeddings Stores the vector representation for each chunk. The vector is generated by the local embedding model and used for semantic similarity search. FTS5 Index Provides fast keyword search over chunk text. This is especially useful for exact terms, code identifiers, error messages, file names, and technical phrases. Metadata Stores attributes such as source path, file type, ingestion time, chunk index, chunk size, and content classification. System State Stores configuration and runtime state, including embedding model identity, vector dimension, chunking settings, and last successful ingestion or indexing operations.

docs.title: Interaction Flow for Ask AI and Deep Dive
docs.text:
The ship_computer.db database interacts directly with the Spock application during user inquiries through the following workflow:

  1. User Input: A user initiates an Ask AI or Deep Dive inquiry through the Engineering Deck interface.
  2. Request Routing: The Orchestrator Hub routes the natural-language query to the RAG API Server.
  3. Hybrid Search Execution: The RAG API Server constructs a search request against ship_computer.db using hybrid logic:
  4. It generates vector embeddings for the user’s query and compares them with stored document vectors for semantic relevance.
  5. It simultaneously runs FTS5 keyword filters to ensure important terms, identifiers, or exact phrases are considered.
  6. Context Retrieval: The database returns the top-ranked text chunks that satisfy both semantic and keyword criteria. For Deep Dive requests, the query expands to include multi-hop retrieval, broader chunk windows, and recursive metadata filtering to assemble a comprehensive context window.
  7. Prompt Assembly: These retrieved chunks are injected into the LLM prompt, allowing the Spock AI Helper to generate accurate, context-aware responses grounded in the local knowledge base.

docs.title: Ask AI vs Deep Dive Retrieval Behavior
docs.text:
Although both Ask AI and Deep Dive use the same underlying database and retrieval infrastructure, they differ in retrieval depth and context assembly:

  • Ask AI:
  • Optimized for fast, direct answers.
  • Usually performs a single hybrid retrieval pass.
  • Returns a small number of highly relevant chunks.

  • Best suited for questions such as “What does this setting do?” or “How do I configure this component?”

  • Deep Dive:

  • Optimized for thorough, multi-step analysis.
  • May perform multiple retrieval passes, also called multi-hop retrieval.
  • Expands the search using terms, entities, or concepts discovered in the first retrieved chunks.
  • Applies broader metadata filters and larger context windows.
  • Best suited for questions such as “Explain the full ingestion pipeline” or “Compare the behavior of these two subsystems.”

In both cases, the database remains the source of truth for retrieved content. The LLM does not invent local documentation facts; it synthesizes the chunks returned by the RAG API Server.

docs.title: Concurrency, Integrity, and Portability
docs.text:
SQLite 3 is well suited to this architecture because the Spock application is local-first and does not require a separate database server.

  • Single-file storage: The entire knowledge base and system state can be stored in one portable file.
  • WAL mode: Allows readers to continue serving RAG queries while the Wiki Agent or Science Station performs ingestion or indexing work.
  • ACID transactions: Ensure that ingestion, chunking, embedding, and indexing operations either complete fully or roll back cleanly.
  • Local operation: No external database service is required, which keeps the system offline-capable and self-contained.

docs.title: Embedding LLM and Vector Database Integration
docs.text: The Spock application relies on a local embedding LLM and a vector-backed retrieval system to bridge natural language queries with structured database content. This integration operates through a deterministic pipeline:

docs.title: Embedding LLM Responsibilities
docs.text:
The embedding LLM, or embedding model, is responsible for converting text into numerical vectors. These vectors represent the semantic meaning of the text in a high-dimensional space.

The embedding model is used in two major phases:

  1. Ingestion Phase:
  2. The Wiki Agent extracts text from documents.
  3. The text is split into chunks.
  4. Each chunk is sent to the local embedding model.

  5. The resulting vector is stored in ship_computer.db.

  6. Query Phase:

  7. The user’s question is sent to the same embedding model.
  8. The model produces a query vector.
  9. The RAG API Server compares the query vector against stored chunk vectors.
  10. Chunks with the closest semantic meaning are ranked and returned.

Using the same embedding model for both ingestion and querying is important because vector similarity is only meaningful when both sides of the comparison are produced by the same model and have the same vector dimension.

docs.title: Vector Database Responsibilities
docs.text:
In this architecture, ship_computer.db acts as the vector database. It stores the embeddings and provides the persistence layer for semantic search.

The vector database is responsible for:

  • Storing chunk embeddings as BLOBs or serialized arrays.
  • Preserving the relationship between a vector and its source chunk.
  • Supporting similarity comparison between the query vector and stored chunk vectors.
  • Providing metadata needed to filter, rank, and cite retrieved content.

Depending on the implementation, vector similarity may be computed in one of two ways:

  • Application-layer similarity: The RAG API Server loads candidate vectors from SQLite and computes cosine similarity in Python.
  • SQLite vector extension: If an extension such as sqlite-vec is available, similarity search can be executed closer to the database layer.

In both cases, the conceptual role is the same: the database stores vectors, and the RAG API Server uses those vectors to find semantically relevant chunks.

docs.title: Deterministic Retrieval Pipeline
docs.text:
The full embedding and vector retrieval pipeline follows a deterministic sequence:

  1. Document Ingestion:
  2. The Science Station or Wiki Agent reads a supported file.
  3. Text is extracted and normalized.

  4. The document is split into manageable chunks.

  5. Embedding Generation:

  6. Each chunk is sent to the local embedding model.
  7. The model returns a fixed-length vector.

  8. The vector is stored alongside the chunk text and metadata.

  9. Keyword Indexing:

  10. The same chunk text is indexed in an FTS5 virtual table.

  11. This creates a fast keyword search path for exact terms and technical identifiers.

  12. Query Embedding:

  13. When the user submits an Ask AI or Deep Dive request, the query text is embedded using the same local embedding model.

  14. Hybrid Search:

  15. The RAG API Server performs vector similarity search using the query vector.
  16. It also performs FTS5 keyword search using the raw query terms.

  17. The two result sets are combined using a ranking strategy such as weighted scoring or reciprocal rank fusion.

  18. Context Assembly:

  19. The top-ranked chunks are selected.
  20. Metadata is used to preserve source information and chunk order.

  21. The chunks are formatted into a prompt for the local LLM.

  22. Response Generation:

  23. The local LLM generates an answer based on the retrieved context.
  24. The response is returned to the user through the Engineering Deck.

docs.title: Hybrid Scoring and Ranking
docs.text:
Hybrid search is used because vector search and keyword search have different strengths.

  • Vector search is strong when the user’s wording differs from the document wording.

  • Example: “How do I make the server start faster?” may match documentation that says “reduce startup latency.”

  • Keyword search is strong when the user includes exact technical terms.

  • Example: “llama-server :8081” or “ship_computer.db” should be matched directly.

The RAG API Server combines both signals so that the final ranking favors chunks that are both semantically relevant and lexically precise.

docs.title: Ask AI and Deep Dive in the Embedding Pipeline
docs.text:
The embedding and vector database pipeline supports both interaction modes:

  • Ask AI:
  • Uses a single query embedding.
  • Performs one hybrid retrieval pass.
  • Returns a compact set of chunks.

  • Produces a concise, grounded answer.

  • Deep Dive:

  • Uses the initial query embedding and retrieval results as a starting point.
  • Extracts additional terms, entities, or concepts from the first retrieved chunks.
  • Performs additional embedding and retrieval passes.
  • Assembles a larger, more comprehensive context window.
  • Produces a more detailed, structured explanation.

This allows the Spock application to answer simple questions quickly while still supporting deeper investigation when the user requests a more thorough analysis.

docs.title: Fallback and Consistency Behavior
docs.text:
Because the system is local and deterministic, the application can maintain consistent behavior even when some components are unavailable.

  • If the embedding model is unavailable, the RAG API Server may fall back to FTS5-only keyword search, depending on configuration.
  • If a document has not been embedded, it may still be searchable through FTS5 if it has been indexed.
  • If a chunk is missing metadata, it may still be retrieved, but citation and filtering accuracy may be reduced.
  • If the database is locked or corrupted, SQLite’s transactional behavior helps prevent partial writes and supports recovery.

This design keeps the Spock application responsive, auditable, and grounded in the local knowledge base stored in ship_computer.db.

docs.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation Architecture
docs.text:
1. Text Chunking & Preprocessing: During ingestion, the Wiki Agent splits documents into semantically coherent chunks, typically 250–500 tokens in length. Overlapping windows are applied to preserve context across chunk boundaries, reducing the risk that important relationships are split between adjacent chunks.

  2. Embedding Generation: The local embedding LLM converts each chunk into a dense, fixed-dimensional vector. These vectors capture semantic relationships, synonyms, and contextual nuances that traditional keyword search cannot reliably detect.

  3. Vector Storage & Indexing: Embeddings are persisted in ship_computer.db alongside chunk identifiers. SQLite stores the vectors efficiently using BLOB serialization, while distance metrics—typically cosine similarity or Euclidean distance—are computed at query time by the RAG API Server.

  4. Query Embedding & Similarity Search: When a user submits a prompt, the same embedding LLM processes the query into a vector of identical dimensionality. The system then performs a nearest-neighbor search against the stored vectors, ranking chunks by semantic proximity.

  5. Hybrid Fusion & Reranking: Vector scores are combined with FTS5 keyword relevance scores using a weighted fusion algorithm. This hybrid approach mitigates the limitations of pure semantic search, such as missing exact identifiers, and the limitations of pure keyword search, such as failing to capture conceptual matches.

  6. Context Window Assembly: The top-ranked chunks are assembled into a structured context payload. For Ask AI, a lightweight, single-pass context window is generated. For Deep Dive, the system iteratively expands the search radius, applies domain-specific filters, and aggregates multi-source chunks to support complex, multi-step reasoning.

  7. Privacy & Offline Operation: Because both the embedding LLM and vector database run locally, no query data or embeddings leave the workstation. This ensures full data sovereignty, predictable local latency, and uninterrupted operation in air-gapped or restricted environments.

docs.title: SQLite 3 ship_computer.db and Spock Application Interaction
docs.text: ship_computer.db is a local SQLite 3 database that serves as the persistent storage layer for the Spock application’s retrieval pipeline. It stores ingested document metadata, text chunks, full-text search indexes, and vector embeddings. The database is local to the workstation and is accessed by the RAG API Server, which provides retrieval and context-assembly services to the Spock application.

docs.title: Role of ship_computer.db
docs.text:
The database has three primary responsibilities:

  • Document and chunk persistence: It stores the source documents, their metadata, and the text chunks produced during ingestion.
  • Vector embedding storage: It stores the dense vector representations generated by the local embedding LLM.
  • Hybrid search support: It supports both semantic vector search and keyword-based full-text search through SQLite FTS5.

The Spock application does not directly perform vector math or database queries for Ask AI and Deep Dive requests. Instead, it sends user prompts to the RAG API Server, which coordinates embedding generation, database retrieval, scoring, fusion, and context assembly.

docs.title: Typical Database Structure
docs.text:
A typical ship_computer.db schema includes the following logical components:

CREATE TABLE documents (
    doc_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    source TEXT,
    title TEXT,
    file_path TEXT,
    content_hash TEXT,
    ingested_at TEXT
);

CREATE TABLE chunks (
    chunk_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    doc_id TEXT,
    sequence INTEGER,
    text TEXT,
    token_count INTEGER,
    metadata_json TEXT,
    FOREIGN KEY (doc_id) REFERENCES documents(doc_id)
);

CREATE TABLE embeddings (
    chunk_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    model_name TEXT,
    dimension INTEGER,
    vector BLOB,
    created_at TEXT,
    FOREIGN KEY (chunk_id) REFERENCES chunks(chunk_id)
);

CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE chunks_fts USING fts5(
    chunk_id UNINDEXED,
    text,
    content='chunks',
    content_rowid='rowid'
);

The embeddings table stores each vector as a binary BLOB. The vector dimension, model name, and creation timestamp are stored alongside the vector to ensure that queries use compatible embeddings and that stale or incompatible vectors can be identified.

docs.title: Ask AI Interaction
docs.text:
For Ask AI inquiries, the Spock application provides a lightweight question-and-answer experience. The interaction flow is as follows:

  1. The user submits a prompt in the Spock application.
  2. The Spock application sends the prompt to the RAG API Server.
  3. The RAG API Server sends the prompt to the local embedding LLM.
  4. The embedding LLM returns a query vector.
  5. The RAG API Server queries ship_computer.db for:
  6. Semantically similar chunks using vector similarity.
  7. Keyword-matching chunks using FTS5.
  8. The RAG API Server fuses the vector and keyword scores.
  9. The top-ranked chunks are assembled into a compact context window.
  10. The context window is used to generate a concise answer.
  11. The answer is returned to the Spock application.

Ask AI is optimized for speed and simplicity. It typically performs a single retrieval pass and returns a focused answer based on the most relevant chunks.

docs.title: Deep Dive Interaction
docs.text:
For Deep Dive inquiries, the Spock application supports more complex, multi-step investigation. The interaction flow is as follows:

  1. The user submits a detailed prompt or research question.
  2. The Spock application sends the prompt to the RAG API Server.
  3. The RAG API Server performs an initial retrieval pass using the embedding LLM and ship_computer.db.
  4. The system evaluates the retrieved chunks and may generate follow-up subqueries.
  5. Additional retrieval passes are performed with:
  6. Expanded similarity thresholds.
  7. Domain-specific filters.
  8. Source or document constraints.
  9. Keyword refinements.
  10. Results from multiple passes are merged, deduplicated, and reranked.
  11. A larger, structured context payload is assembled for multi-step reasoning.
  12. The Spock application receives a more detailed response, often with supporting evidence or citations.

Deep Dive is designed for questions that require synthesis across multiple documents, comparison of concepts, or iterative exploration of related material.

docs.title: How Spock Uses the Embedding LLM and Vector Database
docs.text: The Spock application relies on two local components for retrieval: the embedding LLM and the vector database stored in ship_computer.db.

docs.title: Embedding LLM
docs.text:
The embedding LLM is a local language model used to convert text into numerical vectors. It is used in two places:

  • Ingestion: The Wiki Agent embeds document chunks before storing them in ship_computer.db.
  • Query time: The RAG API Server embeds user prompts before searching the vector store.

Using the same embedding model for both documents and queries ensures that the vectors are comparable. If the model changes, the dimensionality or semantic space may change, so the system should track the model name and vector dimension in the database.

docs.title: Vector Database
docs.text:
The vector database is implemented using SQLite 3 rather than a separate vector database service. This keeps the architecture local, simple, and portable.

The vector database stores:

  • Chunk identifiers.
  • Embedding vectors.
  • Model metadata.
  • Vector dimension.
  • Creation timestamps.

At query time, the RAG API Server:

  1. Loads the query vector.
  2. Reads candidate embedding vectors from ship_computer.db.
  3. Deserializes the BLOB vectors.
  4. Computes similarity scores.
  5. Ranks chunks by relevance.

For normalized vectors, cosine similarity can be computed efficiently as a dot product. For unnormalized vectors, the system may compute cosine similarity or Euclidean distance depending on the configured metric.

docs.title: Hybrid Search
docs.text:
The Spock application does not rely on vector search alone. It combines vector similarity with FTS5 keyword search. This hybrid approach improves recall and precision by handling both semantic and exact-match requirements.

For example:

  • Vector search is useful for conceptual questions such as “What are the risks associated with this system?”
  • FTS5 keyword search is useful for exact identifiers such as part numbers, error codes, or specific technical terms.

The RAG API Server merges these signals into a final ranked context window before passing it to the answer-generation stage.

docs.title: SQLite 3 ship_computer.db
docs.text:
ship_computer.db is the local SQLite 3 database used by the Spock application to store durable, transactional application state. It acts as the system of record for user interactions, conversation history, document metadata, Deep Dive task state, and audit information.

The database is not the primary vector store. Instead, it provides the relational context that allows the Spock application to make Ask AI and Deep Dive responses reproducible, inspectable, resumable, and auditable.

docs.title: Responsibilities
docs.text:
ship_computer.db is responsible for storing:

  • Application configuration and runtime state.
  • User, session, and permission metadata.
  • Ask AI conversation history.
  • Deep Dive request definitions and execution state.
  • Document and chunk metadata.
  • Source references and citation provenance.
  • Model, prompt, and response metadata.
  • Audit logs and operational diagnostics.

This separation allows the application to use SQLite for reliable structured storage while using a vector database for semantic similarity search.

docs.title: Core Data Model
docs.text:
The following tables represent the primary relational structures used by the Spock application.

Table Purpose app_state Stores application-level settings, version information, and runtime flags. users Stores user identities, roles, and access permissions. sessions Tracks active user sessions and interaction context. conversations Stores Ask AI conversation containers. messages Stores individual user and assistant messages within a conversation. deep_dive_requests Stores Deep Dive task definitions, objectives, and status. deep_dive_steps Stores individual execution steps within a Deep Dive workflow. documents Stores source documents, files, or knowledge-base entries. chunks Stores document chunks used for retrieval and citation. chunk_metadata Stores structured metadata associated with each chunk. vector_references Maps SQLite chunk records to vector database identifiers. audit_log Records significant application events for troubleshooting and compliance.

docs.title: Relationship to Ask AI
docs.text:
Ask AI is the conversational interface where users ask natural-language questions and receive generated answers. The Spock application uses ship_computer.db to manage the full lifecycle of an Ask AI interaction.

When a user submits a question, the application performs the following steps:

  1. Resolve the conversation context The application identifies the active conversation, user, and session from ship_computer.db.

  2. Persist the user message The user’s question is stored in the messages table with metadata such as timestamp, user ID, and conversation ID.

  3. Retrieve relevant context The application converts the question into an embedding and queries the vector database for semantically relevant chunks.

  4. Resolve citations The vector database returns chunk identifiers. The application uses those identifiers to look up source documents, chunk text, and metadata in ship_computer.db.

  5. Generate the response The application sends the retrieved context to the language model and receives a generated answer.

  6. Persist the assistant response The generated answer, model metadata, prompt version, retrieval results, and citation references are stored in ship_computer.db.

  7. Enable follow-up questions Because the conversation history is stored in SQLite, the application can reconstruct prior context for subsequent Ask AI questions.

This design ensures that Ask AI responses are not only generated in memory but are also recorded, traceable, and available for later review.

docs.title: Relationship to Deep Dive
docs.text:
Deep Dive is a more structured inquiry workflow where the Spock application performs multi-step analysis, retrieval, and synthesis. ship_computer.db stores the state required to track and resume these workflows.

A Deep Dive request typically includes:

  • A user-defined objective.
  • One or more source documents or knowledge-base scopes.
  • A sequence of analysis steps.
  • Intermediate retrieval results.
  • Generated summaries or findings.
  • Final report metadata.

The application uses ship_computer.db in the following way:

  1. Create the Deep Dive request The user’s objective, scope, and parameters are stored in deep_dive_requests.

  2. Break the request into steps The application creates records in deep_dive_steps for each planned operation, such as retrieval, summarization, comparison, or synthesis.

  3. Track step status Each step is marked as pending, running, completed, failed, or cancelled.

  4. Store intermediate results Retrieved chunks, generated summaries, confidence scores, and source references are stored or referenced in SQLite.

  5. Maintain provenance The application records which documents, chunks, models, and prompts contributed to each finding.

  6. Produce the final report The final Deep Dive output is stored with links to the underlying steps, sources, and metadata.

This allows Deep Dive workflows to be paused, resumed, audited, and reproduced.

docs.title: Data Integrity and Operational Notes
docs.text:
Because ship_computer.db is a local SQLite 3 database, the Spock application should use SQLite features that support reliable local operation:

  • Transactions ensure that multi-step writes either complete fully or roll back cleanly.
  • Foreign keys preserve relationships between users, conversations, messages, documents, and Deep Dive steps.
  • Indexes improve lookup performance for conversation history, document metadata, and audit queries.
  • WAL mode can improve concurrent read performance while the application is writing new interaction data.
  • Backup and restore should treat ship_computer.db as a critical local artifact because it contains user history and workflow state.

docs.title: Embedding LLM and Vector Database
docs.text:
The Spock application uses an embedding LLM, also referred to as an embedding model, to convert natural-language text into numerical vectors. These vectors represent the semantic meaning of the text in a way that can be compared mathematically.

The vector database stores these embeddings and provides fast similarity search. Together, the embedding model and vector database allow the Spock application to retrieve relevant information from large text collections without requiring exact keyword matches.

docs.title: Why Embeddings Are Used
docs.text:
Traditional keyword search works well when the user’s question uses the same words as the source material. However, Ask AI and Deep Dive often require semantic understanding.

For example, a user may ask:

“What should we do if the navigation system loses alignment?”

The relevant document may not contain the exact phrase “navigation system loses alignment.” It may instead discuss:

  • sensor drift
  • attitude correction
  • star tracker recalibration
  • guidance recovery procedures

An embedding model can recognize that these concepts are semantically related, even if the wording differs.

docs.title: Ingestion Pipeline
docs.text:
Before the Spock application can answer questions, source material must be prepared for retrieval.

The ingestion pipeline typically performs the following steps:

  1. Collect source documents Documents may include engineering guides, maintenance procedures, knowledge-base entries, or other approved content.

  2. Normalize and split documents Large documents are divided into smaller chunks that are meaningful enough to retrieve but small enough to use as context.

  3. Generate embeddings Each chunk is passed through the embedding LLM to produce a vector representation.

  4. Store vectors in the vector database The vector database stores the embedding along with metadata such as document ID, chunk ID, source title, section, and access scope.

  5. Record metadata in SQLite ship_computer.db stores the relational metadata for the document and chunk, including the vector database identifier.

This creates a linked system where the vector database handles semantic search and SQLite handles structured metadata and provenance.

docs.title: Ask AI Retrieval Flow
docs.text:
When a user submits an Ask AI question, the Spock application uses the embedding LLM and vector database as follows:

  1. Embed the user question The user’s question is converted into a vector using the same embedding model used during ingestion.

  2. Query the vector database The vector database searches for the most similar stored vectors.

  3. Return candidate chunks The database returns a ranked set of chunks, usually the top N most relevant results.

  4. Filter by metadata The Spock application may filter results based on user permissions, document scope, session context, or Deep Dive constraints.

  5. Resolve source details The application uses the chunk identifiers to retrieve full chunk text and source metadata from ship_computer.db.

  6. Build the prompt The retrieved context is combined with the user’s question and any conversation history.

  7. Generate the answer The language model produces a response based on the retrieved context.

  8. Store the interaction The question, answer, retrieved chunks, model metadata, and citation references are persisted in ship_computer.db.

docs.title: Deep Dive Retrieval Flow
docs.text:
Deep Dive uses the same embedding and vector database infrastructure, but in a more iterative and structured way.

A Deep Dive workflow may perform multiple retrieval passes:

  1. Initial retrieval The application embeds the user’s objective and retrieves broadly relevant chunks.

  2. Step-specific retrieval Each Deep Dive step may generate its own query, such as “find failure modes,” “find recovery procedures,” or “find related maintenance constraints.”

  3. Refined retrieval Results from earlier steps can be used to generate more specific follow-up queries.

  4. Cross-reference analysis The application compares retrieved chunks to identify relationships, contradictions, or supporting evidence.

  5. Citation tracking Every finding is linked back to the chunks and documents that support it.

  6. Report generation The final Deep Dive report is generated from the accumulated context and stored with full provenance.

This allows Deep Dive to move beyond a single answer and produce a structured, evidence-backed analysis.

docs.title: Relationship Between SQLite and the Vector Database
docs.text:
The SQLite database and vector database serve different but complementary roles.

System Primary Role ship_computer.db Stores structured application state, user history, document metadata, and audit information. Vector database Stores embeddings and performs semantic similarity search.

The two systems are linked through identifiers. For example, a chunk stored in the vector database may have a chunk_id that matches a record in the chunks table in ship_computer.db.

This design provides the following benefits:

  • Semantic search is handled by the vector database.
  • Reliable persistence is handled by SQLite.
  • Citations and provenance can be resolved through SQLite metadata.
  • Conversation history remains available even if the vector database is rebuilt.
  • Deep Dive workflows can be resumed using stored step state.

docs.title: Failure and Fallback Behavior
docs.text:
If the vector database is unavailable, the Spock application can still access relational data stored in ship_computer.db. Depending on the implementation, it may provide limited functionality such as:

  • Viewing previous Ask AI conversations.
  • Reviewing stored Deep Dive reports.
  • Searching by document title or explicit keywords.
  • Displaying cached retrieval results.

However, new semantic Ask AI or Deep Dive queries require the embedding model and vector database to retrieve relevant context.

docs.title: Spock Ask AI / Deep Dive
docs.text:
• Mode: deep_dive Activates an in-depth analysis protocol that explores code structure, logic, and potential improvements. This mode is ideal for comprehensive code reviews, identifying inefficiencies, and suggesting best practices for refactoring and optimization.

  • Path filter: D:\Spock-Onboarding Specifies the absolute directory to analyze. Only files located within this path are considered for processing. This ensures that the analysis remains focused on the relevant codebase and avoids unnecessary processing of unrelated files or external dependencies.

  • Language filter: .py,!.md,!.txt,!.rst Defines the file extensions included in the analysis. Python source files (.py) are included, while documentation (.md, .rst) and raw text (.txt) files are excluded using the ! prefix. This filter helps narrow down the scope of the analysis to only the executable source code, improving both efficiency and relevance.

docs.title: Configuration Notes
docs.text:
• Filter Interaction: The Path and Language filters work together to define the final scope. A file must satisfy both conditions (be within the specified path AND match an included language extension) to be analyzed.
  • Exclusion Syntax: In the Language filter, the ! symbol denotes exclusion. Files matching the pattern after the ! will be skipped even if they are within the correct directory.
  • Mode Implications: The deep_dive mode may require more computational resources compared to standard analysis modes due to the extensive logic inspection performed.

docs.title: Database Architecture & Interaction
docs.text: The Spock application utilizes a local SQLite 3 database instance named ship_computer.db to persist data and facilitate queries for both Ask AI and Deep Dive inquiries. This section details the architecture of the database layer and its interaction with the application logic.

docs.title: Database Overview
docs.text:
• File Location: The database file is stored locally within the application's data directory, ensuring fast read/write access without network latency.
  • Engine: SQLite 3 provides a lightweight, serverless relational database engine suitable for local deployment and single-user environments.
  • Persistence: Data generated during analysis sessions, including code snippets, dependency graphs, and AI-generated insights, is stored here to maintain state across sessions.

docs.title: Interaction with Ask AI
docs.text: When the Ask AI mode is active, the application queries ship_computer.db to retrieve context-specific information: - Context Retrieval: The system executes SQL queries to fetch relevant documentation or code history based on user prompts. - Vector Embeddings (Optional): If configured, text data may be stored alongside embeddings in a dedicated table to enable semantic search capabilities within the database. - Response Caching: Generated answers are cached in the database to reduce redundant processing for similar queries.

docs.title: Interaction with Deep Dive
docs.text: The deep_dive mode leverages the relational structure of ship_computer.db for complex analysis: - Schema Traversal: The application performs multi-table joins to understand relationships between modules, dependencies, and functions. - Performance Metrics: Historical execution times and memory usage are logged in the database to identify bottlenecks during deep analysis sessions. - Refactoring Suggestions: Proposed changes or refactoring paths are stored as temporary records within the database before being applied or discarded.

docs.title: Schema Considerations
docs.text: While the specific schema may evolve based on versioning, the core tables typically include: - logs: Stores execution history and timestamps for audit trails. - analysis_results: Contains the output of code reviews and efficiency metrics. - user_preferences: Persists configuration settings like Path filters and Language preferences across sessions.

docs.title: You
docs.text: [Deep Dive] using the Spock python app, can I access mcp 'tools' from here?

docs.title: Computer
docs.text:
Yes, you can access the Spock MCP (Model Context Protocol) tools. Depending on your use case, you can access them directly in-process via Python or externally via the MCP server adapter.

Here is a technical breakdown of how to access these tools using both methods, along with an explanation of how they interact with the underlying data store.

docs.title: SQLite Data Persistence: ship_computer.db
docs.text: Before accessing the tools, it is essential to understand the data layer that powers the Ask AI and Deep Dive inquiries. The Spock application utilizes a local SQLite database file named ship_computer.db. This database serves as the persistent storage for telemetry, health metrics, and context required for AI analysis.

docs.title: Database Role in Ask AI & Deep Dive
docs.text:
• Ask AI Queries: When you ask questions about system status or logs, the MCP tools query specific tables within ship_computer.db to retrieve real-time data (e.g., CPU usage, memory leaks, error counts).
  • Deep Dive Analysis: For complex inquiries, the application performs joins across multiple tables to correlate events over time. The database ensures that historical context is available without requiring external network calls for local diagnostics.

docs.title: Schema Overview
docs.text: The ship_computer.db file typically contains the following core structures: - health_metrics: Stores timestamped snapshots of system health (CPU, RAM, Disk). - logs: Contains raw error logs and event streams. - ai_context: Holds metadata relevant to AI processing sessions.

docs.title: Interaction with MCP Tools
docs.text: When you invoke a tool like spock_health, the underlying logic executes SQL queries against this file via Python's sqlite3 module. This ensures that even when running directly in-process (Method 1), the application reads from the same persistent source of truth as the external server (Method 2).

docs.title: Method 1: Accessing Tools Directly In-Process (Python Code)
docs.text:
If you are writing Python code within the Spock application suite, you do not need to run a background server process to use the tools. You can dynamically load the MCP module and invoke the underlying functions directly.

This approach is currently utilized by the Engineering Deck in D:\Spock-Onboarding\EngineeringDeck\ship_computer_health.py to run diagnostics without PyQt6 GUI overhead.

docs.title: How it works:
docs.text: Because the tools are registered using fastmcp, they are wrapped as FunctionTool objects to standardize their interface. To call them, you access their underlying Python function via the .fn attribute. This abstraction allows the MCP framework to manage metadata (like descriptions and arguments) while still permitting direct execution when needed.

docs.title: Understanding the FastMCP Abstraction Layer
docs.text:
When a tool is registered with fastmcp, it is not immediately callable as a standard function. Instead, it becomes an instance of FunctionTool. - The Wrapper: The object holds metadata (name, description) and the actual logic. - The .fn Attribute: This property exposes the raw Python function wrapped inside the tool object. Accessing .fn bypasses the MCP protocol layer, allowing you to call the function directly with standard arguments.

Here is the implementation pattern from ship_computer_health.py:

import importlib.util
import sys
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Any

# 1. Resolve the path to the MCP server script
ROOT = Path(r"D:\Spock-Onboarding")
mcp_script_path = ROOT / "scripts" / "mcp_spock_server.py"

def load_mcp_tools():
    """Dynamically load the MCP server module without requiring a package install."""
    spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location("mcp_spock_server_tools", mcp_script_path)
    if spec is None or spec.loader is None:
        raise ImportError(f"Cannot load {mcp_script_path}")

    mod = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec)
    sys.modules["mcp_spock_server_tools"] = mod
    spec.loader.exec_module(mod)
    return mod

def call_mcp_tool(tool_name: str, **kwargs: Any) -> Any:
    """Invoke an MCP tool function directly."""
    mod = load_mcp_tools()
    tool = getattr(mod, tool_name, None)
    if tool is None:
        raise AttributeError(f"MCP tool not found: {tool_name}")

    # FastMCP wraps functions; extract the raw callable via '.fn'
    fn = getattr(tool, "fn", None)
    if callable(fn):
        return fn(**kwargs) if kwargs else fn()
    if callable(tool):
        return tool(**kwargs) if kwargs else tool()
    raise TypeError(f"Tool {tool_name} is not callable")

# Example: Call the spock_health tool directly
health_data = call_mcp_tool("spock_health")
print(health_data)

docs.title: Explanation of Key Concepts
docs.text:
• fastmcp: A library used to register and manage tools within the MCP framework. It wraps Python functions into FunctionTool objects for easier integration with external systems and standardizes argument handling.
  • .fn attribute: This is used to access the original Python function inside a FunctionTool object. It is necessary when you want to call the function directly without going through the FunctionTool interface (e.g., bypassing automatic prompt injection or metadata checks).

docs.title: Method 2: Accessing Tools Externally (MCP Server)
docs.text:
If you want an external LLM client (like Cursor, OpenCode, or llama.cpp WebUI) to access these tools, you can run the MCP adapter as a background process.

The server is defined in D:\Spock-Onboarding\scripts\mcp_spock_server.py and supports three transports (configured via the SPOCK_MCP_TRANSPORT environment variable):

  1. stdio (Default): Used by IDEs like Cursor. The IDE spawns the Python process directly and communicates over standard input/output streams.
  2. streamable-http: Exposes a WebUI-compatible endpoint (usually at http://127.0.0.1:8765/mcp). This is useful for browser-based clients.
  3. sse: Legacy Server-Sent Events endpoint. Used primarily for older MCP clients that require event stream connections.

docs.title: 1. Connecting via Cursor / OpenCode (stdio)
docs.text:
Add the following configuration to your global mcp.json file (usually located in %APPDATA%\Cursor\User\globalStorage\moose.geometry-reader\mcp.json or similar IDE config paths):

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "spock": {
      "command": "D:/Spock-Onboarding/.venv/Scripts/python.exe",
      "args": [
        "-u",
        "D:/Spock-Onboarding/scripts/mcp_spock_server.py"
      ]
    }
  }
}

docs.title: 2. Connecting via llama.cpp WebUI (streamable-http)
docs.text:
1. Start the HTTP adapter from the Spock UI (Navigation Station -> Configure Spock AI -> MCP tab) or run it standalone using D:\Spock-Onboarding\spock_mcp_adapter\__main__.py.
  2. In the llama.cpp WebUI, add the server URL: 
    http://127.0.0.1:8765/mcp

docs.title: Available MCP Tools Reference
docs.text: Once connected or imported, the following tools are exposed by mcp_spock_server.py. These tools serve as the API bridge between your LLM client and the ship_computer.db database described above. | Tool Name | Description | Requirements / Dependencies | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | spock_health | Probes the RAG API, database connections, embedding models, and Llama Server instances. | Reads ship_computer.db for connection validation. | | spock_ask | Asks questions over the RAG database using natural language queries. | Requires the RAG API server to be running (:8090). | | spock_search_kb | Performs Full-Text Search (FTS5) keyword searches over the knowledge base. | Direct SQLite read access to ship_computer.db. | | spock_status | Generates a full hardware, GPU, and server readiness status report. | Direct SQLite read + system probes. | | spock_queue | Inspects the current agent execution queue. | Direct SQLite read access. | | spock_captains_log | Fetches recent Captain's Log entries from the database. | Direct SQLite read access. | | spock_llmfit_fit | Ranks local models that fit the host machine's VRAM constraints. | Requires llmfit.exe. | | spock_hardware_plan | Generates a model execution plan (context size, -ngl layers). | Requires llmfit.exe. |

docs.title: Database Architecture: ship_computer.db
docs.text:
The ship_computer.db file serves as the central persistent storage layer for the Spock application, utilizing the SQLite3 database engine. This single-file database manages critical operational data required for both standard queries and advanced analytical tasks.

  • Core Functionality: It acts as the primary repository for knowledge base documents, agent state, system logs, and configuration metadata.
  • Ask AI Interaction: When a user initiates an "Ask AI" inquiry via spock_ask, the RAG API server queries this database to retrieve relevant context chunks. The database supports efficient retrieval through indexes (such as FTS5 for keyword matching) which are essential for generating accurate responses based on stored knowledge.
  • Deep Dive Interaction: For "Deep Dive" inquiries, the application performs complex SQL operations directly against ship_computer.db. This allows for deep analysis of historical data, agent performance metrics, and system logs without requiring external storage access.
  • Schema Overview: The database typically contains tables such as:
    • documents: Stores the raw knowledge base content indexed for retrieval.
    • agents: Tracks active agents and their current state within the queue.
    • logs: Maintains the chronological Captain's Log entries for system auditing.
  • Health Checks: The spock_health tool specifically validates the integrity of this database file to ensure no corruption exists before attempting read/write operations.

docs.title: Explanation of Tool Usage
docs.text:
• spock_health: A diagnostic utility that verifies the operational status of core Spock system components, including the RAG API, database connections (ship_computer.db), embedding models, and the Llama Server. It is essential for identifying potential failures or bottlenecks before they impact operations.
  • spock_ask: Enables users to query the Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) database using natural language questions. This tool retrieves relevant information from the stored knowledge base within ship_computer.db to generate informed responses via the RAG API server.
  • spock_search_kb: Performs keyword-based searches across the knowledge base utilizing Full-Text Search 5 (FTS5), a SQLite extension designed for efficient full-text indexing and retrieval capabilities directly from the database file.
  • spock_status: Generates a comprehensive status report detailing hardware availability, GPU utilization, and server readiness. This tool is critical for monitoring overall system health and performance metrics during operation by reading directly from the database and system probes.
  • spock_queue: Allows users to inspect the current agent execution queue stored in the database. It is useful for managing task prioritization and monitoring the progress of background jobs or automated agents.
  • spock_captains_log: Retrieves recent entries from the Captain's Log, which maintains a chronological record of significant system events, actions, and alerts within the Spock environment stored in ship_computer.db.
  • spock_llmfit_fit and spock_hardware_plan: Specialized utilities for analyzing model execution requirements against host machine capabilities. They assess VRAM availability and hardware constraints to plan optimal Large Language Model (LLM) configurations.

docs.title: Data Persistence Layer: SQLite 3 Database (ship_computer.db)
docs.text: The Spock application utilizes a local SQLite 3 database file named ship_computer.db to persist critical state, context, and knowledge data required for long-running sessions and AI interactions. This database serves as the central memory store for the system's cognitive functions.

docs.title: Database Role in Ask AI and Deep Dive Inquiries
docs.text: The ship_computer.db is integral to the functionality of the Ask AI and Deep Dive features. While the LLM clients handle the generation of responses, the SQLite database manages the context window, historical queries, and persistent knowledge retrieval.

docs.title: 1. Context Management for Ask AI
docs.text: When a user submits an inquiry via the ask_panel or llm_client, the system interacts with ship_computer.db to: * Store Session State: Maintain the current conversation history to ensure context continuity across multiple queries. * Cache Knowledge Snippets: Store retrieved knowledge base entries (from spock_UIEG_KnowledgeBase) that are relevant to the specific query, reducing latency for repeated questions. * Track User Preferences: Save user-specific instructions or constraints applied during the Ask AI session.

docs.title: 2. Deep Dive Analysis
docs.text: The Deep Dive functionality utilizes the database for more intensive data processing: * Persistent Logging: Stores detailed telemetry and interaction logs required for post-session analysis. * Query History Indexing: Maintains an indexed history of complex queries to allow for retrospective review or pattern recognition within the system. * State Recovery: Ensures that if the application restarts, the ship_computer.db allows the Deep Dive session to resume from its last known state without data loss.

docs.title: Schema Overview
docs.text: The database structure is designed for high-read efficiency during AI inference: * sessions Table: Tracks active user sessions and timestamps. * context_window Table: Stores the rolling window of conversation history passed to the LLM client. * knowledge_cache Table: Holds indexed results from external knowledge bases for quick retrieval. * system_state Table: Monitors health metrics and operational status relevant to spock_live_monitor.

docs.title: Interaction Flow
docs.text:
1. Initialization: Upon launch (main.py), the database is initialized or restored from a backup if present.
  2. Query Submission: When a user asks a question, the llm_client queries the database for relevant context before generating a response.
  3. Update: Post-generation, the new interaction is written back to the context_window table to maintain memory.
  4. Deep Dive Trigger: For complex inquiries, the system performs additional reads from the knowledge_cache and writes detailed analysis logs to the database for later review.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The ship_computer.db file serves as the central SQLite 3 database for the Spock application. Unlike external AI models or wiki adapters which may rely on cloud services or separate repositories, ship_computer.db is an embedded, local data store that persists critical system state, knowledge base entries, and operational logs. It ensures high-speed data retrieval for real-time inquiries such as "Ask AI" and complex analytical tasks like "Deep Dive".

docs.title: Schema Architecture
docs.text:
The database schema is designed to support both structured data storage and vectorized search capabilities required for natural language processing. Key tables include:

  • knowledge_base: Stores technical documentation, system manuals, and sensor logs indexed for retrieval.
  • user_queries: Logs historical user interactions, including prompts sent to the AI and responses generated.
  • system_state: Tracks current operational parameters of subsystems (e.g., WarpCore status, Sensor readings).

docs.title: Interaction with Ask AI
docs.text: The "Ask AI" feature leverages ship_computer.db to provide context-aware responses. When a user submits a query: 1. Context Retrieval: The Orchestrator queries the knowledge_base table within ship_computer.db. It retrieves relevant documentation snippets or sensor logs based on semantic similarity (using vector embeddings stored in the database). 2. Inference: These retrieved contexts are passed to the LLMFIT bridge (llmfit_bridge.py) alongside the user's prompt. 3. Response Generation: The AI generates a response grounded in the specific data found in ship_computer.db, ensuring accuracy based on the ship's current state and available documentation.

docs.title: Interaction with Deep Dive
docs.text: The "Deep Dive" feature utilizes the database for complex, multi-step analysis: 1. Complex Query Execution: Users can request detailed analysis of historical trends or system performance. The application constructs complex SQL queries against ship_computer.db to aggregate data from multiple tables (e.g., joining system_state with user_queries). 2. Visualization Data Prep: The database returns structured datasets optimized for the Science Station (app.py) to render charts and graphs. 3. Persistence of Findings: Results from Deep Dive sessions are often saved back into ship_computer.db within a deep_dive_logs table, allowing users to revisit previous analyses without re-running computationally expensive queries.

docs.title: Initialization and Connection
docs.text: The database connection is managed during the bringup process via the __init__.py file in the spock_bringup module. Upon startup: - The application verifies the existence of ship_computer.db. - If missing, a schema initialization script creates the necessary tables and populates default entries from config_defaults. - Connection pooling is configured to handle concurrent requests from the Orchestrator and Science Station efficiently.

docs.title: Ship's Computer
docs.text: The primary SQLite database schema is defined in ship_computer_schema.sql, located in the project root directory. This file contains the complete Data Definition Language (DDL) required to initialize the database structure. It serves as the single source of truth for all table definitions, constraints, and relationships within the system. Upon initialization, this schema generates the ship_computer.db file, which acts as the persistent storage layer for the Spock application.

docs.title: Core Tables
docs.text:
Table Purpose profiles Stores workstation profile configurations. Each row defines a specific set of settings for a user or system workstation. Profiles can be activated or deactivated dynamically based on operational requirements, typically managed via an active status flag. uieg_captures Contains Universal Extractor capture records. This table logs data extracted by the Universal Extractor module for downstream analysis or processing. Each record includes timestamps, source identifiers, and the raw captured payload. kb_entries Holds knowledge-base document entries. This table stores informational content such as documentation, system logs, or learning artifacts. Entries are used for reference, troubleshooting, and system knowledge acquisition. health_snapshots Records historical system health-check data. Each entry captures a snapshot of system metrics at a specific point in time, including CPU usage, memory utilization, and overall system status for monitoring and diagnostics.

The tables are designed to work together across operational context and diagnostic analysis:

  • profiles provides the active workstation or user context that scopes other data.
  • kb_entries stores reference material used by AI-assisted responses and troubleshooting workflows.
  • health_snapshots records point-in-time performance metrics for trend analysis.
  • uieg_captures preserves raw extracted payloads for forensic inspection when anomalies occur.

Where the DDL defines foreign keys, these tables are linked through identifiers such as profile IDs, source IDs, timestamps, or entry references. Even when explicit constraints are not present, application queries should treat them as logically related datasets for filtering and correlation.

docs.title: Schema File
docs.text:
-- ship_computer_schema.sql
-- See project root for full DDL

This SQL file is executed during the database initialization process to create all necessary tables, indexes, views, triggers, or constraints defined in the DDL. Apply this file before running any application logic that depends on the schema. If using a migration tool, ensure the same definitions are represented in migration scripts or seed files so new and existing databases remain consistent.

Initialization guidance:

  • Run the DDL against an empty database unless the statements are explicitly idempotent.
  • If the schema uses foreign keys, enable SQLite foreign-key enforcement with PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON; before executing dependent queries.
  • Verify that expected tables exist by querying sqlite_master or using a database inspection tool after initialization.

docs.title: Spock Application Integration
docs.text: The ship_computer.db database serves as the persistent backend for the Spock application, specifically powering the Ask AI and Deep Dive inquiry modules. The interaction between the database and these features is structured as follows:

docs.title: Ask AI Module
docs.text:
The Ask AI feature utilizes the kb_entries table to provide context-aware responses. When a user submits an inquiry, the system performs semantic search or keyword-based retrieval against the kb_entries table. Semantic ranking is handled in application code, while SQLite stores the text and metadata used for filtering.

  • Data Flow: The application queries kb_entries to retrieve relevant documentation snippets or logs that match the user's intent. Queries are scoped by the active profiles record to ensure context alignment.
  • Context Injection: Retrieved data is formatted into a structured context window and passed to the AI engine. This grounding mechanism ensures responses are accurate, traceable, and constrained to the ship's verified knowledge base.
  • Metadata Filtering: Queries include profile-based filters, timestamp ranges, and document type tags to ensure the AI response adheres to the current operational context, security clearance, and relevance thresholds of the requesting user.
  • Caching & State: Frequently accessed knowledge entries are cached in memory to reduce SQLite I/O latency. The application tracks query history and user feedback to refine future retrieval scoring.

docs.title: Deep Dive Module
docs.text:
The Deep Dive feature leverages historical data stored in health_snapshots and uieg_captures for trend analysis and root-cause investigation.

  • Trend Analysis: The application aggregates metrics from health_snapshots using time-windowed SQL queries. Aggregation functions (AVG, MAX, COUNT) are applied to visualize system performance over time, identifying patterns such as CPU spikes, memory leaks, or network latency degradation.
  • Forensic Logging: When an anomaly is detected or manually triggered, the system retrieves corresponding records from uieg_captures. Raw payloads are decoded and presented alongside metadata for deeper inspection.
  • Correlation: SQL joins are executed to correlate health metrics with specific knowledge-base entries in kb_entries that may explain the observed behavior. This cross-referencing enables automated hypothesis generation for troubleshooting workflows.

  • Query Optimization: To maintain responsiveness, the application uses indexed lookups on timestamp, profile_id, and status columns. Large result sets are paginated, and heavy aggregations are offloaded to background workers when real-time latency is not required. Query considerations for these modules include:

  • Index frequently filtered columns, such as timestamps, profile or context identifiers, status flags, and source IDs.

  • Use bounded queries with time windows, limits, or pagination to avoid scanning large tables unnecessarily.
  • Enforce access controls at the query level by including the appropriate profiles or security filters in every request.
  • For large payloads stored in uieg_captures, retrieve only required fields and consider streaming or paginated reads.

docs.title: SQLite 3 ship_computer.db and Spock Interaction
docs.text:
ship_computer.db is the SQLite 3 database that serves as the relational system of record for the Spock application. It stores structured operational data, user and profile context, knowledge-base metadata, captured payloads, and audit information. The Spock application uses SQLite for deterministic, transactional access to data that must be filtered, joined, and governed by explicit access-control rules.

In production, the database is commonly run in WAL mode with a busy timeout to allow concurrent readers while writes are serialized. This supports the read-heavy patterns typical of Ask AI and Deep Dive workflows, where multiple requests may query the same knowledge-base records, captures, or profile metadata at the same time.

For Ask AI and Deep Dive inquiries, Spock treats ship_computer.db as the authoritative source for:

  • Identity and context: active profile, session context, role, clearance level, and allowed data scopes.
  • Knowledge-base metadata: kb_entries records, document type, source, timestamp, status, and security attributes.
  • Retrieval constraints: time windows, profile filters, status flags, and source restrictions applied before or after semantic search.
  • Large captured data: uieg_captures payloads that may be streamed or paginated when a response requires raw evidence.
  • Auditability: request logs, response citations, feedback, and access decisions.

The typical interaction flow is:

  1. Spock receives an Ask AI or Deep Dive request.
  2. It validates the request against the active profile and security policy.
  3. It constructs a bounded SQLite query that includes the required profiles, clearance, timestamp, and status filters.
  4. It retrieves candidate relational records from kb_entries, uieg_captures, or related tables.
  5. It uses the embedding and vector layer to rank or expand the candidate set semantically.
  6. It returns only the fields needed for the response, preserving citations and access-control metadata.

This design keeps SQLite responsible for exact filtering, authorization, and transactional consistency, while the vector layer provides semantic ranking over unstructured text.

docs.title: Ask AI and Deep Dive Inquiries
docs.text:
Ask AI is a focused, single-turn semantic question. Spock typically retrieves a small number of highly relevant chunks, applies strict profile and clearance filters, and generates a concise, citation-backed answer.

Deep Dive is a broader, iterative investigation.
