  3. Iterative Retrieval For each reasoning step, the system embeds the current subquery and searches the vector database. Retrieved chunks are stored as artifacts and references so that every claim can later be traced to a source.

  4. Tool Execution If the workflow requires external tools, such as wiki lookup, code analysis, or station-specific data access, the tool input and output are recorded. This creates an auditable execution trail.

  5. Checkpointing After each significant step, the application writes a checkpoint to deep_dive_checkpoints. The checkpoint may include:

  6. The current step index.
  7. The reasoning state.
  8. Tool names and inputs.
  9. Tool outputs.
  10. Retrieval pointers.

  11. Intermediate conclusions.

  12. Synthesis Once sufficient evidence has been gathered, the LLM synthesizes the findings into a final response. The final response is written to messages.

  13. Resume Support If the workflow is interrupted, the application can reload the latest checkpoint and continue from the last completed step. This avoids repeating expensive retrieval or tool calls.

  14. Auditability Because each step is persisted, users and operators can inspect how the Deep Dive reached its conclusion, including which sources were consulted and which tools were executed.

docs.title: Query Optimization & Integrity
docs.text: SQLite's ACID compliance ensures data consistency across concurrent station operations. Indexes are applied to conversation_id, timestamp, and user_id fields to accelerate retrieval. The WarpCore module handles connection management and transaction boundaries, reducing lock contention during high-frequency AI interactions.

docs.title: Concurrency and Locking
docs.text:
SQLite is optimized for single-writer workloads. In the Spock application, this means that multiple stations may read from ship_computer.db concurrently, but writes are serialized to preserve integrity.

To improve concurrency, the application may use:

  • WAL mode — Allows readers to continue while a writer is active, reducing read/write blocking.
  • Short transactions — Keeps write locks held for as little time as possible.
  • Retry logic — Handles transient SQLITE_BUSY errors by retrying with backoff.
  • Batched writes — Groups related inserts, such as a message and its references, into a single transaction.

The cache table is designed for frequent reads and writes. Cache entries should include expiration metadata so stale embeddings, retrieval results, or rate-limit tokens can be removed or refreshed safely.

docs.title: Embedding LLM and Vector Database Integration
docs.text:
Spock leverages a dedicated embedding model and a vector database to power semantic search, context retrieval, and knowledge grounding. This architecture enables the application to understand natural language queries and match them against structured and unstructured knowledge bases.

The embedding model is not the same as the generative LLM. The embedding model converts text into numerical vectors. The generative LLM uses those retrieved vectors, along with the associated text chunks, to produce natural language responses.

docs.title: Embedding Generation Pipeline
docs.text: When documents, wiki pages, or user prompts are ingested, the spock_rag_adapter and spock_wiki_adapter pass the text through a lightweight embedding LLM. The model converts raw text into high-dimensional numerical vectors that capture semantic meaning, syntax, and contextual relationships. These vectors are normalized and stored alongside metadata, including source, chunk ID, timestamp, and access permissions.

docs.title: Embedding Model Contract
docs.text:
For retrieval to work correctly, the embedding model must satisfy a consistent contract:

  • Same model for indexing and querying — The model used to embed knowledge base documents must also be used to embed user queries.
  • Stable vector dimensions — The vector database must know the expected dimensionality of the model's output.
  • Normalization — Vectors are typically normalized so that cosine similarity behaves predictably.
  • Deterministic behavior — The same input text should produce the same or nearly the same vector under the same model version.
  • Versioning — If the embedding model changes, the vector index may need to be rebuilt to avoid mixing incompatible vector spaces.

docs.title: Chunking and Metadata
docs.text:
Large documents are split into smaller chunks before embedding. Chunking is important because:

  • Smaller chunks produce more focused semantic representations.
  • Retrieval can return precise passages rather than entire documents.
  • Citations can point to specific sections of a source.
  • Context windows can be filled with the most relevant text.

Each chunk is stored with metadata such as:

  • Source identifier.
  • Source URL or document path.
  • Chunk index.
  • Content hash.
  • Timestamp.
  • Access permissions.
  • Confidence or relevance score, when available.

docs.title: Vector Database Architecture
docs.text:
The vector store operates as a specialized index optimized for similarity search. It supports:

  • Chunking & Indexing — Large documents are split into manageable segments, each assigned a unique vector representation.
  • Distance Metrics — Cosine similarity or Euclidean distance calculations determine how closely a query vector matches stored knowledge vectors.
  • Metadata Filtering — Queries can be constrained by source type, confidence thresholds, or user access levels before similarity scoring occurs.

docs.title: Index and Storage Model
docs.text:
The vector database stores two related pieces of information:

  1. Vector data — The numerical embedding for each chunk.
  2. Payload data — The original text chunk and associated metadata.

During retrieval, the vector database compares the query vector against stored vectors and returns the closest matches. The payload is then used to build the LLM context and generate citations.

The vector database may be local, embedded, or remote. In either case, it is separate from ship_computer.db. The SQLite database stores workflow state and audit records, while the vector database stores semantic search indexes.

docs.title: Similarity Search & Retrieval
docs.text: During an AI interaction, the user's prompt is embedded using the same model that processed the knowledge base. The resulting query vector is passed to the vector database, which returns the top-k most relevant chunks. This retrieval step ensures that the LLM generates responses grounded in verified, up-to-date information rather than relying solely on pre-training data.

docs.title: Retrieval Scoring
docs.text:
The vector database ranks chunks based on similarity. Common scoring approaches include:

  • Cosine similarity — Measures the angle between vectors and is commonly used for normalized embeddings.
  • Euclidean distance — Measures the straight-line distance between vectors.
  • Inner product — Measures vector alignment and is often used with normalized embeddings.

The application may also apply post-retrieval filtering or reranking to improve result quality. For example, it may prioritize chunks from trusted sources, remove duplicates, or enforce access permissions before passing results to the LLM.

docs.title: Integration with Ask AI and Deep Dive Workflows
docs.text:
• Ask AI — For standard inquiries, the vector database performs a single-pass similarity search. Retrieved chunks are injected into the LLM's context window alongside system prompts, enabling fast, accurate answers with inline citations.
  • Deep Dive — Complex queries trigger iterative retrieval. The system performs multiple vector searches across different knowledge domains, aggregates results, and uses the LLM to synthesize findings. Intermediate retrieval states are cached in ship_computer.db to avoid redundant vector lookups and maintain reasoning continuity.

docs.title: Ask AI Retrieval Pattern
docs.text:
For "Ask AI" inquiries, retrieval is optimized for speed and relevance:

  1. The user prompt is embedded.
  2. The vector database returns the top-k most relevant chunks.
  3. Chunks are filtered by permissions and source trust.
  4. Retrieved text is inserted into the LLM prompt.
  5. The LLM generates a response.
  6. Citations are derived from the retrieved chunks.
  7. The response, citations, and metrics are persisted in ship_computer.db.

This pattern is suitable for direct questions where a single retrieval pass is sufficient.

docs.title: Deep Dive Retrieval Pattern
docs.text:
For "Deep Dive" inquiries, retrieval is iterative and stateful:

  1. The initial query is decomposed into subquestions or reasoning steps.
  2. Each subquestion is embedded and searched against the vector database.
  3. Retrieved chunks are evaluated for relevance and completeness.
  4. Additional searches may be issued if the evidence is insufficient.
  5. Tool outputs and intermediate conclusions are checkpointed in ship_computer.db.
  6. The LLM synthesizes the accumulated evidence into a final answer.
  7. All sources, tool calls, and reasoning steps remain available for audit.

This pattern supports complex investigations where the application must gather evidence from multiple sources before producing a final response.

docs.title: Caching and Consistency
docs.text:
The embedding pipeline and vector store are decoupled from the core LLM generation process, allowing independent scaling, model swapping, and knowledge base updates without disrupting active user sessions.

Caching is used to improve performance, but it must be managed carefully:

  • Embedding cache — Avoids re-embedding identical text.
  • Retrieval cache — Avoids repeated vector searches for the same query and knowledge base version.
  • Rate-limit cache — Tracks API usage and prevents exceeding provider limits.
  • Checkpoint cache — Preserves Deep Dive state for resumability.

Cache entries should include versioning or expiration metadata. If the embedding model, chunking strategy, or knowledge base changes, stale cache entries should be invalidated to prevent retrieval from outdated vector data.

docs.title: SQLite3 Implementation (ship_computer.db)
docs.text:
The WarpCore module relies on a single-file SQLite 3 database named ship_computer.db to manage persistent state for the Spock application. This architecture keeps all critical data—user profiles, system configurations, credential references, knowledge-base content, sensor telemetry, and search indices—localized to the host machine, eliminating the need for an external database server or networked data layer.

Key Characteristics: - Portability: The entire database state is encapsulated within a single file, enabling straightforward backup, migration, and restoration using standard file system operations. - Concurrency & Performance: SQLite is optimized for read-heavy workloads, supporting multiple concurrent readers while serializing write operations. This aligns with Spock's primary usage pattern of frequent knowledge-base queries and sensor-data retrieval. To maximize throughput, the database operates in Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) mode, which allows readers to proceed without blocking writers. For write-intensive operations, the application batches updates into short, explicit transactions and uses connection management to minimize lock contention. - Schema Management: Table structures are programmatically managed by WarpCore utilities. Rather than relying on manual migration scripts, the application executes versioned schema updates at runtime. This allows new features—such as additional sensor telemetry tables or research log schemas—to be deployed seamlessly while preserving historical data integrity.

docs.title: Core Data Model
docs.text:
The ship_computer.db database is organized around several logical domains that support both conversational AI responses and structured analytical queries.

  • Identity and Configuration: Stores user profiles, station preferences, authentication references, and application settings.
  • Knowledge Base: Stores document metadata, document chunks, source references, and content used by Ask AI.
  • Vector Search Support: Stores embedding vectors and associated metadata for semantic retrieval.
  • Sensor and Operational Telemetry: Stores time-series data such as warp core efficiency, power distribution, navigation state, and subsystem diagnostics.
  • Research and Audit Logs: Stores user inquiries, generated responses, diagnostic requests, and system events for traceability.
  • Indexes and Caches: Stores B-tree indexes, full-text search indexes, materialized views, and query caches used to accelerate repeated operations.

docs.title: Storage and Indexing Strategy
docs.text:
Spock uses SQLite as both a relational store and a lightweight vector-enabled data layer.

  • B-tree indexes are used for timestamp, component, user, and status filtering in Deep Dive queries.
  • Full-text search indexes, such as SQLite FTS5, may be used for keyword-based retrieval and phrase matching.
  • Vector indexes, such as those provided by sqlite-vec or an in-process vector index, are used for semantic similarity search in Ask AI.
  • Materialized views or cached aggregates may be used for frequently requested analytics, such as rolling averages, threshold breaches, and subsystem summaries.

docs.title: Interaction with Ask AI and Deep Dive Inquiries
docs.text: The database serves as the central memory layer for two distinct operational modes within the Spock application: Ask AI and Deep Dive. These modes leverage different subsets of ship_computer.db and distinct query strategies to deliver tailored responses to user inquiries.

docs.title: Ask AI (Science Station)
docs.text:
• Function: Delivers immediate, context-aware answers to user questions regarding system status, external knowledge, or research queries.
  • Database Interaction: The ScienceStation interfaces with the WarpCore search index and knowledge-base tables stored in ship_computer.db. When a user submits a query, such as "What is the current warp core efficiency?", the application triggers a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline. The pipeline first performs a semantic similarity search against locally indexed content, retrieves the most relevant document chunks, and formats them as context for the language model.
  • Workflow:
  • User submits a natural language query via the ScienceStation interface.
  • WarpCore converts the query into a vector embedding and executes a similarity search against the local index in ship_computer.db.
  • Top-ranked results are extracted, deduplicated, and formatted into a structured context window.
  • The context is passed to the generation layer, and the final synthesized response is returned to the user interface.

docs.title: Deep Dive (Engineering & Navigation Stations)
docs.text:
• Function: Enables complex analytical queries, historical trend tracking, and diagnostic investigations into system logs, sensor history, and operational metrics.
  • Database Interaction: The EngineeringDeck and NavigationStation execute structured SQL queries that perform aggregations, window functions, and multi-table joins across ship_computer.db. For example, analyzing long-range sensor telemetry requires querying the sensor_logs table with time-based filters, grouping by subsystem, and calculating statistical metrics such as moving averages, variance, or threshold breaches. These operations rely heavily on B-tree indexes and precomputed materialized views to maintain sub-second response times.
  • Workflow:
  • User initiates a diagnostic request, such as "Show me warp core fluctuations over the last cycle."
  • WarpCore constructs and executes parameterized SQL queries against ship_computer.db, leveraging indexed columns for timestamp and component filtering.
  • Aggregated results are serialized, visualized through station-specific dashboards, or exported for offline analysis.

docs.title: Ask AI Data Flow in Detail
docs.text:
Ask AI is designed for natural-language interaction and semantic retrieval. The database supports this mode by storing both the source knowledge and the numerical representations used for similarity search.

  1. Query Intake: The ScienceStation receives the user's question and normalizes it for processing.
  2. Embedding Generation: The query text is passed to the embedding model, producing a vector representation of the question's meaning.
  3. Semantic Retrieval: The vector is compared against stored embeddings in ship_computer.db to identify the most relevant knowledge chunks.
  4. Metadata Filtering: Results may be filtered by source type, station context, time range, access level, or document status.
  5. Context Assembly: The selected chunks are ordered, deduplicated, and formatted into a bounded context window suitable for the language model.
  6. Response Generation: The language model uses the retrieved context to produce a grounded answer.
  7. Persistence: The question, retrieved sources, generated answer, and confidence metadata may be stored for audit, feedback, or future retrieval.

docs.title: Deep Dive Data Flow in Detail
docs.text:
Deep Dive is designed for structured analysis of operational data. The database supports this mode by storing time-series telemetry, event logs, and derived analytics in relational tables.

  1. Diagnostic Request: The EngineeringDeck or NavigationStation receives a structured or semi-structured analytical request.
  2. Query Planning: WarpCore determines the relevant tables, time range, subsystem filters, and aggregation requirements.
  3. SQL Execution: Parameterized SQL queries are executed against ship_computer.db, using indexes to accelerate filtering and joins.
  4. Aggregation: The database computes metrics such as averages, maxima, minima, variance, trend deltas, and threshold violations.
  5. Result Presentation: Results are returned to the station interface for visualization, export, or further analysis.
  6. Caching: Frequently requested aggregates may be cached or materialized to reduce repeated computation.

docs.title: Vector Database & Embedding LLM Integration
docs.text:
While ship_computer.db functions as a traditional relational store, Spock extends its capabilities by integrating vector search and embedding models directly into the data layer. This hybrid approach enables semantic understanding without requiring a separate vector database service.

Embedding Generation: When new documents, sensor reports, or system logs are ingested, Spock passes the raw text through a lightweight embedding model, often described as an embedding LLM. More precisely, this is a text-embedding model that converts text into high-dimensional numerical vectors. These vectors capture semantic meaning rather than exact keyword matches. The resulting vectors are stored alongside the original metadata in ship_computer.db, typically as BLOBs, fixed-size binary vectors, or JSON-encoded arrays.

Vector Indexing & Retrieval: To enable fast similarity searches, the application maintains a vector index within SQLite using extensions such as sqlite-vec or an in-process vector index. When a user submits an Ask AI query, the same embedding model processes the prompt to generate a query vector. The database then performs a cosine similarity or Euclidean distance calculation against the stored vectors, returning the top-k most semantically relevant chunks. Full-text search may also be used alongside vector search to improve recall for exact terms, identifiers, and technical phrases.

docs.title: How Spock Uses the Embedding LLM
docs.text:
Spock uses the embedding model as the semantic bridge between natural language and database retrieval.

  • Ingestion: When documents or logs are added, Spock splits the content into manageable chunks and generates an embedding vector for each chunk.
  • Query Encoding: When a user asks a question, Spock encodes the question into a vector using the same embedding model used during ingestion.
  • Semantic Matching: The query vector is compared against stored vectors to find content that is meaningfully related, even if the wording differs.
  • Consistency: Using the same model for both ingestion and querying ensures that the vector space remains consistent.
  • Local Operation: The embedding model can run locally, preserving the offline, single-file architecture of ship_computer.db.

docs.title: How Spock Uses the Vector Database
docs.text:
Spock uses the vector database layer to perform semantic retrieval without requiring an external vector database service.

  • Storage: Embedding vectors are stored in ship_computer.db alongside metadata such as document ID, chunk ID, source type, timestamp, and access level.
  • Indexing: A vector index accelerates nearest-neighbor search over the stored embeddings.
  • Retrieval: Ask AI queries are converted into vectors and matched against the index to retrieve relevant context.
  • Filtering: Vector results can be constrained by metadata, allowing Spock to limit retrieval to specific stations, document types, or time ranges.
  • Hybrid Search: Vector search may be combined with full-text search to balance semantic relevance with exact keyword matching.

docs.title: Hybrid Search and Ranking
docs.text:
For Ask AI, Spock may use a hybrid retrieval strategy rather than relying solely on vector similarity.

  • Semantic Search: Finds conceptually related content using embedding vectors.
  • Keyword Search: Finds exact terms, identifiers, error codes, and technical phrases using full-text search.
  • Scoring and Ranking: Results from both methods are combined, deduplicated, and ranked using relevance scores, recency, source authority, and station context.
  • Context Selection: Only the highest-ranked chunks are included in the language model context to reduce noise and improve response quality.

docs.title: Model and Index Versioning
docs.text:
Because embedding models can change over time, Spock tracks the model version used to generate each stored vector.

  • Version Tracking: Each embedding record includes the model name, version, and dimensionality.
  • Re-embedding: When a new embedding model is deployed, Spock can re-embed existing content to maintain compatibility.
  • Index Compatibility: Vector indexes are rebuilt or migrated when the embedding dimensionality or model changes.
  • Fallback Behavior: If a query vector is incompatible with the stored index, Spock can fall back to keyword search or prompt the user to rebuild the index. RAG Pipeline Integration: The retrieved vector matches are not returned directly to the user. Instead, they are injected into the LLM's context window as grounding evidence. This ensures that generated responses are factually anchored to the ship's local data, reducing hallucination and maintaining operational accuracy. The embedding LLM and vector DB thus work in tandem: the embedding model translates natural language into searchable mathematical representations, while the vector index within ship_computer.db provides low-latency, semantically aware retrieval that powers the Spock application's intelligent query resolution.

docs.title: SQLite 3 ship_computer.db and Spock Application Interaction
docs.text:
ship_computer.db is the local SQLite 3 database that supports the Spock application's retrieval-augmented generation pipeline. It stores the structured data needed to answer user questions from the ship's local knowledge base, including document chunks, metadata, embedding vectors, and query history.

The database acts as the persistent memory layer for Spock. When a user submits an inquiry through Ask AI or Deep Dive, the Spock application does not rely solely on the LLM's internal knowledge. Instead, it first queries ship_computer.db to find relevant local evidence. That evidence is then used to ground the LLM's response.

docs.title: Role of ship_computer.db
docs.text:
The database typically contains the following types of information:

  • Text chunks: Small, meaningful segments of source documents, logs, manuals, or operational records.
  • Metadata: Information such as source file, document title, section, timestamp, author, classification, or operational context.
  • Embedding vectors: Numerical representations of each text chunk, generated by the embedding LLM.
  • Similarity scores: Calculated during retrieval to rank how closely a user query matches stored content.
  • Query and response records: Optional audit data that records user questions, retrieved evidence, and generated answers.

By keeping this data in a local SQLite 3 file, Spock can operate with low latency, reduced network dependency, and strong control over which data is used to generate answers.

docs.title: Ask AI Inquiries
docs.text:
Ask AI is intended for direct, conversational questions. When a user asks a question, Spock performs the following steps:

  1. Query normalization The user's question is cleaned and prepared for embedding. This may include trimming whitespace, removing ambiguous phrasing, or extracting key terms.

  2. Query embedding The embedding LLM converts the question into a vector representation. This vector captures the semantic meaning of the question rather than relying only on keyword matching.

  3. Vector search Spock compares the query vector against the stored embedding vectors in ship_computer.db. The database returns the most semantically similar text chunks.

  4. Evidence ranking Retrieved chunks are ranked by similarity score. Spock may also apply filters based on metadata, such as document type, time range, or operational relevance.

  5. Context assembly The top-ranked chunks are formatted into a structured prompt. Each chunk is usually labeled with its source and relevance information so the LLM can cite or reference the evidence.

  6. LLM response generation The LLM receives the user question together with the retrieved evidence. It is instructed to answer using the provided context and to avoid inventing information that is not present in the local data.

  7. Response delivery The final answer is returned to the user, often with references to the underlying source material.

This workflow allows Ask AI to provide concise, context-aware answers while remaining grounded in the ship's local records.

docs.title: Deep Dive Inquiries
docs.text:
Deep Dive is designed for more complex, analytical, or multi-part questions. Unlike a simple Ask AI query, a Deep Dive request may require broader context, comparison across multiple sources, or step-by-step reasoning.

When a user initiates a Deep Dive inquiry, Spock may perform the following:

  1. Query decomposition The original question is broken into smaller sub-questions or search themes. For example, a question about system performance may be split into queries related to logs, maintenance records, configuration changes, and operational notes.

  2. Multiple retrieval passes Spock may run several vector searches against ship_computer.db to gather a wider set of relevant evidence. This helps ensure that the final answer is not limited to a single document or narrow context.

  3. Cross-source synthesis Retrieved chunks from different sources are compared and synthesized. Spock can identify contradictions, trends, recurring issues, or supporting evidence across the local data set.

  4. Structured reasoning The LLM is prompted to reason through the evidence in a structured way. It may summarize findings, list supporting references, identify gaps, and provide recommendations.

  5. Expanded response The final output is more detailed than a standard Ask AI response. It may include sections such as summary, evidence, analysis, limitations, and suggested next steps.

Deep Dive uses the same core RAG mechanism as Ask AI, but it applies it more extensively. The result is a more thorough, evidence-based analysis that remains anchored to the local data stored in ship_computer.db.

docs.title: How Spock Uses the Embedding LLM and Vector DB
docs.text: The embedding LLM and vector DB are central to Spock's ability to understand natural language questions and retrieve relevant local information.

docs.title: Embedding LLM
docs.text:
The embedding LLM is responsible for converting text into numerical vectors. These vectors represent the semantic meaning of the text in a high-dimensional space.

For example, the phrases:

  • "What is the current status of the navigation system?"
  • "How is the nav system performing right now?"

may not share many exact keywords, but their embeddings will be close together because they express similar meaning.

Spock uses the embedding LLM in two main ways:

  1. During ingestion When documents or records are added to the local knowledge base, Spock splits them into chunks and generates an embedding vector for each chunk. These vectors are stored in ship_computer.db.

  2. During query time When a user asks a question, Spock generates an embedding vector for the question. This vector is then compared against the stored vectors to find the most relevant chunks.

Because both the stored content and the user query are represented in the same embedding space, Spock can perform semantic search rather than simple keyword matching.

docs.title: Vector DB
docs.text:
The vector DB is the retrieval layer that stores and searches embedding vectors. In this architecture, the vector index is maintained within ship_computer.db, allowing Spock to keep retrieval local, fast, and tightly coupled to the application's data.

The vector DB supports the following operations:

  • Vector storage Each text chunk is stored alongside its embedding vector and associated metadata.

  • Similarity search When a query vector is generated, Spock searches for stored vectors that are closest to the query vector. Similarity may be measured using cosine similarity, dot product, or another vector distance metric.

  • Ranked retrieval The database returns the most relevant chunks, usually ordered by similarity score.

  • Metadata filtering Spock can restrict retrieval to specific document types, time periods, sources, or operational categories before or after vector matching.

docs.title: Combined Workflow
docs.text:
The full workflow is as follows:

  1. Source documents are processed and split into meaningful chunks.
  2. The embedding LLM converts each chunk into a vector.
  3. The vectors and metadata are stored in ship_computer.db.
  4. A user submits an Ask AI or Deep Dive inquiry.
  5. Spock converts the user's question into a query vector using the same embedding LLM.
  6. The vector DB searches ship_computer.db for the most similar stored vectors.
  7. The corresponding text chunks are retrieved and ranked.
  8. The retrieved evidence is injected into the LLM's context window.
  9. The LLM generates a grounded response based on the local evidence.
  10. The response is returned to the user, optionally with source references.

This design allows Spock to combine the reasoning ability of an LLM with the precision of local semantic search. The embedding LLM provides meaning-based understanding, while the vector DB provides fast, structured retrieval from the ship's local data. Together, they enable Spock to answer questions accurately, reduce hallucination, and maintain operational relevance.

docs.title: Understanding the spock_-Prefixed Packages
docs.text:
These packages encapsulate core backend services that support the functionality of the UI stations. Each spock_-prefixed package typically functions as a command-line interface (CLI), system adapter, or background daemon that bridges the application with external APIs, local file systems, or infrastructure components. These services are essential for initializing environments, monitoring system health, and maintaining operational continuity. They operate behind the scenes, exposing reusable capabilities and standardized interfaces rather than direct user-facing screens.

In practice, a spock_ package may provide:

  • CLI commands for setup, diagnostics, or maintenance tasks.
  • Service adapters that normalize external API responses into internal data models.
  • Background workers that monitor system state, refresh caches, or process queued jobs.
  • Shared utilities for logging, configuration, authentication, or data transformation.

Because these packages are not primarily user-facing, they are designed to be invoked by other components, such as stations, the orchestrator, or scheduled tasks.

docs.title: Understanding the Star Trek-Named Packages
docs.text:
These packages are named after elements from the Star Trek universe and represent the user-facing components of the application. Each "station" provides a dedicated interface and workflow for interacting with specific functional domains, streamlining tasks such as system setup, diagnostics, real-time monitoring, and research. The station names map directly to their operational purpose: for example, the Science Station facilitates knowledge retrieval and Ask AI workflows, while the Engineering Deck and Navigation Station support deeper operational analysis, system diagnostics, and historical data review.

Stations are the primary surfaces where users interact with the application. They translate user intent into structured requests, coordinate with backend services, and present results in a domain-appropriate format. A station may render forms, dashboards, chat interfaces, diagnostic panels, or analytical reports depending on its purpose.

docs.title: Architectural Roles
docs.text:
The architecture distinguishes between Presentation Layers (Stations) and Infrastructure Layers (Services/Core).

  • Stations serve as primary entry points for user interaction and domain-specific workflows. The Orchestrator is also categorized here; it acts as the central routing hub that coordinates traffic between UI stations and the underlying infrastructure (WarpCore). It manages request distribution, aggregates results from multiple backend services, and ensures consistent, structured responses are returned to the user.
  • Services (prefixed with spock_) handle backend logic, external integrations, data transformation, and system health checks without exposing a primary user interface. They are invoked programmatically by stations or the orchestrator rather than accessed directly by end users.
  • WarpCore functions as the shared kernel, providing persistent storage, configuration management, search indexing, and standardized data access patterns. All other layers depend on WarpCore for state management, query execution, and cross-component data sharing.

This separation allows the application to maintain a clear boundary between user experience, business logic, and data infrastructure. Stations remain focused on interaction, services remain focused on capability, and WarpCore remains focused on consistency, persistence, and shared state.

docs.title: Clarifying Terms
docs.text:
This section defines recurring terms used throughout the architecture description.

  • Station: A user-facing component or workflow surface where users interact with a specific functional domain of the application.
  • Service: A backend package that provides infrastructure, integration, monitoring, or operational capabilities without directly presenting a primary user interface.
  • WarpCore: The shared core module responsible for persistent data access, configuration management, search indexing, and common runtime behavior used by all other components.
  • RAG Pipeline: A retrieval-augmented generation workflow in which the system first retrieves relevant local content from an index, then supplies that evidence as context to a language model to generate accurate, grounded responses.
  • Deep Dive: An analytical mode optimized for historical data exploration, trend analysis, system diagnostics, and complex multi-table relational queries rather than immediate conversational question answering.
  • Embedding Model: A machine-learning model that converts text into numerical vectors, enabling semantic similarity search.
  • Vector Database: A storage system optimized for storing and querying high-dimensional numerical vectors, typically used for semantic search and retrieval.
  • Generative LLM: A large language model that produces natural-language responses, often using retrieved context to ground its output.

docs.title: SQLite 3 ship_computer.db Architecture and Data Flow
docs.text:
The ship_computer.db file is a serverless SQLite 3 database that serves as the relational backbone of the Spock application. Managed by WarpCore, it stores structured metadata, configuration states, query logs, document registries, and relational mappings that complement the unstructured data handled by the vector database. Its lightweight, file-based nature ensures zero-configuration deployment while maintaining ACID compliance for critical application state.

The database is intentionally separate from the vector database. SQLite 3 stores structured, relational, and auditable data, while the vector database stores semantic representations of content. This separation allows Spock to enforce governance, permissions, and analytical queries in SQLite 3 while performing high-dimensional semantic retrieval in the vector store.

docs.title: Core Responsibilities of ship_computer.db
docs.text:
The ship_computer.db database is responsible for maintaining the application’s authoritative structured state. Typical responsibilities include:

  • Document Registry: Tracking which documents exist, their identifiers, sources, versions, and lifecycle status.
  • Metadata Storage: Storing classification tags, creation dates, ownership, sensitivity levels, and other searchable attributes.
  • Permission and Access Control: Recording user roles, allowed scopes, and authorization rules that constrain which content can be retrieved.
  • Query Logging: Capturing user requests, retrieval results, response metadata, and performance data for auditing and diagnostics.
  • Configuration State: Storing application settings, feature flags, station preferences, and integration parameters.
  • System Event History: Recording operational events, health checks, errors, and maintenance actions.
  • Relational Mappings: Linking documents to users, projects, systems, tags, or other entities for analytical queries.

docs.title: Typical Table Categories
docs.text:
While the exact schema may vary by deployment, ship_computer.db commonly contains table categories such as:

  • Documents: Core records representing indexed content items.
  • Document Metadata: Extended attributes associated with each document.
  • Users and Roles: Identity and authorization information.
  • Permissions: Access rules that constrain retrieval and query execution.
  • Query Logs: Historical records of user requests and system responses.
  • System Events: Operational and diagnostic events.
  • Configuration: Application-level settings and runtime state.
  • Index Metadata: Information about vector index versions, rebuild status, or synchronization state.

These tables provide the structured context needed to govern, audit, and analyze the semantic search system.

docs.title: Interaction with Ask AI Inquiries
docs.text:
When a user submits an Ask AI query, the orchestrator first routes the request through WarpCore, which queries ship_computer.db to validate permissions, retrieve user-specific context, and fetch metadata filters (e.g., document source, creation date, or classification tags). The database does not store the raw text or embeddings; instead, it maintains a registry of document IDs and their associated metadata. This relational lookup ensures that only authorized and contextually relevant documents are passed to the vector search stage, preventing hallucination and enforcing data governance.

The Ask AI flow typically follows this sequence:

  1. User submits a natural-language question.
  2. The station forwards the request to the Orchestrator.
  3. The Orchestrator invokes WarpCore to resolve the request context.
  4. WarpCore queries ship_computer.db to:
  5. Validate the user’s identity and permissions.
  6. Determine which document collections are accessible.
  7. Apply metadata filters such as tags, source, date range, or classification.
  8. Retrieve the set of candidate document identifiers.
  9. The filtered document identifiers are used to constrain vector search.
  10. The vector database returns semantically similar content.
  11. The retrieved context is passed to the generative LLM.
  12. The LLM produces a grounded response.
  13. The response, along with metadata and citations, is returned to the station.

In this model, SQLite 3 acts as the governance and filtering layer, while the vector database acts as the semantic retrieval layer. This ensures that Ask AI responses are not only semantically relevant but also authorized, auditable, and contextually constrained.

docs.title: Interaction with Deep Dive Inquiries
docs.text:
Deep Dive workflows rely heavily on ship_computer.db for complex analytical operations. Unlike Ask AI, which prioritizes semantic similarity, Deep Dive executes parameterized SQL queries across multiple tables to aggregate historical metrics, track system events, or correlate logs with configuration changes. The database supports JOIN operations, window functions, and indexed lookups to efficiently process time-series data and relational dependencies. Results are formatted into structured datasets that stations render as charts, tables, or diagnostic reports. Because SQLite 3 handles these queries locally, Deep Dive operations maintain low latency and high throughput without requiring external database servers.

The Deep Dive flow typically follows this sequence:

  1. User selects an analytical task or diagnostic view.
  2. The station constructs a structured query request.
  3. The Orchestrator routes the request to WarpCore.
  4. WarpCore translates the request into parameterized SQL.
  5. SQLite 3 executes relational queries across multiple tables.
  6. Results are aggregated, filtered, or transformed as needed.
  7. The station renders the output as tables, charts, timelines, or diagnostic summaries.

Deep Dive is best suited for questions that require precise relational logic, such as:

  • “Show all system events from the last 30 days grouped by severity.”
  • “List documents modified by a specific user within a date range.”
  • “Correlate configuration changes with error events.”
  • “Identify query patterns that produced the highest latency.”

Because these queries are deterministic and structured, SQLite 3 provides a reliable foundation for analytical workflows without requiring a separate database server.

docs.title: Why SQLite 3 Is Used
docs.text:
SQLite 3 is well suited to the Spock application because it provides:

  • Zero-configuration deployment: No separate database server is required.
  • File-based portability: The database can be copied, backed up, or migrated easily.
  • ACID compliance: Critical application state remains consistent even during concurrent access.
  • Low operational overhead: Ideal for local, embedded, or edge deployments.
  • Strong relational querying: Supports joins, indexes, transactions, and analytical SQL features.
  • Complementarity with vector search: Structured data and semantic data can be managed separately while remaining coordinated through document identifiers.

docs.title: Embedding LLM and Vector Database Integration
docs.text:
The Spock application leverages a dedicated embedding model (often referred to as the embedding LLM) and a vector database to power semantic search and context retrieval. It is important to distinguish between the embedding model, which converts text into numerical vectors, and the generative LLM, which synthesizes final responses.

The embedding model does not generate natural-language answers. Instead, it transforms text into a numerical representation that captures semantic meaning. The vector database stores these numerical representations and enables efficient similarity search. The generative LLM uses the retrieved content as context to produce a coherent, grounded response.

docs.title: Embedding Model Responsibilities
docs.text:
The embedding model is responsible for converting textual content into high-dimensional vectors. These vectors represent the semantic meaning of the text in a way that allows mathematically similar concepts to be close together in vector space.

Its primary responsibilities include:

  • Text Vectorization: Converting documents, chunks, or query strings into numerical embeddings.
  • Semantic Representation: Capturing meaning rather than exact keyword matches.
  • Consistency: Producing embeddings that remain comparable across documents and queries.
  • Dimensionality: Generating vectors of a fixed size suitable for the vector database.
  • Language and Domain Adaptation: Supporting the languages and terminology used by the application.

For example, the phrases “system failure” and “critical error” may not share exact keywords, but their embeddings may be close enough to be retrieved as semantically related.

docs.title: Vector Database Responsibilities
docs.text:
The vector database is responsible for storing embeddings and performing fast similarity searches. It is optimized for high-dimensional numerical data and typically supports distance metrics such as cosine similarity, Euclidean distance, or dot product.

Its primary responsibilities include:

  • Embedding Storage: Persisting vectors associated with document identifiers or content chunks.
  • Similarity Search: Finding the most semantically relevant vectors for a given query embedding.
  • Scalable Retrieval: Returning top-k results efficiently, even as the corpus grows.
  • Metadata Association: Linking vectors to document IDs, metadata, or access-control attributes.
  • Index Management: Maintaining search indexes that support fast approximate or exact nearest-neighbor queries.

The vector database does not replace SQLite 3. Instead, it complements it by handling semantic retrieval while SQLite 3 handles structured governance, permissions, and analytical queries.

docs.title: Ask AI Retrieval Flow
docs.text:
In Ask AI workflows, the embedding model and vector database work together to retrieve relevant context before the generative LLM produces an answer.

The process typically follows these steps:

  1. The user asks a natural-language question.
  2. The station sends the question to the Orchestrator.
  3. WarpCore validates the request and retrieves permission and metadata constraints from ship_computer.db.
  4. The query text is converted into an embedding using the embedding model.
  5. The vector database searches for the most similar document embeddings.
  6. The search is constrained by document identifiers or metadata filters obtained from SQLite 3.
  7. The top relevant content chunks are retrieved.
  8. The retrieved context is formatted into a prompt for the generative LLM.
  9. The generative LLM produces a response grounded in the retrieved evidence.
  10. The station displays the answer, often with citations or source references.

This approach reduces hallucination because the generative LLM is not expected to answer from parametric memory alone. Instead, it uses locally retrieved, authorized content as evidence.

docs.title: Deep Dive Retrieval Flow
docs.text:
Deep Dive workflows may also use the embedding model and vector database, but they place greater emphasis on structured analysis.

In Deep Dive, the system may:

  • Use SQLite 3 to identify relevant time ranges, entities, or event categories.
  • Use the vector database to find semantically related documents or logs.
  • Combine relational results with semantic results to produce a richer analytical view.
  • Use the generative LLM to summarize or explain the combined findings.

For example, a Deep Dive request such as “Explain recent performance degradation in the navigation subsystem” may involve:

  1. Querying ship_computer.db for recent performance events.
  2. Filtering events by subsystem, severity, and time range.
  3. Embedding the query and related event descriptions.
  4. Searching the vector database for semantically related documentation or logs.
  5. Correlating structured events with retrieved context.
  6. Generating a diagnostic summary using the generative LLM.

This hybrid approach allows Spock to combine precise relational analysis with semantic understanding.

docs.title: Hybrid Search and Reranking
docs.text:
In many Spock workflows, retrieval is not purely semantic or purely structured. The system may combine multiple signals:

  • Keyword or metadata filters from SQLite 3.
  • Semantic similarity scores from the vector database.
  • Recency, relevance, or authority weights from structured metadata.
  • Reranking of candidate results before they are passed to the generative LLM.

This hybrid strategy improves accuracy by ensuring that results are both semantically relevant and operationally appropriate.

docs.title: Consistency Between SQLite 3 and the Vector Database
docs.text:
Because the two storage systems serve different purposes, Spock must maintain consistency between them.

Typical consistency mechanisms include:

  • Shared Document Identifiers: SQLite 3 and the vector database reference the same document IDs.
  • Index Metadata: SQLite 3 tracks vector index versions, rebuild status, or synchronization state.
  • Permission Enforcement: SQLite 3 determines which documents are allowed to be searched.
  • Audit Logging: Query results and retrieval metadata are recorded for diagnostics.
  • Reindexing Workflows: When documents are added, updated, or deleted, both systems are updated or invalidated as needed.

This coordination ensures that semantic search remains aligned with the application’s authoritative structured state.

docs.title: Failure Handling and Resilience
docs.text:
The embedding and vector search components are designed to degrade gracefully when possible.

Common failure scenarios include:

  • Embedding model unavailable: The system may fall back to keyword search, metadata filtering, or a limited Deep Dive mode.
  • Vector database unavailable: The system may return structured results from SQLite 3 or indicate that semantic search is unavailable.
  • Stale index: The system may warn that results may be outdated or trigger a reindexing task.
  • Permission mismatch: The system may exclude unauthorized documents before retrieval or after retrieval, depending on the security model.

By separating structured state, semantic retrieval, and generative response, Spock can maintain reliability, auditability, and explainability across both Ask AI and Deep Dive workflows. Embedding Process: During data ingestion, raw documents, logs, and knowledge-base entries are chunked into semantically coherent segments and passed through the embedding model. The model maps each text segment into a high-dimensional vector space in which semantic similarity corresponds to geometric proximity. The resulting vectors, together with their associated document identifiers, chunk identifiers, and metadata pointers, are stored in the vector database. This process is handled asynchronously by Spock background services so that ingestion and indexing do not block user workflows.

Vector Database Role: The vector database indexes these embeddings using approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) algorithms, enabling low-latency similarity searches across large collections of records. When an Ask AI request arrives, the user's query is embedded using the same embedding model, and the vector database performs a cosine similarity or inner-product search to retrieve the top-k most relevant chunks. These chunks are then ranked, deduplicated, and formatted into a context window for the generative LLM.

Integration with the RAG Pipeline: The retrieved context is injected into the prompt template alongside the original user query and system instructions. The generative LLM then produces a response grounded in the retrieved evidence. WarpCore coordinates this handoff, ensuring that vector search results are properly aligned with relational filters from ship_computer.db. This hybrid approach combines the precision of relational metadata filtering with the flexibility of semantic search, allowing Spock to deliver accurate, traceable, and context-aware answers while maintaining strict separation between indexing, retrieval, and generation stages.

SQLite 3 ship_computer.db Role: ship_computer.db is the local SQLite 3 relational database used by the Python-based Spock application to store structured state, metadata, permissions, and audit information. It acts as the system of record for what data exists, who may access it, how data is organized, and what actions have been taken. Unlike the vector database, which optimizes semantic similarity search, ship_computer.db provides deterministic queries, joins, constraints, and transactional consistency.

Typical data stored in ship_computer.db includes: - Documents, logs, and knowledge-base entries - Chunk identifiers and metadata pointers used by the vector database - User, role, and permission records - Ask AI request and response records - Deep Dive session state, steps, evidence, and generated artifacts - Citation and provenance records - System configuration and audit logs

ship_computer.db typically does not store the high-dimensional vectors themselves; those remain in the vector database. Instead, it stores the relational identifiers and metadata needed to connect vector search results back to authoritative application state.

Ask AI Interaction with ship_computer.db: For Ask AI inquiries, ship_computer.db provides the relational context that constrains and enriches semantic retrieval. Before or during vector search, Spock may query the database to resolve the user's identity, validate permissions, apply source filters, and identify relevant document collections. It may also retrieve metadata such as document titles, timestamps, owners, tags, and status to help rank or filter candidate chunks.

After the generative LLM produces an answer, ship_computer.db records the request, the retrieved evidence, the final response, and any citations or provenance links. This allows Spock to maintain traceability, support follow-up questions, and provide auditable answers that can be reviewed or replayed.

Deep Dive Interaction with ship_computer.db: For Deep Dive inquiries, ship_computer.db stores the persistent state of a multi-step investigation. This includes the original question, intermediate prompts, retrieved evidence, generated summaries, hypotheses, task steps, and final deliverables. Because Deep Dive workflows may span multiple turns, tools, or background jobs, the database provides durable storage that survives application restarts and enables resumable sessions.

ship_computer.db also coordinates the relationship between Deep Dive artifacts and the underlying evidence. Each generated claim, summary, or report can be linked to specific chunks, documents, or vector search results, allowing Spock to present citations and explain how the answer was derived.

Embedding LLM and Vector Database Workflow: The embedding LLM, or embedding model, is a specialized model that converts text into numerical vectors. It is not used to generate natural-language answers; instead, it creates a mathematical representation of meaning that can be compared efficiently. During ingestion, Spock chunks source material, sends each chunk to the embedding model, and stores the resulting vector in the vector database.

At query time, Spock embeds the user's question using the same model. The vector database then compares the query vector against stored vectors using an ANN index and a similarity metric such as cosine similarity or inner product. The closest vectors represent the chunks that are semantically most relevant to the question.

The retrieved chunks are then passed through a retrieval pipeline that may include filtering, reranking, deduplication, and context assembly. The final context is combined with the user's question and system instructions in a prompt template. The generative LLM uses that prompt to produce an answer. In this design, the embedding LLM enables semantic matching, the vector database enables fast retrieval, and the generative LLM enables natural-language synthesis.

docs.title: spock_bringup
docs.text: Phase A Bring-Up CLI — acquires resources, starts servers, and validates readiness.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Run the following commands from the project root directory. The text after # is explanatory only; remove it before executing a command in shells that do not treat # as a comment.

.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m spock_bringup acquire    # Acquire system resources required for the bring-up process
.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m spock_bringup up         # Start all servers and services necessary for operation
.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m spock_bringup status     # Check the current status and readiness of the system
.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m spock_bringup down       # Stop all servers and release resources

docs.title: Command Path Variations
docs.text: The command examples above use Windows-specific paths (.venv\Scripts\python.exe). On Unix-like systems (macOS or Linux), replace the path with .venv/bin/python. Ensure the virtual environment is located in the project root directory.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The spock_bringup module is a Python package that provides command-line tools for managing the bring-up and tear-down of a system during Phase A of a deployment process. Phase A refers to the initial infrastructure provisioning stage, where the foundational environment—such as compute instances, networking, and storage—is established before application logic is deployed. The module simplifies resource acquisition, service initialization, system status validation, and resource release when components are no longer needed.

docs.title: Key Concepts
docs.text:
• Acquire: This command provisions the necessary system resources required for the bring-up process, such as compute instances, storage volumes, or network configurations. It verifies that prerequisites are met before deployment proceeds. Because this step may call external cloud provider APIs and wait for resource availability, it can take several minutes to complete.
  • Up: This command starts all servers and services required for normal operation. Depending on the environment, this may include launching application containers, initializing databases, and starting background processes. Verify that required ports are available before running this command to avoid binding conflicts.
  • Status: This command reports the current state of the system in real time. Use it after up to validate readiness, verify whether all services are running, inspect errors, or determine whether the system is ready for use. If status indicates "not ready," resolve the reported issues before proceeding with dependent workloads.
  • Down: This command gracefully shuts down running servers and services and releases allocated resources where appropriate. It helps prevent resource leaks and unnecessary costs. Unless explicitly configured in the teardown script, this command does not delete persistent data.

docs.title: Database Architecture and SQLite Integration
docs.text:
The Spock application uses a local SQLite 3 database file named ship_computer.db to persist critical state information, query logs, and context data required for intelligent processing. Because SQLite is embedded directly within the Python runtime, no external database server is required for deployment, reducing infrastructure complexity and latency.

ship_computer.db serves as the relational source of truth for Spock's operational state, user interactions, session history, and metadata. It works alongside a vector database that stores semantic embeddings used for retrieval-augmented reasoning. The two storage systems are complementary:

  • SQLite 3 (ship_computer.db) stores structured, queryable data such as sessions, prompts, responses, system state, trace IDs, and metadata.
  • Vector database stores high-dimensional embeddings and chunk-level semantic content used to retrieve relevant context for Ask AI and Deep Dive inquiries.

This separation allows Spock to maintain auditable relational state while still performing fast, semantic retrieval over large bodies of text.

docs.title: ship_computer.db Schema and Operational Mechanics
docs.text:
ship_computer.db is a serverless, single-file relational database optimized for concurrent read/write operations during active sessions. The database operates in Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) mode to ensure data integrity while allowing multiple application threads to read historical context without blocking write operations.

The schema is organized around three primary data domains:

  • Query History & Session Logs: Stores timestamps, user prompts, model responses, and session identifiers. This enables audit trails, conversation continuity, and rollback capabilities.
  • Context & Metadata Registry: Maintains structured metadata for documents, system configurations, and user preferences. Foreign keys link this metadata to vector representations and intermediate analysis results.
  • System State & Telemetry: Tracks operational modes (e.g., active, maintenance, degraded), service health metrics, and bring-up checkpoints. This prevents conflicting operations during initialization and enables graceful failover.

All database interactions use parameterized queries and connection pooling to prevent SQL injection, minimize I/O overhead, and ensure thread safety across the Spock application stack.

docs.title: Core Tables and Relationships
docs.text:
A typical ship_computer.db implementation includes tables that support session tracking, query auditing, context management, and Deep Dive workflow persistence. The exact table names may vary by implementation, but the logical structure generally includes the following:

Table Purpose sessions Tracks user or application sessions, including session ID, start time, end time, user identity, and active mode. queries Stores each user prompt or system-generated inquiry, including timestamp, session ID, prompt text, and request type. responses Stores model responses, response metadata, token usage, latency, and associated query ID. documents Stores metadata for source documents, such as title, source, owner, creation time, and processing status. chunks Stores text chunks derived from documents, including chunk ID, document ID, chunk text, position, and embedding reference. vector_references Maps relational chunk IDs to vector database identifiers, embedding model version, and vector storage location. deep_dive_traces Stores top-level Deep Dive workflows, including trace ID, objective, status, start time, and completion time. deep_dive_steps Stores individual reasoning or retrieval steps within a Deep Dive trace, including step order, input context, output result, and retrieved evidence. system_state Stores current operational state, such as active, maintenance, degraded, or initializing. telemetry Stores health metrics, error events, service status, and bring-up checkpoints.

These tables are linked through stable identifiers. For example, a query belongs to a session, a response references a query, a chunk belongs to a document, and a deep_dive_step references both a deep_dive_trace and the chunks or vector_references used during that step.

This design allows Spock to reconstruct the full context of an Ask AI or Deep Dive interaction without relying on the generative model to remember prior state.

docs.title: Concurrency, Safety, and Operational Behavior
docs.text:
SQLite is well suited to Spock's local deployment model because it requires no separate database server, supports file-based persistence, and provides strong transactional guarantees. However, because SQLite allows only one writer at a time, Spock uses a controlled concurrency model.

Key operational behaviors include:

  • WAL mode: Enables readers to continue accessing the database while a writer commits changes. This is useful when Ask AI or Deep Dive workflows need to read historical context while new responses are being logged.
  • Parameterized queries: All SQL statements use bound parameters rather than string concatenation, preventing SQL injection and improving query plan reuse.
  • Connection pooling: Spock maintains a small pool of SQLite connections at the Python level. Each connection is guarded by appropriate locking or thread-affinity rules to avoid unsafe cross-thread access.
  • Busy timeout handling: If a write lock is temporarily held, SQLite can wait for a configurable period before reporting an error. This reduces transient failures during concurrent session activity.
  • Transaction boundaries: Multi-step operations, such as logging a query, storing a response, and updating session state, are committed as a single transaction where appropriate. This prevents partial writes and keeps the audit trail consistent.

This model allows Spock to maintain a reliable local database while supporting interactive AI workflows that may involve frequent reads and writes.

docs.title: Ask AI and Deep Dive Interaction Flow
docs.text:
The database acts as the central memory layer for Spock's advanced reasoning features, enabling stateful, context-aware interactions:

  • Ask AI: When a user submits an inquiry, the application first queries ship_computer.db to retrieve relevant historical context, user preferences, and active system configurations. This contextual payload is injected into the prompt template before being sent to the generative model. By grounding responses in persisted data rather than relying solely on model inference, Ask AI delivers more accurate, consistent, and auditable answers.
  • Deep Dive: For complex, multi-step analysis tasks, the Deep Dive feature writes intermediate results, expanded context windows, and cross-referenced data points back into the database. Each analysis step is logged with a unique trace ID, allowing the application to resume interrupted workflows, backtrack through reasoning chains, and maintain state across long-running sessions without re-fetching raw source data.

docs.title: Ask AI Request Lifecycle
docs.text:
An Ask AI inquiry follows a retrieval-augmented workflow that combines relational context from ship_computer.db with semantic retrieval from the vector database.

  1. Receive the user prompt
  2. Spock receives the user's question or instruction.

  3. The prompt is associated with an active session ID.

  4. Load session and system context

  5. Spock queries ship_computer.db for:

    • Recent conversation history.
    • User preferences.
    • Active system configuration.
    • Relevant document metadata.
    • Prior Ask AI responses related to the current topic.

  6. Prepare the retrieval query

  7. Spock may rewrite or expand the user prompt to improve retrieval quality.

  8. The query is passed to the embedding model to generate a dense vector representation.

  9. Retrieve semantically relevant chunks

  10. Spock searches the vector database for chunks whose embeddings are most similar to the query embedding.
  11. The search may apply metadata filters, such as document type, session scope, user role, or time range.

  12. The top-k results are returned with similarity scores.

  13. Resolve relational metadata

  14. Spock uses the chunk IDs or vector references returned by the vector database to query ship_computer.db.

  15. This retrieves source document metadata, chunk text, permissions, timestamps, and related context.

  16. Build the prompt

  17. Spock assembles a prompt that includes:

    • The user's original question.
    • Retrieved context chunks.
    • Session history.
    • System instructions.
    • Any relevant configuration or policy constraints.

  18. Generate the response

  19. The assembled prompt is sent to the generative model.

  20. The model produces an answer grounded in the retrieved context.

  21. Persist the interaction

  22. Spock writes the query, response, retrieved chunk references, model metadata, and timing information back to ship_computer.db.
  23. This creates an auditable record and provides context for future Ask AI requests.

This lifecycle ensures that Ask AI responses are not based only on the model's internal knowledge. Instead, they are grounded in Spock's persisted application state and retrieved semantic context.

docs.title: Deep Dive Request Lifecycle
docs.text:
Deep Dive is designed for complex, multi-step analysis tasks that require iterative retrieval, reasoning, and state persistence. Unlike a single Ask AI response, a Deep Dive workflow may span multiple retrieval passes, intermediate analyses, and follow-up questions.

  1. Create a Deep Dive trace
  2. Spock creates a new trace ID in ship_computer.db.

  3. The trace records the user's objective, session ID, start time, and initial status.

  4. Break the objective into steps

  5. Spock decomposes the task into smaller analytical steps.

  6. Each step is stored in the deep_dive_steps table with an ordered position and status.

  7. Retrieve context for the first step

  8. Spock generates an embedding for the step's query.
  9. It searches the vector database for relevant chunks.

  10. It resolves chunk metadata from ship_computer.db.

  11. Perform step-level analysis

  12. Spock may call the generative model to summarize, compare, classify, or reason over the retrieved context.

  13. The intermediate result is stored in the database with the trace ID and step ID.

  14. Refine the next query

  15. Based on the intermediate result, Spock generates a follow-up query.

  16. This allows the workflow to explore related concepts, missing evidence, or conflicting information.

  17. Repeat retrieval and reasoning

  18. Each iteration creates additional vector searches and database writes.

  19. Spock records which chunks were used, which were rejected, and why.

  20. Maintain a reasoning chain

  21. The database preserves the sequence of steps, inputs, outputs, and evidence.

  22. This allows Spock to backtrack, resume, or explain how a final conclusion was reached.

  23. Produce the final Deep Dive result

  24. After sufficient evidence has been gathered, Spock synthesizes a final answer or report.

  25. The final result is linked to the trace ID and all contributing steps.

  26. Persist the completed workflow

  27. Spock updates the trace status to completed, failed, or paused.
  28. All intermediate artifacts remain available for audit, debugging, or future continuation.

This design allows Deep Dive to handle long-running analytical tasks without losing context, even if the application is restarted or the user returns later.

docs.title: Embedding LLM and Vector Database Pipeline
docs.text:
Spock separates generative reasoning from semantic retrieval by utilizing a dedicated embedding model alongside a vector database. This architecture enables efficient, high-precision context retrieval before any generative processing occurs.

The embedding model and vector database form the semantic retrieval layer of Spock. They allow the application to find relevant text based on meaning rather than exact keyword matching. This is especially important for Ask AI and Deep Dive, where user questions may be phrased differently from the source material.

docs.title: What the Embedding Model Does
docs.text:
The embedding model converts text into a fixed-size numerical vector, also called an embedding. Each vector represents the semantic meaning of the text in a high-dimensional space. Texts with similar meanings produce vectors that are closer together, while unrelated texts produce vectors that are farther apart.

In Spock, the embedding model is used to encode:

  • User questions.
  • Document chunks.
  • Deep Dive step queries.
  • Intermediate analysis summaries.
  • Metadata-rich context fragments.

Although it is sometimes referred to as an "embedding LLM," the component is typically an encoder model rather than a generative language model. Its purpose is not to produce natural language output, but to produce dense vector representations that can be compared using similarity metrics such as cosine similarity.

Key characteristics of the embedding pipeline include:

  • Deterministic encoding: The same input text, model version, and preprocessing rules produce the same embedding.
  • Semantic similarity: Embeddings capture meaning, allowing Spock to retrieve related content even when exact keywords differ.
  • Chunk-level granularity: Documents are split into smaller chunks so that retrieval can target specific passages rather than entire files.
  • Metadata association: Each embedding is linked to relational metadata in ship_computer.db, such as document ID, chunk ID, session scope, and permissions.
  • Model versioning: Spock stores the embedding model version with each vector reference so that retrieval behavior can be tracked and reproduced.

docs.title: What the Vector Database Stores
docs.text:
The vector database stores the numerical embeddings and the minimal information needed to perform similarity search. It is optimized for fast nearest-neighbor queries over high-dimensional vectors.

A typical vector record includes:

Field Purpose vector_id Unique identifier for the embedding record. chunk_id Identifier for the text chunk in ship_computer.db. document_id Identifier for the source document. session_id Optional session or scope identifier. embedding High-dimensional vector produced by the embedding model. model_version Version of the embedding model used. created_at Timestamp for when the embedding was generated. metadata Additional filters such as document type, owner, language, or classification.

The vector database does not replace ship_computer.db. Instead, it provides fast semantic lookup. After Spock retrieves candidate vector IDs, it uses those IDs to query ship_computer.db for authoritative text, permissions, timestamps, and relational context.

docs.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation Flow
docs.text:
Spock uses the embedding model and vector database as part of a retrieval-augmented generation pipeline. The general flow is as follows:

  1. Chunking
  2. Source documents are split into manageable chunks.

  3. Each chunk is stored in ship_computer.db with metadata.

  4. Embedding

  5. Each chunk is passed through the embedding model.
  6. The resulting vector is stored in the vector database.

  7. A reference to the vector is stored in ship_computer.db.

  8. Query embedding

  9. When a user asks a question, Spock embeds the query using the same embedding model.

  10. Similarity search

  11. Spock searches the vector database for the most similar chunk embeddings.

  12. The search returns a ranked list of candidate chunks.

  13. Metadata filtering

  14. Spock filters results using relational metadata from ship_computer.db.

  15. This ensures that only authorized, relevant, and appropriately scoped content is used.

  16. Context assembly

  17. Spock retrieves the full text of the selected chunks.

  18. It combines them with session history and system instructions.

  19. Generative response

  20. The assembled context is sent to the generative model.

  21. The model produces a response grounded in the retrieved evidence.

  22. Persistence

  23. Spock stores the query, response, retrieved chunk IDs, similarity scores, and model metadata in ship_computer.db.

This pipeline allows Spock to answer questions using current, relevant, and auditable context rather than relying solely on the generative model's internal knowledge.

docs.title: Relationship Between SQLite and the Vector Database
docs.text:
The SQLite database and vector database are tightly coordinated but serve different purposes.

Concern SQLite 3 (ship_computer.db) Vector Database Primary role Relational state, audit logs, session history, system state Semantic similarity search Data type Structured rows, foreign keys, timestamps, text High-dimensional vectors and lightweight metadata Query style SQL queries, joins, filters, transactions Nearest-neighbor vector search Strength Consistency, auditability, transactional writes Fast semantic retrieval over large text corpora Used for Ask AI history, Deep Dive traces, permissions, configuration Finding relevant chunks for user questions and Deep Dive steps

Spock uses stable identifiers to connect the two systems. For example, a vector record may reference a chunk_id, and that chunk_id may exist in ship_computer.db with the full chunk text, document ownership, permissions, and processing status.

This design provides several benefits:

  • Auditability: Every Ask AI and Deep Dive interaction can be traced back to the exact chunks and metadata used.
  • Consistency: Relational state remains authoritative in SQLite, while vector search remains optimized for semantic retrieval.
  • Scalability: Vector search can be optimized independently of the relational schema.
  • Resumability: Deep Dive workflows can be paused and resumed because their state is persisted in SQLite.
  • Security: Permissions and access control can be enforced through relational metadata before context is included in a prompt.

Together, ship_computer.db, the embedding model, and the vector database form the foundation of Spock's context-aware Ask AI and Deep Dive capabilities.

docs.title: Semantic Retrieval Pipeline
docs.text:
1. Text Ingestion & Embedding Generation: Raw documents, logs, and user prompts are passed through a lightweight embedding LLM, such as text-embedding-3-small or an open-source equivalent. This model converts unstructured text into high-dimensional numerical vectors that capture semantic meaning rather than exact keyword matches.

  2. Vector Storage & Indexing: The generated vectors are stored in a vector database, or in a SQLite-vec extension, optimized for similarity search. Each vector is indexed using approximate nearest neighbor, or ANN, algorithms such as HNSW or IVF to enable millisecond-level retrieval even across large datasets.

  3. Semantic Query Resolution: When a user initiates an Ask AI or Deep Dive request, the same embedding model converts the query into a vector. The vector database performs a similarity search, typically using cosine distance or inner product, to retrieve the most semantically relevant chunks from the knowledge base.

  4. Context Assembly & Generation: Retrieved chunks are ranked, filtered by relevance thresholds, and assembled into a structured context window. This context is merged with metadata from ship_computer.db and passed to the primary generative LLM. The model then synthesizes a response grounded in both real-time vector retrieval and persistent relational state.

This decoupled pipeline ensures that Spock scales efficiently: the embedding model handles semantic matching, the vector database manages high-dimensional search, SQLite maintains relational integrity and session state, and the generative LLM focuses exclusively on reasoning and response formulation.

docs.title: SQLite 3 ship_computer.db
docs.text:
