  6. Caching & Feedback Loop: Frequently accessed embeddings and their corresponding vector IDs are cached in memory to reduce redundant model calls. User interactions and AI response quality metrics are logged back into ship_computer.db, enabling periodic retraining or index optimization to improve retrieval accuracy over time.

docs.title: How the Spock Application Uses the Embedding LLM and Vector DB
docs.text: The Spock application uses the embedding model and vector database as a semantic retrieval layer. The embedding model is not the same as the response-generating LLM; it converts text into numerical vectors that can be compared by similarity. The vector database stores those vectors along with metadata, allowing the application to find conceptually relevant content even when the user’s wording differs from the source material.

docs.title: Ingestion and Indexing
docs.text:
When knowledge base documents are added to the system, the Spock application performs the following steps:

  1. It normalizes and chunks the document into semantically coherent passages.
  2. It generates an embedding vector for each chunk.
  3. It stores the vector in the vector database.
  4. It stores associated metadata, such as source identifier, document title, date, credibility score, and chunk identifier.
  5. It records the chunk reference in ship_computer.db so that retrieval results can be audited and linked to specific inquiries.

This separation allows the vector database to optimize similarity search while SQLite remains the system of record for application state and audit history.

docs.title: Query-Time Retrieval
docs.text:
When a user submits a question, the Spock application uses the embedding model to convert the question into a vector. It then queries the vector database for the most similar stored chunks. The vector database returns candidate chunks ranked by similarity score.

The application may then apply additional filtering and ranking logic, such as:

  • Restricting results to a specific source or document type.
  • Prioritizing recent or high-credibility content.
  • Excluding chunks already used in the current Deep Dive session.
  • Reranking candidates using lexical overlap, metadata rules, or a secondary relevance model.

The final set of chunks is injected into the prompt context for the response-generating LLM.

docs.title: Ask AI vs Deep Dive Retrieval
docs.text:
The two inquiry pathways use the embedding and vector database differently.

  • Ask AI treats each question as independent. The application embeds the current question, retrieves the most relevant chunks, and generates a response without relying on prior conversational state.
  • Deep Dive treats the question as part of an ongoing investigation. The application embeds the current question, retrieves relevant chunks, and also consults prior session context from ship_computer.db. This allows the system to refine the query, avoid repeating previously retrieved material, and maintain continuity across multiple turns.

docs.title: Hybrid SQLite and Vector Search
docs.text:
The Spock application does not rely on vector search alone. It combines semantic retrieval with structured database queries.

For example, the application may:

  • Use the vector database to find chunks semantically related to “reactor containment failure.”
  • Use SQLite to filter those chunks by date range, source credibility, or session scope.
  • Use SQLite to determine whether a chunk has already been retrieved in the current Deep Dive session.
  • Use SQLite to store the final ranked context for audit and reproducibility.

This hybrid model gives the application both semantic flexibility and operational control.

docs.title: Caching, Feedback, and Optimization
docs.text:
To improve performance and accuracy, the Spock application maintains a feedback loop.

  • Embeddings for frequently used text chunks are cached to avoid repeated model calls.
  • Vector search results are logged in ship_computer.db with their similarity scores and inquiry context.
  • Response quality signals, such as user corrections, follow-up questions, or explicit feedback, are stored for later analysis.
  • Periodic jobs can use this data to tune chunking strategies, adjust similarity thresholds, rebuild indexes, or retrain retrieval components.

This allows the system to improve over time while preserving a clear audit trail of how each response was constructed.

docs.title: Interaction with Spock Application
docs.text: The database is accessed from the Python backend through the standard sqlite3 library or an ORM layer such as SQLAlchemy. The interaction model supports responsive, lightweight operations for health checks, inquiry tracking, and session persistence, while offloading heavier AI computations to dedicated processing pipelines.

docs.title: ship_computer.db Schema and Interaction Model
docs.text:
ship_computer.db is a SQLite 3 relational database that serves as the persistent state layer for the Spock application. It is optimized for low-latency reads and writes, handling metadata, audit trails, and session state rather than raw AI model weights or large binary payloads. The schema is structured around three core tables:

  • inquiries: Stores metadata for every Ask AI request, including a unique identifier, user/session context, timestamp, query text, AI response payload, and processing status (pending, processing, completed, failed). Indexed on status and created_at for efficient filtering and health monitoring.
  • sessions: Manages multi-turn Deep Dive interactions. Each record contains a session ID, initialization timestamp, current step index, and a TEXT field containing serialized JSON context state. Foreign keys link back to the originating user or system actor.
  • knowledge_base: Acts as a structured cache for retrieved documents, embeddings metadata, and intermediate reasoning artifacts. It stores document IDs, source references, vector database identifiers, and relevance scores. Foreign keys tie entries to specific inquiries or sessions to maintain traceability.

SQLite 3 is configured with WAL (Write-Ahead Logging) mode to allow concurrent reads during writes, and PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL is enforced at startup. Indexes are applied to foreign keys and frequently queried columns to prevent full-table scans. The application interacts with ship_computer.db using parameterized queries to prevent SQL injection, and all state mutations are wrapped in explicit transactions to guarantee atomicity.

docs.title: Relationships and Data Flow
docs.text:
The tables in ship_computer.db are designed to preserve a clear audit trail for every AI interaction.

  • An inquiries row represents a single Ask AI request and its lifecycle.
  • A sessions row represents a multi-step Deep Dive interaction and its evolving context.
  • A knowledge_base row represents a retrieved or generated artifact that supports an inquiry or session.

In practice, the database records what happened, when it happened, and which retrieved evidence was used. The actual semantic search and vector similarity calculations are performed outside SQLite, typically in a dedicated vector database or in-memory ANN index. SQLite stores the resulting references, scores, and response metadata so that the Spock application can reconstruct, audit, and resume interactions reliably.

docs.title: Ask AI Inquiry Flow
docs.text:
1. Ingestion: When a user submits an Ask AI query, the application writes a record to the inquiries table with a status of pending. The record captures the raw prompt, metadata, and a unique tracking ID.
  2. Retrieval: The system queries the knowledge_base to fetch relevant context needed to answer the prompt. Metadata filters and vector similarity scores are joined to surface the most semantically relevant documents.
  3. Completion: Once the AI engine generates a response, the result is stored in the response_payload column, and the inquiry record is updated to completed. Processing duration and token metrics are logged for observability.

docs.title: Deep Dive Inquiry Flow
docs.text:
1. Session Initialization: A Deep Dive session creates a new entry in the sessions table, establishing a unique context identifier for the multi-step interaction. Initial parameters, depth limits, and user preferences are serialized and stored.
  2. Contextual Storage: As the AI explores the topic, intermediate results, retrieved documents, and reasoning traces are appended to the knowledge_base or linked via foreign keys to the session ID. Each step updates the session's current_step and state_snapshot fields.
  3. State Persistence: Unlike standard queries, Deep Dive sessions maintain state across multiple steps. The database uses explicit transactions so that if a step fails, incomplete updates can be rolled back, preserving data integrity for the current session. Checkpointing is performed at logical boundaries to enable recovery without reprocessing.

docs.title: Embedding LLM and Vector Database Integration
docs.text:
The Spock application relies on a dedicated embedding LLM and a vector database to power semantic retrieval for both Ask AI and Deep Dive workflows. The integration follows a decoupled pipeline:

  • Embedding Generation: Incoming user queries and indexed knowledge documents are passed through a lightweight embedding model (e.g., text-embedding-3-small or an open-source equivalent). The model converts text into high-dimensional dense vectors that capture semantic meaning rather than lexical matching.
  • Vector Storage & Indexing: Generated embeddings are stored in a vector database optimized for approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search. The vector DB maintains an HNSW or IVF index to enable low-latency similarity lookups across large collections of vectors. Each vector record is linked to a metadata payload containing document IDs, source URLs, and chunk boundaries.
  • Similarity Search & Reranking: During retrieval, the user's query is embedded in real-time and used to query the vector DB using cosine similarity or inner product distance. Top-k results are returned, optionally passed through a cross-encoder reranker to refine relevance before context injection.
  • Integration with Inquiry Flows: The vector DB does not store conversational state; it strictly handles semantic lookup. Once relevant chunks are retrieved, their metadata and content are cached in ship_computer.db's knowledge_base table for auditability. The AI completion engine then receives the original prompt augmented with the retrieved context, ensuring grounded, traceable responses.

docs.title: How the Spock Application Uses the Embedding LLM and Vector DB
docs.text:
The embedding LLM and vector database work together to convert natural-language questions into semantic searches over a knowledge corpus.

  1. Document Preparation: Source documents are chunked into smaller passages suitable for retrieval. Each chunk is assigned metadata such as document ID, source reference, section, and creation timestamp.
  2. Embedding Indexing: Each chunk is passed through the embedding LLM to produce a vector representation. These vectors are stored in the vector database alongside their metadata.
  3. Query Embedding: When a user submits an Ask AI or Deep Dive prompt, the Spock application sends the prompt to the same embedding model used for indexing. This ensures that queries and documents exist in the same vector space.
  4. Semantic Retrieval: The query vector is compared against the indexed document vectors using a similarity metric such as cosine similarity. The vector database returns the most relevant chunks.
  5. Context Assembly: The retrieved chunks are ranked, filtered, and assembled into a context block. This context is appended to the user prompt before it is sent to the generative AI model.
  6. Response Grounding: The generative model produces an answer using both the user prompt and the retrieved context. The resulting response is stored in ship_computer.db, along with references to the evidence used.

This separation allows the Spock application to keep semantic search fast and scalable while using SQLite for durable, transactional state management.

docs.title: Technical Considerations
docs.text:
• Concurrency: SQLite supports concurrent readers and a single writer. WAL mode improves read/write overlap, but the application should avoid long-running write transactions.
  • Security: All SQL access should use parameterized queries. Sensitive prompt data should be encrypted at rest where required by policy.
  • Performance: Frequently accessed columns should be indexed. Large response payloads should be stored efficiently, and heavy vector search work should remain outside SQLite.
  • Observability: Inquiry status, processing duration, token usage, and retrieval scores should be logged to support debugging and performance monitoring.
  • Recovery: Deep Dive sessions should checkpoint state at logical boundaries so that failed steps can be retried without corrupting prior session data.
  • Backup: Because ship_computer.db contains operational state and audit data, it should be included in regular backup and restore procedures.

  • Connection Management: The application uses context managers or equivalent connection handling to ensure each SQLite connection is opened, used, and closed within a single operation. This prevents resource leaks in long-running processes. Because SQLite supports one writer at a time, the application avoids connection pooling and instead creates short-lived connections per request or per thread. Each connection sets appropriate busy_timeout, journal_mode, and synchronous pragmas, and connections are not shared across threads unless explicitly configured for safe single-thread use.

  • Transaction Isolation: Writes to ship_computer.db are performed inside transactions so that inquiry history, session state, and Deep Dive step state remain atomic. Read-heavy operations use DEFERRED transactions, allowing readers to proceed while a writer waits for locks. Batch state updates use IMMEDIATE transactions to acquire the write lock early and reduce lock contention. EXCLUSIVE transactions are reserved for rare maintenance operations that must prevent concurrent readers and writers.

  • Readiness Check Integration: The spock_probe module verifies database connectivity as part of its readiness contract. If the connection to ship_computer.db fails, the server is marked as "Not Ready," preventing traffic routing until the dependency is restored. Health checks include file-system accessibility, WAL checkpoint status, schema version validation, and basic query execution against a known metadata table.

  • Storage & Maintenance: Periodic VACUUM and ANALYZE operations are scheduled during low-traffic windows to reclaim fragmented space and refresh query planner statistics. Automated backups are performed using SQLite's online backup API to create consistent, zero-downtime snapshots without blocking normal application traffic.

docs.title: SQLite 3 ship_computer.db and Spock Interaction
docs.text: ship_computer.db is the local SQLite 3 database that provides durable, transactional state for the Spock application. It is the system of record for inquiry metadata, session context, response history, Deep Dive execution state, citations, feedback, and maintenance information. It does not replace the vector database; instead, it stores the operational state needed to make Ask AI and Deep Dive requests reproducible, auditable, and resumable.

docs.title: Role in Ask AI
docs.text:
For an Ask AI inquiry, Spock uses ship_computer.db to:

  • Create an inquiry record before calling external services.
  • Store the user's question, session identifier, model version, prompt template, and request timestamp.
  • Load prior conversation context, user preferences, and previous citations.
  • Record the vector database query, retrieved chunk identifiers, and similarity scores.
  • Store the final answer, token usage, latency, error state, and user feedback.
  • Support replay, audit, and debugging by preserving the exact context used to generate the answer.

docs.title: Role in Deep Dive
docs.text:
For a Deep Dive inquiry, Spock uses ship_computer.db to persist a multi-step research workflow:

  • Create a Deep Dive run with a unique identifier, objective, status, and owner.
  • Store the generated research plan and each sub-question as individual steps.
  • Record the vector database queries, retrieved evidence, intermediate summaries, and confidence signals for each step.
  • Track step completion, retries, timeouts, and partial failures.
  • Store the final synthesized report, citations, assumptions, and artifacts.
  • Allow the run to be resumed after interruption by reading the last committed step state.

This design keeps long-running Deep Dive work durable even if the process restarts or a downstream service temporarily fails.

docs.title: Embedding LLM and Vector Database Integration
docs.text: Spock uses an embedding LLM and a vector database to perform semantic retrieval for both Ask AI and Deep Dive inquiries. The embedding LLM converts text into dense numerical vectors, and the vector database stores those vectors alongside metadata so that Spock can find semantically relevant evidence quickly.

docs.title: Embedding LLM
docs.text:
The embedding LLM is a model that maps text chunks, user questions, and metadata into fixed-size vector representations. Spock uses it to:

  • Embed document chunks before storing them in the vector database.
  • Embed user questions at query time.
  • Embed sub-questions and intermediate findings during Deep Dive execution.
  • Compare semantic similarity between the user's intent and candidate evidence.

The embedding model version is recorded in ship_computer.db so that Spock can detect when embeddings need to be regenerated after a model upgrade.

docs.title: Vector Database
docs.text:
The vector database is the semantic search layer. It stores:

  • Vector embeddings for document chunks, notes, reports, and other evidence.
  • Metadata such as source identifier, document title, section, timestamp, classification, and Deep Dive run association.
  • Indexes that support fast approximate nearest-neighbor search.

Spock uses the vector database to:

  • Retrieve the most relevant chunks for an Ask AI question.
  • Gather evidence for each Deep Dive sub-question.
  • Apply metadata filters to limit results to authorized or contextually relevant sources.
  • Support hybrid retrieval by combining vector similarity with keyword or structured filters.

docs.title: Retrieval Flow
docs.text:
1. Spock receives an Ask AI or Deep Dive request.
  2. Spock validates readiness and loads relevant context from ship_computer.db.
  3. Spock sends the user question or sub-question to the embedding LLM.
  4. The embedding LLM returns a query vector.
  5. Spock queries the vector database for the nearest matching evidence vectors.
  6. Spock applies metadata filters, reranks candidates, and selects the final context set.
  7. Spock stores the retrieved identifiers and scores in ship_computer.db.
  8. Spock passes the selected context to the answer-generation model.
  9. Spock records the final response, citations, and execution metadata.

docs.title: Consistency and Failure Handling
docs.text:
ship_computer.db remains the authoritative store for inquiry state, while the vector database remains the authoritative store for embeddings and semantic search. If the vector database is unavailable, Spock can mark the request as degraded, fall back to previously stored context when appropriate, or return a readiness error depending on the operation. If the embedding LLM is unavailable, Spock cannot generate new query vectors and should avoid returning stale semantic results unless the operation explicitly permits cached retrieval.

This separation allows Spock to maintain durable request state in SQLite while using the vector database for high-performance semantic search.

docs.title: spock_status
docs.text: Displays the current system status, including server health, resource usage, and readiness flags.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m spock_status

Note: The command above calls the Python interpreter inside a Windows virtual environment directly, so activation is not required. If you activate the virtual environment first, run python -m spock_status instead. On Linux/macOS, use ./venv/bin/python -m spock_status, or activate the environment with source venv/bin/activate and then run python -m spock_status.

docs.title: SQLite 3 ship_computer.db and Spock integration
docs.text:
ship_computer.db is the local SQLite 3 database used by the Spock application as the structured source of truth for operational state and inquiry metadata. It stores data that is deterministic, queryable, and suitable for relational access, such as:

  • server health and readiness flags
  • resource usage snapshots
  • service status and dependency checks
  • Ask AI request metadata
  • Deep Dive investigation records
  • evidence references, citations, and result summaries
  • embedding metadata, such as chunk identifiers, source paths, timestamps, and vector store references

The database is not used to store large vector embeddings directly. Instead, it stores the relational context needed to explain, audit, and retrieve the data that the vector database returns.

docs.title: Ask AI interaction
docs.text:
When a user submits an Ask AI inquiry, Spock uses ship_computer.db to:

  1. Validate that the system is ready to answer.
  2. Load relevant status, configuration, and recent operational context.
  3. Record the user question, timestamp, model version, and retrieval parameters.
  4. Store the final answer, confidence indicators, and source references.
  5. Provide citations that can be traced back to structured records in the database.

For Ask AI, the database provides the factual and operational context, while the vector database provides semantic similarity over unstructured text.

docs.title: Deep Dive interaction
docs.text:
Deep Dive inquiries are more investigative and may require multiple retrieval and reasoning steps. Spock uses ship_computer.db to:

  • create a Deep Dive session record
  • track each step of the investigation
  • store structured queries and their results
  • link vector search results to source documents and database records
  • preserve intermediate findings, hypotheses, and evidence
  • produce a final report with auditable references

This separation allows Deep Dive to combine precise SQL queries with semantic search. For example, Spock can query ship_computer.db for all failed readiness checks in the last hour, then use the vector database to find related logs, runbooks, or explanatory text that match the failure context.

docs.title: Embedding LLM and vector database usage
docs.text: The Spock application uses an embedding LLM to convert text into numerical vectors. These vectors represent semantic meaning, allowing the application to find related content even when the wording differs from the user's question.

docs.title: Embedding process
docs.text:
1. Spock receives a user question or a document chunk.
  2. The text is normalized and split into manageable chunks if necessary.
  3. The embedding LLM converts each chunk into a vector.
  4. The vector is stored in the vector database along with metadata, such as source, timestamp, chunk ID, and content type.
  5. ship_computer.db stores the relational metadata needed to reference, audit, and display that content.

docs.title: Retrieval process
docs.text:
When Spock needs to answer an Ask AI or Deep Dive inquiry:

  1. The user question is embedded using the same embedding LLM.
  2. The vector database searches for the nearest vectors to the question vector.
  3. Spock retrieves the associated text chunks and metadata.
  4. Results are filtered, ranked, and combined with structured data from ship_computer.db.
  5. The final context is passed to the language model that generates the response.

docs.title: Why both SQLite and a vector database are used
docs.text:
SQLite 3 provides exact, relational access to structured operational data. The vector database provides approximate semantic search over unstructured text. Together, they allow Spock to answer questions that require both precise status data and contextual understanding.

For example:

  • Ask AI: "Why is the server not ready?" Spock queries ship_computer.db for readiness flags and resource usage, then searches the vector database for related logs or documentation.
  • Deep Dive: "Investigate the recent readiness failures." Spock creates a session in ship_computer.db, retrieves structured failure records, searches semantically for possible causes, and stores the evidence trail for review.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The spock_status module provides a command-line interface (CLI) for monitoring system health and status. It is intended for development and operations environments, allowing teams to quickly assess the state of a server or application without performing detailed manual inspection.

The module can also serve as a source of operational context for the Spock application. When status metrics, service checks, or readiness signals are persisted or exposed through the Spock data layer, they can be used to support "Ask AI" and "Deep Dive" inquiries that require current or historical system state.

docs.title: Functionality
docs.text:
• Server Health: Verifies the operational status of critical running services, validates network connectivity, and monitors active system processes where available.
  • Resource Usage: Reports real-time statistics for CPU load, memory consumption, and disk space availability. The exact metrics may vary by operating system and permissions.
  • Readiness Flags: Returns boolean indicators or exit codes that indicate whether the system meets the criteria required for deployment, testing, or production use. Exit codes are useful for scripts, CI/CD pipelines, and automated monitoring tools.

docs.title: Technical Details
docs.text: The module is implemented in Python and should be run from a virtual environment that contains its dependencies. It relies on system-level metrics and may require appropriate permissions to access certain resources, such as network sockets, process lists, or protected files. On Windows, Linux, and macOS, the available data can differ depending on user privileges and OS APIs.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Python Environment: A compatible Python version must be installed in the virtual environment, along with any required third-party packages.
  • Permissions: The user executing the module may need elevated privileges to read system logs, inspect processes, or access protected network interfaces.

docs.title: Database Architecture
docs.text: The Spock application uses a SQLite 3 database file named ship_computer.db to persist data and manage state for advanced inquiry features. This section explains how the database supports "Ask AI" and "Deep Dive" inquiries, and how it can provide context for status-related reporting when applicable.

docs.title: SQLite 3 Storage Layer
docs.text:
The ship_computer.db file serves as the local relational database engine for the Spock application. It is implemented using Python's built-in sqlite3 library, so no external database server or additional installation step is required.

  • File-Based Persistence: Unlike server-based databases such as PostgreSQL or MySQL, SQLite stores all data in a single disk file. This makes it well suited to portable applications and environments where network overhead should be minimized.
  • ACID Compliance: Despite its lightweight design, the database follows ACID principles (Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability). This helps preserve data integrity even if the application crashes during a write operation.
  • Schema Management: The application manages the schema for ship_computer.db. Required tables are created during initialization or when a feature first needs them, rather than requiring manual database setup.
  • Write-Ahead Logging (WAL): The application configures the database to operate in WAL mode where supported to optimize concurrent read/write operations. This helps ensure that status checks and AI query routing do not unnecessarily block each other, maintaining low latency during high-throughput periods.
  • Local Transaction Control: SQLite transactions are managed by the application process. This allows Spock to group related writes, such as storing a user query, retrieved context, and generated response, into a single consistent operation.
  • Portability and Simplicity: Because the database is file-based, it can be copied, backed up, or restored as part of the application data directory. This is useful for local development, edge deployments, and environments where a separate database service is not desired.

docs.title: Ask AI and Deep Dive Integration
docs.text:
The database plays an important role in powering the intelligent features of the Spock application, specifically "Ask AI" and "Deep Dive". These features rely on structured data retrieval from ship_computer.db.

  • Ask AI Queries: When a user initiates an "Ask AI" inquiry, the system parses natural-language requests into constrained SQL queries, query plans, or semantic retrieval requests. The database stores historical context, logs, metadata, and prior interactions needed to generate accurate responses. Frequently accessed tables are indexed to reduce latency for AI inference pipelines.
  • Deep Dive Inquiries: For complex analytical tasks labeled as "Deep Dive", the application performs multi-table joins and aggregations within ship_computer.db. This enables detailed analysis of system logs, performance metrics, user activity, and status history without transferring large datasets to external servers. Results can be summarized or returned as structured data for display.
  • Data Isolation: To maintain security and stability, database access is restricted to the application process. Direct modification by external scripts or users should be avoided; file permissions, OS-level controls, and parameterized queries help prevent unauthorized changes to the data store.
  • Context Persistence: The database records the inputs, outputs, and intermediate context used by AI features. This supports auditability, debugging, response consistency, and the ability to reconstruct why a particular answer was generated.
  • Status Context: When spock_status metrics are stored in ship_computer.db, Ask AI and Deep Dive can reference recent health checks, resource usage, service states, and readiness flags as part of their response context.

docs.title: Schema Design and Query Routing
docs.text:
To support both conversational and analytical workloads, ship_computer.db utilizes a normalized schema with dedicated indexing strategies:

  • Core Tables: The database maintains tables for sessions, queries, responses, system_metrics, and context_logs. Each record includes timestamps, user/session identifiers, and status flags to enable precise filtering.
  • Indexing Strategy: Primary keys are indexed by SQLite's rowid mechanism. Foreign keys are not automatically indexed, so the application creates indexes on commonly joined columns. Additional B-tree indexes are applied to frequently filtered columns such as query_type, status_code, and timestamp to accelerate WHERE and ORDER BY clauses during Deep Dive aggregations.
  • Query Routing: The application's query router evaluates incoming requests and directs them to the appropriate execution path. Simple status checks use lightweight SELECT statements with LIMIT clauses, while Deep Dive operations trigger batched reads and bounded result sets to prevent memory exhaustion.
  • Read-Only Enforcement: AI and Deep Dive query paths should use read-only connections or transaction modes where possible. This reduces the risk of accidental writes during analytical operations.
  • Query Limits: The application enforces timeouts, row limits, and resource caps on generated SQL to protect the local database and the host system from expensive or runaway queries.

docs.title: Detailed Inquiry Data Flow
docs.text:
The following flow describes how ship_computer.db participates in Spock's inquiry features:

  1. Intake: The user submits an "Ask AI" or "Deep Dive" request through the Spock interface.
  2. Session Tracking: The application creates or updates a session record in ship_computer.db, capturing the user, timestamp, request type, and environment context.
  3. Intent Classification: The request is classified as a simple status question, a conversational AI question, or a complex analytical Deep Dive request.
  4. Context Retrieval: The application retrieves relevant structured data from ship_computer.db, such as recent metrics, prior queries, service states, or status flags.
  5. Semantic Retrieval: If the request requires conceptual matching, the application also queries the vector database for relevant text chunks, logs, or documentation.
  6. Query Execution: For Deep Dive requests, the application may generate constrained SQL, execute joins and aggregations, and apply limits to keep the operation safe and efficient.
  7. Response Generation: The retrieved context is assembled into a prompt or structured report. An LLM or summarization engine may generate the final user-facing answer.
  8. Persistence: The final response, retrieved context, query plan, and execution metadata are stored back into ship_computer.db for audit and future reference.

docs.title: Operational Considerations
docs.text:
• Backups: Because ship_computer.db is a single file, it can be backed up using file-level copy, snapshot, or application-managed export mechanisms.
  • Migrations: Schema changes should be applied through controlled migration steps to avoid corrupting existing inquiry history.
  • Retention: Large tables such as context_logs and system_metrics may require retention policies to prevent unbounded growth.
  • Monitoring: The application should track query latency, failed queries, database size, and WAL file growth to detect performance or storage issues.
  • Concurrency: SQLite is best suited to single-writer workloads. The application should serialize writes and use short transactions to avoid lock contention.

docs.title: Embedding LLM and Vector Database Integration
docs.text: While ship_computer.db handles structured relational data, the Spock application leverages an embedding LLM and a companion vector database to enable semantic understanding and context-aware retrieval. This hybrid architecture ensures that both precise data lookups and conceptual matching are supported.

docs.title: Embedding Generation and Semantic Search
docs.text:
The embedding LLM, or embedding model, converts text into numerical vector representations. These vectors capture semantic meaning, allowing the application to find related content even when the exact wording differs from the user's question.

  • Text Normalization: Before embedding, the application normalizes text by trimming whitespace, removing unnecessary markup, and standardizing timestamps or identifiers where appropriate.
  • Chunking: Long documents, logs, or responses are split into smaller chunks. Each chunk is embedded separately so that retrieval can return the most relevant portion of a larger text source.
  • Embedding Generation: The embedding model maps each chunk into a fixed-length vector. Similar concepts produce vectors that are closer together in vector space, while unrelated concepts produce vectors that are farther apart.
  • Semantic Search: When a user asks a question, the application embeds the question and searches the vector database for the most similar stored chunks. Similarity is typically measured using cosine distance, dot product, or another vector distance metric.
  • Hybrid Search: In addition to semantic search, the application may combine keyword search, metadata filters, and structured SQLite queries. This hybrid approach improves recall for technical terms, identifiers, and exact values that pure semantic search may miss.

docs.title: Vector Database Storage and Retrieval
docs.text:
The vector database stores embeddings alongside metadata that describes the source and context of each vector.

  • Vector Records: Each record contains an embedding vector, a unique identifier, a text chunk or reference, and metadata such as source type, timestamp, session ID, document ID, and content category.
  • Metadata Filtering: The application can restrict vector searches to specific sessions, time ranges, document types, or status categories. This prevents irrelevant results from being returned.
  • Similarity Ranking: The vector database returns the top-k most similar records based on the embedded query. The application can then rerank these results using recency, relevance score, source authority, or business rules.
  • Local or Embedded Deployment: The vector database may be implemented as an embedded local store or a lightweight companion service. In either case, it is designed to work alongside ship_computer.db without requiring a large external infrastructure stack.
  • Indexing: Vector indexes are used to accelerate similarity search. The application may rebuild or refresh indexes when new content is added or when the underlying text corpus changes significantly.

docs.title: Hybrid Retrieval and Context Assembly
docs.text:
Spock combines structured and semantic retrieval to build a complete context for each inquiry.

  • Structured Retrieval: ship_computer.db provides precise data such as metric values, query history, response records, status flags, and session metadata.
  • Semantic Retrieval: The vector database provides conceptually related text, such as similar past questions, relevant log excerpts, documentation snippets, or explanatory notes.
  • Context Assembly: The application merges these results into a bounded context window. It prioritizes the most relevant and recent items, removes duplicates, and enforces token or size limits before sending the context to the response generator.
  • Answer Grounding: The final answer should be grounded in the retrieved context. If the context is insufficient, the application should indicate uncertainty rather than fabricating details.
  • Explainability: Because both structured and semantic sources are recorded, the application can explain which data contributed to a response, improving debugging and user trust.

docs.title: End-to-End Inquiry Flow
docs.text:
The following flow describes how the embedding LLM and vector database work with ship_computer.db:

  1. User Request: The user submits an "Ask AI" or "Deep Dive" question.
  2. Query Embedding: The application converts the user's question into an embedding vector.
  3. Vector Search: The vector database returns the most semantically similar stored chunks.
  4. Structured Search: The application queries ship_computer.db for relevant sessions, metrics, logs, responses, or status records.
  5. Result Fusion: The application combines vector search results with structured database results, applying filters, rankings, and deduplication.
  6. Context Construction: The application builds a concise context package that includes the most relevant facts, examples, and historical references.
  7. Response Generation: An LLM or summarization engine uses the context to generate a natural-language answer or structured report.
  8. Result Storage: The final answer, retrieved context, vector search metadata, and database query results are stored for audit and future retrieval.

docs.title: Caching, Consistency, and Failure Handling
docs.text:
• Embedding Cache: Frequently used text chunks may have cached embeddings to reduce repeated model inference costs.
  • Vector Index Refresh: New or updated content should be embedded and added to the vector index in a controlled manner to avoid serving stale or inconsistent results.
  • Database Consistency: ship_computer.db remains the source of truth for structured records. The vector database is treated as a derived index that can be rebuilt if necessary.
  • Graceful Degradation: If the vector database is unavailable, the application can fall back to structured SQLite queries and keyword search, though semantic matching will be reduced.
  • Timeouts and Limits: Vector searches and embedding generation should have timeouts and result limits to prevent slow or expensive operations from blocking the user interface.

docs.title: Security and Privacy
docs.text:
• Data Minimization: Only content necessary for inquiry support should be embedded and stored in the vector database.
  • Access Control: Both ship_computer.db and the vector database should be protected by file permissions, application authentication, and OS-level controls.
  • Sensitive Data Handling: Logs, prompts, and responses may contain sensitive information. The application should apply redaction, retention limits, and encryption where appropriate.
  • Audit Logging: Access to inquiry context, vector search results, and generated responses should be logged to support accountability and troubleshooting.
  • Isolation: AI retrieval paths should not expose raw database internals or vector store internals to end users. Only approved, summarized, or structured results should be returned.
  • Text-to-Vector Conversion: The embedding LLM converts natural language inputs, system logs, and documentation snippets into high-dimensional dense vectors. These vectors capture semantic meaning rather than relying on exact keyword matches.
  • Dimensionality and Model Selection: The application uses a lightweight, locally hosted embedding model optimized for technical and operational text. Vectors are typically 384 to 1536 dimensions, balancing accuracy with memory efficiency.
  • Similarity Scoring: Retrieved vectors are scored using cosine similarity or dot product metrics. Thresholds are dynamically adjusted based on query confidence to filter out irrelevant context before passing data to the generative LLM.

docs.title: Vector Database Architecture
docs.text:
• Storage and Indexing: The vector database stores embeddings alongside metadata pointers that link back to records in ship_computer.db. It utilizes Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) indexing (e.g., HNSW or IVF) to enable sub-millisecond search times across millions of vectors.
  • Synchronization: A background sync process ensures that new logs, metrics, and user queries are embedded and indexed incrementally. This prevents search latency from degrading during peak usage.
  • Hybrid Retrieval: When a query arrives, the system performs a dual lookup: exact matches are pulled from SQLite, while semantic matches are retrieved from the vector store. Results are fused using a weighted ranking algorithm before context assembly.

docs.title: Integration with Ask AI and Deep Dive Workflows
docs.text:
• Ask AI Context Assembly: For conversational inquiries, the embedding LLM first generates a query vector. The vector database retrieves the top-k semantically relevant documents or log entries. These are combined with relational metadata from ship_computer.db to construct a precise prompt context, reducing hallucination and improving response accuracy.
  • Deep Dive Analytical Enhancement: During complex investigations, the vector store identifies conceptually related events that may not share explicit identifiers. For example, a spike in memory usage can be correlated with deployment logs or error traces that mention similar subsystems, even if they lack direct foreign key relationships.
  • Fallback and Caching: If the embedding pipeline experiences latency or temporary unavailability, the application gracefully falls back to keyword-based SQLite queries. Frequently used vector results are cached in memory to minimize redundant embedding computations and database round trips.

docs.title: Layers
docs.text:
The application is organized into functional layers that separate user interaction, content ingestion, retrieval-augmented generation, model/hardware management, and persistence.

Layer Components Evidence UI / Stations NavigationStation, EngineeringDeck, ScienceStation, Bringup Menu PyQt6-based desktop applications or panels Wiki agent / ingest wiki_agent, starfleet_universal_extractor, onboarding skills Pipeline from agent_queue to extracted documents and embeddings RAG / Ask AI deep_dive, llm_client, spock_rag_adapter, AskAiPanel Hybrid search over local knowledge, context packing, and chat LLM calls Hardware / models spock_scanner_core, model_selector, host_recipe, llmfit VRAM-aware model selection and launch configuration Persistence WarpCore.settings_store, ship_computer.db SQLite database with FTS5 full-text search and embedding storage Python packages present bootstrap_wizard, EngineeringDeck, LongRangeSensors, model_selector, NavigationStation, Orchestrator, ScienceStation, spock_bringup, spock_bringup_menu, spock_codebase_knowledge, spock_live_monitor, spock_mcp_adapter, spock_onboarding, spock_probe, spock_progress_log, spock_rag_adapter, spock_shell, spock_status, spock_wiki_adapter, tests Filesystem scan of Python packages and modules

docs.title: Layer notes
docs.text:
• UI / Stations: The user-facing layer consists of a desktop UI built with PyQt6. "Stations" represent distinct operational views or workspaces, including navigation, engineering, science, and bringup/onboarding interfaces.
  • Wiki agent / ingest: This layer transforms raw wiki content into structured knowledge. It enqueues onboarding items, extracts text and metadata, persists documents, and generates embeddings for semantic search.
  • RAG / Ask AI: This layer answers user questions by combining local retrieval with an LLM. Hybrid search indicates that the system uses both keyword/full-text matching and vector/embedding similarity before assembling prompt context.
  • Hardware / models: This layer manages model availability and launch behavior, particularly regarding GPU memory or VRAM constraints. It selects appropriate model sizes, quantizations, ports, and runtime settings tailored to the host machine.
  • Persistence: The system stores configuration, documents, search indexes, embeddings, and operational state in SQLite. FTS5 provides full-text search capability, while stored embeddings support semantic retrieval.

docs.title: SQLite 3 Persistence: ship_computer.db
docs.text: ship_computer.db serves as the centralized persistence layer for the Spock application. Built on SQLite 3, it combines relational storage, full-text indexing, and vector data management into a single, lightweight database file.

docs.title: Schema and Storage Strategy
docs.text:
• Document & Metadata Tables: Store raw and processed wiki content, codebase artifacts, and associated metadata such as source paths, timestamps, authorship, and classification tags. These tables provide the authoritative record of what has been ingested and how each item should be interpreted.
  • FTS5 Virtual Table: An integrated Full-Text Search 5 index enables high-performance keyword matching, phrase queries, and boolean filtering across all ingested text. This supports exact-term retrieval, which is especially useful for technical identifiers, error messages, configuration keys, and domain-specific terminology.
  • Embedding Storage: High-dimensional vectors generated during ingestion are serialized, typically as BLOBs or JSON arrays, and stored alongside their corresponding document or chunk identifiers. This eliminates the need for an external vector database while still enabling semantic similarity search.
  • Configuration & State: WarpCore.settings_store maps to dedicated tables that track user preferences, hardware recipes, model launch parameters, and runtime telemetry. This allows the application to restore prior state and maintain consistent behavior across sessions.

docs.title: Embedding LLM and Vector Database
docs.text:
Spock uses an embedding model, often described in this architecture as the embedding LLM, to convert text into dense numerical vectors. These vectors represent the semantic meaning of a passage rather than its exact wording. For example, a question about "how to configure the model port" can be matched to a document that says "set the launch port in the host recipe," even if the two texts share few keywords.

The vector database is not a separate server or external service. It is implemented inside ship_computer.db as one or more SQLite tables that store embedding vectors together with metadata such as document ID, chunk ID, embedding model name, vector dimension, and creation timestamp. This design keeps the entire knowledge base local, portable, and easy to back up.

During ingestion, Spock processes source content in the following way:

  1. Raw wiki pages, codebase artifacts, or onboarding items are extracted and normalized.
  2. The content is split into manageable chunks so that retrieval can return relevant passages rather than entire documents.
  3. Each chunk is passed through the embedding model to produce a vector.
  4. The vector is serialized and stored in the embedding table.
  5. The same chunk is also indexed in the FTS5 table for keyword-based retrieval.

During query time, Spock uses the same embedding model to convert the user's question into a query vector. It then compares that vector against stored embeddings to find semantically similar passages. Because SQLite does not natively provide a universal vector index, similarity scoring is typically performed by the application layer, often using cosine similarity or dot-product scoring over candidate vectors. The result is a ranked set of semantically relevant documents or chunks.

This embedding-based retrieval complements FTS5. FTS5 excels at exact keyword matching, while the embedding vector store excels at conceptual matching. Together, they allow Spock to answer questions that require both precise terminology and broader semantic understanding.

docs.title: Interaction with Ask AI and Deep Dive
docs.text:
• Ask AI: When a user submits a conversational query, the RAG adapter executes a hybrid search against ship_computer.db. It first runs an FTS5 query to capture exact keyword matches and domain-specific terminology. Simultaneously, it retrieves the top-K semantically similar documents using stored embeddings. Results are ranked, deduplicated, and packed into a structured context window before being forwarded to the chat LLM. This allows Ask AI to produce grounded answers that are based on local knowledge rather than relying solely on the model's general training data.
  • Deep Dive: This mode triggers a more granular, multi-hop retrieval strategy. Instead of a single query pass, Deep Dive iteratively expands context by following metadata relationships, traversing codebase dependencies, or recursively querying related wiki nodes. The database supports this through indexed foreign keys, transactional read consistency, and optimized batch retrieval queries that minimize I/O latency during complex explorations. Deep Dive can therefore move from an initial answer to a broader investigation, pulling in related configuration files, code references, wiki pages, and operational notes as needed.

docs.title: Ask AI and Deep Dive Query Flow
docs.text:
The following flow describes how ship_computer.db participates in both Ask AI and Deep Dive inquiries.

  1. Query intake: The user submits a question through the Ask AI panel or initiates a Deep Dive request.
  2. Query preparation: Spock normalizes the question, extracts key terms, and prepares it for both lexical and semantic retrieval.
  3. Keyword retrieval: An FTS5 query is executed against the full-text index to find documents containing exact terms, phrases, or technical identifiers.
  4. Semantic retrieval: The question is embedded using the same embedding model used during ingestion. The resulting query vector is compared against stored embeddings to find conceptually similar passages.
  5. Result fusion: Keyword and vector results are combined, ranked, and deduplicated. This hybrid approach reduces the risk of missing relevant content that is either semantically similar but lexically different, or lexically exact but contextually weak.
  6. Context assembly: The highest-ranked passages are packed into a prompt context window. Metadata such as source, title, and classification may be included to help the LLM interpret the evidence.
  7. Answer generation: The chat LLM receives the assembled context and generates a response. For Ask AI, this is typically a direct answer. For Deep Dive, the response may include follow-up retrieval targets.
  8. Iterative expansion: In Deep Dive mode, Spock may inspect the retrieved documents for related links, code references, configuration keys, or metadata relationships. It then issues additional queries against ship_computer.db to expand the evidence base.
  9. State persistence: Query results, session state, and operational telemetry may be written back to SQLite so that the application can resume, audit, or refine the investigation later.

This flow allows Spock to treat ship_computer.db as both a knowledge store and a retrieval engine. FTS5 provides fast lexical search, the embedding tables provide semantic search, and the relational schema provides the structure needed to connect documents, metadata, configuration, and application state.

docs.title: Data flow (ingest → Ask AI)
docs.text:
1. Wiki scan / watcher enqueues onboarding work A scanner or file watcher detects new wiki content and places it into an onboarding queue in ship_computer.db. The extractor processes queued items, producing structured documents, metadata, and associated embeddings.

  2. Ask AI / Deep Dive retrieves relevant context When a user asks a question, the RAG layer queries ship_computer.db. It combines SQLite FTS5 full-text search with embedding similarity to identify the most relevant documents, metadata, or codebase knowledge. The selected context is then packed into an LLM prompt.

  3. Settings and host recipes control runtime behavior WarpCore.settings_store and related recipe/configuration data dictate how the application launches models, which ports are utilized, where scan roots are located, and what hardware constraints must be respected.

[ASK USER] Confirm intended production topology (single host vs dual-GPU). This matters because it affects model placement, VRAM allocation, port configuration, scan-root discovery, and whether components run locally on one machine or across multiple GPUs/hosts.

docs.title: SQLite 3 ship_computer.db
docs.text: ship_computer.db is the local SQLite 3 database that acts as the operational state store for the Spock application. It is not merely a passive file; it is the shared source of truth for onboarding work, extracted knowledge, embeddings, retrieval indexes, and runtime configuration.

docs.title: Core responsibilities
docs.text:
• Onboarding queue: stores pending wiki pages, files, or code artifacts that need extraction, chunking, embedding, and indexing.
  • Document store: stores normalized documents, chunks, source paths, titles, timestamps, content hashes, and metadata needed for citation and filtering.
  • Embedding store: stores vector representations for each document chunk or query-relevant unit, typically as BLOB values with dimensionality and model identifier.
  • Full-text index: uses SQLite FTS5 to provide keyword search over document text, titles, and selected metadata.
  • Settings and recipes: stores WarpCore.settings_store values and host recipes that control model endpoints, ports, scan roots, GPU/CPU placement, and hardware constraints.

docs.title: Expected table relationships
docs.text:
A practical schema would include tables such as:

  • onboarding(id, source_path, content_hash, status, created_at, updated_at, error)
  • documents(id, source_id, title, path, content, content_hash, created_at, updated_at)
  • chunks(id, document_id, ordinal, text, token_count, metadata_json)
  • embeddings(id, chunk_id, model, dimension, vector_blob, created_at)
  • documents_fts as an FTS5 virtual table linked to chunks or documents
  • settings(key, value_json, updated_at)
  • recipes(id, name, host, gpu, ports_json, scan_roots_json, constraints_json)

These tables allow the application to perform atomic updates: a new wiki page can be queued, extracted, chunked, embedded, and indexed in a single transaction, reducing the risk of partial state.

docs.title: How Ask AI uses the database
docs.text:
For an Ask AI request, the application:

  1. Normalizes the user question.
  2. Queries FTS5 for exact or near-exact keyword matches.
  3. Encodes the question with the embedding LLM.
  4. Compares the query vector against stored chunk embeddings.
  5. Ranks the combined results using keyword relevance, semantic similarity, recency, source type, and access constraints.
  6. Selects the highest-scoring chunks and formats them into a prompt for the generative LLM.

docs.title: How Deep Dive uses the database
docs.text:
Deep Dive extends the same retrieval path with a more exhaustive strategy:

  • It may issue multiple retrieval passes, using the initial answer or intermediate findings to generate follow-up queries.
  • It can traverse related documents through shared metadata, source paths, or linked references.
  • It may retrieve codebase knowledge, configuration recipes, and settings context in addition to wiki content.
  • It assembles a larger, more structured context block while still respecting token limits and relevance thresholds.

This makes ship_computer.db the central coordination point between ingestion, semantic search, configuration, and answer generation.

docs.title: Embedding LLM and Vector Database Integration
docs.text: The Spock application relies on a dedicated embedding LLM and an integrated vector storage mechanism to power semantic retrieval. This pipeline bridges raw text ingestion with intelligent, context-aware querying.

docs.title: Embedding LLM Workflow
docs.text:
• Ingestion Phase: As documents are extracted by the wiki agent, the embedding LLM processes each text chunk independently. It converts unstructured content into fixed-dimensional numerical vectors that capture semantic meaning, syntactic structure, and domain-specific relationships.
  • Query Phase: When a user submits a prompt via Ask AI or Deep Dive, the same embedding LLM encodes the query into a vector of identical dimensionality. This ensures mathematical compatibility for similarity comparison.
  • Model Selection & Optimization: The embedding model is typically smaller and faster than generative chat models, allowing it to run efficiently on CPU or low-VRAM GPU configurations. Quantization and batching are applied during ingestion to maintain throughput without sacrificing vector fidelity.

docs.title: Vector Database Operations
docs.text:
• Storage Architecture: Rather than relying on a standalone vector database, Spock leverages ship_computer.db as a unified vector store. Embeddings are persisted alongside document metadata, enabling atomic transactions and simplified backup/recovery procedures.
  • Similarity Search: During retrieval, the application computes cosine similarity or dot product distances between the query vector and stored document vectors. Indexing strategies, such as approximate nearest neighbor algorithms or SQLite vector extensions, can accelerate search operations and target sub-second response times even across large knowledge bases.
  • Hybrid Ranking: Raw similarity scores are combined with FTS5 keyword relevance metrics using a weighted ranking algorithm. This hybrid approach mitigates the limitations of pure vector search, such as poor handling of exact identifiers or rare technical terms, while preserving semantic flexibility.
  • Context Assembly: Top-ranked results are filtered by metadata constraints, such as recency, source type, or access level, truncated to fit token limits, and formatted into a structured context block. This block is injected into the system prompt before the generative LLM produces the final response.

docs.title: End-to-end embedding and retrieval flow
docs.text:
1. Chunking: The extractor splits source content into manageable chunks that preserve meaning while remaining small enough for efficient embedding and prompt inclusion.
  2. Embedding: Each chunk is passed through the embedding LLM to produce a dense vector representation.
  3. Persistence: The vector, chunk text, document metadata, and source information are written to ship_computer.db.
  4. Query encoding: The user’s Ask AI or Deep Dive prompt is encoded with the same embedding model.
  5. Candidate retrieval: The system retrieves candidates using both FTS5 keyword search and vector similarity search.
  6. Reranking: Candidates are scored using semantic similarity, keyword relevance, metadata filters, and freshness or access constraints.
  7. Prompt construction: The highest-scoring context is assembled into a structured prompt for the generative LLM.

docs.title: Why SQLite is used as the vector store
docs.text:
• Simplicity: SQLite provides a single-file database that is easy to deploy, inspect, and back up.
  • Atomicity: Document, chunk, embedding, and index updates can be committed together, reducing inconsistent state.
  • Portability: The database can be copied, restored, or migrated without requiring a separate vector database service.
  • Hybrid search: SQLite FTS5 and vector storage can coexist in the same database, enabling combined keyword and semantic retrieval.
  • Operational constraints: For local or single-host deployments, SQLite avoids the complexity of running a separate vector database cluster.

• Deterministic: This section was produced by a repeatable scanning process. Given the same repository state, scanner version, and filter configuration, it will consistently produce the same concerns list rather than relying on nondeterministic model generation or sampling.
  • High-churn files: Files that have been modified frequently in Git history. High churn can indicate active development, instability, or areas where behavior changes often; it serves as a heuristic for prioritizing review, not as proof of defects.
  • Filtered scan: The scanner excluded directories listed by .gitignore, scan.skip_dirs, and built-in extras before reporting TODO/FIXME hits or file statistics. This prevents generated artifacts, caches, dependencies, and large model/data blobs from dominating the results.
  • Raw scan excerpt: A short, unprocessed sample of what the scanner observed in a source file. It is shown as evidence that the scanner can detect TODO-like markers, but it does not imply that every line in the excerpt represents an unresolved concern.
  • llama.cpp blobs: Large binary or model-related files associated with llama.cpp. They are skipped because they often contain repeated strings and would artificially inflate TODO/FIXME counts.

docs.title: Concerns (deterministic)
docs.text:
What “deterministic” means here: This section was generated automatically by the acquire_codebase_knowledge script using a fixed, reproducible rule set (“deterministic fill”). No manual curation was applied; given the same scan input and configuration, it will always produce the same output.

  • The filtered concern list reports no actionable TODO, FIXME, or HACK markers in the reviewed source set.

What “filtered scan” means: The scanner walks the repository but excludes directories listed in .gitignore, the scan.skip_dirs configuration, and a set of built-in extras (for example, .cache, node_modules, and __pycache__). Only files outside those excluded trees are searched for marker comments.

docs.title: Summary versus raw evidence
docs.text: The filtered concern list is intended to highlight actionable review targets in first-party source code. The later “Raw scan excerpt” preserves unprocessed scanner output and may therefore still contain [TODO] placeholder strings, scanner internals, or diagnostic text that is not treated as an actionable concern.

The number shown before each path is the count of commits that touched that file during the scan window. Higher churn can indicate active development, instability, or frequent refactoring, making those files useful review targets.
