docs.title: SQLite 3 ship_computer.db
docs.text:
ship_computer.db is the local SQLite 3 database used by the Spock application as its primary structured state store. It provides persistent, transactional storage for application metadata, user sessions, configuration, research artifacts, and audit trails.

In the context of Ask AI and Deep Dive inquiries, ship_computer.db is not primarily responsible for semantic search. Instead, it acts as the system of record for:

  • user questions and assistant responses,
  • Deep Dive run state and intermediate steps,
  • retrieved evidence references,
  • model and prompt configuration,
  • document and chunk metadata,
  • application logs and maintenance events,
  • resumable workflow state.

The vector database, by contrast, is optimized for similarity search over embedded text. ship_computer.db stores the structured facts about what was asked, what was retrieved, what was generated, and how the process progressed.

docs.title: Role in Ask AI
docs.text:
Ask AI is the interactive question-and-answer surface of Spock. When a user submits an inquiry, the application typically performs the following steps:

  1. Normalize the request
  2. Trim and validate the user question.
  3. Resolve the active workspace, project, or document scope.

  4. Apply any user-selected filters, such as source type, date range, or document category.

  5. Load configuration

  6. Read model settings, context limits, retrieval settings, and prompt templates from ship_computer.db or related configuration tables.

  7. Retrieve relevant context

  8. Convert the user question into an embedding using the embedding model.
  9. Query the vector database for the most relevant chunks.

  10. Optionally rerank or filter results using metadata stored in ship_computer.db.

  11. Generate the answer

  12. Assemble a prompt from the user question, retrieved context, and system instructions.
  13. Send the prompt to the selected language model.

  14. Return the generated answer to the user.

  15. Persist the interaction

  16. Store the user question, assistant response, model used, prompt metadata, retrieved chunk identifiers, and timestamps in ship_computer.db.

This persistence allows Spock to support conversation history, answer auditing, debugging, and later review of why a particular answer was produced.

docs.title: Role in Deep Dive
docs.text:
Deep Dive is a more extensive research workflow than a single Ask AI question. It is designed for multi-step investigation, where Spock may need to:

  • break a broad question into subquestions,
  • retrieve evidence from multiple sources,
  • summarize intermediate findings,
  • identify gaps,
  • refine the search,
  • produce a final structured report.

ship_computer.db supports this workflow by storing the state of each Deep Dive run. A typical Deep Dive record may include:

  • the original user request,
  • the generated research plan,
  • each step executed,
  • the subquestions asked,
  • the chunks or documents retrieved at each step,
  • intermediate summaries,
  • final report content,
  • model and prompt versions,
  • timing and status information.

This makes Deep Dive resumable and inspectable. If a run is interrupted, Spock can reload the last completed step from ship_computer.db and continue without losing prior work.

docs.title: Representative tables
docs.text:
The exact schema may vary by implementation, but a typical ship_computer.db used by Spock may contain tables such as the following:

  • ask_ai_sessions
  • Stores one row per Ask AI conversation.

  • Tracks session start time, active workspace, model, and status.

  • ask_ai_messages

  • Stores individual user and assistant messages.

  • Includes message role, content, model, token counts, and timestamps.

  • retrieval_events

  • Records each retrieval operation.

  • Stores query text, embedding model, vector database query parameters, and retrieved chunk identifiers.

  • deep_dive_runs

  • Stores one row per Deep Dive investigation.

  • Tracks the original question, status, start time, completion time, and final report location.

  • deep_dive_steps

  • Stores each step in a Deep Dive workflow.

  • Includes step order, subquestion, retrieved evidence, summary, and status.

  • document_registry

  • Tracks documents known to Spock.

  • Stores source path, document type, hash, last modified time, and ingestion status.

  • chunk_registry

  • Tracks text chunks derived from documents.

  • Stores chunk text or chunk hash, source document, chunk index, and vector identifier.

  • model_settings

  • Stores selected models, embedding model, context size, temperature, and prompt settings.

  • application_logs

  • Stores operational logs, warnings, and maintenance events.

docs.title: Typical Ask AI data flow
docs.text:
A simplified Ask AI flow using ship_computer.db and the vector database is:

User question
    |
    v
Spock application
    |
    |-- Load settings from ship_computer.db
    |-- Embed question using embedding model
    |-- Query vector database for similar chunks
    |-- Retrieve chunk metadata from ship_computer.db
    |-- Assemble prompt
    |-- Generate answer with language model
    |-- Store question, answer, and retrieval trace in ship_computer.db
    v
Answer returned to user

docs.title: Typical Deep Dive data flow
docs.text:
A simplified Deep Dive flow is:

User research request
    |
    v
Spock application
    |
    |-- Create deep_dive_runs row in ship_computer.db
    |-- Generate research plan
    |-- For each step:
    |       |-- Create deep_dive_steps row
    |       |-- Embed subquestion
    |       |-- Query vector database
    |       |-- Store retrieved chunk references
    |       |-- Generate intermediate summary
    |       |-- Update step status
    |-- Generate final report
    |-- Mark run complete in ship_computer.db
    v
Deep Dive report returned to user

docs.title: Operational notes
docs.text:
Because ship_computer.db is a SQLite 3 database, it is well suited to local, file-based, low-overhead persistence. Spock can use it without requiring a separate database server.

Common operational practices include:

  • enabling WAL mode for better concurrent read/write behavior,
  • using transactions when writing multi-step Deep Dive state,
  • storing content hashes to detect changed documents,
  • using foreign keys to keep sessions, messages, and retrieval events consistent,
  • periodically running integrity checks and maintenance tasks,
  • retaining enough metadata to reproduce or audit an Ask AI or Deep Dive result.

docs.title: Embedding LLM and vector database
docs.text:
Spock uses an embedding model, often referred to in this context as the embedding LLM, to convert text into numerical vectors. These vectors are stored in a vector database, which enables fast similarity search over large collections of text.

This mechanism is central to both Ask AI and Deep Dive. It allows Spock to find relevant passages, code excerpts, wiki entries, logs, or research notes without requiring the user to know the exact wording of the source material.

docs.title: What the embedding LLM does
docs.text:
An embedding model maps text into a high-dimensional numerical space. Similar meanings tend to produce vectors that are close together, while unrelated meanings tend to produce vectors that are farther apart.

For example:

  • “How do I tune the context size?”
  • “What settings control prompt length?”
  • “How can I increase the amount of context passed to the model?”

These phrases may not share many exact words, but their embeddings may be close enough for the vector database to retrieve them as related.

The embedding model is different from the generative language model used to produce answers. The embedding model is primarily used for:

  • indexing text,
  • representing semantic meaning numerically,
  • enabling similarity search.

The generative model is used for:

  • answering questions,
  • summarizing evidence,
  • producing Deep Dive reports.

docs.title: What the vector database stores
docs.text:
The vector database stores the numerical embeddings and the metadata needed to retrieve and cite the original text. A typical vector record may include:

  • vector identifier,
  • embedded text or chunk text,
  • source document path,
  • document type,
  • chunk index,
  • content hash,
  • timestamp,
  • workspace or project identifier,
  • embedding model name,
  • embedding dimension,
  • optional metadata such as tags, author, or category.

The vector database is optimized for approximate nearest-neighbor search. Given a query vector, it can quickly return the most similar stored vectors.

docs.title: How Spock uses the embedding LLM and vector database
docs.text: The overall process has two main phases: indexing and retrieval.

docs.title: Indexing phase
docs.text:
When Spock ingests a document, wiki page, code file, log, or research artifact, it may perform the following steps:

  1. Read the source content
  2. Spock reads the file or content source.

  3. It records the source path, type, and modification time.

  4. Chunk the content

  5. Long documents are split into smaller chunks.

  6. Chunking may be based on character count, token count, headings, paragraphs, or semantic boundaries.

  7. Embed each chunk

  8. Each chunk is passed to the embedding model.

  9. The model produces a vector representation of the chunk.

  10. Store the vector and metadata

  11. The vector is written to the vector database.

  12. The chunk text, source metadata, and identifiers are stored in ship_computer.db or associated metadata tables.

  13. Track ingestion state

  14. Spock records whether the document was successfully indexed.
  15. It may store content hashes so unchanged documents are not re-embedded unnecessarily.

docs.title: Retrieval phase
docs.text:
When a user asks a question through Ask AI or initiates a Deep Dive, Spock performs the following steps:

  1. Embed the query

  2. The user question or subquestion is converted into a vector using the same embedding model used during indexing.

  3. Search the vector database

  4. Spock queries the vector database for the nearest neighbors.

  5. It may request a configurable number of results, such as top 5, top 10, or top 20.

  6. Apply filters

  7. Results may be filtered by workspace, document type, date, source path, or other metadata.

  8. Rerank or score results

  9. Spock may use similarity scores, metadata relevance, or a reranking model to improve result quality.

  10. Assemble context

  11. The selected chunks are combined into a prompt context.

  12. Spock must respect the context window limit of the selected language model.

  13. Generate a response

  14. The generative language model uses the retrieved context to answer the question or produce a Deep Dive section.

  15. Record the retrieval trace

  16. The query, retrieved chunk identifiers, scores, and model settings are stored in ship_computer.db for auditability.

docs.title: Ask AI usage pattern
docs.text:
Ask AI is optimized for fast, direct answers. Its retrieval strategy usually favors:

  • low latency,
  • a small number of highly relevant chunks,
  • strict context limits,
  • clear citations or source references.

A typical Ask AI retrieval configuration may include:

  • top-k retrieval size,
  • maximum context tokens,
  • minimum similarity threshold,
  • source filters,
  • prompt template,
  • model temperature,
  • maximum response length.

Ask AI may use a single retrieval pass. For example:

User: How can I tune the context size in Spock?

Spock:
1. Embed the question.
2. Retrieve the five most relevant chunks.
3. Filter chunks to documentation and configuration files.
4. Build a prompt with the question and retrieved chunks.
5. Generate an answer.
6. Store the question, answer, and retrieved chunk IDs.

docs.title: Deep Dive usage pattern
docs.text:
Deep Dive is optimized for thoroughness rather than speed. It may use multiple retrieval passes, each focused on a different aspect of the research question.

A Deep Dive workflow may include:

  • initial broad retrieval,
  • extraction of key themes,
  • generation of follow-up subquestions,
  • targeted retrieval for each subquestion,
  • comparison of evidence,
  • identification of contradictions or gaps,
  • synthesis of a final report.

For example:

User: Explain how Ask AI and Deep Dive work in Spock and how context size can be tuned.

Deep Dive:
1. Retrieve general documentation about Ask AI.
2. Retrieve documentation about Deep Dive.
3. Retrieve configuration files related to context size.
4. Retrieve code files that assemble prompts.
5. Summarize each area.
6. Identify where context limits are enforced.
7. Produce a structured report with citations.

Because Deep Dive may retrieve many chunks, it must manage context carefully. It may summarize intermediate results before passing them to the final answer model, reducing the amount of raw text that must fit into the final prompt.

docs.title: Relationship between ship_computer.db and the vector database
docs.text:
The two storage systems have different responsibilities.

Component Primary responsibility Typical contents ship_computer.db Structured application state sessions, messages, runs, steps, settings, logs, metadata Vector database Semantic similarity search embeddings, chunk text, vector metadata

In practice, they work together:

  • The vector database finds relevant text.
  • ship_computer.db records what was found, why it was found, and how it was used.
  • The generative language model produces the final answer or report.
  • The embedding model supports both indexing and query-time retrieval.

docs.title: Context size and retrieval tuning
docs.text:
Context size is one of the most important tuning areas for Ask AI and Deep Dive. It affects answer quality, latency, cost, and reliability.

Key tuning parameters include:

  • Chunk size
  • Smaller chunks can be more precise but may lack surrounding context.

  • Larger chunks provide more context but may include irrelevant material.

  • Top-k retrieval count

  • A higher top-k value retrieves more candidates.

  • A lower top-k value reduces noise and prompt size.

  • Similarity threshold

  • A higher threshold returns only very similar chunks.

  • A lower threshold may include more diverse but less relevant results.

  • Maximum context tokens

  • This limits how much retrieved text can be included in the prompt.

  • It must remain within the selected model’s context window.

  • Reranking

  • Reranking can improve precision by reordering retrieved chunks before prompt assembly.

  • Source filters

  • Restricting retrieval to specific document types or workspaces can improve relevance.

  • Summarization depth

  • Deep Dive may summarize intermediate evidence to keep the final prompt manageable.

docs.title: Embedding model consistency
docs.text: For reliable retrieval, Spock should use the same embedding model for indexing and querying. If the embedding model changes, previously stored vectors may no longer be comparable to new query vectors. In that case, Spock may need to re-embed indexed content or maintain separate vector collections for different embedding models.

docs.title: Local and offline operation
docs.text:
Because Spock is described as a Python and SQLite application, it is likely designed to operate locally. This means:

  • ship_computer.db can be a local file,
  • the vector database can be local or embedded,
  • the embedding model can run locally,
  • the generative model can run locally or through a configured endpoint.

This local architecture supports privacy, reproducibility, and offline use, while still allowing Spock to perform semantic search and AI-assisted research.

docs.title: ship_computer.db Architecture and Query Routing
docs.text:
ship_computer.db is a SQLite 3 database that serves as the persistent state layer for the Spock application. It is configured to run in Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) mode to support concurrent read/write operations without locking the entire database during active AI inference or document indexing.

The database stores relational metadata, query history, session state, configuration, and references to vector artifacts. It is not the primary vector index itself; instead, it provides durable, transactional context around vector search, LLM workflows, and Deep Dive research state.

docs.title: Core Schema Components
docs.text:
• queries: Stores user prompts, timestamps, routing flags (ask_ai vs deep_dive), and associated session IDs.
  • documents: Contains metadata for ingested wiki pages, ship logs, and research artifacts, including file paths, chunk boundaries, and content hashes.
  • embeddings_index: Maps document chunks to their corresponding vector identifiers and stores dimensionality, model version, and index metadata.
  • session_state: Tracks multi-turn conversation context, intermediate research steps, and cached LLM responses for Deep Dive workflows.
  • config: Holds runtime parameters such as context window limits, temperature settings, and active model paths.

docs.title: SQLite 3 Storage and Concurrency Model
docs.text:
SQLite 3 is used as a lightweight, file-based relational store that can run locally without a separate database server. This makes it well suited for Spock’s local or embedded deployment model.

Key storage characteristics include:

  • WAL mode: Allows readers to continue accessing the database while a writer commits changes. This is important when Spock is indexing documents, updating session state, or writing query logs while another request is being processed.
  • Single-writer model: SQLite permits one writer at a time, but multiple readers can operate concurrently. Spock should serialize write-heavy operations such as document ingestion, embedding updates, and Deep Dive checkpoint commits.
  • Transactions: Multi-step operations, especially Deep Dive state updates, should be wrapped in transactions so that partial failures do not leave inconsistent session state.
  • Foreign-key relationships: The schema should enforce relationships between queries, documents, embeddings_index, and session_state to preserve referential integrity.
  • Indexes: Frequently queried fields such as session_id, query_type, document_id, chunk_id, and created_at should be indexed to keep lookup latency low.

docs.title: Interaction with Ask AI
docs.text:
When a user initiates an Ask AI inquiry, the application performs a lightweight, stateless lookup:

  1. The prompt is logged to the queries table with a type='ask_ai' flag.
  2. The system checks the session_state table for recent context to maintain conversational continuity.
  3. If a cached response exists for a semantically similar query, it is returned immediately to reduce latency. Exact-match caching may use a content hash, while approximate caching may use vector proximity.
  4. Otherwise, the query is routed to the embedding pipeline, and the resulting context is assembled for the generative LLM.

Ask AI is optimized for fast, single-turn or lightly contextual responses. It may use recent conversation history, but it does not require the durable multi-step state machine used by Deep Dive.

docs.title: Interaction with Deep Dive
docs.text:
Deep Dive inquiries require stateful, multi-step research tracking:

  1. The initial prompt creates a new session_id in session_state.
  2. As the AI iterates through sub-queries, each intermediate finding, source citation, and reasoning step is persisted to ship_computer.db.
  3. The database acts as a checkpoint system: if the application restarts or a step fails, Deep Dive resumes from the last committed state rather than re-executing completed research branches.
  4. Final synthesized reports are linked back to the original queries record, enabling auditability and reproducibility.

Deep Dive treats ship_computer.db as a durable workflow store. It records not only the final answer, but also the research path that produced the answer.

docs.title: Ask AI vs Deep Dive State Management
docs.text:
Workflow State Model Persistence Focus Recovery Behavior Ask AI Stateless or lightly stateful Query log, optional cache, recent context Re-executes the request if needed Deep Dive Stateful and resumable Session state, sub-queries, citations, checkpoints, final report Resumes from last committed step

Ask AI prioritizes low latency and simple retrieval. Deep Dive prioritizes completeness, traceability, and fault tolerance.

docs.title: Embedding LLM and Vector Database Workflow
docs.text: Spock separates text representation from text generation by utilizing a dedicated embedding model alongside a vector storage layer. This architecture enables efficient semantic retrieval before any generative processing occurs.

docs.title: Embedding Model Role
docs.text:
The embedding LLM, more precisely an embedding model, converts unstructured text into fixed-length numerical vectors. Unlike generative models, it does not produce natural language output. Its sole responsibility is to map documents, logs, and user queries into a shared mathematical space where semantic similarity correlates with geometric proximity.

In Spock, the embedding model is used for two main purposes:

  • Document embedding: Converts ingested wiki pages, ship logs, and research artifacts into searchable vector representations.
  • Query embedding: Converts user prompts into vectors that can be compared against stored document vectors.

The embedding model should be stable and versioned. If the model changes, existing vectors may no longer be comparable to newly generated vectors, so Spock should track model version in embeddings_index and re-embed affected content when necessary.

docs.title: Vector Database Integration
docs.text:
Spock leverages a vector database to store and query embeddings. This may be implemented through a SQLite extension such as sqlite-vec, or through a lightweight standalone vector index that is referenced from ship_computer.db.

  • Indexing Strategy: Vectors are organized using Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) algorithms such as HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) or IVF (Inverted File Index). This allows low-latency retrieval across large chunk collections without exhaustive linear scans.
  • Distance Metric: Cosine similarity or L2 Euclidean distance is used to rank relevance. Higher scores indicate stronger semantic alignment between the user query and stored knowledge.
  • Chunking & Metadata Filtering: Before embedding, documents are split into logical chunks, such as paragraphs, code blocks, or log entries. Each chunk retains metadata tags that allow the vector DB to apply hybrid filtering, such as restricting results to a specific ship log date range or wiki category.

docs.title: Embedding LLM and Vector Database Relationship
docs.text:
The embedding model and vector database work together as a semantic retrieval layer.

  1. Ingestion: Spock reads a document, splits it into chunks, and sends each chunk to the embedding model.
  2. Vector storage: The resulting vectors are stored in the vector database, while chunk metadata is stored in ship_computer.db.
  3. Query time: Spock embeds the user’s question using the same embedding model.
  4. Semantic search: The vector database finds the nearest stored vectors.
  5. Metadata join: Spock uses ship_computer.db to resolve vector identifiers back to document chunks, sources, citations, and metadata.

This separation allows Spock to keep relational data, session state, and vector search in distinct but coordinated layers.

docs.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) Pipeline
docs.text:
1. Query Embedding: The user’s prompt is passed through the embedding model to generate a query vector.
  2. Vector Search: The vector DB retrieves the top-K most relevant document chunks based on similarity scoring.
  3. Context Assembly: Retrieved chunks are concatenated with system prompts, conversation history, and routing instructions.
  4. Generative Inference: The assembled context is fed to the primary LLM, which synthesizes a response grounded in the retrieved data.
  5. Caching & Feedback: Successful retrievals and responses are optionally logged back to ship_computer.db to improve future latency and enable query optimization.

docs.title: Ingestion and Query Path
docs.text:
The full Spock retrieval path can be summarized as follows:

Ingestion path

  1. Source document is registered in documents.
  2. Document is chunked into logical units.
  3. Each chunk is embedded by the embedding model.
  4. Vector identifiers, dimensions, and model version are recorded in embeddings_index.
  5. Chunk metadata, such as source path, date range, category, and content hash, is stored in SQLite.

Query path

  1. User prompt is recorded in queries.
  2. Prompt is embedded using the same embedding model used for ingestion.
  3. Vector database performs ANN search over stored chunk vectors.
  4. Results are filtered using metadata from ship_computer.db.
  5. Relevant chunks are assembled into a prompt context.
  6. Generative LLM produces the final answer.
  7. For Deep Dive, intermediate steps and final report are persisted for auditability and resumability.

This separation of concerns ensures that Spock maintains low memory overhead, scales efficiently with growing knowledge bases, and provides traceable, source-grounded answers for both quick inquiries and complex research tasks.

docs.title: Filter note
docs.text:
Markers under skipped trees (data/, models/, … from .gitignore / scan.skip_dirs) are omitted so large vendored artifacts—such as llama.cpp model blobs—do not dominate the report.

Why the filter matters: Large binary or generated directories (for example, data/ and models/, which may contain llama.cpp files) can produce many false-positive marker hits from embedded, generated, or third-party code. Excluding them keeps the concerns list focused on first-party source code.

• Paths use Windows-style backslashes because they were captured on that platform; they are equivalent to forward-slash repository paths.
  • [TODO] strings inside spock_codebase_knowledge may be template placeholders, not real work items.
  • Duplicate lines can appear when the scanner reports multiple matching patterns or repeated section output; treat them as evidence of a reporting artifact unless confirmed in source.
  • The final line in the original excerpt appears truncated and should not be interpreted as a complete marker hit.

docs.title: SQLite 3 ship_computer.db
docs.text: ship_computer.db is the SQLite 3 database used by the Spock application to store structured, queryable application state. It is the relational backbone for the knowledge base, scan results, user queries, and response metadata. It works alongside the vector database, which stores high-dimensional embeddings for semantic search.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The database provides a durable, local, transactional store for data that must be filtered, joined, audited, or cited. It is especially useful for:

  • Storing source-file metadata and scan evidence.
  • Tracking TODO, FIXME, and HACK markers.
  • Recording Ask AI and Deep Dive sessions.
  • Linking generated answers back to specific chunks, files, and scan runs.
  • Preserving citation and provenance information.

docs.title: Relationship to the vector database
docs.text:
The vector database stores embeddings, while ship_computer.db stores the relational context around those embeddings.

For example:

  • The vector database can return a vector ID or chunk ID for a semantically similar passage.
  • Spock then uses that ID to query ship_computer.db for the file path, line range, document title, scan run, and related markers.
  • This allows Spock to combine semantic relevance with precise, citable source information.

docs.title: Typical data stored in ship_computer.db
docs.text:
A representative schema may include tables such as:

Table Purpose documents Stores one row per scanned file or document. chunks Stores text chunks derived from documents. markers Stores TODO, FIXME, HACK, and other code markers. scan_runs Stores metadata about each scan execution. ask_ai_queries Stores user questions submitted through Ask AI. deep_dive_sessions Stores Deep Dive investigation sessions. deep_dive_steps Stores intermediate retrieval and reasoning steps. citations Stores evidence used to support an answer. embeddings_meta Stores metadata linking chunks to vector records.

docs.title: Ask AI interaction
docs.text:
When a user submits an Ask AI question, Spock uses ship_computer.db in several ways:

  1. Query recording

  2. Spock stores the user’s question, timestamp, and session context.

  3. Filter extraction

  4. Spock may extract filters such as file path, package name, marker type, or scan run.

  5. Candidate retrieval

  6. Spock queries the database for relevant documents, chunks, and markers.

  7. Vector search coordination

  8. Spock sends the question to the embedding model and searches the vector database.

  9. The vector database returns candidate chunk IDs or vector IDs.

  10. Context enrichment

  11. Spock joins the returned IDs back to ship_computer.db to retrieve:

    • File path
    • Line numbers
    • Chunk text
    • Related markers
    • Scan metadata

  12. Answer generation

  13. Spock builds a prompt using the retrieved context.

  14. The language model generates the answer.

  15. Citation storage

  16. Spock stores the answer and the evidence used to produce it.

docs.title: Deep Dive interaction
docs.text:
Deep Dive is a more investigative mode. It may require multiple retrieval passes and broader context than a single Ask AI response.

ship_computer.db supports Deep Dive by:

  • Creating a session record for the investigation.
  • Storing each sub-question or retrieval step.
  • Tracking which chunks, files, and markers were considered.
  • Preserving the order of evidence discovery.
  • Linking final conclusions back to specific source records.

A typical Deep Dive flow is:

  1. User asks a complex question.
  2. Spock creates a Deep Dive session.
  3. Spock decomposes the question into sub-questions.
  4. For each sub-question:
  5. Spock performs relational queries against ship_computer.db.
  6. Spock performs semantic search using the vector database.
  7. Spock merges and reranks results.
  8. Spock accumulates evidence across steps.
  9. Spock generates a detailed answer with citations.
  10. Spock stores the final session, steps, and citations.

docs.title: Why SQLite 3 is used
docs.text:
SQLite 3 is well suited to this role because it is:

  • Local and file-based.
  • Easy to deploy without a separate database server.
  • Transactional.
  • Well suited to metadata, audit logs, and citation tracking.
  • Compatible with Python’s standard sqlite3 module.

It is not intended to replace the vector database. Instead, it provides the structured context needed to make vector search results useful, traceable, and citable.

docs.title: Embedding LLM and vector database
docs.text: The Spock application uses an embedding model—referred to in this architecture as the embedding LLM—to convert text into numerical vectors. These vectors are stored in a vector database and used to find semantically similar content.

docs.title: What the embedding LLM does
docs.text:
The embedding LLM does not generate natural-language answers. Its role is to encode text into a fixed-size numerical representation.

For example:

  • A source-code chunk is converted into a vector.
  • A user question is converted into a vector.
  • Similar meanings produce vectors that are close together in vector space.

This allows Spock to search for relevant content even when the user’s wording does not exactly match the source text.

docs.title: How embeddings are created
docs.text:
During indexing, Spock typically:

  1. Reads source files or documents.
  2. Splits them into chunks.
  3. Sends each chunk to the embedding model.
  4. Receives a vector for each chunk.
  5. Stores the vector in the vector database.
  6. Stores metadata about the chunk in ship_computer.db.

The metadata may include:

  • Chunk ID
  • File path
  • Line range
  • Document title
  • Scan run ID
  • Embedding model name
  • Vector dimension

docs.title: How the vector database is used
docs.text:
The vector database stores embeddings and supports similarity search. It may be implemented using a dedicated vector store or a SQLite-compatible vector extension.

When Spock needs to answer a question, it:

  1. Embeds the user’s question using the same embedding model used during indexing.
  2. Searches the vector database for the closest vectors.
  3. Retrieves the top matching chunks.
  4. Uses those chunks as context for answer generation.

docs.title: Ask AI using the embedding LLM and vector database
docs.text:
For Ask AI, the flow is:

  1. User submits a question.
  2. Spock embeds the question.
  3. Spock queries the vector database for similar chunks.
  4. Spock retrieves the corresponding records from ship_computer.db.
  5. Spock builds a prompt containing:
  6. The user’s question
  7. Relevant source chunks
  8. File and line metadata
  9. Related markers, if present
  10. The language model generates an answer.
  11. Spock stores the answer and citations.

This allows Ask AI to answer questions using both semantic relevance and precise source context.

docs.title: Deep Dive using the embedding LLM and vector database
docs.text:
Deep Dive uses the same embedding and vector search mechanism, but over multiple steps.

For each Deep Dive step:

  1. Spock generates or refines a sub-question.
  2. Spock embeds the sub-question.
  3. Spock searches the vector database.
  4. Spock retrieves related records from ship_computer.db.
  5. Spock may expand the search using:
  6. Related files
  7. Related chunks
  8. Related markers
  9. Nearby code sections
  10. Spock reranks the evidence.
  11. Spock continues until enough context is gathered.
  12. Spock produces a detailed, cited answer.

docs.title: Why both stores are needed
docs.text:
The vector database provides semantic search, while ship_computer.db provides structured context.

Together they allow Spock to:

  • Find relevant content by meaning.
  • Retrieve exact file and line information.
  • Preserve citations.
  • Support multi-step Deep Dive investigations.
  • Keep answers grounded in the scanned codebase.

docs.title: SQLite 3 Database (ship_computer.db) Integration
docs.text: The ship_computer.db file is a SQLite 3 relational database that serves as the structured knowledge backbone for the Spock application. It stores normalized metadata, scan artifacts, codebase topology, and cached inference results. Unlike raw file scans, this database provides fast, indexed, and transaction-safe access to project intelligence, enabling Spock to route queries efficiently based on intent.

docs.title: Database Schema and Responsibilities
docs.text:
The database is organized around stable identifiers and normalized relationships. A typical schema includes:

Table Purpose files Stores file-level metadata such as path, hash, language, size, last modified time, branch, and commit. modules Stores logical module or package information, including name, path, owner, description, and dependency relationships. dependencies Stores directed relationships between files, modules, functions, or packages, including dependency type and confidence. scan_results Stores security, quality, or architecture scan findings, including severity, rule, line range, commit, and timestamp. query_cache Stores cached Ask AI responses, query hashes, context snapshots, model identifiers, and expiration metadata. sessions Stores Deep Dive session state, including user, mode, creation time, and last active time. annotations Stores user-created notes, highlights, and navigation state tied to files, line ranges, or modules. embeddings_metadata Stores chunk identifiers, file paths, line ranges, embedding model, and pointers to the corresponding vector records in the vector database.

This design keeps ship_computer.db focused on exact, queryable facts. The vector database stores high-dimensional embeddings, while SQLite stores the metadata needed to interpret, filter, cite, and cache those results.

docs.title: Interaction with "Ask AI" Inquiries
docs.text:
When a user submits an Ask AI query, Spock treats the request as a semantic or factual question about the codebase. The workflow leverages ship_computer.db as follows:

  1. Context Retrieval: Spock executes parameterized SQL queries against indexed tables (e.g., files, modules, dependencies, scan_results) to fetch relevant documentation, recent changes, and architectural summaries.
  2. Prompt Grounding: Retrieved rows are serialized into a structured context window. The database ensures that only verified, first-party metadata is injected, reducing hallucination risk.
  3. Response Caching: Once the LLM generates a response, Spock stores the query hash, context snapshot, and final answer in a query_cache table. Subsequent identical or highly similar queries are served directly from SQLite, bypassing redundant LLM calls and reducing latency.

In practice, Ask AI may combine SQLite context with vector search. SQLite provides the authoritative project facts, while the vector database helps Spock find semantically relevant code or documentation when the user's wording does not match exact identifiers.

docs.title: Interaction with "Deep Dive" Inquiries
docs.text:
Deep Dive requests require granular, relational analysis rather than broad semantic matching. Spock uses ship_computer.db to:

  1. Traverse Dependency Graphs: Complex JOIN queries and recursive common table expressions map module relationships, import chains, and function call hierarchies stored in normalized adjacency tables.
  2. Filter by Metadata: Users can constrain deep dives by commit hash, author, file type, or scan severity. SQLite’s WHERE and GROUP BY clauses efficiently filter large result sets without loading them into memory.
  3. State Persistence: Deep Dive sessions maintain temporary working tables that track user navigation paths, highlighted code regions, and custom annotations. These are committed to ship_computer.db to preserve session continuity across application restarts.

Because Deep Dive is relationship-heavy, SQLite’s transactional integrity ensures that partial updates do not corrupt the working graph. This makes it suitable for exploratory workflows where users repeatedly refine filters, expand dependency paths, and annotate code regions.

docs.title: Ask AI vs. Deep Dive: Retrieval Strategy
docs.text:
• Ask AI favors semantic retrieval and cached answers. It may use vector search first, then SQLite for grounding, validation, and citation.
  • Deep Dive favors relational traversal and exact metadata. It may use SQLite first, then vector search to explain relationships or locate conceptually related code.

docs.title: Embedding LLM and Vector Database Workflow
docs.text: While ship_computer.db handles structured, exact-match, and relational queries, the Spock application relies on an embedding LLM and a vector database to power semantic understanding and fuzzy code retrieval. This hybrid architecture ensures that both precise structural data and conceptual meaning are accessible.

docs.title: Role of the Embedding LLM
docs.text:
The embedding LLM is not the same as the primary answer-generating LLM. Its purpose is to convert text, code, comments, documentation, and scan summaries into numerical vectors. Each vector represents the meaning of a chunk in a high-dimensional space. Similar concepts produce vectors that are close together, while unrelated concepts are farther apart.

This allows Spock to answer questions such as "Where is the retry logic for failed API calls?" even when the user's wording does not match the code identifiers exactly. The embedding model provides the semantic bridge between natural language questions and codebase content.

docs.title: Embedding Generation Pipeline
docs.text:
1. Chunking & Preprocessing: Source files, documentation, and scan outputs are split into semantic chunks (typically 256–512 tokens). Headers, docstrings, and comments are preserved to maintain context.
  2. Vectorization: The embedding LLM converts each chunk into a high-dimensional vector (e.g., 768 or 1536 dimensions). These vectors capture syntactic patterns, semantic intent, and code semantics.
  3. Indexing: Vectors are stored in the vector database alongside metadata pointers (file path, line range, chunk ID). The database builds an approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) index (e.g., HNSW or IVF) to enable low-latency similarity searches.

docs.title: Vector Database Responsibilities
docs.text:
The vector database is responsible for storing and searching embeddings. It typically stores:

  • The embedding vector for each chunk.
  • A stable chunk identifier.
  • Metadata such as file path, line range, language, commit, and scan severity.
  • An ANN index that supports fast similarity search.

During retrieval, Spock embeds the user's question using the same embedding model and asks the vector database for the nearest neighbors. The vector database returns candidate chunks ranked by similarity, often using cosine distance or dot product. Spock then uses ship_computer.db to validate metadata, apply filters, deduplicate results, and attach citations.

docs.title: Query Routing & Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
docs.text:
When Spock receives a natural language prompt, it determines whether to route the request through the relational database, the vector store, or both:

  • Semantic Routing: The query itself is embedded and compared against a lightweight intent classifier. Conceptual questions ("How does authentication work?") trigger vector search, while structural questions ("List all imports in auth.py") trigger SQLite queries.
  • Hybrid Retrieval: For complex prompts, Spock executes parallel lookups. Vector search returns semantically relevant code snippets, while ship_computer.db supplies exact file paths, version history, and dependency constraints.
  • Context Assembly: Retrieved vectors and relational rows are merged, deduplicated, and ranked by relevance score. The final context window is formatted into a system prompt that includes explicit instructions, code boundaries, and citation markers.
  • Inference & Feedback Loop: The primary LLM generates the response. If the user marks the answer as helpful or requests clarification, Spock logs the interaction in ship_computer.db and optionally adjusts retrieval parameters, re-embeds affected chunks, or updates ranking heuristics for improved future retrieval.

This dual-storage approach ensures Spock delivers accurate, traceable, and context-aware responses while maintaining performance at scale.

docs.title: Explanation of Terms
docs.text:
• Deterministic: The concerns listed above are generated automatically by the spock_codebase_knowledge scan pipeline. No manual curation is applied; given an identical repository state, filter configuration, and environment settings, the pipeline produces reproducible output.
  • Filtered scan: The scan process excludes file paths defined in .gitignore, scan.skip_dirs, and built-in exclusion patterns (e.g., .venv, node_modules, __pycache__). Only files residing outside these excluded directories are processed for analysis.
  • High-churn files: Files ranked by the frequency of Git commits that modified them within the scanned history. A higher commit count indicates frequent modification, which may signal active development, architectural instability, or a need for architectural review.
  • [TODO] placeholders in the raw excerpt: These are literal string values emitted by populate.py when the scan cannot resolve specific metadata (e.g., missing README.md or undetected test frameworks). They serve as template fallbacks for the documentation generator and do not represent actionable TODO comments within the source code.
  • TODO_LIMIT: A configuration constant in scan.py that caps the number of TODO/FIXME/HACK annotations reported per scan (currently set to 60). This prevents a single noisy file from disproportionately dominating the analysis output.

docs.title: SQLite 3 ship_computer.db Architecture & Query Routing
docs.text: The ship_computer.db file serves as the primary relational storage layer for the Spock application. Built on SQLite 3, it provides structured, ACID-compliant persistence for scan artifacts, metadata indexes, and query routing logic. Its design complements the unstructured vector storage by handling deterministic lookups, relationship mapping, and state management.

docs.title: Schema & Data Organization
docs.text: The database is partitioned into logical tables that track: - File Metadata: Absolute paths, file types, line counts, and last-modified timestamps. - Scan Artifacts: Parsed AST nodes, dependency graphs, linting results, and architectural concerns. - Query History & Caching: Cached responses, user prompts, and execution timestamps to enable session continuity and reduce redundant LLM calls. - Routing Flags: Boolean and categorical markers that determine whether a query should be routed to the relational engine, the vector engine, or a hybrid pipeline.

docs.title: Interaction with "Ask AI" Inquiries
docs.text: When a user submits an "Ask AI" prompt, Spock first queries ship_computer.db to establish baseline context: 1. Intent Classification: The prompt is parsed for keywords and structural markers. The database checks routing flags to determine if the query requires code-level precision or high-level architectural reasoning. 2. Relational Context Retrieval: If the query references specific modules, functions, or configuration files, Spock executes targeted SELECT statements to fetch exact file paths, version history, and associated metadata. 3. Prompt Assembly: Retrieved relational data is formatted into a structured context block. This ensures the LLM receives precise, verifiable references rather than relying solely on semantic approximation.

docs.title: Interaction with "Deep Dive" Inquiries
docs.text: "Deep Dive" requests require multi-hop reasoning across codebases, dependencies, and historical changes. ship_computer.db facilitates this through: 1. Graph Traversal: The database stores adjacency lists for import/export relationships and function call chains. Spock executes recursive CTEs (Common Table Expressions) to map dependency trees up to a configurable depth. 2. Temporal Analysis: Commit metadata and churn metrics are joined with file paths to surface historically volatile or frequently refactored components. 3. Hybrid Routing: For complex architectural questions, Spock uses the relational layer to filter the vector search space. For example, it may restrict vector retrieval to files modified in the last 30 days or belonging to a specific service tier, drastically reducing noise and improving response accuracy.

docs.title: Embedding LLM & Vector Database Integration
docs.text: While ship_computer.db handles structured data, Spock leverages an embedding LLM and a dedicated vector database to process unstructured code, documentation, and natural language queries. This integration powers semantic search and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) workflows.

docs.title: Embedding Generation Pipeline
docs.text:
1. Chunking Strategy: Source files and documentation are split into semantic chunks, typically 500–1000 tokens, with overlapping windows to preserve context across function boundaries, class definitions, and Markdown sections. Chunk boundaries, line ranges, and content hashes are recorded in ship_computer.db so that retrieval results can be traced back to their source files.
  2. Vectorization: Each chunk is passed through a code-aware embedding model optimized for source code and technical documentation. The model outputs a fixed-dimensional vector, such as 768 or 1536 dimensions, that captures syntactic and semantic relationships. The same embedding model is used for both corpus chunks and user queries so that similarity comparisons remain consistent.
  3. Metadata Tagging: Every vector is paired with relational metadata, including file path, language, commit hash, scan timestamp, chunk ID, and vector ID, before ingestion. This metadata enables hybrid filtering, permission checks, and deterministic retrieval constraints during query time.

docs.title: Vector Database Storage & Indexing
docs.text: The vector database stores embeddings in an optimized index structure, such as HNSW or IVF-PQ, that supports approximate nearest-neighbor search with low latency. Key characteristics include: - Dynamic Indexing: New scan results are batched and upserted asynchronously to prevent blocking the main application thread. - Namespace Partitioning: Vectors are partitioned by repository, branch, or service tier to isolate search scopes and prevent cross-context contamination. - TTL & Eviction: Stale embeddings are automatically purged or re-embedded when underlying files are modified, ensuring the vector space reflects the current repository state. ship_computer.db tracks file hashes, scan status, and chunk validity to determine when embeddings should be invalidated or refreshed.

docs.title: RAG Workflow for Ask AI & Deep Dive
docs.text:
When a query reaches the vector layer, Spock executes the following sequence: 1. Query Embedding: The user's prompt is transformed into a vector using the same embedding model applied to the corpus. 2. Similarity Search: The vector database performs a cosine similarity or inner-product search against the indexed corpus. Top-K results are returned based on a configurable relevance threshold. 3. Metadata Filtering & Re-ranking: Results are cross-referenced with ship_computer.db to apply hard filters, such as excluding test files, generated code, secrets, or unauthorized repositories. A lightweight cross-encoder or LLM-based re-ranker may then be applied to refine relevance. 4. Context Injection: The highest-scoring chunks are concatenated into a structured prompt template. The embedding LLM is not used for generation; it strictly handles representation. The primary generative LLM receives the enriched context and produces the final response. 5. Feedback Loop: User interactions, retrieved chunk IDs, response latency, and accuracy metrics are logged to ship_computer.db, enabling continuous tuning of chunking strategies, similarity thresholds, and routing heuristics.

This dual-layer architecture ensures Spock balances deterministic precision, via SQLite, with semantic flexibility, via embeddings, delivering accurate, context-aware responses for both straightforward inquiries and complex architectural deep dives.

docs.title: SQLite 3 ship_computer.db Integration
docs.text:
ship_computer.db is the structured, relational foundation of the Spock application. It is a SQLite 3 database that stores deterministic state, metadata, permissions, scan history, query logs, and feedback data. Unlike the vector database, which is optimized for semantic similarity, ship_computer.db is optimized for exact lookups, joins, filtering, transactional consistency, and auditability.

In this architecture, SQLite 3 serves as the system of record for the following concerns:

  • Repository and scan state: Which repositories have been scanned, which branches were analyzed, and when the last successful scan occurred.
  • File inventory: File paths, languages, sizes, content hashes, modification timestamps, and classification flags such as test, generated, documentation, or production code.
  • Chunk metadata: Stable chunk identifiers, line ranges, token counts, content hashes, embedding model versions, and references to the corresponding vector IDs.
  • Query history: Ask AI and Deep Dive prompts, retrieved chunk IDs, response metadata, latency, and user feedback.
  • Configuration and routing rules: Thresholds, allowed file types, excluded paths, repository scopes, and feature flags.
  • Maintenance state: Embedding invalidation, re-embedding queues, failed scans, and data freshness indicators.

A typical ship_computer.db schema may include tables such as:

  • repositories: repository identifiers, remote URLs, default branches, and ownership metadata.
  • scans: scan runs, commit hashes, start and completion timestamps, status, and error details.
  • files: file paths, language, size, content hash, classification flags, and last-modified timestamps.
  • chunks: chunk IDs, file references, line ranges, token counts, content hashes, and vector IDs.
  • query_logs: session IDs, user IDs, query mode, prompt text, retrieved chunk IDs, response IDs, and latency.
  • feedback: user ratings, comments, and correction signals tied to specific query logs.
  • settings: application configuration, retrieval thresholds, and routing preferences.
  • permissions: repository, branch, or file-level access controls used to constrain retrieval.

docs.title: How ship_computer.db Supports Ask AI
docs.text:
Ask AI is designed for fast, scoped, and contextually grounded answers. When a user submits an Ask AI prompt, Spock uses ship_computer.db to establish the deterministic boundaries of the search before any semantic retrieval occurs.

The interaction typically follows this flow:

  1. Scope Resolution Spock resolves the active repository, branch, service tier, and user permissions from ship_computer.db. This ensures that the vector search is limited to the correct codebase and that the user cannot retrieve content they are not authorized to access.

  2. Filter Construction SQLite provides structured filters such as:

  3. Include production code and exclude test files.
  4. Exclude generated files, vendored dependencies, or secrets.
  5. Prioritize recently modified files.

  6. Restrict results to a specific module, directory, or language.

  7. Vector Retrieval The embedding model converts the user prompt into a vector, and the vector database returns semantically similar chunks.

  8. Metadata Joining Spock joins the returned vector IDs back to ship_computer.db to retrieve file paths, chunk line ranges, commit hashes, and classification flags. This step converts raw semantic matches into auditable, repository-aware results.

  9. Context Assembly Only chunks that pass the SQLite-defined filters are included in the prompt sent to the generative LLM. This prevents the model from answering based on irrelevant, stale, or unauthorized content.

  10. Logging and Feedback The prompt, retrieved chunk IDs, response metadata, and user feedback are written back to ship_computer.db. This creates a durable audit trail and supports future tuning of retrieval behavior.

For Ask AI, SQLite provides precision and control, while the vector database provides semantic recall. The result is a response that is both contextually relevant and constrained to the correct repository state.

docs.title: How ship_computer.db Supports Deep Dive
docs.text:
Deep Dive is intended for more complex architectural analysis, such as understanding a subsystem, tracing dependencies, comparing implementation patterns, or explaining how multiple modules interact. In this mode, Spock relies more heavily on ship_computer.db because the query often requires structured traversal, not just semantic similarity.

The interaction typically includes:

  1. Initial Semantic Retrieval Spock begins with an embedding-based search to identify the most relevant chunks, files, and modules.

  2. Structured Expansion Using ship_computer.db, Spock expands the initial result set by following relational relationships, such as:

  3. Files that import or reference the matched file.
  4. Other chunks in the same module or package.
  5. Documentation files associated with the same component.
  6. Recent changes to the same file or directory.

  7. Related configuration, tests, or interface definitions.

  8. Hybrid Search For Deep Dive queries that include exact identifiers, function names, class names, or error strings, Spock may combine vector search with SQLite full-text search, such as FTS5. This allows the application to match both semantic intent and exact code symbols.

  9. Iterative Context Building Deep Dive may perform multiple retrieval passes. Each pass can use the previous results to refine the next query. ship_computer.db stores intermediate state, including visited files, candidate chunks, excluded paths, and retrieval steps, so the process remains reproducible and debuggable.

  10. Architecture-Aware Ranking SQLite metadata can be used to boost or suppress results based on architectural relevance. For example, Spock may prioritize:

  11. Public API surfaces.
  12. Core service files.
  13. Recently changed modules.
  14. Files with high coupling or dependency significance.

  15. Documentation that explicitly describes the subsystem.

  16. Response Grounding The final Deep Dive response is grounded in a larger, more structured context than Ask AI. SQLite ensures that the context is not only semantically relevant but also consistent with the repository structure, permissions, and current scan state.

  17. Auditability Because Deep Dive can involve multiple retrieval steps, ship_computer.db records the sequence of queries, retrieved chunks, filters applied, and final response. This is especially useful for debugging why a particular architectural explanation was produced.

docs.title: Relationship Between SQLite and the Vector Database
docs.text:
The SQLite database and vector database are complementary rather than redundant.

Concern ship_computer.db Vector Database Primary purpose Structured metadata, permissions, state, and audit logs Semantic similarity search Query style Exact matches, joins, filters, and transactions Approximate nearest-neighbor search Data type Relational rows, hashes, timestamps, flags High-dimensional embeddings Strength Deterministic, auditable, and precise Flexible, semantic, and cross-language Weakness if used alone Cannot infer meaning from natural language Cannot enforce exact repository constraints

In practice, Spock uses the vector database to find semantically relevant content and ship_computer.db to validate, filter, enrich, and log that content. This separation allows the application to answer natural language questions while still respecting the deterministic structure of the codebase.

docs.title: Maintenance and Data Freshness
docs.text:
ship_computer.db also plays a central role in keeping the vector index accurate over time.

When Spock detects that a file has changed, it can:

  • Compare the new content hash against the stored hash.
  • Mark affected chunks as stale.
  • Invalidate or delete the corresponding vector IDs.
  • Queue the changed file for re-chunking and re-embedding.
  • Record the scan result and update the repository state.

This ensures that Ask AI and Deep Dive do not rely on outdated code, documentation, or architecture descriptions. It also allows Spock to maintain a clear history of when each chunk was embedded, which embedding model was used, and whether the underlying source file has changed since the last scan.

docs.title: Observed conventions
docs.text:
• Python packages use PascalCase or snake_case directory names and include an __init__.py file.
  • Wiki agent skills are implemented as methods on the Skills class and validated through WarpCore.skills.
  • Prefer spock_shell.paths for resolving ROOT and database paths rather than hard-coding path values.
  • [TODO] The scan did not detect a root-level ruff, black, or flake8 configuration file.

docs.title: Conventions explained
docs.text:
• A Python package directory is an explicit directory that contains __init__.py; the observed convention allows either PascalCase or snake_case naming for such directories.
  • The Skills / WarpCore.skills convention describes how agent capabilities are exposed as callable methods and validated through the WarpCore.skills registry.
  • Using spock_shell.paths centralizes path resolution, which helps keep ROOT and database path handling consistent across environments and prevents path-related runtime errors.
  • The TODO item records a scan finding about missing linting/formatting configuration; it is not itself a confirmed project rule.

docs.title: Error handling
docs.text:
• Skills return SkillResult(ok, evidence, log_lines) instead of raising exceptions into the queue loop.
  • GUI long-running work uses a wait cursor and a busy QProgressBar via spock_shell.busy_ui.

docs.title: Error handling explained
docs.text:
• SkillResult is a structured result object that reports whether a skill succeeded (ok), provides supporting evidence, and includes relevant log lines. By returning this value instead of raising exceptions, the queue loop can record failures, continue processing subsequent items, and avoid unhandled exception crashes.
  • The GUI pattern communicates that long operations are in progress by showing a wait cursor or busy progress indicator. spock_shell.busy_ui centralizes this behavior so user-facing code does not need to manage Qt cursor and progress-bar state manually.

docs.title: Raw scan excerpt
docs.text: No linting or formatting config files found in project root.

docs.title: Evidence

docs.title: Database Overview and Schema
docs.text:
ship_computer.db is the SQLite 3 database that provides persistent state for the Spock application. It is the system of record for application metadata, query history, session context, skill state, and references to external knowledge assets such as document chunks and vector-store identifiers.

The database is optimized for read-heavy workloads and uses SQLite's ACID behavior to keep state consistent while multiple skills or background jobs may read and write data. It does not replace the vector database; instead, it stores the metadata needed to locate, validate, cache, and audit the data used by Ask AI and Deep Dive.

Core tables include:

  • documents: Stores metadata about ingested files, including file path, content hash, source type, ingestion timestamp, and processing status.
  • embeddings_index: Maps document chunks to vector-store identifiers, chunk text or chunk references, embedding model version, and retrieval metadata.
  • query_log: Records user prompts, skill invocations, routing decisions, response summaries, latency, token usage, and retrieval metrics for auditing and analytics.
  • sessions: Tracks active conversation contexts, user preferences, temporary state, and multi-turn interaction history.
  • skills_registry: Maintains skill configuration, availability status, dependency information, and version metadata for agent skills.

docs.title: Interaction with Ask AI Inquiries
docs.text:
When a user submits an "Ask AI" inquiry, the Spock application treats the request as a lightweight retrieval-augmented generation task. The skill first resolves the database path through spock_shell.paths, then checks ship_computer.db for cached responses, recent session context, or previously resolved intents.

If a sufficiently similar cached response exists, the application may return the cached result to reduce latency and avoid unnecessary LLM calls. If no cache exists, the application embeds the user prompt using the embedding LLM, searches the vector database for relevant chunks, and retrieves the associated document metadata from ship_computer.db.

The raw prompt, timestamp, routing decision, retrieved chunk identifiers, and final response summary are written to query_log. If the request is part of a multi-turn conversation, the relevant context is also stored in sessions. The final answer and supporting citations are returned to the user through a SkillResult, with evidence and log lines available for inspection.

docs.title: Interaction with Deep Dive Inquiries
docs.text:
"Deep Dive" requests trigger a more intensive retrieval-augmented generation workflow. The application uses ship_computer.db to identify high-relevance document clusters and to apply metadata filters such as date ranges, source credibility, topic tags, document type, and ingestion status.

The database returns structured pointers to the vector store, including chunk identifiers, vector-store IDs, and metadata needed to fetch dense vector representations or precomputed chunk text. The Spock application then performs one or more vector searches, reranks candidates, and may issue follow-up embeddings to explore related concepts.

Throughout the Deep Dive process, intermediate reasoning steps, retrieved context chunks, confidence scores, filter selections, and final evidence chains are persisted in ship_computer.db. This allows the application to produce transparent, traceable outputs and lets users review the evidence that supported the final answer. Because Deep Dive can be long-running, the GUI uses spock_shell.busy_ui to show a wait cursor or busy progress indicator while the skill executes.

docs.title: Ask AI and Deep Dive Data Flow
docs.text:
1. The user submits an Ask AI or Deep Dive request through the Spock GUI or shell.
  2. The request is routed to the appropriate skill method on the Skills class.
  3. The skill validates its configuration through WarpCore.skills and resolves the database and vector-store paths using spock_shell.paths.
  4. The skill reads sessions and query_log to determine whether cached context or prior results are available.
  5. The user prompt is converted into an embedding by the embedding LLM.
  6. The vector database is searched for the most relevant chunks.
  7. ship_computer.db is used to resolve chunk metadata, document provenance, and citation information.
  8. The generative LLM produces an answer using the retrieved context.
  9. The response, evidence, metrics, and log lines are written back to ship_computer.db.
  10. The skill returns a SkillResult containing success status, evidence, and diagnostic log lines.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The embedding LLM and vector database provide semantic search for the Spock application. The embedding LLM converts text into numerical vectors that represent meaning. The vector database stores those vectors and supports similarity search, allowing the application to find relevant document chunks even when the user's wording differs from the source text.

This layer is separate from the generative LLM that writes the final answer. The embedding LLM is used for retrieval; the generative LLM is used for synthesis.

docs.title: Ingestion Pipeline
docs.text:
When documents are added to the Spock knowledge base, the application processes them through an ingestion pipeline:

  1. The source file is read and validated.
  2. The document is split into manageable chunks, such as paragraphs, sections, or token-limited blocks.
  3. Each chunk is embedded using the embedding LLM.
  4. The resulting vector is stored in the vector database.
  5. Metadata about the document, chunk, embedding model, and vector-store identifier is written to ship_computer.db.
  6. The documents table records the source file, hash, ingestion timestamp, and processing status.
  7. The embeddings_index table records the mapping between the chunk and its vector-store identifier.

This design keeps the vector database focused on high-dimensional similarity search while ship_computer.db remains the authoritative source for application state, provenance, and audit information.

docs.title: Query Pipeline
docs.text:
When the application needs to answer a question, it uses the following query pipeline:

  1. The user prompt is normalized and embedded using the same embedding LLM used during ingestion.
  2. The query vector is sent to the vector database.
  3. The vector database returns the nearest neighbor chunks, usually a configurable top-k set.
  4. The application retrieves metadata for those chunks from ship_computer.db.
  5. Optional reranking, filtering, or scoring is applied to improve relevance.
  6. The selected chunks are passed to the generative LLM as context.
  7. The generative LLM produces an answer grounded in the retrieved evidence.
  8. The final answer, citations, retrieval metrics, and log lines are returned to the user and recorded in ship_computer.db.

docs.title: How Ask AI Uses the Embedding LLM and Vector Database
docs.text:
Ask AI uses the embedding LLM and vector database for fast, single-pass retrieval. The user prompt is embedded once, the vector database is searched once, and the most relevant chunks are used to generate a concise answer.

Ask AI is optimized for low latency. It may use cached embeddings, cached responses, or session context from ship_computer.db when available. If the vector database returns weak matches, the skill may return a lower-confidence answer, request clarification, or fall back to a generic response depending on the configured policy.

docs.title: How Deep Dive Uses the Embedding LLM and Vector Database
docs.text:
Deep Dive uses the embedding LLM and vector database more aggressively. It may perform multiple retrieval passes, expand the search with related terms, retrieve document clusters, and apply metadata filters from ship_computer.db.

Deep Dive is optimized for completeness and traceability. It may retrieve more chunks than Ask AI, compare confidence scores, and preserve intermediate retrieval results in ship_computer.db. This allows the final answer to include an evidence chain showing which documents, chunks, and metadata filters contributed to the response.

docs.title: Relationship to ship_computer.db
docs.text:
The vector database stores the high-dimensional vectors used for similarity search. ship_computer.db stores the application-level state needed to use those vectors safely and transparently.

In practice, the two systems work together as follows:

  • The vector database answers: "Which chunks are semantically similar to this prompt?"
  • ship_computer.db answers: "What document did this chunk come from, when was it ingested, which embedding model created it, what metadata applies, and what was the user's prior context?"
  • The Spock application combines both results to produce grounded, auditable answers for Ask AI and Deep Dive.

docs.title: Failure and Fallback Behavior
docs.text:
If the embedding LLM is unavailable, the skill should return a SkillResult with ok=False, evidence explaining the failure, and log lines describing the missing dependency or error.

If the vector database is unavailable or returns no results, the application may fall back to cached responses, session context, or a clearly labeled non-grounded answer, depending on the configured policy. In all cases, the failure or fallback is recorded in query_log so the behavior can be audited.

docs.title: Embedding LLM and Vector Database Integration
Embedding Model Workflow
docs.text: Spock uses a dedicated embedding model, separate from the generative LLM, to convert unstructured text into high-dimensional numerical vectors. When new documents or user queries are processed, the text is first chunked, cleaned, and normalized. The embedding model then generates fixed-length vectors that capture semantic meaning rather than simple lexical overlap. These vectors are optimized for cosine similarity or inner-product distance metrics, enabling efficient semantic search across large knowledge bases.

docs.title: Vector Database Retrieval and RAG Pipeline
docs.text: The generated vectors are stored in a vector database optimized for approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search. When an Ask AI or Deep Dive request is initiated, Spock embeds the user's prompt using the same embedding model and queries the vector database for the most contextually relevant document chunks. The retrieved chunks are ranked, filtered by metadata constraints, and supplied to the generative LLM as context. This retrieval-augmented generation pipeline grounds responses in verified, up-to-date information rather than relying solely on the model's pre-training data.

docs.title: Separation of Concerns: Embedding vs. Generative LLM
docs.text: The architecture strictly separates the embedding model from the generative LLM to optimize performance, cost, and accuracy. The embedding model is lightweight, fast, and designed exclusively for vectorization and similarity matching; it does not generate natural language. The generative LLM is responsible for synthesizing coherent, context-aware responses using the retrieved chunks and associated metadata. This division allows Spock to scale retrieval operations independently, update embedding models without disrupting response generation, and maintain clear audit trails for both semantic search and language synthesis stages.

docs.title: SQLite 3 ship_computer.db and Spock Integration
docs.text:
SQLite 3 ship_computer.db serves as Spock's local relational store for operational state, document metadata, retrieval context, and audit information. It is the system of record for what Spock is allowed to use, what has been retrieved, and how each Ask AI or Deep Dive response was produced. The vector database stores high-dimensional vectors for fast semantic search, while ship_computer.db stores the durable, queryable facts that make those search results meaningful and traceable.

Typical responsibilities of ship_computer.db include: - Storing document and chunk records, including source, title, owner, permissions, status, and content hash. - Mapping each chunk to its vector database identifier, embedding model version, and vector status. - Recording user sessions, prompts, retrieved chunk IDs, generated responses, citations, and confidence signals. - Maintaining Deep Dive state, such as active constraints, explored chunks, follow-up questions, and intermediate findings. - Providing transactional consistency, so a chunk is not considered available for retrieval until its metadata and vector reference are committed. - Supporting audit and compliance by preserving the exact context used for each generated answer.

In practice, Spock uses SQLite 3 for deterministic filtering and state management, while it uses the vector database for probabilistic semantic ranking. This combination allows Spock to answer questions with both relevance and accountability.

docs.title: Ask AI and Deep Dive Interaction with ship_computer.db
docs.text:
For Ask AI inquiries, Spock treats the request as a bounded question that should be answered from the most relevant available context. The application first loads the user's session, permissions, and allowed source scope from ship_computer.db. It then embeds the prompt, searches the vector database, and retrieves candidate chunks. Before passing those chunks to the generative LLM, Spock validates them against SQLite-stored metadata, such as document status, access rights, freshness, and source reliability. The final answer, retrieved chunk IDs, citations, and response metadata are written back to ship_computer.db so the interaction can be reviewed, replayed, or audited.

For Deep Dive inquiries, Spock treats the request as a multi-step investigation rather than a single lookup. ship_computer.db stores the Deep Dive session state, including the original objective, refined sub-questions, applied filters, previously retrieved chunks, and intermediate conclusions. As the investigation progresses, Spock may issue multiple embedding searches, compare results, eliminate duplicates, and request additional context. SQLite 3 ensures that the application does not lose track of what has already been examined, prevents redundant retrieval, and preserves a clear chain of evidence from the initial question to the final synthesized answer.

docs.title: How Spock Uses the Embedding LLM and Vector Database
docs.text:
Spock uses the embedding model and vector database as a semantic retrieval layer that connects user intent to the most relevant stored knowledge. The embedding model converts both stored content and incoming questions into the same numerical vector space. Because both sides of the search use the same model, a user question such as "what are the risks in this deployment plan?" can match a document chunk that does not contain the exact phrase "risks" but still discusses failure modes, rollback constraints, or operational exposure.

During ingestion, Spock processes source material into manageable chunks, normalizes the text, and generates a vector for each chunk. The vector is stored in the vector database alongside a stable identifier and metadata. The corresponding chunk record, permissions, and vector identifier are stored in ship_computer.db. This dual storage model gives Spock fast semantic search while preserving durable, inspectable context.

During retrieval, Spock embeds the user's prompt and asks the vector database for the nearest vectors. The vector database returns candidate chunks based on semantic proximity. Spock then applies business rules from ship_computer.db, such as access control, document status, source priority, and freshness. The surviving chunks are ranked, deduplicated, and assembled into a context window for the generative LLM. The generative LLM uses that context to produce an answer, while the embedding model and vector database remain responsible only for finding the right material.

This design gives Spock three important properties: - Relevance: semantic search finds conceptually related content, not just keyword matches. - Grounding: generated answers are constrained by retrieved, citable evidence. - Traceability: SQLite 3 preserves the exact chunks, metadata, and session state used to produce each response.
