docs.title: SQLite 3 Database Architecture: ship_computer.db
docs.text:
The ship_computer.db file serves as the central relational database for the Spock application, leveraging SQLite 3 for lightweight, serverless, and zero-configuration data persistence. It acts as the authoritative source of truth for application state, user configurations, session tracking, audit logging, and metadata indexing.

Unlike the vector database, which is optimized for semantic similarity and approximate nearest-neighbor search, ship_computer.db manages structured relational data required for deterministic operations, workflow orchestration, and reproducible application behavior. In practice, the two storage layers are complementary:

  • SQLite 3 (ship_computer.db) stores exact records, timestamps, identifiers, task states, configuration values, and audit trails.
  • The vector database stores high-dimensional embeddings and supports semantic retrieval over text content.

This separation allows Spock to combine deterministic state management with flexible semantic search.

docs.title: Core Schema & Functional Domains
docs.text:
• Configuration & State Management: Stores persistent user preferences, model selection policies (first_models_last.json mappings), hardware profiles, and runtime environment variables. This ensures settings survive application restarts without requiring external configuration services.

  • Health & Maintenance Tracking: Modules such as db_maintenance.py and EngineeringDeck/ship_computer_health.py write diagnostic metrics, uptime logs, and system integrity checks to dedicated tables. This enables proactive monitoring, troubleshooting, and automated recovery routines.

  • Session & Workflow Metadata: Tracks active and historical sessions for both interactive and background processes, including progress markers, error states, resource allocation records, and workflow checkpoints.

  • Audit & Traceability: Records user actions, AI query submissions, Deep Dive task execution, document ingestion events, and maintenance operations. This provides a durable audit trail for debugging, compliance, and reproducibility.

docs.title: Interaction with "Ask AI" Inquiries
docs.text:
When a user initiates an "Ask AI" query via chat_ai_helper.py or EngineeringDeck/ask_panel.py, the application performs the following relational operations:

  1. Context Retrieval & Caching: The database stores recent conversation history, prompt templates, cached LLM responses, and retrieval metadata. This reduces redundant API calls, maintains conversational continuity, and allows the application to reconstruct prior context after restarts.

  2. Rate Limiting & Cost Tracking: Each query is logged with timestamps, token usage estimates, model identifiers, latency measurements, and response status. This data is used to enforce usage policies, detect anomalies, and provide transparent cost and performance reporting.

  3. Response Validation: Before delivering an AI-generated response, the system cross-references the output against stored safety filters, domain-specific constraints, and user-defined guardrails stored in the relational schema.

  4. Retrieval Coordination: For questions that require external knowledge, ship_computer.db stores references to relevant documents, chunks, source identifiers, and vector database search results. This allows the application to combine semantic retrieval with deterministic citation and provenance tracking.

docs.title: Interaction with "Deep Dive" Inquiries
docs.text:
The "Deep Dive" feature, orchestrated by deep_dive.py, relies heavily on ship_computer.db for stateful, long-running analytical workflows:

  1. Task Queue & Progress Logging: Deep Dive operations are broken into discrete steps such as crawling, parsing, chunking, embedding, analysis, and reporting. Each step's status, completion percentage, timestamps, and intermediate artifacts are recorded in the database, allowing users to pause, resume, or inspect progress without losing context.

  2. Document & Source Indexing: When LongRangeSensors or spock_wiki_adapter ingest external documents, the database stores source URLs, file hashes, ingestion timestamps, processing flags, and content fingerprints. This prevents duplicate processing and ensures traceability for every piece of retrieved information.

  3. Result Aggregation: Final analysis outputs, extracted entities, cross-referenced findings, and generated summaries are stored in structured tables. This enables the UI to render detailed reports, generate citations, and allow users to export or archive Deep Dive sessions.

  4. Embedding Pipeline State: The database tracks which documents and chunks have been embedded, which embedding model version was used, and whether re-embedding is required after model or chunking changes. This prevents inconsistent semantic indexes and supports safe upgrades.

docs.title: Embedding LLM & Vector Database Integration
docs.text: The Spock application uses an embedding LLM and a vector database to support semantic understanding, retrieval, and knowledge synthesis. This layer is especially important for "Ask AI" and "Deep Dive" workflows, where the application must locate relevant information from large or unstructured text sources.

docs.title: 1. Text Chunking
docs.text:
Before embedding, Spock breaks source content into manageable chunks. Chunking may be based on:

  • Paragraph boundaries
  • Section headings
  • Token limits
  • Document structure
  • Semantic boundaries

Each chunk is assigned a stable identifier and associated metadata, such as:

  • Source document ID
  • Source URL or file path
  • Chunk index
  • Content hash
  • Ingestion timestamp
  • Processing status
  • Embedding model version

This metadata is stored in ship_computer.db, while the resulting vector is stored in the vector database.

docs.title: 2. Embedding Generation
docs.text:
The embedding LLM converts each text chunk into a dense numerical vector. This vector represents the semantic meaning of the chunk in a high-dimensional space. Similar concepts are placed closer together, while unrelated concepts are placed farther apart.

The embedding process is deterministic for a given model version and input text, but the resulting vectors are not human-readable. They are optimized for mathematical similarity comparison.

Spock records the following information in the relational database:

  • Which embedding model was used
  • When the embedding was generated
  • Which chunk was embedded
  • Whether the embedding succeeded
  • Whether the chunk requires re-embedding

This allows the application to maintain consistency when models, prompts, or chunking strategies change.

docs.title: 3. Vector Database Storage
docs.text:
The vector database stores the generated embeddings alongside lightweight metadata required for retrieval. Unlike SQLite, the vector database is optimized for approximate nearest-neighbor search, allowing Spock to quickly find semantically similar chunks even when the user's query does not match the source text exactly.

For example, a user may ask:

"What are the risks associated with autonomous navigation failures?"

The vector database can retrieve relevant chunks containing related concepts such as:

  • "sensor degradation"
  • "decision latency"
  • "failover procedures"
  • "navigation uncertainty"

even if those exact phrases do not appear in the user's question.

docs.title: 4. Semantic Retrieval for "Ask AI"
docs.text:
During an "Ask AI" inquiry, Spock may use the vector database to retrieve context relevant to the user's question. The typical flow is:

  1. The user submits a question.
  2. The question is embedded using the same or a compatible embedding model.
  3. The vector database searches for the most semantically similar chunks.
  4. Retrieved chunks are ranked by similarity score.
  5. Relevant metadata is joined from ship_computer.db.
  6. The retrieved context is included in the prompt sent to the generative LLM.
  7. The final response is validated, logged, and returned to the user.

This approach allows Spock to answer questions using grounded, source-backed context rather than relying solely on the LLM's internal knowledge.

docs.title: 5. Semantic Retrieval for "Deep Dive"
docs.text:
For "Deep Dive" workflows, the embedding and vector database layers support deeper analysis over large document sets. The process typically includes:

  1. Ingesting documents from external sources.
  2. Parsing and normalizing content.
  3. Chunking documents into semantic units.
  4. Generating embeddings for each chunk.
  5. Storing vectors in the vector database.
  6. Recording chunk metadata in ship_computer.db.
  7. Performing similarity searches, clustering, or cross-document comparison.
  8. Aggregating findings into structured reports.

This enables Spock to identify related concepts across multiple sources, detect recurring themes, and produce citations that trace back to the original documents.

docs.title: 6. Relationship Between SQLite and the Vector Database
docs.text:
The relational database and vector database work together as follows:

  • SQLite stores exact, queryable state: It records what was ingested, when it was processed, which model was used, what the task status is, and what the final results were.

  • The vector database stores semantic representations: It stores embeddings and supports similarity search over text content.

  • SQLite provides provenance: It links vector search results back to source documents, chunks, users, sessions, and workflows.

  • The vector database provides flexibility: It allows Spock to retrieve relevant information even when the user's wording differs from the source material.

This hybrid architecture gives Spock both deterministic reliability and semantic adaptability.

docs.title: Database Lifecycle & Maintenance
docs.text:
Database lifecycle operations are managed through db_maintenance.py and reset_ship_computer.py.

  • db_maintenance.py: Handles schema migrations, integrity checks, vacuuming, index optimization, and cleanup of stale records.

  • reset_ship_computer.py: Provides safe state clearing for troubleshooting, development, or recovery scenarios.

The relational layer ensures deterministic consistency, while the vector layer handles semantic flexibility. Together, they allow Spock to manage complex AI workflows with traceability, resumability, and semantic retrieval.

docs.title: Embedding LLM and Vector Database Integration
docs.text: The Spock application implements a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline that separates semantic retrieval from generative reasoning. This architecture relies on two distinct AI components: an Embedding LLM for vectorization and a Vector Database for similarity retrieval. Together, they enable context-aware, grounded responses for both Ask AI and Deep Dive workflows.

docs.title: The Embedding LLM: Semantic Translation
docs.text:
The embedding model is a specialized neural network trained to map unstructured text into high-dimensional numerical vectors, commonly called embeddings. Unlike a generative LLM, it does not produce conversational text. Instead, it captures semantic meaning, context, and relationships between words, phrases, and documents.

  • Chunking Strategy: Raw documents, wiki pages, logs, and external search results are split into manageable chunks, typically 250–500 tokens, to preserve contextual boundaries while fitting within the model’s context window.
  • Vectorization: Each chunk is passed through the configured embedding LLM, managed via llm_client.py and model_selector/embedding_panel.py. The model outputs a fixed-length vector where geometric proximity correlates with semantic similarity.
  • Metadata Attachment: Each vector is paired with structured metadata, such as source ID, document type, timestamp, confidence score, and retrieval context, before storage. This enables precise filtering, attribution, and traceability during retrieval.

docs.title: The Vector Database: High-Dimensional Indexing
docs.text:
The vector database, exposed via rag_api_server.py and spock_rag_adapter, stores embeddings in an optimized index structure, such as HNSW or IVF, designed for fast approximate nearest neighbor, or ANN, search.

  • Storage & Indexing: Vectors are persisted alongside their metadata. The index is periodically rebuilt or updated as new documents are ingested by LongRangeSensors or spock_wiki_adapter.
  • Similarity Search: When a query arrives, the same embedding LLM converts the user’s prompt into a vector. The vector database then performs a cosine similarity, dot product, or Euclidean distance calculation to identify the most relevant document chunks.
  • Hybrid Filtering: Results are filtered using metadata constraints, such as “only return engineering logs from the last 30 days,” before being passed to the generative LLM. This improves relevance, reduces hallucination, and respects domain boundaries.

docs.title: SQLite 3 ship_computer.db Integration
docs.text:
The SQLite 3 database ship_computer.db is Spock’s local relational store for application state, user interactions, retrieval metadata, and workflow checkpoints. It does not replace the vector database; instead, it coordinates the surrounding Spock application and provides durable, queryable context for both Ask AI and Deep Dive inquiries.

  • Persistent Application State: ship_computer.db stores sessions, prompts, responses, model selections, retrieval results, citations, and workflow status. This allows Spock to resume conversations, audit AI behavior, and maintain continuity across restarts.
  • Ask AI Support: During an Ask AI inquiry, chat_ai_helper.py can use ship_computer.db to load prior conversation context, record the user’s prompt, store retrieved chunk references, and persist the final generated response. This creates a traceable chain from user question to retrieved evidence to AI answer.
  • Deep Dive Support: During a Deep Dive inquiry, deep_dive.py can use ship_computer.db to track research phases, intermediate findings, evidence links, and completion status. This allows the workflow to checkpoint progress, recover from interruptions, and cross-reference earlier findings in later phases.
  • Relationship to the Vector Database: The vector database is optimized for fast semantic similarity search, while ship_computer.db is optimized for structured queries, transactions, and application state. A typical design stores vector references, chunk IDs, scores, and metadata in SQLite, while the actual high-dimensional vectors remain in the vector database.
  • Typical Data Domains: Common tables or data domains include sessions, messages, documents, chunks, embeddings, retrieval results, Deep Dive runs, findings, model configuration, and audit logs.
  • Operational Benefits: Because SQLite is embedded, local, and transactional, ship_computer.db supports offline operation, low-latency state access, and reliable persistence without requiring a separate database server.

docs.title: How Spock Uses the Embedding LLM and Vector Database
docs.text:
Spock uses the embedding LLM and vector database as a semantic retrieval layer that grounds generative AI responses in relevant local and external knowledge.

  1. Ingestion: Documents, wiki pages, logs, and sensor-derived data are chunked, embedded, and stored in the vector database with metadata.
  2. Query Embedding: When a user submits an Ask AI or Deep Dive prompt, Spock sends the prompt to the configured embedding LLM to produce a query vector.
  3. Similarity Retrieval: spock_rag_adapter queries the vector database for the most semantically similar chunks, using ANN search and metadata filters.
  4. Context Assembly: The retrieved chunks, along with their metadata and scores, are assembled into a context window for the generative LLM.
  5. Grounded Generation: The generative LLM produces a response using the retrieved context, reducing reliance on ungrounded parametric knowledge.
  6. Persistence: ship_computer.db records the prompt, retrieved evidence, response, model used, and workflow state for auditability and continuity.
  7. Deep Dive Iteration: In Deep Dive mode, intermediate findings are embedded and stored so later phases can retrieve and cross-reference earlier analysis.
  8. Model Management: model_selector can swap embedding models or generative models, while the vector database and SQLite metadata track model versions to prevent incompatible vector mixing.

docs.title: Integration with Spock Workflows
docs.text:
• Ask AI Pipeline: User prompts are embedded, matched against the vector store, and the top-k relevant chunks are injected into the generative LLM’s context window. The LLM synthesizes a response grounded in the retrieved data, while chat_ai_helper.py manages turn-taking and context window optimization.
  • Deep Dive Pipeline: For complex, multi-step analysis, the vector database acts as a dynamic knowledge base. As deep_dive.py iterates through research phases, intermediate findings are embedded and stored. Subsequent steps query the vector store to cross-reference new data with previously analyzed material, enabling recursive reasoning and comprehensive synthesis.
  • Model Flexibility: The model_selector subsystem allows users to swap embedding models based on hardware constraints or accuracy requirements. The vector database abstracts the underlying model version, ensuring backward compatibility and supporting migration by re-embedding or maintaining versioned indexes.

This separation of concerns ensures that Spock maintains high retrieval accuracy, scales efficiently with growing document corpora, and delivers auditable, traceable AI interactions.

docs.title: SQLite 3 Database (ship_computer.db) Architecture
docs.text: The Spock application relies on a local SQLite 3 database named ship_computer.db to persist structured metadata, query history, configuration states, and cached inference results. SQLite is selected for its zero-configuration deployment, ACID compliance, and efficient read/write performance for single-user or low-concurrency workloads typical of local AI assistant applications.

docs.title: Interaction with Spock: Ask AI and Deep Dive Inquiries
docs.text:
When a user initiates an Ask AI or Deep Dive inquiry, the Spock application orchestrates a multi-step interaction with ship_computer.db:

  1. Context Retrieval & Grounding: Before routing the prompt to the LLM, Spock queries the database for relevant historical context, user preferences, and previously resolved entities. This ensures responses are grounded in the user's specific project state and conversation history.
  2. Query Logging & State Management: Each inquiry is logged with timestamps, session IDs, and metadata tags. For Deep Dive requests, which typically involve multi-turn reasoning or extensive codebase traversal, the database tracks intermediate reasoning steps, cached embeddings, and dependency graphs to prevent redundant computation and maintain traceability.
  3. Result Caching & Deduplication: To optimize latency and reduce token consumption, Spock checks ship_computer.db for semantically similar past queries. If a match exceeds a configured similarity threshold, the cached response is returned or used as a prefix for incremental generation.
  4. Transaction Safety: All write operations during inquiry processing are wrapped in SQLite transactions. This guarantees data integrity and prevents partial writes even if the application encounters interruptions during long-running Deep Dive operations.
  5. Schema Versioning: The database includes a version-tracking table that allows Spock to apply incremental schema migrations safely, ensuring backward compatibility as new inquiry features are introduced.

docs.title: Database responsibilities
docs.text:
ship_computer.db is the system of record for structured application state. It is responsible for:

  • Preserving user sessions, inquiry history, and conversation context.
  • Storing configuration, preferences, and feature flags.
  • Tracking codebase chunks, content hashes, and version metadata.
  • Recording embedding metadata, vector index references, and retrieval provenance.
  • Caching normalized prompts, responses, and intermediate Deep Dive results.
  • Providing auditability for Ask AI and Deep Dive outputs.
  • Supporting safe schema migrations and local backups.

docs.title: Core tables and their roles
docs.text:
The exact table names may vary by implementation, but the logical schema typically includes the following categories:

Table or table group Purpose schema_version Tracks database schema version and applied migrations. sessions Stores user or application session identifiers, start/end times, and session-level settings. inquiries Records each Ask AI or Deep Dive request, including type, status, timestamps, and parent/child relationships. messages Stores user prompts, assistant responses, system prompts, and message metadata. entities Tracks named entities, files, functions, classes, documents, or concepts referenced during an inquiry. codebase_chunks Stores chunk identifiers, source paths, content hashes, line ranges, and version information. embeddings_metadata Stores embedding model, vector dimension, content hash, vector store reference, and creation time. response_cache Caches normalized prompts, similarity scores, response payloads, and cache validity metadata. preferences Stores user or workspace preferences that influence retrieval, grounding, and response style. audit_log Records significant events, errors, fallbacks, and permission or policy decisions.

docs.title: Ask AI detailed flow
docs.text:
An Ask AI inquiry is a grounded, usually single-turn question that Spock answers using local context, conversation history, and semantic retrieval.

  1. Intake and session binding Spock creates or reuses a session and records the inquiry in ship_computer.db. The record includes the prompt, user context, timestamp, and inquiry type.

  2. Structured context lookup Before calling the model, Spock queries the database for relevant session state, recent messages, user preferences, and previously resolved entities. This helps the response reflect the user's current project and conversation.

  3. Semantic retrieval Spock embeds the user prompt using the embedding model and queries the vector database for semantically similar code chunks, documents, or conversation summaries. SQLite stores the metadata needed to retrieve, filter, and cite those results.

  4. Prompt assembly Spock combines the user prompt, retrieved context, preferences, and any cached or previously resolved information into a structured prompt for the answer-generation model.

  5. Response generation and persistence After the model returns an answer, Spock stores the response, citations, token usage, latency, and confidence or grounding metadata in ship_computer.db.

  6. Caching and deduplication Spock may store a normalized prompt hash and embedding reference in the response cache. If a later Ask AI request is sufficiently similar, Spock can return the cached answer or use it as a grounding prefix, reducing latency and token usage.

docs.title: Deep Dive detailed flow
docs.text:
A Deep Dive inquiry is a longer, multi-step investigation. It may involve repeated retrieval, code traversal, dependency analysis, and synthesis of a detailed report.

  1. Run creation Spock creates a Deep Dive run record in ship_computer.db, including the objective, scope, constraints, and initial context.

  2. Planning and decomposition Spock breaks the objective into subquestions or investigation steps. Each step is stored as a child inquiry or task record so the process can be inspected, resumed, or replayed.

  3. Iterative retrieval For each step, Spock embeds the subquestion, queries the vector database, and retrieves relevant chunks. It may also use SQLite to filter by file path, entity, version, or session scope.

  4. Evidence accumulation Retrieved chunks, code symbols, dependency relationships, and intermediate conclusions are stored with provenance metadata. This allows Spock to cite sources and avoid repeating work.

  5. Checkpointing Because Deep Dive operations can be long-running, Spock commits intermediate state to SQLite at safe points. If the process is interrupted, Spock can resume from the last committed checkpoint.

  6. Synthesis and final report Spock synthesizes the accumulated evidence into a final answer or report. The final output, citations, reasoning steps, and performance metrics are persisted for auditability.

docs.title: Transaction safety and consistency
docs.text: All write operations during Ask AI and Deep Dive processing are wrapped in SQLite transactions. This ensures that partial writes are not committed if an error occurs. For long-running Deep Dive operations, Spock uses incremental commits and checkpoints to preserve progress while maintaining data integrity.

docs.title: Schema versioning and migrations
docs.text: The database includes a version-tracking mechanism that allows Spock to apply incremental schema migrations safely. This supports backward compatibility and controlled introduction of new inquiry features, retrieval fields, or caching columns.

docs.title: Embedding LLM and Vector DB
docs.text: Spock uses an embedding model, often referred to in this architecture as the embedding LLM, together with a vector database, or vector DB, to provide semantic retrieval. The embedding model converts text into numerical vectors, and the vector DB indexes those vectors for fast similarity search. This allows Spock to find relevant code, documentation, conversation history, or project knowledge even when the wording of the user's question differs from the wording of the stored content.

docs.title: Purpose of the embedding and vector layer
docs.text:
The embedding and vector layer provides semantic grounding for Spock's AI responses. It complements ship_computer.db by handling approximate similarity search, while SQLite handles exact structured state, metadata, history, and provenance.

Together, they enable Spock to:

  • Retrieve relevant context for Ask AI questions.
  • Support iterative evidence gathering during Deep Dive investigations.
  • Reduce reliance on brittle keyword matching.
  • Improve answer relevance, citation quality, and consistency.
  • Cache and reuse embeddings for repeated or similar content.

docs.title: How Spock uses the embedding LLM
docs.text:
The embedding LLM is a model that produces fixed-size vector representations of text. It is separate from the answer-generation model that produces natural-language responses.

Spock uses the embedding model in the following ways:

  1. Chunk embedding Code files, documentation, conversation summaries, and other knowledge sources are split into chunks. Each chunk is embedded into a vector.

  2. Prompt embedding When a user submits an Ask AI or Deep Dive request, Spock embeds the prompt or subquestion to create a query vector.

  3. Similarity comparison The query vector is compared against stored vectors using a similarity metric, commonly cosine similarity.

  4. Caching Embeddings are cached by content hash. If a chunk has not changed, Spock reuses the existing vector instead of re-embedding it.

  5. Re-embedding on change When code, documentation, or conversation context changes, Spock re-embeds affected chunks and updates the vector database.

docs.title: How Spock uses the vector DB
docs.text:
The vector DB stores embeddings and supports approximate nearest-neighbor search. It may be implemented as a local vector store or a SQLite-backed vector index, depending on the deployment. In either case, Spock abstracts the storage behind a retrieval interface.

The vector DB is used to:

  • Store embeddings for code chunks, documents, entities, and conversation summaries.
  • Index vectors for fast similarity search.
  • Return the most relevant chunks for a given query vector.
  • Support metadata filtering, such as file path, session, project, version, or content type.
  • Enable reranking or hybrid retrieval when combined with keyword search.

docs.title: Ask AI usage pattern
docs.text:
For an Ask AI inquiry, Spock typically follows this pattern:

  1. Receive the user's question.
  2. Embed the question using the embedding model.
  3. Query the vector DB for the most relevant chunks.
  4. Use SQLite to retrieve metadata, preferences, session context, and citation information.
  5. Assemble a grounded prompt for the answer-generation model.
  6. Store the response, retrieved context, and provenance in ship_computer.db.

This pattern allows Spock to answer questions with context that is semantically related to the user's request, rather than relying only on exact keyword matches.

docs.title: Deep Dive usage pattern
docs.text:
For a Deep Dive inquiry, Spock uses the embedding and vector layer repeatedly:

  1. Decompose the investigation into subquestions.
  2. Embed each subquestion.
  3. Retrieve relevant chunks for each subquestion.
  4. Store retrieved evidence and intermediate conclusions in SQLite.
  5. Use the accumulated evidence to generate follow-up subquestions.
  6. Continue until the investigation reaches a stopping condition.
  7. Synthesize the final report and persist the full reasoning trail.

This iterative use of embeddings and vector search allows Deep Dive to explore a codebase or knowledge base more thoroughly than a single retrieval pass.

docs.title: Caching, invalidation, and consistency
docs.text:
Spock uses caching to improve performance and reduce repeated embedding work.

  • Embedding cache: Stored by content hash, model name, and vector dimension.
  • Response cache: Stored by normalized prompt, context version, and similarity threshold.
  • Invalidation: Triggered when source content, schema version, embedding model, or retrieval policy changes.
  • Consistency: SQLite remains the source of truth for metadata and provenance, while the vector DB is treated as a derived index that can be rebuilt if necessary.

docs.title: Failure handling and fallback
docs.text:
If the embedding model or vector DB is unavailable, Spock can degrade gracefully by:

  • Falling back to SQLite-based keyword or metadata search.
  • Returning a limited answer with a warning that semantic retrieval is unavailable.
  • Logging the failure in the audit log.
  • Retrying embedding or vector search operations when appropriate.

This design keeps the core application functional while preserving transparency about the level of grounding available for each response.

docs.title: Embedding LLM and Vector Database Integration
docs.text: Spock leverages a dedicated embedding model (typically a lightweight, locally-hosted transformer or distilled LLM) to convert unstructured text, code snippets, and documentation into high-dimensional numerical vectors. These vectors are stored in a vector database (or a vector-capable SQLite extension) to enable fast semantic similarity search and retrieval-augmented generation.

docs.title: How Spock Utilizes Embeddings and Vector Search
docs.text:
The embedding and vector search pipeline operates as follows:

  • Ingestion & Chunking: Raw documents, code files, and wiki entries are parsed and split into semantic chunks. Each chunk is passed through the embedding LLM to generate a fixed-length vector representation that captures contextual meaning rather than exact keyword matches.
  • Vector Indexing: The generated vectors are indexed using approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) algorithms (e.g., HNSW or IVF) to enable sub-millisecond retrieval. Metadata such as file paths, line numbers, chunk IDs, and source types are attached to each vector for traceability and filtering.
  • Semantic Query Routing: When a user submits a query, Spock first embeds the prompt using the same model. The resulting query vector is compared against the indexed corpus to retrieve the most contextually relevant chunks based on cosine similarity or inner product distance.
  • Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG): The top-k retrieved chunks are injected into the LLM's context window alongside the original prompt. This grounding mechanism significantly reduces hallucination and ensures that Ask AI and Deep Dive responses are directly tied to verified project data.
  • Dynamic Re-embedding & Index Maintenance: As the codebase or documentation evolves, Spock triggers incremental re-embedding jobs. The vector index is updated asynchronously to maintain search accuracy without blocking user interactions, and stale vectors are automatically pruned based on file modification timestamps.

docs.title: Bootstrap
docs.text: The bootstrap process initializes the Spock environment from a clean state. To ensure the desktop menu launches quickly without waiting for all dependencies, the process is divided into two phases: Phase A (approximately 280 MB) and Phase B (bringing the total size to approximately 990 MB). These sizes are approximate and may vary depending on the platform, package versions, and existing system components.

docs.title: Phase A — Environment setup and the UI tier
docs.text:
.\bootstrap.ps1 -NonInteractive -EmitEvents -NoHandOffGui

Phase A prepares only the dependencies required for the Bringup menu and lightweight bringup operations:

  1. Locates or installs Python 3.14
  2. Creates the virtual environment (.venv) and the required folder structure
  3. Installs requirements-ui.txt — PyQt6, requests, psutil, huggingface_hub
  4. Validates the UI gate (import PyQt6)

Phase A intentionally halts at the point required for python -m spock_bringup_menu to open the desktop interface. This prevents file-locking conflicts during Phase B, as the Bringup menu may keep Python and PyQt files in use while running. Subsequent bringup steps (3–5: acquire, bring up servers, status) operate on this tier as well, because they only require lightweight packages such as requests and huggingface_hub.

docs.title: Phase B — Full dependency tier
docs.text:
.\bootstrap_phase_b_job.ps1 -InstallRoot . -FullDeps -Validate

Run from Bringup step 2 (or the console menu). It re-enters bootstrap.ps1 -FromStep pip_full and installs only the full dependency tier. It does not reinstall the UI packages, because the Bringup menu is typically still holding that virtual environment open, and Windows may lock loaded files (WinError 32).

Phase B assumes Phase A has already completed successfully. If the virtual environment or UI-tier packages are missing, run Phase A first before attempting Phase B.

  1. Installs requirements-full.txt — extractors (PyMuPDF, python-docx, openpyxl, pandas, beautifulsoup4, lxml, Pillow), watchdog, PyQt6-WebEngine, keyring, reportlab, google-auth, nvidia-ml-py
  2. Pulls in requirements-mcp.txt (fastmcp, authlib, starlette)
  3. Retries pip a few times if a file is briefly locked by Defender, Explorer, or another Spock window
  4. Writes bootstrap_full_deps.ok, the marker file read by spock_onboarding.readiness, spock_bringup, and spock_status

If Phase B still fails with Windows Error 32 on a site-packages path, close every other Spock or Python window that uses this .venv, then re-run step 2. As a last resort, exit Bringup and run the Phase B script from a plain PowerShell prompt. Do not delete or recreate the virtual environment unless absolutely necessary; if you do, rerun Phase A before Phase B.

Phase B is required before Wiki Scan and the UIEG crawler; both validate their imports first and redirect to step 2 when packages are missing. -HeavyDeps / -SkipHeavyDeps still function as aliases for -FullDeps / -SkipFullDeps. Use skip flags only in constrained environments, because features that depend on the full tier will remain unavailable until Phase B completes successfully.

Server launch is not part of Phase B — that is handled in Bringup step 4 (spock_bringup up).

docs.title: Step order
docs.text:
The bootstrap.ps1 script executes a logical sequence of internal functions: python, install_root, folders, venv, pip_wizard, pip_full, validate. Use -FromStep or -OnlyStep to re-enter partway through the process; note that pip_full performs no operations unless the -FullDeps flag is passed.

Typical usage:

  • Phase A runs the initial steps and stops after UI validation, leaving a usable Bringup environment.
  • Phase B re-enters at pip_full with -FullDeps, installs the remaining packages, and then validates readiness.

docs.title: Script Reference
docs.text: Script Purpose bootstrap.ps1 Main bootstrap orchestrator for both tiers; can be run directly or re-entered from later steps bootstrap_phase_b_job.ps1 Phase B full-tier install, intended to run outside the GUI when possible spock_menu.ps1 Interactive menu wrapper for common Spock operations

docs.title: Database Architecture
docs.text: The Spock application uses a local SQLite 3 database file named ship_computer.db to persist state between sessions. This database serves as the central repository for user context, conversation history, document metadata, retrieval results, and analysis metadata required by the Ask AI and Deep Dive modules. Unlike the virtual environment managed during bootstrap, which can be rebuilt from package requirements, the database is designed to be durable and supports the read-heavy access patterns typical of LLM-assisted workflows.

docs.title: Database Location and Lifecycle
docs.text:
The ship_computer.db file resides in Spock's resolved data directory. Depending on the installation layout and OS conventions, this may be under the application root, a user-specific application-data folder, or a dedicated data/ subdirectory. It is not part of the Python virtual environment and should not be moved into .venv.

  • Initialization: The database is created automatically upon first run if it does not exist. Spock initializes the required tables and indexes for Ask AI and Deep Dive during startup.
  • Persistence: Data persists across restarts of the Spock application and bootstrap phases unless explicitly deleted or reset by a user action.
  • Locking: SQLite uses file-level locking to coordinate access. Although package installation does not normally modify the database, open Spock processes may hold connections that can cause SQLITE_BUSY errors during concurrent writes or schema changes. Close idle Bringup, Ask AI, or Deep Dive windows before running maintenance operations when possible.

docs.title: ship_computer.db and Ask AI / Deep Dive Interaction
docs.text: ship_computer.db is the durable local state store for Spock's conversational and analytical features. It is not the primary vector index, but it is the source of truth for the metadata that makes Ask AI and Deep Dive responses reproducible, auditable, and resumable.

docs.title: Role in Ask AI
docs.text:
Ask AI is a conversational interface that answers user questions using local context, retrieved documents, and prior conversation state. ship_computer.db supports this workflow by storing:

  • Session state: The active Ask AI conversation, including session identifiers, timestamps, and user context.
  • Message history: User prompts, assistant responses, system prompts, and intermediate context used to generate each answer.
  • Retrieval context: The document chunks, sources, and metadata that were selected for a given question.
  • Citations and provenance: References to the files, pages, sections, or records that contributed to an answer.
  • Feedback and corrections: Optional user feedback, such as accepted, rejected, or corrected responses, which can be used to improve future retrieval or prompting.

A typical Ask AI interaction follows this pattern:

  1. The user submits a question in the Ask AI interface.
  2. Spock loads the active session and recent conversation history from ship_computer.db.
  3. The query is embedded using the configured embedding LLM.
  4. The vector database is searched for semantically similar chunks.
  5. Candidate chunks are filtered, ranked, and combined into a prompt context.
  6. The LLM generates an answer.
  7. Spock writes the question, answer, retrieved chunks, citations, and metadata back to ship_computer.db.

This design allows Ask AI to maintain continuity across restarts, show users where an answer came from, and support follow-up questions without reprocessing the entire corpus.

docs.title: Role in Deep Dive
docs.text:
Deep Dive is a more structured analytical workflow. It is designed for questions that require multiple retrieval passes, evidence comparison, and step-by-step reasoning. ship_computer.db supports Deep Dive by storing:

  • Run metadata: The Deep Dive run identifier, start time, completion status, and user intent.
  • Decomposed subquestions: The individual questions or hypotheses generated during the analysis.
  • Retrieval steps: Each search performed, including query text, embedding vector reference, top-k results, and filters applied.
  • Evidence records: The chunks, documents, and metadata selected as supporting evidence.
  • Intermediate conclusions: Partial findings produced during the analysis.
  • Final report data: The synthesized answer, citations, confidence notes, and unresolved gaps.

A typical Deep Dive interaction follows this pattern:

  1. The user starts a Deep Dive with a broad analytical question.
  2. Spock creates a new run record in ship_computer.db.
  3. The application decomposes the question into subquestions or evidence requirements.
  4. For each subquestion, Spock embeds the query and searches the vector database.
  5. Retrieved chunks are stored as evidence records with provenance.
  6. The LLM compares evidence, identifies contradictions, and builds intermediate conclusions.
  7. The final answer is generated with citations to the stored evidence.
  8. The complete run, including intermediate steps, is persisted in ship_computer.db so the user can review, resume, or export the analysis.

This makes Deep Dive more transparent than a single-turn Ask AI response because the database preserves the reasoning path, not just the final answer.

docs.title: Embedding LLM and Vector Database Integration
docs.text: Spock uses an embedding LLM and a vector database to convert natural-language questions and document content into a form that can be compared semantically. This is the core mechanism behind Ask AI and Deep Dive retrieval.

docs.title: Embedding LLM
docs.text:
The embedding LLM is a model that converts text into a fixed-size numerical vector, also called an embedding. Unlike a generative LLM, which produces text, an embedding LLM produces a representation of meaning.

For example:

  • A document chunk about “network latency during peak load” is converted into a vector.
  • A user question about “why the system slows down at busy times” is converted into another vector.
  • If the two concepts are semantically related, their vectors will be close together in vector space.

Spock uses the embedding LLM in two main ways:

  1. Indexing: When documents are ingested, their text is split into chunks and each chunk is embedded.
  2. Querying: When a user asks a question, the question is embedded and compared against the stored chunk embeddings.

The embedding model should be deterministic for a given input so that repeated queries produce consistent retrieval results. If the model changes, existing embeddings may no longer be comparable to new ones, and the vector index may need to be rebuilt.

docs.title: Vector Database
docs.text:
The vector database stores embeddings and the metadata needed to retrieve them. It may be implemented as a SQLite-backed vector store or as a separate vector database service, depending on the deployment. In either case, Spock abstracts the vector store behind a retrieval interface.

The vector database typically stores:

  • Vector ID: A unique identifier for the embedding.
  • Embedding vector: The numerical representation of the text chunk.
  • Chunk text: The original text that was embedded.
  • Document reference: The source file, record, or page.
  • Metadata: Section, author, timestamp, classification, language, or other filters.
  • Index version: The embedding model or index generation used to create the vector.

The vector database supports similarity search, allowing Spock to find the most relevant chunks for a query. Depending on the implementation, this may use exact nearest-neighbor search, approximate nearest-neighbor search, or a hybrid search that combines vector similarity with keyword matching.

docs.title: How Spock Uses the Embedding LLM and Vector Database Together
docs.text:
The full retrieval pipeline works as follows:

  1. Document ingestion

    • Spock reads documents from local files, wikis, or other sources.
    • Documents are parsed into text using the appropriate extractor.
    • Text is split into chunks of a suitable size for retrieval.
    • Each chunk is embedded using the embedding LLM.
    • The chunk, metadata, and vector are stored in the vector database.
    • A reference to the chunk and vector is stored in ship_computer.db.

  2. Query preparation

    • The user submits a question through Ask AI or Deep Dive.
    • Spock normalizes the query and may add context from the active session.
    • The query is embedded using the same embedding LLM used for indexing.

  3. Vector search

    • Spock searches the vector database for the closest matching chunk embeddings.
    • Filters may be applied based on document type, date, user permissions, or metadata.
    • The top-k results are returned.

  4. Reranking and context assembly

    • Spock may rerank the retrieved chunks using metadata, recency, source reliability, or keyword overlap.
    • The selected chunks are assembled into a prompt context for the generative LLM.

  5. Answer generation

    • The generative LLM produces an answer using the retrieved context.
    • Citations are generated from the metadata associated with the retrieved chunks.

  6. Persistence

    • The query, retrieved chunks, citations, answer, and run metadata are written to ship_computer.db.
    • This allows the user to inspect the evidence, resume a Deep Dive, or audit an Ask AI response.

docs.title: Relationship Between ship_computer.db and the Vector Database
docs.text:
ship_computer.db and the vector database serve different but complementary roles.

Component Primary Responsibility ship_computer.db Durable application state, conversation history, run metadata, citations, provenance, and user context Vector database High-performance semantic search over embedded text chunks Embedding LLM Converts text into numerical vectors for semantic comparison

In a standard Spock deployment, ship_computer.db stores the human-readable and application-level records, while the vector database stores the numerical embeddings used for retrieval. If the vector database is rebuilt, Spock can often re-embed the source chunks and restore search capability. If ship_computer.db is deleted, however, conversation history, Deep Dive runs, citations, and user context may be lost.

docs.title: Failure Modes and Recovery
docs.text:
Several failure modes can affect the embedding and retrieval pipeline:

  • Missing embedding model: Spock cannot embed new queries or documents. Ask AI and Deep Dive may be unavailable until the model is restored.
  • Stale embeddings: If the embedding model changes, old vectors may no longer match new query vectors. Reindexing is required.
  • Vector database unavailable: Retrieval fails, but ship_computer.db may still contain prior answers and metadata.
  • Corrupted or missing chunks: If the source text is unavailable, citations may be incomplete even if the vector index exists.
  • Concurrent writes: Multiple Spock processes writing to ship_computer.db may cause SQLITE_BUSY errors. Closing idle windows or using a single active process reduces this risk.

For recovery, Spock should prefer rebuilding the vector index from the stored source chunks before deleting ship_computer.db. The vector index is derived data; ship_computer.db contains the durable application state.

docs.title: ship_computer.db Schema and Core Tables
docs.text:
The ship_computer.db file is the local SQLite 3 database used by the Spock application. It is optimized for high-concurrency reads and structured writes using SQLite 3's Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) mode. The schema is partitioned into logical domains to isolate conversation state, document metadata, analysis results, and vector embeddings.

Table Purpose Key Columns conversations Tracks individual Ask AI sessions id, title, created_at, updated_at, user_id messages Stores prompt/response pairs and system instructions id, conversation_id, role, content, token_count, timestamp documents Catalogs ingested files for Deep Dive analysis id, file_path, hash, mime_type, ingestion_status, metadata_json analysis_results Caches Deep Dive extraction outputs and summaries id, document_id, query_hash, result_json, confidence_score vector_store Holds dense embeddings for semantic retrieval id, document_id, chunk_id, embedding_vector, metadata

All tables utilize B-tree indexes on foreign keys and timestamp columns to accelerate JOIN operations and chronological queries. Transaction isolation is set to DEFERRED for reads and IMMEDIATE for batch writes, ensuring consistency without blocking concurrent UI threads.

docs.title: Schema Design Notes
docs.text:
The schema is designed to keep Spock's interactive and analytical workflows separate while still allowing them to share a single local database.

  • conversations represents a user-facing Ask AI session. Each conversation has a stable identifier, a human-readable title, and timestamps that support history browsing, sorting, and session restoration.
  • messages stores the ordered exchange of user prompts, assistant responses, system instructions, and tool-related messages. The role column distinguishes message types, while token_count supports context-window management, cost tracking, and rate-limiting.
  • documents tracks files that have been ingested for Deep Dive analysis. The hash column enables change detection, while ingestion_status allows Spock to distinguish between pending, processing, completed, and failed documents.
  • analysis_results stores structured outputs produced by Deep Dive pipelines. Caching these results prevents repeated extraction work and allows Spock to reuse previously computed summaries, entities, tables, or other structured findings.
  • vector_store stores dense vector embeddings for document chunks. These embeddings are used for semantic retrieval in both Ask AI and Deep Dive workflows.

docs.title: SQLite 3 Operational Details
docs.text:
Spock relies on SQLite 3 as an embedded, file-based database engine. This gives the application local persistence, low operational overhead, and strong ACID behavior without requiring a separate database server.

  • WAL mode allows readers to continue accessing the database while a writer is committing changes. This is important for Spock because the UI may read conversation history or document metadata while background ingestion or embedding jobs are writing new data.
  • PRAGMA synchronous=NORMAL reduces fsync overhead compared with the default FULL setting while still providing a practical durability level for local application data.
  • Deferred reads allow multiple read transactions to proceed without immediately acquiring exclusive locks.
  • Immediate writes are used for batch operations so that writers can acquire the necessary lock before modifying multiple rows, reducing the chance of write conflicts.
  • B-tree indexes on foreign keys, timestamps, and frequently filtered columns improve query performance for common operations such as loading recent messages, finding documents by status, or retrieving analysis results by document.

docs.title: Ask AI and Deep Dive Integration
docs.text:
The ship_computer.db acts as the state backbone for both interactive and analytical workflows:

  • Ask AI: When a user initiates a query, Spock retrieves the relevant conversation_id and fetches the last N messages from the messages table to reconstruct the context window. System prompts, tool-use instructions, and user preferences are merged at query time. Responses are written back to messages with token usage metrics, enabling cost tracking and rate-limiting logic.
  • Deep Dive: This module performs structured document analysis. Upon ingestion, files are registered in documents and processed through extraction pipelines. Results are cached in analysis_results to avoid redundant processing. When a user requests a Deep Dive inquiry, Spock queries analysis_results using semantic and metadata filters, then assembles a structured context payload that is injected into the LLM prompt. The database ensures that analysis state survives application restarts and can be versioned or rolled back if needed.

Both modules leverage SQLite's PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL and PRAGMA synchronous=NORMAL settings to balance durability with performance. Read queries are heavily cached at the application layer, while writes are batched to minimize I/O latency.

docs.title: Ask AI Interaction
docs.text:
Ask AI uses ship_computer.db as the persistent store for conversational state.

  1. Session lookup: Spock identifies the active conversation using the conversations table.
  2. Context reconstruction: Spock reads recent rows from messages in chronological order to build the prompt context.
  3. Prompt assembly: System instructions, user preferences, tool definitions, and retrieved semantic context are combined into the final LLM prompt.
  4. Response persistence: The assistant response is inserted into messages with metadata such as token count, model identifier, and timestamp.
  5. State updates: The conversation's updated_at timestamp is refreshed so that the UI can display the most recently active sessions first.

This design allows Ask AI to resume conversations after application restarts, support multiple simultaneous sessions, and maintain a durable audit trail of prompts and responses.

docs.title: Deep Dive Interaction
docs.text:
Deep Dive uses ship_computer.db to manage document ingestion, analysis caching, and structured retrieval.

  1. Document registration: When a file is added, Spock inserts a row into documents with the file path, hash, MIME type, and initial ingestion status.
  2. Ingestion tracking: As the file is parsed, chunked, embedded, and analyzed, Spock updates the ingestion_status and related metadata.
  3. Analysis caching: Structured extraction outputs are stored in analysis_results, keyed by document and query hash where applicable.
  4. Semantic retrieval: When a Deep Dive question is asked, Spock may retrieve relevant chunks from vector_store and combine them with cached analysis results.
  5. Result assembly: The retrieved context is formatted into a structured payload for the LLM, allowing the model to answer with grounding in the ingested document.

By persisting both raw document metadata and derived analysis results, Spock can avoid repeating expensive extraction work while still supporting incremental updates when source documents change.

docs.title: Shared Database Behavior
docs.text:
Ask AI and Deep Dive share the same database file, but they operate on different logical domains.

  • Ask AI primarily reads and writes conversations and messages.
  • Deep Dive primarily reads and writes documents, analysis_results, and vector_store.
  • Both workflows may use vector_store for semantic retrieval.
  • Both workflows benefit from WAL mode because UI reads and background writes can occur concurrently.
  • Both workflows rely on transactional writes to ensure that partially completed operations do not corrupt user-visible state.

docs.title: Embedding LLM and Vector Database Workflow
docs.text:
Spock integrates a local embedding LLM and a vector database to enable semantic search and context-aware retrieval. The workflow operates as follows:

  1. Text Chunking & Preprocessing: Ingested documents are split into overlapping text chunks (typically 512–1024 tokens) with metadata preservation (source, page, section headers).
  2. Embedding Generation: Each chunk is passed through the embedding LLM (e.g., a lightweight transformer model optimized for dense vector representation). The model outputs a fixed-dimensional vector (e.g., 768 or 1536 dimensions) that captures semantic meaning.
  3. Vector Storage: Embeddings are stored in the vector_store table within ship_computer.db. SQLite's vector extension (or a compatible in-process vector index) enables approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search without requiring external services.
  4. Semantic Retrieval: When Ask AI or Deep Dive requires contextual grounding, the user query is embedded using the same model. Spock executes a vector similarity search (cosine or dot product) against the vector_store index, retrieving the top-K most relevant chunks.
  5. Context Assembly & Reranking: Retrieved chunks are filtered by metadata constraints, deduplicated, and optionally reranked using a lightweight cross-encoder or heuristic scoring. The final context window is assembled and injected into the primary LLM prompt.
  6. Caching & Incremental Updates: Embeddings are cached to prevent redundant model inference. When documents are updated or deleted, Spock invalidates the corresponding vector entries and triggers incremental re-embedding only for affected chunks.

This architecture ensures low-latency retrieval, offline capability, and strict data locality. The embedding LLM runs in a dedicated inference thread with memory pooling, while the vector database leverages SQLite's ACID guarantees to maintain consistency between document state and semantic indexes.

docs.title: Embedding LLM Role
docs.text:
The embedding LLM is responsible for converting text into numerical vector representations that can be compared mathematically.

  • It does not generate natural-language answers.
  • It produces fixed-size dense vectors for text chunks and user queries.
  • It enables Spock to measure semantic similarity between a question and document content.
  • It runs locally or in a controlled inference environment, preserving data locality and reducing dependence on external services.
  • It is used during ingestion to embed document chunks and during retrieval to embed user queries.

Because the same embedding model is used for both document chunks and queries, Spock can compare vectors in the same semantic space.

docs.title: Vector Database Role
docs.text:
The vector database provides the storage and search layer for embeddings.

  • It stores each chunk's embedding vector in the vector_store table.
  • It preserves metadata needed for filtering, such as document ID, chunk ID, source file, page, section, and ingestion timestamp.
  • It supports similarity search using cosine similarity, dot product, or another configured distance metric.
  • It allows Spock to retrieve the most relevant chunks for a query without scanning the entire document corpus.
  • It can be implemented using a SQLite vector extension or an in-process vector index that integrates with the local database.

The vector database is not a replacement for relational storage. It complements the relational tables by enabling semantic matching, while documents, analysis_results, and messages continue to provide structured state and auditability.

docs.title: Retrieval and Context Assembly
docs.text:
When Spock needs grounded context, it follows a retrieval pipeline.

  1. Query embedding: The user's question or Deep Dive prompt is converted into an embedding vector.
  2. Similarity search: Spock searches vector_store for the closest matching chunk embeddings.
  3. Metadata filtering: Results are filtered by document status, user scope, file type, date range, or other constraints.
  4. Deduplication: Near-duplicate chunks are removed to avoid redundant context.
  5. Reranking: Optional reranking improves precision by scoring the relationship between the query and each candidate chunk.
  6. Prompt injection: The selected chunks are formatted into the LLM prompt with source attribution where appropriate.

This process allows Spock to answer questions using relevant document evidence rather than relying solely on the model's prior knowledge.

docs.title: Consistency, Caching, and Updates
docs.text:
Spock maintains consistency between document state and vector state.

  • If a document is deleted, its associated chunks and embeddings are removed or marked inactive.
  • If a document is modified, Spock compares the new file hash with the stored hash.
  • Only changed chunks are re-embedded when possible.
  • Embedding results are cached to avoid repeated inference for unchanged content.
  • Analysis results are cached in analysis_results so that repeated Deep Dive queries can reuse prior work.
  • SQLite transactions ensure that partial updates do not leave the database in an inconsistent state.

This combination of local persistence, semantic retrieval, and incremental updates allows Spock to provide responsive Ask AI and Deep Dive experiences while maintaining a durable, inspectable, and locally controlled data store.

docs.title: Interaction with Ask AI
docs.text:
The Ask AI module leverages ship_computer.db to support Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and session management. The database provides the persistent context needed to retrieve relevant source material, maintain conversation continuity across application restarts, and correctly attribute responses to specific user inquiries.

  1. Conversation History: Stores user prompts and model responses in the conversations table. This enables multi-turn sessions to preserve contextual memory, allowing the generative LLM to reference prior exchanges without requiring the user to repeat information.
  2. Knowledge Base Indexing: Stores metadata for document chunks alongside serialized embedding vectors or pointers to an external vector index. During query processing, Ask AI uses this data to efficiently locate and retrieve the most relevant document fragments.
  3. Session State: Tracks the active session identifier, turn ordering, and attribution metadata. This ensures that responses are correctly linked to the originating user prompt and that conversation threads remain isolated and traceable.

Schema Overview (Ask AI): - conversations: Stores chat history (id, user_query, model_response, timestamp) along with session identifiers and message metadata required for contextual continuity. - knowledge_chunks: Stores retrieved document fragments (chunk_id, content, source_url, embedding_vector). Depending on the deployment configuration, embeddings may be stored directly in the database or represented as foreign keys/references to an external vector store.

The fields above represent the core data structures utilized by Ask AI. Additional columns may be present for version control, relevance scoring, source provenance, or token usage accounting.

docs.title: Interaction with Deep Dive
docs.text:
The Deep Dive module performs intensive, multi-step analysis on user-provided inputs and requires structured storage for complex intermediate states and final outputs. The database supports full auditability, streamlined debugging, and the reuse of computationally expensive operations.

  1. Analysis Logs: Records each step executed during a deep dive (e.g., text extraction, parsing, cross-referencing, validation) in job and log tables such as analysis_jobs. This enables operators to monitor progress, inspect intermediate outputs, and diagnose failures without re-running the entire pipeline.
  2. Entity Extraction: Persists identified entities, attributes, and relationships extracted from source documents. Depending on the analysis type, this data is stored as structured relational rows or serialized within result metadata for flexible querying.
  3. Result Caching: Stores the outputs of heavy computations keyed to input hashes or identifiers. When equivalent inputs are submitted, Spock checks the cache first, allowing it to return prior results instantly instead of reprocessing identical source material.

Schema Overview (Deep Dive): - analysis_jobs: Tracks active, queued, and completed analysis tasks (job_id, input_file, status, completion_time) along with lifecycle metadata such as error codes and resource consumption. - extraction_results: Stores parsed data from specific files (file_path, extracted_text, metadata_json). Entity graphs, relationship mappings, or cache flags may be embedded within the JSON payload or normalized into adjacent tables for optimized querying.

The fields above describe the foundational Deep Dive records. Additional columns may exist for input hashing, detailed error tracing, execution timing, or result versioning.

docs.title: Connection Management
docs.text:
The Python application connects to the SQLite database using the standard sqlite3 module. The helper function below establishes a new connection for each request or operation, which is appropriate for local development and single-process deployments. If the application scales to multiple worker processes or threads, prefer short-lived connections per unit of work or introduce a managed connection pooling layer. Never share a raw SQLite connection across threads without explicit synchronization.

import sqlite3

# Standard connection pattern for Spock
def get_db_connection():
    conn = sqlite3.connect("ship_computer.db")
    conn.row_factory = sqlite3.Row  # Enable dictionary-like access
    return conn

Setting conn.row_factory to sqlite3.Row allows query results to be accessed by column name rather than positional index. This improves code readability, reduces indexing errors, and simplifies schema evolution.

Best Practices: - Transactions: All write operations (e.g., persisting conversation history or caching analysis results) should be wrapped in transactions to guarantee atomicity. In Python, a with conn: context manager automatically commits on success and rolls back if an unhandled exception occurs. - Connection Lifecycle: Close connections promptly after use. Prefer explicit try/finally blocks, or a custom context manager that closes the connection, to release file handles and prevent resource leaks. The built-in with conn: context manager manages transactions, not connection closure. - Write-Ahead Logging (WAL): Enable WAL mode (PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL;) to improve concurrent read performance and reduce lock contention during frequent writes. - Vacuuming & Maintenance: Periodic maintenance (e.g., VACUUM, ANALYZE) may be required if the database grows significantly or experiences heavy fragmentation. If Spock includes automated idle-time maintenance, rely on that; otherwise, schedule manual vacuuming during low-traffic windows.

docs.title: SQLite 3 ship_computer.db and Spock Interaction
docs.text: ship_computer.db is a local SQLite 3 database file that serves as Spock's relational store of record. It is used for durable application state, audit trails, session continuity, and lightweight retrieval metadata. In most Spock deployments, it does not replace the vector database; instead, it coordinates the data that the vector database indexes and the results that Spock returns to the user.

docs.title: Role in the Spock Application
docs.text:
• Durable state: Persists conversations, analysis jobs, extraction results, and cache entries so that Spock can resume work after restarts.
  • Auditability: Records who asked what, when, which sources were used, and which pipeline steps succeeded or failed.
  • Retrieval coordination: Stores chunk identifiers, source metadata, and optional embedding references that allow Spock to connect vector search results back to readable content.
  • Caching and reuse: Stores hashes, job outputs, and intermediate artifacts so expensive Deep Dive operations can be repeated without recomputation.
  • Local deployment: Because SQLite is embedded, Spock can run with minimal infrastructure while still providing transactional consistency for local or single-node deployments.

docs.title: Ask AI Inquiry Flow
docs.text:
When a user submits an Ask AI inquiry, Spock typically uses ship_computer.db in the following sequence:

  1. Resolve the session: Spock reads or creates a session identifier and loads prior conversation turns from conversations.
  2. Prepare retrieval context: Spock determines which knowledge base, source filters, or user permissions apply to the inquiry.
  3. Retrieve relevant chunks: Spock uses the vector database to find semantically similar chunks, then uses knowledge_chunks to load the chunk text, source URL, and provenance metadata.
  4. Build the prompt: Spock combines the user's current question, relevant conversation history, and retrieved source material into a prompt for the generative LLM.
  5. Store the response: After the LLM returns an answer, Spock writes the user prompt, model response, retrieved chunk references, relevance scores, and token usage to conversations or related metadata tables.
  6. Maintain continuity: The stored turn becomes part of the session history for future Ask AI inquiries.

This design keeps the vector database focused on similarity search while SQLite remains the source of truth for conversation history, source attribution, and operational metadata.

docs.title: Deep Dive Inquiry Flow
docs.text:
When a user submits a Deep Dive inquiry, Spock uses ship_computer.db to manage the full lifecycle of the analysis:

  1. Create the job: Spock inserts a row into analysis_jobs with the input identifier, status, timestamps, and any user or session context.
  2. Execute pipeline steps: As Spock extracts text, identifies entities, cross-references sources, and validates results, it writes step logs and intermediate artifacts to the database.
  3. Use semantic search: If the Deep Dive pipeline needs to compare new material against existing knowledge, Spock embeds the extracted text and queries the vector database for related chunks or entities.
  4. Persist results: Final or intermediate outputs are stored in extraction_results or adjacent tables, often with JSON payloads for flexible structures such as entity graphs.
  5. Cache expensive work: Spock stores result hashes and cached outputs so that equivalent Deep Dive inputs can be served from the database instead of re-running the pipeline.
  6. Support debugging: Operators can inspect job status, step logs, extracted entities, and cached results without relying on transient in-memory state.

docs.title: Typical Data Responsibilities
docs.text: Concern Stored in ship_computer.db Stored in vector DB Conversation history Yes No Session identifiers Yes No Document chunk text Yes, or referenced by ID No, unless duplicated for search Chunk metadata Yes Yes, as searchable metadata Embedding vectors Optional for small deployments Primary store Similarity search No, or limited Yes Analysis job state Yes No Extraction results Yes No Result cache Yes No

docs.title: Embedding LLM and Vector Database
docs.text: Spock uses an embedding LLM and a vector database to support semantic retrieval for both Ask AI and Deep Dive. The embedding LLM converts text into numerical vectors, and the vector database stores those vectors and finds the most similar ones to a user's inquiry.

docs.title: Embedding LLM
docs.text:
An embedding LLM is a model that maps text into a fixed-length vector of floating-point numbers. For example, a document chunk such as "The reactor coolant loop uses a closed-loop heat exchange design" may be converted into a vector with hundreds or thousands of dimensions. Texts with similar meaning produce vectors that are geometrically close, while unrelated texts produce vectors that are farther apart.

Spock uses the embedding LLM in two main ways:

  • Indexing: When source documents are added to the knowledge base, Spock splits them into chunks, embeds each chunk, and stores the resulting vector in the vector database.
  • Querying: When a user asks an Ask AI question or submits a Deep Dive input, Spock embeds the query or extracted text and uses that vector to search for semantically related content.

The embedding LLM is distinct from the generative LLM that writes natural-language answers. The embedding model is responsible for understanding meaning for retrieval, while the generative model is responsible for composing the final response.

docs.title: Vector Database
docs.text:
The vector database is the component that stores embedding vectors and performs fast similarity search. It may be a local library such as FAISS or Chroma, or a managed service such as Qdrant, Milvus, or pgvector. The exact implementation is deployment-specific, but its role in Spock is consistent:

  1. Store vectors: Each vector is associated with a chunk identifier, source metadata, and optional filters such as document type, date, or user scope.
  2. Build an index: The vector database creates an index that enables approximate nearest-neighbor search, allowing Spock to find relevant chunks quickly even when the knowledge base is large.
  3. Return candidates: Given a query vector, the vector database returns the top-k most similar chunks, often ranked by cosine similarity, dot product, or another distance metric.
  4. Support filtering: Spock can restrict search to specific sources, sessions, document categories, or permission scopes before or during vector search.

docs.title: How Spock Uses Them Together
docs.text:
For Ask AI, Spock typically follows this RAG pattern:

  1. The user submits a question.
  2. Spock embeds the question using the embedding LLM.
  3. Spock queries the vector database with that embedding.
  4. The vector database returns the most relevant chunk identifiers.
  5. Spock uses those identifiers to retrieve chunk text and metadata from ship_computer.db.
  6. Spock constructs a prompt that includes the question, conversation history, and retrieved context.
  7. The generative LLM produces an answer grounded in the retrieved material.
  8. Spock stores the answer and retrieval metadata in ship_computer.db.

For Deep Dive, Spock may use the same embedding and vector search capabilities in a more analytical way:

  1. Spock extracts text, entities, or claims from the user's input.
  2. Spock embeds those extracted items.
  3. Spock searches the vector database for related documents, prior analyses, or known entities.
  4. Spock compares, clusters, or cross-references the results as part of the Deep Dive pipeline.
  5. Spock stores the semantic matches, extracted entities, and final report in ship_computer.db.

docs.title: Relationship Between SQLite and the Vector Database
docs.text:
SQLite and the vector database serve different purposes:

  • SQLite is the relational, transactional store for Spock's durable state: conversations, jobs, logs, extraction results, cache entries, and chunk metadata.
  • Vector database is the semantic search engine for embeddings: it stores vectors and returns the most similar chunks or entities.
  • Spock is the orchestrator: it decides what to embed, what to search, how to combine results, and what to persist.

In a small deployment, Spock may store embedding vectors directly in ship_computer.db as BLOBs or use a SQLite vector extension. In a larger deployment, Spock usually stores only chunk identifiers and metadata in SQLite while the vector database holds the high-dimensional vectors and search index. This separation keeps SQLite lightweight and transactional while allowing the vector database to scale with the size of the knowledge base.

docs.title: ship_computer.db Interaction Architecture
docs.text:
ship_computer.db is the SQLite 3 persistence layer for the Spock application. It stores application state, conversation history, document chunks, analysis job metadata, cached extraction results, and operational telemetry. In a Python deployment, Spock typically accesses this database through the standard sqlite3 module or a thin data-access layer that enforces parameterized queries, transaction boundaries, and connection lifecycle management.

The database is designed to support two primary workloads:

  • Ask AI: A conversational, retrieval-augmented generation workflow where the user asks natural-language questions and Spock returns grounded answers using relevant document context.
  • Deep Dive: A structured analysis workflow where Spock processes one or more sources, extracts entities, relationships, summaries, or other analytical artifacts, and stores the results for later review.

The interaction follows a consistent request-response lifecycle:

  1. Request Ingestion

When a user submits a query or file, Spock generates a unique session or job identifier and writes an initial record to the appropriate table:

  • conversations for Ask AI requests.
  • analysis_jobs for Deep Dive requests.

This establishes an audit trail, enables crash recovery, and anchors subsequent operations to a stable identifier.

  1. Context Retrieval and Routing

  2. For Ask AI, Spock retrieves relevant document fragments from knowledge_chunks using semantic similarity. The retrieved chunks, together with recent conversation history from conversations, are assembled into a prompt context window for the generative LLM.

  3. For Deep Dive, Spock first checks extraction_results for a cached output. If a valid cache hit exists, the pipeline short-circuits and returns the stored result. Otherwise, Spock executes the analysis pipeline and logs each stage back to the database.

  4. LLM or Processing Execution

The assembled context is passed to the generative LLM or analysis engine. Intermediate states, such as streaming tokens, partial entity graphs, extraction progress, or pipeline stage status, may be written to staging or event tables to support real-time UI updates and recovery from interruptions.

  1. Response Persistence

Once processing completes, the final output, metadata, and performance metrics are committed to the database.

  • For Ask AI, Spock updates the conversations table with the model response, token usage, latency, model identifier, and any retrieval metadata.

  • For Deep Dive, Spock populates extraction_results, updates the job status to completed, and records completion timestamps, confidence scores, and processing metrics.

  • Cleanup and Indexing

Background tasks periodically prune expired sessions, archive stale jobs, update relevance or access metadata, and maintain database indexes. This helps query performance remain predictable as the database grows.

This architecture ensures that every interaction is traceable, stateful, and resilient to interruptions while maintaining a clear separation between conversational data and analytical workloads.

docs.title: Detailed SQLite 3 ship_computer.db Model
docs.text:
ship_computer.db is a single-file SQLite 3 database. It is well suited to Spock because it provides ACID transactions, JSON support, full-text search, and low operational overhead without requiring a separate database server.

The database is organized around several core concerns:

Concern Purpose Conversations Stores Ask AI user prompts, assistant responses, session context, and model metadata. Documents and chunks Stores ingested source material and the text fragments used for retrieval. Embeddings Stores vector representations of chunks and, where applicable, query vectors.
