Analysis jobs Tracks Deep Dive request lifecycle, configuration, status, and progress. Extraction results Stores cached Deep Dive outputs, including entities, relationships, summaries, and confidence data. Operational metadata Stores model versions, pipeline stages, errors, timing, and maintenance state.

A typical logical schema includes the following tables or table groups:

docs.title: conversations
docs.text:
Stores Ask AI interaction records. Depending on implementation, this table may represent one row per conversation or one row per message.

Representative fields:

  • id: Primary key.
  • session_id: Groups related messages into a single conversation.
  • user_id: Identifies the user or tenant.
  • role: user, assistant, system, or tool.
  • content: Prompt or response text.
  • model: Generative model identifier.
  • retrieval_metadata: JSON payload describing retrieved chunks, scores, and filters.
  • token_count: Input and output token usage.
  • latency_ms: Processing time.
  • created_at: Timestamp.
  • updated_at: Timestamp.

This table supports conversation continuity, prompt assembly, audit logging, and response replay.

docs.title: documents
docs.text:
Stores source documents that have been ingested into Spock.

Representative fields:

  • id: Primary key.
  • title: Human-readable document name.
  • source_type: File, URL, API, or manual entry.
  • source_uri: Original location or identifier.
  • content_hash: Hash used for deduplication and cache validation.
  • status: pending, processed, failed, or archived.
  • created_at: Timestamp.
  • updated_at: Timestamp.

This table provides the source of truth for document identity and lifecycle.

docs.title: knowledge_chunks
docs.text:
Stores the text fragments used for retrieval and context assembly.

Representative fields:

  • id: Primary key.
  • document_id: Foreign key to documents.
  • chunk_index: Position of the chunk within the source document.
  • content: Chunk text.
  • token_count: Approximate token length.
  • metadata_json: Source, permissions, language, section, or other filters.
  • embedding_model: Identifier of the embedding model used.
  • embedding_version: Version or hash of the embedding model.
  • embedding_blob: Binary vector representation, when stored locally.
  • created_at: Timestamp.

This table is central to Ask AI retrieval and Deep Dive evidence gathering.

docs.title: analysis_jobs
docs.text:
Stores Deep Dive job state.

Representative fields:

  • id: Primary key.
  • job_id: Public or external job identifier.
  • user_id: Requesting user or tenant.
  • source_id: Related document or source identifier.
  • status: queued, running, completed, failed, or cancelled.
  • request_json: Original user request and configuration.
  • config_json: Pipeline settings, extraction targets, and model parameters.
  • progress: Percentage or stage indicator.
  • error_message: Failure details, if present.
  • started_at: Timestamp.
  • completed_at: Timestamp.

This table allows Spock to track long-running analytical work and resume or inspect it later.

docs.title: extraction_results
docs.text:
Stores completed Deep Dive outputs.

Representative fields:

  • id: Primary key.
  • job_id: Foreign key to analysis_jobs.
  • result_json: Final structured output.
  • entities_json: Extracted entities.
  • relations_json: Extracted relationships or graph edges.
  • summary: Natural-language summary.
  • confidence: Overall confidence or quality score.
  • model: Analysis model identifier.
  • created_at: Timestamp.

This table enables cache hits, result comparison, and historical review.

docs.title: pipeline_events
docs.text:
Stores intermediate processing events for Deep Dive and, where useful, Ask AI.

Representative fields:

  • id: Primary key.
  • job_id: Related job or conversation identifier.
  • stage: Pipeline stage name.
  • status: started, completed, failed, or skipped.
  • payload_json: Stage-specific data.
  • created_at: Timestamp.

This table supports debugging, progress reporting, and crash recovery.

docs.title: sessions
docs.text:
Stores active user or application sessions.

Representative fields:

  • id: Primary key.
  • user_id: User or tenant identifier.
  • created_at: Timestamp.
  • expires_at: Expiration timestamp.
  • metadata_json: Client, device, or feature flags.

This table supports session pruning and access control.

docs.title: Ask AI Data Flow in ship_computer.db
docs.text:
Ask AI is a retrieval-augmented conversational workflow. The database participates at every stage.

  1. Session and message creation

Spock creates or reuses a session identifier and writes the user prompt to conversations.

  1. History retrieval

Spock loads recent messages for the session to provide conversational context. The number of messages included is controlled by token budget, latency requirements, and product policy.

  1. Query embedding

The user prompt, optionally combined with recent context, is converted into an embedding vector using the configured embedding model.

  1. Vector or full-text retrieval

Spock searches the vector store or local SQLite vector index for the most similar knowledge_chunks. If semantic search is unavailable, it may fall back to SQLite FTS5 or keyword search.

  1. Metadata filtering

Retrieved chunks are filtered by permissions, source type, recency, language, or other metadata before being included in the prompt.

  1. Prompt assembly

Spock combines the filtered chunks, conversation history, system instructions, and user question into a structured prompt.

  1. Generative LLM call

The prompt is sent to the generative LLM. Streaming tokens may be displayed in the UI while the final response is being generated.

  1. Response persistence

The assistant response, retrieval metadata, model identifier, token usage, and latency are written back to conversations.

  1. Post-processing

Spock may update access counts, relevance scores, or session metadata. It may also log retrieval quality signals for later evaluation.

docs.title: Deep Dive Data Flow in ship_computer.db
docs.text:
Deep Dive is a structured analytical workflow. The database is used to track job state, cache results, and preserve intermediate artifacts.

  1. Job creation

Spock creates an analysis_jobs record with status queued or running. The request payload, source identifiers, and configuration are stored in JSON fields.

  1. Cache check

Spock checks extraction_results for a valid cached result. A cache is considered valid when the source content hash, extraction configuration, model version, and schema version match the current request.

  1. Source preparation

If no cache hit exists, Spock loads the relevant document or chunks from documents and knowledge_chunks.

  1. Retrieval and evidence selection

For complex Deep Dive requests, Spock may use semantic search to identify the most relevant chunks before passing them to the analysis model.

  1. Analysis execution

The analysis engine extracts entities, relationships, summaries, or other requested artifacts. Stage transitions are recorded in pipeline_events.

  1. Result validation

Spock validates the output against the expected schema, applies confidence scoring, and normalizes the result.

  1. Result persistence

The final result is written to extraction_results, and the corresponding analysis_jobs record is updated to completed.

  1. Failure handling

If processing fails, Spock records the error in analysis_jobs and pipeline_events. The job may be retried, depending on configuration.

docs.title: Transactions, Concurrency, and Recovery
docs.text:
Because Spock is a Python application using SQLite 3, transaction management is important for consistency.

  • Parameterized queries prevent SQL injection.
  • Short transactions reduce lock contention.
  • WAL mode can improve concurrent read performance while writes are in progress.
  • Foreign keys help maintain referential integrity between documents, chunks, jobs, and results.
  • Idempotent job processing allows Spock to safely retry failed stages without duplicating results.
  • Event logging enables reconstruction of pipeline state after an interruption.

For long-running Deep Dive jobs, Spock should avoid holding database locks during LLM calls. Instead, it should persist job state before external processing, update progress in small transactions, and commit final results only after validation.

docs.title: Embedding LLM and Vector Database Integration
docs.text:
Spock uses an embedding model and a vector database to power semantic search and context retrieval. The embedding model converts text into numerical vectors, while the vector database stores those vectors and supports efficient similarity search.

Together, they allow Spock to retrieve contextually relevant information rather than relying only on exact keyword matching.

docs.title: Embedding Model Role
docs.text:
The embedding model is a non-generative language model that maps text into a fixed-dimensional vector space. In Spock, it is used for two purposes:

  1. Document embedding

During ingestion, document chunks are converted into vectors and stored with their metadata.

  1. Query embedding

During Ask AI or Deep Dive requests, the user prompt is converted into a vector using the same embedding model.

Using the same model for both documents and queries is essential because similarity is only meaningful when both sides of the comparison exist in the same vector space.

The embedding model captures semantic meaning, syntax, and contextual relationships. As a result, queries such as “What risks are mentioned in the contract?” can retrieve chunks containing “liability,” “indemnification,” or “breach,” even if the exact words do not match.

docs.title: Vector Database Role
docs.text:
The vector database stores embeddings and supports nearest-neighbor search. It may be:

  • An external vector database such as Chroma, Qdrant, Milvus, or Weaviate.
  • A local vector index such as FAISS.
  • A SQLite-based vector extension such as sqlite-vec, when the deployment is small or self-contained.

The vector database is responsible for:

  • Storing high-dimensional vectors.
  • Maintaining an approximate nearest-neighbor index.
  • Returning the top-K most similar chunks for a query vector.
  • Supporting metadata filters, such as permissions, source type, or recency.
  • Enabling fast search without scanning every stored vector.

docs.title: Ingestion Pipeline
docs.text:
When a document is added to Spock, the following steps occur:

  1. Document normalization

Spock extracts text from the source format, removes unnecessary markup, and normalizes encoding.

  1. Chunking

The document is split into overlapping or non-overlapping chunks. Chunk size is chosen to balance retrieval precision with context completeness.

  1. Metadata extraction

Spock records source, title, section, permissions, language, and other attributes.

  1. Embedding generation

Each chunk is passed through the embedding model to produce a vector.

  1. Persistence

The chunk text, metadata, embedding model identifier, and vector are stored in ship_computer.db or an external vector database.

  1. Index update

The vector index is updated so the new chunk can be retrieved immediately.

docs.title: Query-Time Retrieval Pipeline
docs.text:
During an Ask AI or Deep Dive request, Spock performs the following steps:

  1. Query preparation

Spock may rewrite, expand, or decompose the user prompt to improve retrieval quality.

  1. Query embedding

The prepared query is converted into a vector using the same embedding model used for document chunks.

  1. Vector search

Spock queries the vector database for the top-K most similar chunks. Similarity is typically measured using cosine similarity or inner product distance.

  1. Metadata filtering

Results are filtered by access permissions, source type, recency, language, or other business rules.

  1. Reranking

Optional reranking may reorder candidates using a cross-encoder, keyword score, or business-specific relevance heuristic.

  1. Context assembly

The final chunks are formatted into the LLM prompt with citations or source identifiers.

  1. Response generation

The generative LLM produces an answer grounded in the retrieved context.

docs.title: Local SQLite Vector Storage
docs.text:
For small or self-contained deployments, Spock can store embeddings directly in ship_computer.db.

In this mode:

  • Embeddings are stored as BLOB values in knowledge_chunks or a dedicated vector table.
  • The embedding model name and version are stored alongside each vector.
  • Similarity search may use brute-force comparison for small datasets or a SQLite vector extension for larger datasets.
  • FTS5 can provide keyword-based fallback search.

This approach keeps the deployment simple and portable, but it is best suited to moderate data volumes.

docs.title: External Vector Database
docs.text:
For larger deployments, Spock can use an external vector database.

In this mode:

  • ship_computer.db remains the system of record for conversations, jobs, documents, and metadata.
  • The external vector database stores embeddings and provides high-performance ANN search.
  • Spock synchronizes chunk metadata between SQLite and the vector store.
  • Deletions, updates, and re-indexing are coordinated to prevent stale vectors.

This separation allows Spock to scale retrieval independently from transactional application state.

docs.title: Fallback, Versioning, and Re-indexing
docs.text:
Spock should treat embedding search as a preferred path, not the only path.

  • If the embedding service is unavailable, Spock can fall back to SQLite FTS5 or keyword search.
  • If the vector database is unavailable, Spock can return cached results, limited context, or a degraded response with a clear notice.
  • Embedding vectors are versioned with the model identifier and model version.
  • If the embedding model changes, Spock triggers a background re-indexing job so that new queries are compared against vectors generated by the current model.
  • Old vectors may be retained temporarily for rollback or comparison, then pruned after validation.

This integration ensures that Spock retrieves contextually relevant information, improves response accuracy, reduces hallucination, and supports efficient handling of complex, multi-document inquiries.

docs.title: Profiles
docs.text: Profiles store per-workstation configurations, such as model selections, ports, paths, and preferences. They allow settings to be customized for a particular workstation without altering the configuration of other workstations.

docs.title: Storage
docs.text:
Profiles are managed by WarpCore.profile_store and persisted to SQLite 3. The central database file is ship_computer.db, which stores profile configurations alongside core operational data required by the Spock application. This includes structured records for Ask AI inquiries, which are focused on information retrieval, and Deep Dive inquiries, which are focused on complex analysis and multi-step reasoning. Key tables include profiles, inquiries, and results.

Database interactions are wrapped in explicit transactions, with automatic rollback available when an operation fails. This ensures that configuration and inquiry data remain consistent across both successful and failed updates.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
from WarpCore.profile_store import ProfileStore

store = ProfileStore()
profile = store.get_active()
print(profile.model_name)

This example retrieves the currently active profile using ProfileStore.get_active() and prints its model name, assuming the returned profile object exposes a model_name attribute. Callers should verify that get_active() returns a valid profile instance before accessing its attributes to prevent NoneType errors.

docs.title: Creating a Profile
docs.text:
store = ProfileStore()
store.create(name="workstation-1", model="llama-3-8b", port=8081)

This creates a new profile named workstation-1 with the specified model and port, then persists it to SQLite. Once created, the profile can be reused in subsequent sessions or operations that require workstation-specific settings. Profiles may also store additional configuration values, such as file paths, API keys, or UI preferences, depending on the application's schema design.

docs.title: Lifecycle Management
docs.text: Profiles are managed as persistent records within the store: they can be created, retrieved, updated, and deleted when no longer needed. Removing unused profiles prevents stale configurations from accumulating in the database. For example, a profile can be removed with store.delete(name="workstation-1"). The store automatically handles foreign key constraints to ensure related inquiry and result records are archived or cleaned up according to the defined retention policy.

docs.title: Database Core: ship_computer.db and Spock Integration
docs.text: The ship_computer.db file serves as the central SQLite 3 database for the application, managing both profile configurations and core operational data required by the Spock application. This database is structured to support reliable, auditable queries for AI-driven tasks, specifically handling Ask AI inquiries and Deep Dive inquiries.

docs.title: Schema Overview
docs.text:
The database schema normalizes data while maintaining strict transactional safety. Normalization reduces redundant storage of profile settings, inquiry metadata, and results, making updates easier to maintain. Transactional safety ensures that related changes are committed together or not at all. Key tables include:

  • profiles: Stores configuration details for each workstation, including model paths, API ports, preference flags, and active status indicators.
  • inquiries: Logs metadata for every Ask AI or Deep Dive request, including timestamps, user identifiers, query hashes, session IDs, and inquiry type flags.
  • results: Stores the output of AI processing, linked to specific inquiry IDs for retrieval, auditing, and caching. Deep Dive inquiries may contain multiple result rows representing intermediate reasoning steps.

Depending on the deployment, additional tables or external stores may also be used for inquiry_steps, embeddings, vector_chunks, or checkpoint data. In such cases, ship_computer.db remains the authoritative relational store for profiles, inquiry metadata, and final or intermediate results, while the vector database stores semantic representations used for retrieval.

docs.title: Embedding LLM and Vector Database
docs.text:
Spock uses an embedding LLM, or a dedicated embedding model, to convert text into numerical vector representations. These vectors capture semantic meaning, allowing Spock to compare the similarity between a user query and stored content without relying only on keyword matching.

The embedding process works as follows:

  1. Text preparation: Spock receives a user query, document chunk, intermediate reasoning artifact, or other text item.
  2. Embedding generation: The embedding LLM converts the text into a fixed-size vector.
  3. Vector storage: The vector, along with associated metadata, is stored in the vector database.
  4. Semantic search: When a new query is submitted, Spock embeds the query and searches the vector database for the most similar stored vectors.
  5. Context assembly: The retrieved chunks or artifacts are ranked, filtered, and assembled into a context window for the generative model or analysis engine.

The vector database is responsible for storing and querying these embeddings efficiently. It may be implemented as a separate vector database service or as a SQLite-backed vector extension, depending on the deployment. In either case, Spock treats it as a semantic index that supports fast approximate nearest-neighbor search.

For Ask AI inquiries, the embedding LLM and vector database are used primarily for retrieval. Spock embeds the user's question, searches the vector database for relevant documents, notes, or prior results, and then provides the most relevant context to the generative model. This allows the model to answer from grounded, workstation-specific information rather than relying solely on its internal knowledge.

For Deep Dive inquiries, the embedding LLM and vector database support multi-step reasoning. Spock may embed the initial question, intermediate hypotheses, retrieved evidence, and generated analysis steps. During each reasoning step, Spock can query the vector database to find relevant prior context, compare new findings against earlier artifacts, and retrieve supporting evidence. This helps the application maintain continuity across long-running analyses and reduces the risk of losing important context between steps.

The vector database does not replace ship_computer.db. Instead, it complements it. ship_computer.db stores structured, transactional records such as profiles, inquiry metadata, result payloads, and audit information. The vector database stores semantic representations used for similarity search and context retrieval. Together, they allow Spock to combine reliable relational persistence with flexible semantic search.

docs.title: Spock Application Interaction
docs.text:
The Spock application interacts with ship_computer.db through a managed database layer that controls connection pooling, query optimization, and write ordering. This interaction ensures that:

  1. Ask AI Inquiries: When a user submits an Ask AI query, the system logs the request in inquiries, retrieves relevant context via semantic search, and stores the final response in results. This supports historical tracking of knowledge retrieval while minimizing direct exposure of sensitive raw data to the generative model.
  2. Deep Dive Inquiries: For complex tasks requiring multi-step reasoning, the database persists intermediate states, checkpoint tokens, and final outputs. This allows an interrupted Deep Dive session to resume from the last committed transaction in ship_computer.db without losing computational progress.

docs.title: Ask AI and Deep Dive Inquiry Processing
docs.text:
Spock treats Ask AI and Deep Dive as distinct inquiry types because they have different processing requirements.

Ask AI is optimized for fast, grounded information retrieval. A typical Ask AI flow is:

  1. The user submits a question.
  2. Spock creates an inquiry record in inquiries.
  3. Spock loads the active profile to determine the model, retrieval settings, and workstation-specific preferences.
  4. Spock embeds the question using the embedding LLM.
  5. Spock queries the vector database for the most relevant chunks, documents, or prior results.
  6. Spock ranks and filters the retrieved context.
  7. Spock sends the question and selected context to the generative model.
  8. Spock stores the final answer in results.
  9. The inquiry, result, and related metadata remain available for auditing, replay, or follow-up questions.

Deep Dive is optimized for complex, multi-step analysis. A typical Deep Dive flow is:

  1. The user submits a complex task or research question.
  2. Spock creates an inquiry record in inquiries and marks it as a Deep Dive inquiry.
  3. Spock breaks the task into reasoning steps, sub-questions, or analysis checkpoints.
  4. For each step, Spock may embed the step's context and query the vector database for relevant evidence.
  5. Spock generates intermediate reasoning artifacts, such as hypotheses, summaries, comparisons, or partial conclusions.
  6. Spock persists intermediate results and checkpoints in results or related step tables.
  7. If the session is interrupted, Spock can resume from the last committed checkpoint.
  8. When the analysis is complete, Spock stores the final output in results and links it back to the original inquiry.

This separation allows Spock to provide quick answers for simple retrieval tasks while preserving enough state to support long-running, iterative analysis.

docs.title: Data Flow and Audit Trail
docs.text:
Each AI-driven request follows a consistent lifecycle:

  1. Spock creates or identifies an inquiry record in inquiries.
  2. The application retrieves profile settings and any relevant context needed for the task.
  3. The model or analysis engine produces a response or intermediate result.
  4. The final output is written to results and linked back to the original inquiry via foreign keys.

This flow provides an auditable trail that connects user intent, system configuration, and generated output without requiring raw sensitive data to be retained in every result record. Indexes on inquiry_id, timestamp, and user_id ensure rapid retrieval for logging and debugging.

docs.title: Transactional Integrity
docs.text: All interactions between Spock and the SQLite database are wrapped in explicit transactions. This prevents partial writes, such as an incomplete Deep Dive analysis, from leaving orphaned data in the database. If a query fails or a timeout occurs, the transaction is rolled back automatically, maintaining the consistency of the ship_computer.db file across all sessions. SQLite's Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) mode is enabled to allow concurrent reads during heavy write operations, ensuring the application remains responsive during intensive AI workloads.

docs.title: Embedding LLM and Vector Database Integration
docs.text:
The Spock application uses a dedicated embedding LLM and a vector database to provide semantic search and context retrieval. This design separates raw document storage from AI reasoning, allowing fast, relevance-driven retrieval for both Ask AI and Deep Dive workflows.

The embedding LLM converts text into numerical vectors that represent meaning. The vector database stores those vectors and supports similarity search. SQLite 3, through ship_computer.db, stores relational metadata, permissions, session state, audit records, and synchronization information. Together, these components allow Spock to retrieve relevant context, enforce access control, and maintain a reliable record of AI-assisted analysis.

docs.title: Embedding Pipeline Architecture
docs.text:
When a user submits a query or when new documents are ingested, Spock routes the text through the embedding LLM. The model transforms unstructured text into high-dimensional dense vectors, also called embeddings. These vectors capture semantic similarity rather than exact keyword matches.

The resulting vectors are stored in a vector database optimized for Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) search. ANN search allows Spock to find the most similar vectors quickly, even when the index contains a large number of document chunks.

The vector database operates alongside ship_computer.db. The vector store holds the numerical embeddings and lightweight payload references, while SQLite 3 holds the authoritative relational metadata needed for permissions, citations, session tracking, and auditability.

docs.title: Semantic Retrieval for Ask AI
docs.text:
For Ask AI inquiries, the embedding pipeline enables rapid context assembly:

  1. The user's question is converted into an embedding vector.
  2. The vector database performs a similarity search against indexed document chunks and returns the most semantically relevant passages.
  3. Spock uses ship_computer.db to resolve vector IDs to document chunks, verify access permissions, retrieve source metadata, and rank or filter candidates.
  4. The selected chunks are formatted into a context window.
  5. The generative LLM receives the original query and the retrieved context, producing a grounded, citation-ready response.

This retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) approach reduces hallucination and ensures Ask AI responses are tied to verified source material.

docs.title: Context Management for Deep Dive
docs.text:
Deep Dive inquiries require sustained context across multiple reasoning steps. The embedding LLM and vector database support this by:

  • Chunking and Indexing: Long documents, reports, or conversation histories are split into manageable segments, embedded, and indexed for fast lookup.
  • Dynamic Context Refreshing: As the Deep Dive session progresses, intermediate outputs, hypotheses, and analysis notes are embedded and stored. The vector database re-ranks relevant context based on the evolving query trajectory, helping the generative model focus on the most pertinent information.
  • State Checkpointing: Vector metadata is synchronized with ship_computer.db at each reasoning step. If a session is interrupted, Spock can reconstruct the semantic context from stored checkpoints and resume analysis without reprocessing previously evaluated data.

docs.title: Vector-Relational Synchronization
docs.text:
To maintain data integrity, Spock synchronizes vector database operations with the relational schema:

  • Every vector insertion or update generates a corresponding metadata record in ship_computer.db, linking vector IDs to inquiry sessions, user profiles, document sources, and access permissions.
  • Batch operations are coordinated with database transactions where possible. Because the vector database and SQLite 3 are separate stores, Spock uses idempotent writes, reconciliation logs, and periodic verification to prevent drift.
  • Periodic reconciliation jobs verify that vector embeddings correspond to their source documents, flagging or re-embedding corrupted, stale, or permission-mismatched entries.

This hybrid architecture combines the speed and semantic accuracy of vector search with the reliability and auditability of SQLite 3, providing a robust foundation for Spock's AI-driven workflows.

docs.title: SQLite 3 ship_computer.db Integration
docs.text: ship_computer.db is the local SQLite 3 database used by Spock to manage relational state. It is not the primary store for large-scale vector search. Instead, it provides the structured, transactional, and auditable layer that surrounds the vector database.

docs.title: Core Responsibilities
docs.text:
ship_computer.db is responsible for:

  • Document and chunk metadata: source file, title, author, version, ingestion timestamp, content hash, and chunk boundaries.
  • Vector linkage: mapping vector IDs to document chunks, embedding model versions, and index identifiers.
  • Access control: user roles, document permissions, session-scoped permissions, and audit-relevant access decisions.
  • Ask AI state: inquiry records, query text, retrieved context, generated responses, citations, and feedback.
  • Deep Dive state: session records, reasoning steps, checkpoints, intermediate artifacts, status, and resume information.
  • Synchronization and reconciliation: logs of vector insertions, updates, deletions, failed operations, and consistency checks.

docs.title: Conceptual Schema
docs.text:
A simplified schema might include the following tables:

CREATE TABLE documents (
    document_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    title TEXT NOT NULL,
    source_uri TEXT,
    content_hash TEXT NOT NULL,
    created_at TEXT NOT NULL,
    updated_at TEXT NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE chunks (
    chunk_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    document_id TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES documents(document_id),
    chunk_index INTEGER NOT NULL,
    content TEXT NOT NULL,
    token_count INTEGER,
    created_at TEXT NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE vector_metadata (
    vector_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    chunk_id TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES chunks(chunk_id),
    embedding_model TEXT NOT NULL,
    embedding_version TEXT NOT NULL,
    index_name TEXT NOT NULL,
    created_at TEXT NOT NULL,
    updated_at TEXT NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE sessions (
    session_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id TEXT NOT NULL,
    mode TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (mode IN ('ask_ai', 'deep_dive')),
    status TEXT NOT NULL,
    created_at TEXT NOT NULL,
    updated_at TEXT NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE inquiry_events (
    event_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    session_id TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES sessions(session_id),
    step_index INTEGER,
    event_type TEXT NOT NULL,
    payload_json TEXT,
    created_at TEXT NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE permissions (
    permission_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id TEXT NOT NULL,
    document_id TEXT REFERENCES documents(document_id),
    access_level TEXT NOT NULL,
    granted_at TEXT NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE sync_state (
    sync_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    operation TEXT NOT NULL,
    vector_id TEXT,
    chunk_id TEXT,
    status TEXT NOT NULL,
    error_message TEXT,
    created_at TEXT NOT NULL
);

The exact schema may vary by deployment, but the important architectural point is that SQLite 3 stores the relational facts needed to interpret, secure, and audit vector search results.

docs.title: Ask AI Interaction
docs.text:
During an Ask AI inquiry, ship_computer.db participates in the following sequence:

  1. Inquiry creation: Spock records the user, session, timestamp, and original question.
  2. Permission resolution: Spock checks which documents and chunks the user may access.
  3. Vector search: The embedding LLM converts the question into a vector, and the vector database returns candidate vector IDs.
  4. Metadata resolution: Spock joins vector IDs to vector_metadata, chunks, and documents to retrieve readable text, source information, and citation data.
  5. Context filtering: Chunks that fail permission checks, are stale, or are outside the requested scope are removed.
  6. Response storage: The final answer, retrieved context, citations, model version, and user feedback are stored for audit and follow-up.

This allows Ask AI to be both semantically flexible and operationally accountable.

docs.title: Deep Dive Interaction
docs.text:
For Deep Dive, ship_computer.db provides durable session state. Each reasoning step can be recorded as an event or checkpoint, including:

  • the current question or hypothesis,
  • the vector IDs used to retrieve context,
  • the chunks selected for the generative LLM,
  • the intermediate output produced,
  • the status of the step,
  • and any errors or reconciliation flags.

When a Deep Dive session resumes, Spock reads the latest checkpoint from ship_computer.db, reconstructs the semantic context from the referenced vector IDs, and continues from the recorded state. This prevents loss of analytical progress and supports reproducible review of how a conclusion was reached.

docs.title: How Spock Uses the Embedding LLM and Vector Database
docs.text: Spock uses the embedding LLM and vector database as a semantic retrieval layer. The embedding LLM is responsible for converting text into a numerical representation that can be compared by similarity. The vector database is responsible for storing those representations and returning the closest matches to a query vector.

docs.title: Embedding LLM Responsibilities
docs.text:
The embedding LLM:

  • Converts user questions, document chunks, and Deep Dive intermediate outputs into dense vectors.
  • Preserves semantic relationships so that conceptually similar text produces nearby vectors.
  • Enables retrieval by meaning rather than exact phrase matching.
  • Supports consistent indexing and querying when the same model version is used for both ingestion and search.

The embedding LLM does not generate the final user-facing answer. Its role is to create searchable representations of text.

docs.title: Vector Database Responsibilities
docs.text:
The vector database:

  • Stores embeddings for indexed document chunks and, where appropriate, intermediate Deep Dive artifacts.
  • Supports ANN search to find the most similar vectors to a query embedding.
  • Returns vector IDs and optional payload data, such as chunk references or source identifiers.
  • Enables fast retrieval over large corpora without requiring full-text keyword matching.

The vector database does not replace relational storage. It does not own permissions, audit logs, session state, or document lifecycle metadata. Those responsibilities remain in ship_computer.db.

docs.title: Ingestion Flow
docs.text:
When Spock ingests a document:

  1. The document is validated and stored as a relational record in ship_computer.db.
  2. The document is split into chunks suitable for embedding and retrieval.
  3. Each chunk is sent to the embedding LLM.
  4. The resulting vector is stored in the vector database.
  5. A metadata record is written to ship_computer.db, linking the vector ID to the chunk, document, embedding model, and index.
  6. Permissions and audit metadata are associated with the document and chunk.

docs.title: Query Flow
docs.text:
When Spock answers a question:

  1. The user query is embedded using the same embedding LLM used during ingestion.
  2. The vector database searches for the nearest vectors.
  3. Candidate vector IDs are returned to Spock.
  4. Spock resolves those IDs against ship_computer.db to obtain chunk text, document metadata, and access permissions.
  5. The context is filtered, ranked, and formatted.
  6. The generative LLM produces the final response using the query and retrieved context.
  7. The response and retrieval metadata are recorded in ship_computer.db.

docs.title: Why This Separation Matters
docs.text:
Separating the embedding LLM, vector database, and SQLite 3 database gives Spock three distinct capabilities:

  • Semantic retrieval through embeddings and ANN search.
  • Relational integrity through SQLite 3 transactions, foreign keys, and audit records.
  • Operational control through permissions, session checkpoints, and reconciliation.

This separation allows Spock to scale vector search independently while preserving a reliable, inspectable record of every Ask AI and Deep Dive interaction.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Global and per-profile settings are managed by WarpCore.settings_store, which persists data in ship_computer.db. This database acts as the persistent state store for user preferences, runtime configurations, and session metadata. Canonical port mappings, documentation URLs, and context / max_tokens defaults are defined in WarpCore/service_endpoints.py and seeded via WarpCore/config_defaults.py.

Per-profile settings allow different model or embedding profiles to use distinct endpoints and context limits, while global settings provide shared fallback values when a profile-specific value is not defined.

docs.title: Service ports (defaults)
docs.text:
Role Default App config / env Embeddings 8080 embed_port, embedding_profile.embeddings_url, SPOCK_EMBED_PORT Chat 8081 llama_port, SPOCK_CHAT_PORT Llama WebUI proxy 8082 mcp.webui_port, SPOCK_MCP_WEBUI_PORT RAG API 8090 rag_api.port, SPOCK_RAG_PORT MCP HTTP 8765 mcp.http_port, SPOCK_MCP_PORT AI Helper docs 8000 docs_port, SPOCK_DOCS_PORT

The values in the App config / env column represent alternative sources for the same logical endpoint. A full URL setting, such as embedding_profile.embeddings_url, may include a port and can be used to specify the complete endpoint address.

Context Settings: embed_n_ctx, chat_n_ctx, and chat_max_tokens control the model's context window size and maximum output length. These are configured via Configure Spock AI → Llama.cpp.

  • embed_n_ctx: Maximum number of tokens that can be processed for embedding-related context.
  • chat_n_ctx: Maximum number of tokens available to the chat model during inference.
  • chat_max_tokens: Maximum number of tokens allowed in a generated response.

These settings can be edited in the Configure Spock AI interface, or set using SPOCK_* environment variables before launching the application. If installing a second instance on the same machine, ensure that different ports are used or stop the first instance to avoid binding conflicts.

docs.title: SQLite 3 ship_computer.db
docs.text:
ship_computer.db is a local SQLite 3 database used by the Spock application as its primary persistent state store. It is embedded in the application, meaning it does not require a separate database server. The database stores configuration, session state, document metadata, retrieval results, and other data needed to support Ask AI and Deep Dive inquiries.

In practice, ship_computer.db may contain logical data groups such as:

  • Settings: global and per-profile configuration values.
  • Profiles: model, embedding, endpoint, and context-window settings.
  • Sessions: conversation state, user prompts, assistant responses, and follow-up context.
  • Documents: metadata for uploaded or indexed documents, including source, title, owner, and status.
  • Chunks: document fragments used for retrieval, including chunk text, position, and associated document.
  • Embeddings: vector representations of chunks or queries, either stored directly in SQLite or referenced from an external vector database.
  • Retrieval results: cached or logged search results, similarity scores, and selected context for a given inquiry.
  • Usage or audit data: timestamps, profile selections, model endpoints, and request metadata.

The exact table names and schema may vary by deployment, but the database serves as the durable record of what the user configured, what content was indexed, and how the application answered previous questions.

docs.title: How Ask AI uses ship_computer.db
docs.text:
Ask AI is a direct question-and-answer mode. When a user submits an Ask AI request, Spock uses ship_computer.db to resolve the active configuration and to preserve the resulting conversation.

A typical Ask AI flow is:

  1. Resolve the active profile Spock reads the selected or default profile from the database. This profile determines which embedding endpoint, chat endpoint, context limits, and model settings should be used.

  2. Load context settings Values such as embed_n_ctx, chat_n_ctx, and chat_max_tokens are read from the profile or global settings. These values control how much context can be sent to the embedding model and how much output the chat model may generate.

  3. Prepare the user query The user's question is normalized and prepared for retrieval. Depending on the implementation, Spock may also include recent conversation context from the session stored in the database.

  4. Retrieve relevant content The query is converted into an embedding and used to search the vector database. The retrieved chunks, their scores, and their source metadata are used to build the prompt for the chat model.

  5. Generate the answer The chat model receives the user question, retrieved context, and any system instructions. It returns a natural-language answer.

  6. Persist the interaction Spock stores the user question, assistant answer, selected profile, retrieved chunk references, and timestamps in ship_computer.db. This allows the conversation to continue, be reviewed later, or be used for follow-up questions.

docs.title: How Deep Dive uses ship_computer.db
docs.text:
Deep Dive is a more thorough inquiry mode. Instead of answering from a single retrieval pass, Deep Dive may perform multiple retrieval steps, expand the search, compare sources, and synthesize a longer response.

ship_computer.db supports Deep Dive by storing both the final answer and the intermediate state of the investigation.

A typical Deep Dive flow is:

  1. Create or resume a Deep Dive session Spock creates a session record in the database. This record tracks the user's original request, the active profile, and the current stage of the analysis.

  2. Perform initial retrieval The user's request is embedded and used to search the vector database. The most relevant chunks are selected.

  3. Generate follow-up queries The chat model may identify gaps in the retrieved context and generate additional search queries. These queries are embedded and used to retrieve more content.

  4. Accumulate evidence Retrieved chunks, similarity scores, source documents, and intermediate summaries are stored or referenced in the database. This allows Spock to avoid repeating work and to maintain a consistent evidence set.

  5. Synthesize the final response The chat model combines the accumulated context into a detailed answer, report, or analysis.

  6. Persist the Deep Dive result The final response, supporting citations, retrieved chunk references, and session state are written to ship_computer.db. This enables the user to return to the Deep Dive later, ask follow-up questions, or review the sources used.

docs.title: Embedding LLM and vector database
docs.text: Spock uses an embedding LLM and a vector database to support retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG. The embedding LLM converts text into numerical vectors, and the vector database stores and searches those vectors to find content that is semantically similar to the user's question.

docs.title: Embedding LLM
docs.text:
The embedding LLM is a model that produces dense vector representations of text. Unlike the chat model, it does not generate natural-language answers. Instead, it maps text into a fixed-size numerical vector that captures semantic meaning.

In Spock, the embedding LLM is typically exposed through the embeddings endpoint, commonly on port 8080. The active embedding profile determines which endpoint, model, and context settings are used.

The embedding LLM is used for:

  • Document chunking and indexing When documents are added to Spock, they are split into chunks. Each chunk is sent to the embedding LLM and converted into a vector.

  • Query embedding When a user asks a question in Ask AI or Deep Dive, the question is sent to the embedding LLM and converted into a query vector.

  • Semantic matching The query vector is compared against stored chunk vectors to find the most relevant content.

The embed_n_ctx setting controls how much text the embedding model can process at once. If a chunk or query exceeds this limit, Spock must truncate, split, or otherwise manage the input before sending it to the embedding endpoint.

docs.title: Vector database
docs.text:
The vector database stores the embeddings produced by the embedding LLM. Each vector is associated with metadata, such as the source document, chunk identifier, profile, timestamp, and relevance score.

The vector database may be implemented in one of two ways:

  • SQLite-backed vector storage Vectors are stored directly in ship_computer.db, often as binary BLOB values. This keeps the system self-contained and simple to deploy.

  • External vector database Vectors are stored in a dedicated vector database, while ship_computer.db stores metadata, session state, and references to the external vectors.

In either case, the vector database enables similarity search. When Spock receives a query vector, it searches for the closest stored vectors, usually using cosine similarity or another distance metric. The top matching chunks are returned with their scores and metadata.

docs.title: Typical Ask AI and Deep Dive retrieval flow
docs.text:
The following flow describes how Spock uses the embedding LLM and vector database for both Ask AI and Deep Dive:

  1. User submits a question The question is received by the Spock application.

  2. Active profile is resolved Spock reads the selected profile from ship_computer.db and determines the embedding endpoint, chat endpoint, and context limits.

  3. Question is embedded The question is sent to the embedding LLM endpoint. The model returns a vector representation of the question.

  4. Vector search is performed The query vector is compared against stored chunk vectors in the vector database. The most similar chunks are selected.

  5. Retrieved context is assembled Spock combines the selected chunks, their metadata, and any session context into a prompt for the chat model.

  6. Chat model generates a response The chat model uses the retrieved context to answer the user's question.

  7. Result is persisted The question, answer, profile, retrieved chunk references, and session state are stored in ship_computer.db.

For Ask AI, this process is usually a single retrieval-and-answer cycle. For Deep Dive, the process may repeat with additional queries, broader retrieval, and intermediate summaries until the application has enough context to produce a detailed response.

docs.title: Configuration Hierarchy
docs.text:
Settings follow a strict precedence order where higher-priority sources override lower-priority ones:

  1. Hardcoded Defaults: Values defined in WarpCore/config_defaults.py and WarpCore/service_endpoints.py.
  2. Environment Variables: SPOCK_* variables (e.g., SPOCK_CHAT_PORT) override defaults if set before startup.
  3. Database/UI Config: Persistent settings saved to ship_computer.db or modified via the Configure Spock AI UI take precedence over environment variables for runtime behavior.

In practice, a fresh installation uses hardcoded defaults unless SPOCK_* environment variables are present at startup. Once a value is saved in the database through the application UI, that stored value becomes the active setting until it is explicitly changed again.

docs.title: SQLite Database Architecture & Interaction
docs.text:
The ship_computer.db file is a local SQLite 3 database that serves as the central repository for application state. It interacts with the Spock application to manage persistent data required for both Ask AI and Deep Dive inquiries.

ship_computer.db is responsible for storing the information Spock needs to preserve continuity across sessions, restore user preferences, resume interrupted work, and coordinate with external or embedded model services. It is not primarily used to store large model weights or raw vector indexes, but it does store the metadata, configuration, session state, and indexing status needed to locate, validate, and reuse those resources.

Database Management: * Storage Engine: Uses SQLite 3 for lightweight, serverless storage optimized for desktop applications. The database operates in WAL (Write-Ahead Logging) mode to allow concurrent reads while writes are occurring, preventing lock contention during active AI sessions. * Access Layer: The WarpCore.settings_store module abstracts direct database access, providing a clean, type-safe API for reading and writing configuration values, session metadata, and analysis checkpoints. * Initialization: The database schema is auto-generated on first launch using the structure and seed values defined in WarpCore/config_defaults.py. Subsequent launches validate the schema version and apply incremental migrations if necessary.

Interaction with Ask AI: For Ask AI inquiries, the database stores and retrieves: * User Preferences: Specific context window sizes (embed_n_ctx, chat_n_ctx) and token limits (chat_max_tokens) that dictate how much input context the model can process and how long a generated response may be. * Session State: Metadata regarding active chat sessions, including conversation history pointers, selected model profiles, and prompt templates. This ensures continuity between user interactions without reloading the entire context into memory. * Configuration Overrides: Any UI modifications made in Configure Spock AI are written here, ensuring that Ask AI uses the most recent settings rather than static environment variables or hardcoded defaults.

Interaction with Deep Dive: For Deep Dive inquiries (long-context analysis), the database supports: * Session Persistence: Maintains state for long-running analysis tasks, including document ingestion progress, chunking strategies, and intermediate reasoning steps. This prevents data loss if the application restarts unexpectedly. * Analysis Logs & Checkpoints: Stores configuration snapshots and vector indexing status associated with specific deep dive sessions, allowing users to resume, branch, or review past analyses without reprocessing source documents. * Resource Management: Tracks active connections, embedding cache status, and memory allocation limits to optimize performance during heavy computational tasks. The database also logs rate-limiting states and fallback routing decisions when primary endpoints are unavailable.

Loading Configuration: To retrieve the current application state from the database, use the following import:

from WarpCore.settings_store import load_app_config

# Load persisted configuration from the database
cfg = load_app_config("ship_computer.db")

The path should point to the actual ship_computer.db file. If the application uses a default storage location, pass that resolved path instead of a relative filename. The settings_store automatically handles connection pooling, schema validation, and graceful fallback to defaults if the database is corrupted or missing.

docs.title: Embedding LLM and Vector Database Workflow
docs.text:
Spock uses an embedding LLM and a vector database to turn unstructured text into searchable, semantically meaningful representations. This allows the application to retrieve relevant context for Ask AI and to analyze large document sets during Deep Dive without relying solely on keyword matching or manual indexing.

An embedding LLM is a model that converts text into a fixed-length numeric vector, also called an embedding. Each vector represents the semantic meaning of the text in a high-dimensional space. Text with similar meaning produces vectors that are close together, while unrelated text produces vectors that are farther apart.

A vector database stores these embeddings along with metadata such as source document, chunk ID, timestamp, model version, and content hash. During a query, Spock embeds the user's question or analysis prompt, searches the vector database for the most similar stored vectors, and then uses the associated text chunks as context for the chat or reasoning model.

docs.title: How Spock Uses the Embedding LLM
docs.text:
1. Text Preparation: Spock normalizes and chunks incoming text. For Ask AI, this may include the user's question, recent conversation context, and selected reference material. For Deep Dive, this includes source documents, reports, logs, or other long-form content.

  2. Embedding Generation: The embedding LLM converts each text chunk into a vector. The model profile, context length, batch size, and endpoint selection are read from ship_computer.db or the active configuration hierarchy.

  3. Cache Validation: Before generating new embeddings, Spock checks whether an equivalent embedding already exists. The cache key is typically derived from the text content, embedding model identifier, model version, dimensionality, and relevant settings. If a valid cached embedding exists, Spock reuses it to reduce latency and cost.

  4. Vector Storage: New embeddings are written to the vector database. ship_computer.db stores the metadata needed to locate and validate those vectors, including vector store path, index name, schema version, embedding model fingerprint, and ingestion status.

  5. Query Embedding: When the user submits an Ask AI question or starts a Deep Dive analysis, Spock embeds the query using the same embedding model used for the stored content. This ensures that query vectors and document vectors exist in the same semantic space.

  6. Similarity Search: Spock performs a nearest-neighbor search against the vector database. The most relevant chunks are returned based on similarity score, metadata filters, and any active session constraints.

  7. Context Assembly: The retrieved chunks are ranked, deduplicated, and assembled into a prompt context. Token limits from ship_computer.db determine how much context can be included in the final model request.

  8. Model Response: The chat or reasoning LLM generates a response using the assembled context. For Ask AI, this produces a conversational answer. For Deep Dive, this may produce summaries, comparisons, extracted insights, or multi-step analysis.

docs.title: How the Vector Database Supports Ask AI
docs.text:
For Ask AI, the vector database enables fast retrieval of relevant context from previously indexed material. Instead of sending the entire conversation history or all available documents to the model, Spock retrieves only the most relevant chunks.

This improves: * Response relevance: The model receives context that is semantically related to the user's question. * Latency: Smaller prompts reduce inference time. * Cost: Fewer tokens are sent to the model. * Consistency: Session metadata in ship_computer.db ensures the same model profile, context limits, and retrieval settings are used across interactions.

docs.title: How the Vector Database Supports Deep Dive
docs.text:
For Deep Dive, the vector database supports long-context analysis by breaking large documents into manageable chunks and indexing them for semantic search.

During a Deep Dive session, Spock may: * Ingest multiple source documents. * Chunk documents using a strategy stored in ship_computer.db. * Generate embeddings for each chunk. * Store vectors and metadata in the vector database. * Record ingestion progress and checkpoints in ship_computer.db. * Resume interrupted indexing if the application restarts. * Reuse existing embeddings when documents or model settings have not changed.

This allows Deep Dive to analyze large corpora incrementally and to recover from failures without reprocessing every document from scratch.

docs.title: Relationship Between ship_computer.db and the Vector Database
docs.text:
ship_computer.db and the vector database serve different but complementary roles.

Component Primary Responsibility ship_computer.db Stores configuration, session state, user preferences, checkpoints, model settings, and vector index metadata. Vector database Stores embeddings and performs similarity search over semantic content. Embedding LLM Converts text into vectors for storage and query matching. Chat/Reasoning LLM Generates answers or analysis using retrieved context.

In a typical Spock workflow, ship_computer.db tells the application which embedding model to use, where the vector database is located, which chunks have already been indexed, and how to reconstruct the active session. The vector database then provides the semantic search capability needed to retrieve relevant content for the model.

docs.title: Failure Handling and Fallback Behavior
docs.text:
If the embedding endpoint is unavailable, rate-limited, or misconfigured, Spock can fall back to a secondary endpoint or cached embeddings, depending on the active configuration. ship_computer.db records the fallback decision, rate-limit state, and last successful model version so the application can resume consistently.

If the vector database is missing or corrupted, Spock can rebuild the index from source documents when available. The rebuild process uses the chunking strategy and embedding settings stored in ship_computer.db, ensuring that the regenerated index matches the user's intended configuration.

docs.title: Embedding LLM & Vector Database Integration
docs.text:
The Spock application relies on a coordinated pipeline between an embedding LLM, a vector database, and the primary chat LLM to power retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for both Ask AI and Deep Dive workflows.

Embedding LLM Role: The embedding model (typically running on port 8080) converts unstructured text into high-dimensional dense vectors. Unlike the chat LLM, which generates human-readable text, the embedding model is optimized for semantic similarity. When a user submits a query or uploads a document, Spock routes the text through the embedding endpoint to generate fixed-length vector representations that capture contextual meaning rather than exact keyword matches.

Vector Database Role: The vector database stores these embeddings alongside metadata (source document, chunk ID, timestamp, and profile tags). It maintains an optimized index (e.g., HNSW or IVF) that enables sub-millisecond similarity searches. When Spock needs to retrieve relevant context, it queries the vector database using cosine similarity or inner product distance metrics to find the most semantically related chunks.

Ask AI Retrieval Flow: 1. Query Embedding: The user's prompt is sent to the embedding LLM and converted into a query vector. 2. Similarity Search: The vector database retrieves the top-k most relevant document chunks based on the query vector. 3. Context Assembly: Retrieved chunks are concatenated with the user's prompt and system instructions, respecting the chat_n_ctx limit stored in ship_computer.db. 4. LLM Inference: The augmented prompt is sent to the chat LLM (port 8081), which generates a grounded response. 5. State Persistence: Session metadata and retrieval statistics are logged to ship_computer.db for continuity and debugging.

Deep Dive Analysis Flow: 1. Document Ingestion & Chunking: Large documents are split into manageable segments using configurable token limits and overlap strategies. 2. Batch Embedding: Chunks are processed in parallel batches through the embedding LLM to maximize throughput. 3. Vector Indexing: Embeddings are written to the vector database with deep-dive-specific metadata tags. 4. Iterative Retrieval & Reasoning: The chat LLM performs multi-step analysis, querying the vector database at each reasoning step to gather evidence, cross-reference findings, and maintain logical consistency. 5. Checkpointing: Intermediate analysis states, vector cache status, and resource utilization metrics are persisted to ship_computer.db, enabling seamless session resumption and audit trails.

Coordination with ship_computer.db: The SQLite database acts as the control plane for the embedding and vector pipeline. It stores: * Embedding model profiles and endpoint configurations. * Vector index metadata, cache invalidation flags, and synchronization timestamps. * Rate-limit counters and fallback routing rules when the primary embedding service is overloaded. * Session-specific vector query logs for Deep Dive traceability.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
The following example shows how to resolve effective endpoint and context values from an already loaded configuration object.

from WarpCore.service_endpoints import resolve_ports, resolve_ctx, docs_base_url

# Resolve ports from the current app configuration object
ports = resolve_ports(app_config)   # dict: embed, chat, rag, mcp_http, docs, …
ctx = resolve_ctx(app_config)       # embed_n_ctx, chat_n_ctx, chat_max_tokens
print(docs_base_url(app_config))    # Base URL for documentation endpoints

docs.title: Copy Map
docs.text: The copy map tracks which files were adapted from the original Spock-UIE-Wiki-KB-HUB project during migration to the current codebase. This document provides a high-level summary of architectural changes and file renames. For the complete, low-level file-to-file mapping, see COPY_MAP.md in the project root.

docs.title: Key Adaptations
docs.text: Original Spock-Onboarding Changes UIE-Wiki-KB.py Spock-UIE-Wiki-KB.py Refactored for modularity to improve maintainability and scalability. This allows functionality to be updated or extended without affecting unrelated parts of the codebase. UIEG_KnowledgeBase.py spock_UIEG_KnowledgeBase.py Extracted into a standalone module to promote reusability and separation of concerns. The knowledge-base logic can now be used independently and is less tightly coupled to other components. Monolithic UI spock_shell/ Split into 24 focused modules to improve code organization and simplify maintenance. This makes individual user-interface components easier to read, test, and update.

docs.title: Column Notes
docs.text:
• Original: The file or component name in the source Spock-UIE-Wiki-KB-HUB project.
  • Spock-Onboarding: The corresponding file, module, or directory in the current codebase after migration.
  • Changes: The primary architectural reason for the rename, extraction, or refactor.

docs.title: Architectural Context
docs.text:
This section explains the architectural terms used above:

  • Modularity: The original implementation contained tightly coupled logic within single files. Refactoring into modular units allows specific features to be updated or tested in isolation, reducing the risk of regressions during development.
  • Separation of Concerns: Logic previously mixed with data handling—for example, in UIEG_KnowledgeBase.py—has been decoupled. This ensures that knowledge-base functionality can operate independently of main application logic, which simplifies unit testing and database management.
  • Monolithic UI: Refers to the original implementation where user-interface code was consolidated in one location or tightly coupled structure. The new spock_shell/ directory distributes this code across specialized modules, allowing developers to target specific UI components without impacting the entire application.

docs.title: Database Architecture
docs.text: The Spock application relies on a persistent data store managed by SQLite 3, specifically instantiated as ship_computer.db. This database serves as the central repository for knowledge retrieval, state management, and analytical processing required by the application's core features.

docs.title: Role of ship_computer.db
docs.text:
Unlike client-server relational databases that require separate server processes, SQLite is embedded directly within the application runtime. This design choice minimizes infrastructure overhead while providing ACID-compliant transactional integrity when the application uses appropriate transaction handling, journaling modes such as WAL, and concurrency controls. The database is responsible for:

  1. Knowledge Persistence: Storing structured data related to the knowledge base, document metadata, and context windows.
  2. State Management: Maintaining session history, user interaction logs, and application configuration states.
  3. Query Execution: Providing the underlying data schema for analytical operations, full-text search, and vector similarity retrieval.

docs.title: SQLite Operational Model
docs.text:
ship_computer.db is a single-file database that is accessed directly by the Spock application. This embedded model provides several operational benefits:

  • Low Deployment Complexity: The database does not require a separate database server, service account, or network endpoint.
  • Data Locality: Relational data, metadata, and vector embeddings can be stored in the same file, reducing integration overhead.
  • Transactional Consistency: SQLite supports atomic transactions, allowing the application to update knowledge entries, session state, and interaction logs consistently.
  • Concurrency Control: SQLite uses file-level locking and journaling mechanisms to coordinate access. In read-heavy workloads, WAL mode can improve concurrent read performance while preserving write consistency.
  • Extension Support: Optional SQLite extensions, such as FTS5 for full-text search or vector-oriented extensions where available, can extend the database's retrieval capabilities.

docs.title: Interaction with Application Features
docs.text: The database interacts directly with specific high-level features of the Spock application, particularly Ask AI and Deep Dive inquiries. The data flow is structured as follows:

docs.title: Ask AI Inquiries
docs.text:
• Functionality: Provides immediate, context-aware answers based on retrieved knowledge base content.
  • Database Interaction: When a user submits an inquiry, the application first queries ship_computer.db to retrieve relevant text chunks, metadata, or cached results associated with the query topic. Semantic search leverages precomputed vector embeddings stored directly in SQLite, while keyword-based fallback retrieval utilizes SQLite's FTS5 extension. The database returns the top-k most relevant documents, which are then formatted into a prompt context window for the generative model.
  • Read/Write Pattern: Primarily read-heavy during inference to minimize latency. Write operations occur asynchronously during knowledge ingestion, context window updates, or when query results are cached for future requests.

docs.title: Deep Dive Inquiries
docs.text:
• Functionality: Enables complex analysis, multi-step reasoning, cross-referencing, and historical data exploration.
  • Database Interaction: These inquiries trigger more intensive database transactions. The application executes complex SQL queries that join multiple tables to correlate disparate data points, such as user session history, knowledge-base entries, and previous analysis outputs. The database may also store intermediate reasoning steps and chain-of-thought artifacts to support iterative exploration.
  • Read/Write Pattern: Balanced read/write workload. The application persists analysis results, intermediate computation states, and audit records to enable reproducibility and longitudinal tracking of user research paths.

docs.title: Embedding LLM and Vector Database Integration
docs.text:
Spock utilizes an embedding LLM and a vector storage layer to enable semantic search and context retrieval. Although SQLite is traditionally a relational database, in this architecture it functions as a lightweight vector database through the following pipeline:

  1. Document Ingestion & Chunking: Raw documents or knowledge base entries are parsed and split into manageable text chunks. Metadata such as source, timestamp, category, and document identifier is extracted and normalized.
  2. Embedding Generation: Each text chunk is passed through an embedding LLM, such as a transformer-based model optimized for dense vector representation. The model outputs a fixed-dimensional floating-point vector that captures the semantic meaning of the text.
  3. Vector Storage in SQLite: The generated vectors are stored in ship_computer.db as BLOB or REAL array columns alongside their corresponding text chunks and metadata. Because SQLite does not have a native array type, vectors are commonly stored either as a packed binary BLOB or as a fixed number of REAL columns. This eliminates the need for a separate vector database service while maintaining data locality.
  4. Similarity Search & Retrieval: When a query is submitted, the same embedding LLM converts the user's prompt into a vector. The application then performs a similarity search, typically using cosine similarity or Euclidean distance, against the stored vectors. Depending on the implementation, this computation may occur in application memory or leverage SQLite extensions optimized for vector math.
  5. Context Assembly: The top-ranked vectors are mapped back to their original text chunks. These chunks are assembled into a structured context window, which is injected into the prompt for the primary generative LLM to produce the final response.

This integrated approach ensures low-latency retrieval, simplified deployment, and consistent transactional behavior across both relational and vector data operations.

docs.title: Embedding LLM Responsibilities
docs.text:
The embedding LLM is a specialized model used to convert text into numerical vector representations. It is distinct from the generative LLM that produces natural-language answers.

  • Semantic Encoding: The embedding LLM maps text into a high-dimensional vector space where semantically similar texts are located closer together.
  • Fixed-Dimension Output: Each text chunk and user query is represented by a vector of the same dimension, enabling consistent similarity comparison.
  • Retrieval Support: The embedding LLM enables the application to find relevant knowledge chunks without relying solely on exact keyword matching.
  • Query Normalization: User questions, paraphrases, and natural-language prompts are converted into the same vector space as the stored knowledge base.
  • Caching Opportunity: Embeddings for stable knowledge chunks can be precomputed and reused, reducing repeated inference cost during retrieval.

docs.title: Vector Search Mechanics
docs.text:
The vector search process is the core mechanism that connects user intent to relevant knowledge base content.

  1. Query Embedding: The user's Ask AI or Deep Dive prompt is converted into a vector using the embedding LLM.
  2. Candidate Retrieval: The application compares the query vector against stored vectors in ship_computer.db.
  3. Similarity Scoring: Each stored vector is scored using a similarity metric such as cosine similarity, dot product, or Euclidean distance.
  4. Top-k Selection: The highest-scoring vectors are selected, typically the top-k most relevant chunks.
  5. Reranking or Filtering: Optional metadata filters, recency rules, category constraints, or reranking models may refine the candidate set.
  6. Context Construction: The selected chunks are ordered and formatted into a prompt context for the generative LLM.

For small to medium knowledge bases, this approach can be performed efficiently within the application. For larger corpora, the architecture can be extended with SQLite vector extensions, application-level indexing, or an external vector database while preserving the same logical retrieval workflow.

docs.title: Ask AI Data Flow
docs.text:
The Ask AI feature is optimized for fast, context-aware responses.

  1. User Submission: The user submits a question or prompt.
  2. Query Embedding: The application converts the prompt into a vector using the embedding LLM.
  3. Semantic Retrieval: The application searches ship_computer.db for the most relevant knowledge chunks.
  4. Fallback Retrieval: If semantic results are insufficient, the application may use FTS5 keyword search to recover relevant text.
  5. Context Assembly: The retrieved chunks are combined into a structured prompt context.
  6. Answer Generation: The generative LLM produces a response using the retrieved context.
  7. Persistence: The query, retrieved context, response, latency, and metadata are stored for auditing, caching, and future analysis.

docs.title: Deep Dive Data Flow
docs.text:
The Deep Dive feature is optimized for iterative, multi-step analysis.

  1. Analysis Planning: The application interprets the user's request and determines which data sources, sessions, knowledge entries, or prior analyses are relevant.
  2. Multi-Table Retrieval: The application executes SQL queries that join knowledge base entries, interaction logs, session state, and previous Deep Dive outputs.
  3. Intermediate State Storage: Intermediate reasoning steps, retrieved evidence, and computation states are persisted to ship_computer.db.
  4. Iterative Refinement: The application may perform additional retrieval, filtering, or analysis passes based on intermediate results.
  5. Synthesis: The generative LLM synthesizes the accumulated evidence into a detailed response.
  6. Audit and Reproducibility: The final analysis, supporting evidence, and execution metadata are stored to support review, comparison, and longitudinal tracking.

docs.title: Schema Overview
docs.text:
While specific table structures may evolve with feature requirements, the core schema is intended to reduce data redundancy through normalization. Key logical tables typically include:

  • knowledge_base: Stores static knowledge entries, document chunks, and associated metadata.
  • sessions: Tracks active user sessions, authentication tokens, and timestamps.
  • interactions: Logs specific Ask AI or Deep Dive queries, response payloads, and latency metrics for audit trails and model fine-tuning.
  • embeddings: Holds vector representations linked to knowledge base entries, enabling semantic retrieval.

docs.title: Schema Verification
docs.text: The table names above describe expected logical entities rather than guaranteed physical names. For authoritative definitions, inspect the current ship_computer.db schema using .schema in the SQLite CLI or review the application's database migration scripts that create and update those tables.

docs.title: Overview

This modular design enables independent scaling, simplified testing, and clear separation of concerns across development, documentation, and deployment pipelines.
