  3. LLM Synthesis: The combined context is injected into the prompt template for the primary LLM. The model generates a comprehensive response, grounding its recommendations in verified documentation and live system data. Citations and source references are automatically appended to maintain transparency and traceability.

docs.title: How the Spock Application Uses the Embedding LLM and Vector Database
docs.text:
The Spock application uses the embedding LLM and vector database as a semantic retrieval layer for Ask AI and Deep Dive inquiries. The embedding model is not used to generate the final answer directly. Instead, it converts text into numerical vectors that can be compared by meaning.

The vector database stores those vectors alongside the original text chunks and metadata. When a user asks a question, the application embeds the question, searches the vector database for semantically similar content, and retrieves the most relevant documentation, procedures, incident notes, or architecture references.

For Ask AI, this process supports quick, natural-language answers. The application can combine the retrieved semantic context with live structured data from ship_computer.db, allowing the LLM to answer questions that require both current system state and documented guidance.

For Deep Dive, the application can use the vector database to gather broader context across multiple documents and historical records. It can then correlate that context with telemetry, logs, maintenance history, and incident data from SQLite to support multi-step troubleshooting, root-cause analysis, and procedural recommendations.

This architecture ensures that Ask AI and Deep Dive inquiries benefit from precise, real-time telemetry while leveraging semantic understanding for complex troubleshooting, procedural guidance, and cross-system analysis.

docs.title: SQLite 3 ship_computer.db Integration
docs.text: ship_computer.db is the local SQLite 3 database used by the Spock application as the structured source of truth for operational, diagnostic, and maintenance data. It complements the vector database by storing data that can be queried with precise filters, timestamps, numeric thresholds, and relational joins.

docs.title: Purpose and Scope
docs.text:
The SQLite 3 database is used for data that requires exact matching, time-based filtering, aggregation, and deterministic querying. This includes telemetry readings, system alerts, maintenance records, incident history, diagnostic results, and operational state information.

Unlike the vector database, which is optimized for semantic similarity, ship_computer.db is optimized for structured queries. It allows the Spock application to answer questions such as:

  • What is the current temperature of the propulsion system?
  • Which alerts were active in the last 24 hours?
  • What maintenance tasks were completed for the life support system last month?
  • Which incidents are associated with a specific subsystem?
  • What is the latest status of a known fault code?

docs.title: Data Model Overview
docs.text:
The exact schema may vary by deployment, but ship_computer.db typically contains structured tables or views representing the following data areas:

Data Area Example Content Use in Spock Telemetry Sensor readings, timestamps, units, thresholds Provides current and historical operational state Alerts and Events Fault codes, severity, active/cleared status Supports troubleshooting and incident awareness Maintenance Records Tasks, completion status, technicians, notes Provides procedural and historical maintenance context Incident Reports Incident ID, affected systems, root cause, resolution Supports Deep Dive analysis and pattern recognition System Metadata Subsystems, components, versions, configuration Enables filtering and cross-system correlation Audit Logs User actions, system changes, access events Supports traceability and operational accountability

The database is typically accessed through Python’s sqlite3 module using parameterized SQL queries. This allows the Spock application to retrieve only the relevant rows needed for a given Ask AI or Deep Dive request.

docs.title: How Ask AI Uses ship_computer.db
docs.text:
For Ask AI inquiries, the Spock application uses ship_computer.db to obtain precise, current, or recent structured facts. This is especially useful when the user asks about live system state, recent alerts, thresholds, or completed maintenance actions.

A typical Ask AI flow is:

  1. The user asks a natural-language question.
  2. The Spock application interprets the intent of the question.
  3. It queries ship_computer.db for relevant structured data, such as current telemetry, active alerts, or recent maintenance records.
  4. It may also query the vector database for relevant documentation or procedural guidance.
  5. The structured and semantic context is combined into a prompt for the primary LLM.
  6. The LLM generates a concise, grounded answer with citations to the relevant data sources.

For example, if a user asks, “What is the current status of the propulsion system?”, the application can query ship_computer.db for the latest propulsion telemetry, active alerts, and recent maintenance notes. It can then use the vector database to retrieve relevant operational procedures or known fault guidance. The final answer can include both the current state and the recommended next steps.

docs.title: How Deep Dive Uses ship_computer.db
docs.text:
For Deep Dive inquiries, the Spock application uses ship_computer.db as the primary structured evidence store. Deep Dive is intended for more complex investigations that require correlation across time, systems, incidents, maintenance actions, and operational logs.

A typical Deep Dive flow is:

  1. The user requests an in-depth analysis of a system, incident, or anomaly.
  2. The Spock application identifies the relevant subsystems, time range, and data sources.
  3. It queries ship_computer.db for telemetry trends, alert history, maintenance records, incident reports, and related system events.
  4. It queries the vector database for semantic context, such as troubleshooting guides, historical incident summaries, architecture notes, and procedural documentation.
  5. The application correlates structured evidence with semantic context.
  6. The primary LLM synthesizes a detailed report, including likely causes, supporting evidence, recommended actions, and source references.

For example, if a user asks for a Deep Dive into repeated propulsion anomalies, the application may query ship_computer.db for temperature spikes, pressure deviations, fault codes, maintenance history, and related alerts. It may then retrieve vector database content describing known propulsion failure modes, diagnostic procedures, and historical incident resolutions. The final output can present a timeline, probable root causes, and recommended maintenance or diagnostic actions.

docs.title: Query and Context Patterns
docs.text:
The Spock application typically converts SQLite query results into prompt-friendly context. This may include:

  • Timestamps and time ranges
  • Sensor values and units
  • Alert severity and status
  • Maintenance task completion details
  • Incident IDs and resolution notes
  • System or subsystem identifiers
  • Row identifiers or record keys for citation

This context is then combined with vector database results, which may include:

  • Document title or source name
  • Section or chunk identifier
  • Metadata tags
  • Semantic relevance score
  • Original text excerpt

The combined context is used to ground the LLM response and reduce the likelihood of unsupported or hallucinated recommendations.

docs.title: Relationship to the Embedding and Vector Layers
docs.text:
The SQLite 3 database and the vector database serve different but complementary roles.

Layer Best For Example Question ship_computer.db Exact values, timestamps, thresholds, alerts, maintenance records “What was the propulsion temperature at 14:32?” Vector database Semantic meaning, procedures, historical context, documentation “What should be checked when propulsion temperature spikes?” Primary LLM Synthesis, explanation, recommendation, report generation “What is the likely cause and what should we do next?”

The Spock application uses ship_computer.db for factual, structured evidence and the vector database for semantic, document-based context. The primary LLM then combines both to produce a coherent, traceable, and operationally useful response.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before running the Engineering Deck, ensure the following environment requirements are met:

  • Python Environment: A Python virtual environment, such as .venv, must be created and configured for the project.
  • Dependencies: All required Python packages must be installed within the virtual environment before execution.
  • Operating System / Shell: The provided usage commands are optimized for Windows PowerShell. Run them in a PowerShell terminal, or adapt the syntax if using another shell such as WSL, Bash, or Zsh.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
To run the Engineering Deck, execute the following command from the project root directory:

Windows (PowerShell): 

.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m spock_maintenance

Linux / macOS / WSL: 

./.venv/bin/python -m spock_maintenance

(If your virtual environment directory is named venv instead of .venv, adjust the path accordingly: ./venv/bin/python -m spock_maintenance)

This command starts the application using the Python interpreter located in the virtual environment. The -m flag instructs Python to execute the spock_maintenance package as a module. Ensure the virtual environment exists and contains all required dependencies. Explicitly invoking the virtual environment’s interpreter bypasses the need to activate the environment first, though activation remains an option if preferred.

docs.title: LLM Client
docs.text: The LLM client provides a unified interface for communicating with local LLM inference backends and other OpenAI-compatible services. It abstracts the differences between various LLM servers and APIs, allowing developers to interact with different models through a consistent API without implementing custom connection logic for each backend.

docs.title: Components
docs.text: Module Role llm_client Main client library that provides core functionality for interacting with LLMs lm_studio_api Wrapper for the LM Studio API, enabling communication with the LM Studio GUI-based inference tool through its HTTP endpoint llama_server_manager Manages the lifecycle of the llama.cpp server, including starting, stopping, and monitoring server health status gemini_openai_models Registry for Gemini and OpenAI models, facilitating compatibility mapping between different model families to ensure consistent API usage

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
from llm_client import LLMClient

# Initialize the client with the base URL of the inference server.
client = LLMClient(base_url="<inference-server-url>")

# Send a chat request to the selected backend.
response = client.chat("What is the meaning of life?")

docs.title: Message Format and Parameters
docs.text: The example above demonstrates a high-level abstraction where the prompt is passed as a plain string. In production scenarios, requests should be structured using message objects (e.g., system, user, and assistant roles) to support multi-turn conversations, system instructions, and tool calling. The client automatically serializes these message objects into the JSON payload format expected by the underlying OpenAI-compatible backend.

docs.title: Supported Backends
docs.text:
• LM Studio — A local GUI-based inference tool for running LLMs on a machine. It exposes an OpenAI-compatible API endpoint, allowing developers to manage models and interact with them without requiring detailed knowledge of the underlying server configuration.
  • llama.cpp — A lightweight C++ inference server optimized for performance and resource efficiency. It is well suited for running large language models on devices with limited computational resources by using quantization techniques (e.g., GGUF format) to reduce memory footprint while maintaining acceptable accuracy.
  • OpenAI-compatible APIs — Any server that implements the OpenAI chat format, typically over HTTP/REST. This allows integration with a wide range of LLM services, including commercial and open-source models that follow the standard OpenAI API specification.

docs.title: SQLite 3 ship_computer.db
docs.text: The ship_computer.db file is a SQLite 3 database that stores structured information about the ship’s computer systems, components, operational state, maintenance history, and related technical documentation. It serves as the primary structured data source for the Spock application, especially for Ask AI and Deep Dive inquiries.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The database provides a reliable, queryable foundation for answering questions about the ship’s computer environment. Unlike unstructured text, the data in ship_computer.db is organized into tables and relationships, which allows the Spock application to perform precise lookups, joins, aggregations, and time-based filtering before sending relevant context to the LLM.

Typical data stored in ship_computer.db may include:

  • Ship and computer identifiers
  • Hardware specifications
  • Software versions
  • Component inventory
  • Operational status
  • Error logs
  • Maintenance records
  • Configuration snapshots
  • User or system activity records
  • Links to related documentation or knowledge-base entries

docs.title: Schema Overview
docs.text:
A typical ship_computer.db schema may contain tables such as:

Table Description ships Core ship records, including ship ID, name, class, and status computers Computer systems associated with each ship components Hardware or software components installed on each computer status_events Time-stamped operational status changes error_logs Captured errors, warnings, and diagnostic messages maintenance_records Maintenance actions, repairs, and inspections documents References to manuals, guides, or technical notes document_chunks Chunked text segments used for retrieval and embedding embeddings Vector representations of document chunks, if stored in SQLite

The exact schema may vary depending on the deployment, but the key design principle is that ship_computer.db stores structured, relational data that can be queried deterministically before being used to inform LLM responses.

docs.title: Ask AI Interaction
docs.text:
Ask AI is intended for direct, conversational questions about the ship’s computer systems. When a user submits an Ask AI request, the Spock application typically follows this flow:

  1. Receive the user question

  2. Example: “What is the current status of the navigation computer?”

  3. Interpret the intent

  4. The application determines whether the question requires structured data, documentation, or both.

  5. Query ship_computer.db

  6. The application runs targeted SQL queries to retrieve relevant records.

  7. For example, it may query the computers and status_events tables to find the latest status for a specific computer.

  8. Assemble context

  9. The retrieved rows are formatted into a concise context block.

  10. This context may include identifiers, timestamps, status values, and related component information.

  11. Send the prompt to the LLM

  12. The LLM client sends the user question and the structured context to the selected model.

  13. The model generates a natural-language answer grounded in the retrieved data.

  14. Return the response

  15. The Spock application presents the answer to the user, optionally including source references or data provenance.

This approach allows Ask AI to answer questions quickly while reducing the risk of hallucination, because the LLM is provided with concrete data from the database rather than relying solely on its internal knowledge.

docs.title: Deep Dive Interaction
docs.text:
Deep Dive is intended for more complex investigations that require multiple data sources, historical analysis, and cross-referencing. Compared with Ask AI, Deep Dive may involve:

  • Multiple database queries
  • Joins across several tables
  • Time-range filtering
  • Aggregation of logs or events
  • Retrieval of related documentation
  • Vector search over technical text
  • Multi-step reasoning by the LLM

A typical Deep Dive flow is:

  1. Receive a complex question

  2. Example: “Why did the navigation computer experience repeated failures during the last 72 hours?”

  3. Break the question into subtasks

  4. Identify the relevant computer
  5. Retrieve recent status events
  6. Retrieve error logs
  7. Retrieve maintenance records

  8. Find related documentation or known issues

  9. Query ship_computer.db

  10. The application may execute several SQL statements, such as:

    • Find the computer by name or ID
    • Retrieve status events within a time window
    • Retrieve error logs associated with that computer
    • Retrieve recent maintenance actions
    • Join component data to identify affected subsystems

  11. Retrieve unstructured context

  12. If the question requires explanatory context, the application may also search the vector database for relevant documentation chunks.

  13. Combine structured and unstructured evidence

  14. The application merges database results with retrieved text snippets.

  15. It may rank or prioritize the most relevant evidence before sending it to the LLM.

  16. Generate a detailed explanation

  17. The LLM produces a structured response that may include:
    • Summary of findings
    • Timeline of events
    • Likely causes
    • Recommended actions
    • References to logs, records, or documentation

Deep Dive is therefore a retrieval-augmented workflow in which ship_computer.db provides the factual backbone, while the LLM provides interpretation and synthesis.

docs.title: Data Flow
docs.text:
The interaction between ship_computer.db and the Spock application can be summarized as follows:

User Question
    ↓
Spock Application
    ↓
Intent Detection / Query Planning
    ↓
SQLite 3 `ship_computer.db`
    ↓
Structured Context
    ↓
Optional Vector Search
    ↓
LLM Client
    ↓
Generated Answer
    ↓
User

In this flow, the database is not directly “talking” to the LLM. Instead, the Spock application acts as the orchestrator: it queries the database, formats the results, and supplies them as context to the LLM through the LLM client.

docs.title: Example Queries
docs.text: The following examples illustrate the kinds of queries the Spock application may run against ship_computer.db.

docs.title: Find a computer by name
docs.text:
SELECT id, ship_id, name, status
FROM computers
WHERE name = 'Navigation Computer';

docs.title: Retrieve recent status events
docs.text:
SELECT timestamp, event_type, status, details
FROM status_events
WHERE computer_id = 12
  AND timestamp >= datetime('now', '-72 hours')
ORDER BY timestamp DESC;

docs.title: Retrieve recent error logs
docs.text:
SELECT timestamp, severity, message, component_id
FROM error_logs
WHERE computer_id = 12
  AND timestamp >= datetime('now', '-72 hours')
ORDER BY timestamp DESC;

docs.title: Retrieve related maintenance records
docs.text:
SELECT performed_at, technician, action, notes
FROM maintenance_records
WHERE computer_id = 12
ORDER BY performed_at DESC
LIMIT 10;

These queries provide the factual context that the LLM can use to answer user questions accurately.

docs.title: Embedding LLM and Vector Database
docs.text: The Spock application may also use an embedding LLM and a vector database to support semantic search over unstructured or semi-structured text. This is especially useful for Deep Dive inquiries, where the answer may depend on manuals, troubleshooting guides, incident reports, or other technical documents that are not easily captured by simple SQL queries.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
An embedding LLM converts text into numerical vectors, also called embeddings. These vectors represent the semantic meaning of the text in a high-dimensional space. Similar meanings produce similar vectors, which allows the application to find relevant passages by measuring vector similarity rather than relying only on keyword matching.

The vector database stores these embeddings and supports efficient similarity search. Together, the embedding LLM and vector database enable the Spock application to answer questions such as:

  • “What are the recommended troubleshooting steps for a navigation computer timeout?”
  • “Are there known issues with this component after firmware update 4.2?”
  • “What does the maintenance manual say about thermal throttling on this system?”

docs.title: Ingestion Pipeline
docs.text:
Before text can be searched semantically, it must be processed and stored. A typical ingestion pipeline includes the following steps:

  1. Collect source documents
  2. Technical manuals
  3. Maintenance guides
  4. Error reference documents
  5. Incident reports
  6. Component datasheets

  7. Operational procedures

  8. Chunk the text

  9. Long documents are split into smaller, meaningful segments.

  10. Chunking helps improve retrieval precision and keeps context within the LLM’s token limits.

  11. Generate embeddings

  12. Each chunk is passed to the embedding LLM.

  13. The model returns a vector representation of the chunk.

  14. Store metadata

  15. Alongside each vector, the application stores metadata such as:

    • Document ID
    • Chunk ID
    • Source title
    • Section heading
    • Page or paragraph location
    • Timestamp
    • Related ship or computer ID, if applicable

  16. Index the vectors

  17. The vector database indexes the embeddings for fast similarity search.

docs.title: Embedding Model
docs.text:
The embedding LLM is typically a separate model from the chat LLM used for answer generation. It is optimized for producing dense vector representations of text.

Key characteristics of an embedding model include:

  • Deterministic output — The same input text should produce the same embedding under the same model version.
  • Semantic sensitivity — Text with similar meaning should produce similar vectors.
  • High-dimensional output — Embeddings may have hundreds or thousands of dimensions.
  • Model versioning — Changing the embedding model may require re-embedding existing content.

The Spock application may use a local embedding model, a hosted embedding API, or another OpenAI-compatible embedding endpoint, depending on the deployment environment.

docs.title: Vector Storage
docs.text:
The vector database may be implemented in several ways:

  • A dedicated vector database such as Chroma, Qdrant, Milvus, or Weaviate
  • A SQLite-based vector extension such as sqlite-vec
  • An in-memory vector index for smaller deployments
  • A hybrid store where metadata remains in ship_computer.db while vectors are stored separately

If the vector store is separate from ship_computer.db, the Spock application must maintain consistent references between the two systems. For example, a vector record may include a document_id that maps back to a row in the documents table.

docs.title: Query Pipeline
docs.text:
When the Spock application needs semantic search, it follows a process similar to the following:

  1. Receive the user question

  2. Example: “What should I check if the navigation computer reports intermittent timeouts?”

  3. Embed the query

  4. The application sends the question to the embedding LLM.

  5. The model returns a query vector.

  6. Search the vector database

  7. The vector database finds the most similar stored embeddings.

  8. The application retrieves the corresponding text chunks and metadata.

  9. Filter by metadata

  10. The application may filter results by:

    • Ship ID
    • Computer ID
    • Document type
    • Time range
    • Relevance score

  11. Rank and select context

  12. The application selects the most relevant chunks.

  13. It may combine vector similarity with keyword matching or metadata filters.

  14. Send context to the chat LLM

  15. The retrieved chunks are included in the prompt.
  16. The chat LLM generates an answer grounded in the retrieved evidence.

docs.title: Hybrid Search
docs.text:
In many cases, the best results come from combining structured search with semantic search. This is known as hybrid search.

For example, the Spock application may:

  • Use SQL to find the correct computer and time range
  • Use vector search to find relevant troubleshooting documentation
  • Combine both result sets into a single context block

This approach is more robust than using either method alone because:

  • SQL provides precise, deterministic filtering
  • Vector search provides semantic flexibility
  • The LLM can synthesize both structured and unstructured evidence

docs.title: Context Assembly
docs.text:
Before sending the prompt to the LLM, the Spock application assembles a context block that may include:

  • User question
  • Relevant database rows
  • Retrieved document chunks
  • Metadata such as timestamps and source references
  • Instructions for the LLM to answer only from the provided context

A simplified prompt structure may look like this:

You are an assistant for the Spock ship computer system.
Answer the user's question using only the provided context.
If the answer is not present in the context, say that the information is unavailable.

Context:
- Computer: Navigation Computer
- Status: Degraded
- Recent Error: Timeout detected in navigation service
- Document Chunk: "If navigation timeouts occur, verify network latency, firmware version, and thermal status."

User Question:
What should I check if the navigation computer reports intermittent timeouts?

This structure helps ensure that the LLM remains grounded in the retrieved data and documentation.

docs.title: Failure Handling
docs.text:
Because the embedding and vector search pipeline depends on multiple components, the Spock application should handle failures gracefully.

Common failure modes include:

  • Embedding model unavailable
  • Vector database unreachable
  • Missing or stale embeddings
  • Low-relevance search results
  • Mismatch between document metadata and database records

Recommended handling strategies include:

  • Fall back to structured database queries if vector search fails
  • Return a clear message if no relevant context is found
  • Log retrieval failures for diagnostics
  • Re-embed content after model or schema changes
  • Validate metadata consistency between ship_computer.db and the vector store

docs.title: Relationship Between ship_computer.db and the Vector Database
docs.text:
The two data stores serve complementary roles:

Data Store Role ship_computer.db Stores structured, relational data about ships, computers, components, status, logs, and maintenance Vector database Stores semantic embeddings of unstructured or semi-structured text for similarity search

The Spock application uses both when appropriate:

  • Use ship_computer.db for precise, factual queries
  • Use the vector database for semantic retrieval over documents and guides
  • Use the LLM to interpret and synthesize the combined context

This separation allows the application to maintain accurate structured data while still benefiting from flexible, meaning-based search over technical content.

docs.title: Database Architecture
docs.text: The database layer provides persistent storage for LLM interactions. It uses SQLite, with the primary database file named ship_computer.db. This enables the Spock application to retain query history, associated context, and generated results for later retrieval, auditing, or review.

docs.title: Database Schema Overview
docs.text: Table Purpose queries Stores submitted prompts or question text, session information, feature type, and request metadata context Stores contextual material supplied to the LLM for a query, including source identifiers, text snippets, and relevance scores results Stores generated model responses, performance metrics, token usage, model version, and execution status

docs.title: Interaction with Spock Application
docs.text:
The Spock application uses this client as its integration point for AI-assisted features such as Ask AI and Deep Dive. For each request, Spock supplies a user prompt and any relevant context; the LLM client forwards that information to the selected backend and records the interaction in ship_computer.db. The stored records include entries in queries, context, and results, which support traceability of what was asked, what context was provided, and what response was returned.

The client exposes lightweight CRUD methods that Spock calls synchronously after each inference cycle. A typical write sequence is:

  1. Insert a queries record to capture the user prompt and request metadata.
  2. Insert one or more context records to capture the sources, chunks, and relevance scores used for the request.
  3. Insert a results record to capture the model response, latency, token usage, and execution status.
  4. Commit the transaction. If any step fails, the transaction is rolled back to prevent partial writes.

This design keeps the Spock application responsible for user experience and workflow orchestration, while the database client remains responsible for durable logging and retrieval of AI interactions.

docs.title: SQLite 3 Database: ship_computer.db Architecture
docs.text:
ship_computer.db is a local, file-based SQLite 3 relational database designed for low-latency, zero-configuration persistence. It operates in WAL journal mode to improve data integrity and concurrency during read/write operations from the Spock application. The schema is normalized to separate user intent, retrieved context, and model outputs, enabling efficient querying and historical analysis.

  • queries Table: Acts as the primary ledger for user interactions. Each record contains a unique identifier, timestamp, session ID, raw user prompt, and metadata tags such as feature flag, user role, and request source. This table serves as the anchor for all downstream logging.
  • context Table: Stores the semantic context injected into the LLM prompt. Records include a foreign key linking to the parent queries entry, source identifiers such as document ID, URL, or knowledge base path, raw text snippets, chunk identifiers, and relevance scores returned by the vector search engine. This enables developers to audit which documents influenced a specific response.
  • results Table: Captures the LLM's output along with performance metrics. Fields include the generated response text, token usage for input and output, latency, model version, and execution status such as success, timeout, or error. This facilitates cost tracking, performance monitoring, and response caching.

All database operations are wrapped in transactional blocks to prevent partial writes during network timeouts or backend failures. The client exposes lightweight CRUD methods that Spock calls synchronously after each inference cycle.

docs.title: Reference Schema
docs.text:
The following schema illustrates the core relationships and fields used by the Spock application.

CREATE TABLE queries (
    query_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
    session_id TEXT NOT NULL,
    feature TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (feature IN ('ask_ai', 'deep_dive', 'other')),
    user_role TEXT,
    prompt TEXT NOT NULL,
    metadata_json TEXT,
    created_at TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT (datetime('now'))
);

CREATE TABLE context (
    context_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
    query_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES queries(query_id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    source_type TEXT,
    source_id TEXT,
    source_path TEXT,
    chunk_id TEXT,
    text_snippet TEXT,
    relevance_score REAL,
    embedding_id TEXT,
    retrieved_at TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT (datetime('now'))
);

CREATE TABLE results (
    result_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
    query_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES queries(query_id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    response_text TEXT,
    model_name TEXT,
    model_version TEXT,
    input_tokens INTEGER,
    output_tokens INTEGER,
    latency_ms INTEGER,
    status TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('success', 'timeout', 'error', 'cancelled')),
    error_message TEXT,
    cache_key TEXT,
    created_at TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT (datetime('now'))
);

CREATE INDEX idx_queries_session ON queries(session_id, created_at);
CREATE INDEX idx_context_query ON context(query_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_results_query ON results(query_id);

The queries table is the parent record for a single user request. The context table may contain multiple rows for one query, especially in Deep Dive workflows where several retrieved chunks are used. The results table stores the final response and operational metrics for that query.

docs.title: Spock Application Integration: Ask AI and Deep Dive Workflows
docs.text:
The Spock application leverages the LLM client and ship_computer.db to power two distinct AI inquiry modes, each with different data flow and logging requirements:

  • Ask AI: Designed for direct, conversational Q&A. When a user submits a prompt, Spock routes it directly to the LLM client with minimal or no external context. The client forwards the request to the configured backend, receives the response, and logs a single entry across the three database tables. This workflow prioritizes speed and simplicity, making it ideal for general knowledge questions, code snippets, or quick clarifications.
  • Deep Dive: Engineered for complex, research-oriented inquiries requiring domain-specific knowledge. Spock initiates a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline. The user prompt is first processed to extract semantic intent, triggering a vector similarity search. Retrieved documents are chunked, ranked, and injected into the system prompt as structured context. The LLM client then orchestrates the multi-step inference, logging each context chunk in the context table and the final synthesized response in the results table. This workflow ensures traceability, allowing users to click through source references and verify how the model constructed its answer.

Both workflows share the same underlying client abstraction, but Deep Dive dynamically adjusts timeout thresholds, token limits, and retry logic to accommodate heavier computational loads.

docs.title: Ask AI Logging Pattern
docs.text:
In Ask AI, the database write is typically compact:

  • One queries row records the user's prompt.
  • Zero or more context rows record any optional context supplied by the user or application.
  • One results row records the model response and execution metadata.

Because Ask AI is optimized for low latency, Spock may skip vector search entirely or use a lightweight context source when appropriate.

docs.title: Deep Dive Logging Pattern
docs.text:
In Deep Dive, the database write is more detailed:

  • One queries row records the original research question.
  • Multiple context rows record each retrieved chunk, source, relevance score, and embedding identifier.
  • One results row records the synthesized answer, model version, token usage, latency, and status.

This pattern supports audit trails, source verification, and debugging of retrieval quality.

docs.title: Embedding LLM and Vector Database Integration
docs.text: While the primary LLM client handles generative tasks, the Spock application relies on a separate embedding LLM and a vector database to power semantic search and context retrieval. These components operate in tandem to bridge the gap between unstructured data and the generative model.

docs.title: Role of the Embedding LLM
docs.text:
The embedding LLM is a specialized model that converts text into dense numerical vectors, also called embeddings. Unlike the primary generative LLM, the embedding LLM does not produce natural-language answers. Instead, it produces fixed-length vector representations that capture semantic meaning. Texts with similar meaning are mapped to nearby points in vector space, enabling similarity search.

Spock uses the embedding LLM in two main phases:

  1. Indexing: When documents, knowledge-base entries, or other source material are added to Spock, the application chunks the text and sends each chunk to the embedding LLM. The resulting vectors are stored in the vector database along with metadata such as document ID, chunk ID, source path, permissions, and timestamp.
  2. Querying: When a user submits a Deep Dive request, Spock sends the user prompt to the same embedding LLM to create a query vector. This vector is then compared against stored vectors to find the most semantically relevant chunks.

Using the same embedding model for indexing and querying is important because vectors from different models are not guaranteed to be comparable. If Spock changes the embedding model, it should reindex existing content or maintain versioned embeddings to preserve search accuracy.

docs.title: Role of the Vector Database
docs.text:
The vector database stores embeddings and their associated metadata. It is optimized for high-dimensional nearest-neighbor search, allowing Spock to quickly identify the most relevant chunks from a large corpus.

For each stored vector, the vector database typically retains:

  • The embedding vector itself.
  • A unique chunk or document identifier.
  • Source metadata such as document ID, URL, file path, or knowledge-base location.
  • Access-control metadata such as user role, group, or permission scope.
  • Timestamps and version information.
  • Optional relevance or confidence scores computed during retrieval.

During a Deep Dive request, the vector database performs a similarity search using the query embedding. It returns the top-k most relevant chunks, ranked by similarity score. Spock can then filter these results by permissions, freshness, or source type before injecting them into the LLM prompt.

docs.title: How Spock Uses the Embedding LLM and Vector Database Together
docs.text:
The full retrieval flow for a Deep Dive inquiry is:

  1. Prompt preparation: Spock receives the user's question and prepares it for semantic search.
  2. Query embedding: Spock sends the prompt to the embedding LLM and receives a query vector.
  3. Vector search: Spock queries the vector database for the nearest stored vectors.
  4. Filtering and ranking: Spock applies metadata filters, permission checks, and relevance ranking to select the best context chunks.
  5. Context assembly: Spock formats the selected chunks into a structured prompt context, including source references for traceability.
  6. Generation: Spock sends the prompt and context to the primary LLM through the LLM client.
  7. Logging: The LLM client records the query, retrieved context, and final response in ship_computer.db.

This separation of concerns allows Spock to use the embedding LLM for semantic matching, the vector database for fast retrieval, and the primary LLM for answer synthesis. It also makes the system easier to debug: if a Deep Dive answer is incorrect, developers can inspect the retrieved chunks in the context table and determine whether the issue was retrieval, ranking, prompt construction, or model generation.

docs.title: Ask AI vs. Deep Dive Use of Embeddings
docs.text:
Ask AI may not require vector search when the question can be answered from the model's general knowledge or from a small, explicitly supplied context. In that case, Spock may bypass the embedding LLM and vector database entirely, or use them only for optional lightweight retrieval.

Deep Dive relies more heavily on the embedding LLM and vector database because it is designed to answer questions that require access to specific documents, internal knowledge, or domain-specific material. The vector search step is what allows Deep Dive to ground its responses in relevant source content rather than relying solely on the generative model's prior knowledge. 1. Embedding Generation: When a user submits a query—particularly in Deep Dive mode—Spock passes the prompt to a dedicated embedding model (for example, text-embedding-3-small or a local equivalent). The model converts the text into a high-dimensional numerical vector that captures semantic meaning rather than literal keyword matches. This vector is used as a search key for related content.

  1. Vector Similarity Search: Spock sends the generated query vector to the vector database, which indexes pre-embedded documents, knowledge-base articles, and system logs. Using similarity measures such as cosine similarity or inner-product distance, the vector database retrieves the top-N most relevant passages. Each result includes a similarity score and metadata pointers that identify the source document, section, timestamp, or log entry.

  2. Context Assembly & Injection: Spock aggregates the retrieved passages, trims or ranks them to fit the LLM's context window, and formats them into a structured prompt template. The LLM client then appends this context to the system message before forwarding the complete payload to the inference backend. This allows the generative model to answer using grounded, relevant material rather than relying only on its internal knowledge.

  3. Logging & Traceability: The vector database does not store conversation history. Instead, the LLM client writes the retrieved context snippets, their source IDs, similarity scores, and related metadata into the context table in ship_computer.db. This decouples real-time vector search from persistent relational logging, ensuring that the application maintains a complete audit trail without bloating the vector index.

This architecture ensures that the generative LLM remains focused on reasoning and synthesis, while the embedding model and vector database handle precise, scalable information retrieval. The separation of concerns also allows Spock to swap embedding models or vector backends independently without disrupting the core inference pipeline.

docs.title: SQLite 3 ship_computer.db
docs.text:
ship_computer.db is a local SQLite 3 database used by the Spock application for durable, transactional storage of application state and inquiry history. It is separate from the vector database: SQLite stores structured records, while the vector database stores high-dimensional embeddings and performs similarity search.

For Ask AI inquiries, Spock uses ship_computer.db to record the user's question, the selected mode, the model response, the retrieved context, and any relevant metadata. This gives the application a persistent record of what was asked, what context was used, and what answer was produced.

For Deep Dive inquiries, Spock uses the same database to store richer audit information, including multiple retrieval steps, source identifiers, similarity scores, timestamps, and the final synthesized answer. This supports traceability, debugging, and later review of how the application arrived at a detailed response.

Typical responsibilities of ship_computer.db include:

Area Purpose context Stores retrieved passages, source IDs, similarity scores, and context metadata used for an inquiry. Conversation records Stores user prompts, assistant responses, mode, and timestamps. Settings and state Stores user preferences, active model configuration, and application state. Audit trail Provides a durable record of Ask AI and Deep Dive activity for review and debugging.

The database is not used as the primary vector index. Embeddings and similarity search remain in the vector database, while SQLite provides reliable local persistence and relational querying.

docs.title: Embedding LLM and Vector Database
docs.text: Spock uses an embedding model to translate natural-language text into numerical vectors. These vectors represent semantic meaning, so similar concepts are close together in vector space. The vector database stores these vectors alongside metadata and uses them to find relevant content quickly.

docs.title: How Spock uses the embedding LLM
docs.text:
1. Spock receives a user query from Ask AI or Deep Dive.
  2. It sends the query to the embedding model.
  3. The embedding model returns a vector representation of the query.
  4. Spock uses that vector to search the vector database for semantically related passages.

The embedding model is not responsible for generating the final answer. Its role is to create a searchable representation of the query so that Spock can retrieve relevant context.

docs.title: How Spock uses the vector database
docs.text:
1. The vector database contains pre-embedded documents, knowledge-base articles, logs, and other indexed content.
  2. Spock submits the query vector to the vector database.
  3. The vector database compares the query vector against stored vectors using a similarity metric.
  4. It returns the top-N most relevant passages, each with a similarity score and metadata.
  5. Spock uses those passages to build the context for the generative LLM.

docs.title: Ask AI versus Deep Dive
docs.text:
In Ask AI, Spock typically performs a focused retrieval step: it embeds the question, retrieves a small set of relevant passages, and asks the generative LLM to answer directly.

In Deep Dive, Spock may perform broader or iterative retrieval: it can embed multiple query variants, retrieve more passages, rank or filter results, and assemble a larger context before asking the generative LLM to synthesize a detailed answer. In both cases, the final answer is generated by the LLM, while the embedding model and vector database provide the relevant supporting material.

docs.title: Database Architecture
docs.text: The ship_computer.db SQLite 3 database serves as the persistent storage layer for the Spock application, specifically managing data related to AI inquiries such as "Ask AI" and "Deep Dive". This database stores context, query history, and generated insights locally, eliminating reliance on external cloud services for state management and ensuring data sovereignty.

docs.title: Database Schema Overview
docs.text:
The ship_computer.db file is optimized for the high-frequency read/write operations required by the LLM client and Spock application. Key tables include:

  • queries: Stores incoming prompts and metadata, including timestamps, user/session IDs, request type (ask_ai or deep_dive), execution status, and correlation identifiers. This table provides a complete audit trail for every AI interaction and enables precise tracking of request lifecycles.
  • context: Maintains session history and retrieval context used for multi-turn conversations. It stores conversation turns, referenced data points, vector search results, and scope boundaries required to reconstruct the prompt environment accurately. Each entry is linked to a specific session ID to prevent context bleeding between independent inquiries.
  • results: Caches generated responses from LLM backends to prevent redundant inference calls. Cached results support response replay, debugging, and a consistent user experience when identical or highly similar requests are repeated. The table also stores token usage metrics and latency data for performance monitoring.
  • vector_metadata: Acts as a relational bridge between the vector database and SQLite. It maps vector IDs to source documents, conversation threads, and access permissions, ensuring that semantic search results can be traced back to their origin within the relational schema.

docs.title: Interaction with Spock Application
docs.text:
The Spock application orchestrates the data flow between the user interface, the LLM client, and ship_computer.db. When a user initiates an inquiry, the following workflows execute:

  1. Ask AI: The Spock application first queries the context table to retrieve relevant session history and previously resolved references. This enriched context is appended to the user's prompt before transmission to the LLM client. The resulting response is logged in the results table, and the updated conversation state is persisted back to context. If the query matches a previously cached prompt within a defined similarity threshold, the system bypasses the LLM and serves the cached result directly.
  2. Deep Dive: For complex, multi-step analysis, the system breaks down the inquiry into discrete reasoning stages. Intermediate steps, tool outputs, and chain-of-thought traces are written to the queries and context tables with incremental status flags. This granular logging allows users to inspect the AI's decision-making process, verify data sources, and resume interrupted analyses without losing state. Each reasoning step is tagged with a parent-child correlation ID to reconstruct the full analytical tree.

The LLM client interacts with this database exclusively through the Spock application's internal API. This abstraction ensures that all inference requests are logged, stateful sessions survive application restarts, and data integrity is maintained via SQLite's ACID compliance. Connection pooling and WAL (Write-Ahead Logging) mode are enabled to optimize concurrent read/write performance during active sessions.

docs.title: Local Storage and Recovery
docs.text: Because ship_computer.db is a local SQLite 3 file, it provides an embedded, low-dependency storage solution ideal for single-user or workstation deployments. The Spock application treats this database as the authoritative source for AI interaction state. While generated model outputs depend on backend availability and caching policies, all session metadata, context windows, and user prompts remain locally accessible and recoverable. Automatic checkpointing and periodic vacuuming are scheduled to prevent database bloat and maintain query performance over extended usage periods.

docs.title: Embedding LLM and Vector Database Integration
docs.text: The Spock application leverages a dedicated embedding LLM and an integrated vector database to enable semantic search and dynamic context retrieval. This subsystem operates alongside ship_computer.db to bridge raw user queries with relevant knowledge bases and conversation history. - Embedding Generation: When a user submits a query, uploads a document, or initiates a session, the Spock application routes the text through a lightweight embedding LLM. This model converts natural language into high-dimensional numerical vectors that capture semantic meaning, intent, and contextual relationships rather than relying on exact keyword matches. - Vector Storage & Indexing: Generated vectors are stored in a vector database optimized for similarity search. The index uses approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) algorithms to enable low-latency retrieval even as the corpus scales. Metadata linking each vector to its source document, conversation thread, or context window is persisted in ship_computer.db for traceability and access control. - Semantic Retrieval Workflow: During an "Ask AI" or "Deep Dive" request, the user's prompt is first embedded. The vector database performs a similarity search against the indexed corpus, retrieving the most contextually relevant chunks. These retrieved segments are then recorded in the context table, ranked by relevance score, and formatted into the final prompt sent to the primary generative LLM. - State Management & Separation of Concerns: The vector database handles high-speed similarity matching and memory-efficient indexing, while ship_computer.db maintains the relational mapping between vectors, sessions, and user metadata. This architecture ensures that semantic search remains performant without compromising the durability, query flexibility, and transactional safety of the relational database. Context windows are dynamically assembled by merging vector search results with relational session history, providing the LLM with both semantic relevance and conversational continuity.

docs.title: SQLite 3 ship_computer.db
docs.text:
ship_computer.db is the durable relational database used by the Spock application to manage application state, user context, document metadata, retrieval results, and audit information. It is built on SQLite 3 and is intended to provide ACID transactions, structured querying, and persistent storage for the parts of the system that require relational integrity.

The database does not perform vector similarity search. Instead, it stores the relational metadata needed to interpret, authorize, trace, and reuse the results returned by the vector database.

docs.title: Core Responsibilities
docs.text:
ship_computer.db is responsible for:

  • Storing user, session, and conversation state.
  • Tracking uploaded documents, source files, and derived text chunks.
  • Mapping vector database identifiers back to application-level entities.
  • Recording retrieval results for "Ask AI" and "Deep Dive" requests.
  • Maintaining the context table used to assemble prompts for the generative LLM.
  • Enforcing application-level access control and auditability.
  • Preserving session history so that later requests can reference prior context.

docs.title: Representative Tables
docs.text:
The exact schema may vary by implementation, but a typical ship_computer.db design includes tables such as the following:

Table Purpose users Stores user identities, roles, and access permissions. sessions Stores conversation sessions, including session ID, user ID, creation time, and status. messages Stores user prompts, assistant responses, and message ordering. documents Stores uploaded or indexed source documents, including title, source, owner, and visibility. chunks Stores text chunks derived from documents, including chunk text, position, and document reference. vector_refs Maps application-level chunks to vector database identifiers and embedding metadata. context Stores retrieval results selected for a specific request, including relevance score and rank. audit_log Records access, retrieval, and generation events for traceability.

docs.title: Key Relationships
docs.text:
The relational model connects the major entities in the system:

  • A user owns or participates in one or more sessions.
  • A session contains one or more messages.
  • A document is split into one or more chunks.
  • A chunk may have one or more vector_refs.
  • A vector_ref links a chunk to a vector stored in the external vector database.
  • A context row records that a particular chunk was selected for a particular request.

This structure allows Spock to answer questions such as:

  • Which user made this request?
  • Which session did this request belong to?
  • Which document or chunk was used as context?
  • Which vector database identifier represented that chunk?
  • What relevance score was returned?
  • When was the context assembled?
  • Which LLM response was generated from that context?

docs.title: Interaction with Ask AI and Deep Dive
Ask AI Workflow
docs.text:
"Ask AI" is typically a single-turn or lightweight multi-turn semantic retrieval workflow. The Spock application uses ship_computer.db to manage the surrounding state while the vector database performs similarity search.

A typical Ask AI sequence is:

  1. The user submits a prompt.
  2. Spock loads or creates the relevant session in ship_computer.db.
  3. Spock records the user message in the messages table.
  4. Spock sends the prompt to the embedding LLM.
  5. The embedding LLM returns a query vector.
  6. Spock sends the query vector to the vector database.
  7. The vector database returns candidate vector identifiers and similarity scores.
  8. Spock uses vector_refs to resolve those identifiers back to application-level chunks.
  9. Spock checks permissions and document visibility using users, documents, and related tables.
  10. Spock inserts the selected chunks into the context table with their relevance scores and ranks.
  11. Spock assembles the final prompt using the session history and retrieved context.
  12. Spock sends the prompt to the primary generative LLM.
  13. Spock stores the assistant response in messages.
  14. Spock records audit information in audit_log.

In this workflow, ship_computer.db provides the durable record of what was asked, what was retrieved, what was authorized, and what was generated.

docs.title: Deep Dive Workflow
docs.text:
"Deep Dive" is a more iterative retrieval and synthesis workflow. It may involve multiple retrieval passes, follow-up subqueries, context expansion, and repeated prompt assembly.

A typical Deep Dive sequence is:

  1. The user submits a complex question or research request.
  2. Spock creates or loads a Deep Dive session in ship_computer.db.
  3. Spock records the initial user message.
  4. Spock embeds the initial prompt using the embedding LLM.
  5. Spock performs an initial similarity search in the vector database.
  6. Spock resolves the returned vector identifiers to chunks using vector_refs.
  7. Spock filters the results using access control and document metadata.
  8. Spock stores the first retrieval pass in the context table.
  9. Spock may generate follow-up subqueries or refinement prompts.
  10. Each subquery is embedded and searched again.
  11. New retrieval results are merged, deduplicated, and re-ranked.
  12. The updated context is persisted in ship_computer.db.
  13. Spock assembles a richer prompt for the generative LLM.
  14. The final answer, intermediate steps, and retrieved context are stored for traceability.

For Deep Dive, ship_computer.db is especially important because it preserves the multi-step reasoning path. It allows Spock to reconstruct which chunks were considered, which retrieval passes were performed, and how the final context was assembled.

docs.title: Role of the Embedding LLM
docs.text:
The embedding LLM is a specialized model used to convert text into numerical vectors. Unlike the primary generative LLM, the embedding LLM is not expected to produce natural-language answers. Its purpose is to represent text in a mathematical space where semantically similar texts are located near one another.

The embedding LLM is used for:

  • User prompts.
  • Uploaded documents.
  • Document chunks.
  • Conversation history, when needed.
  • Follow-up subqueries in Deep Dive workflows.

The resulting vectors capture semantic meaning rather than exact keyword overlap. For example, a query about "how to recover a failed deployment" may be semantically close to a document chunk discussing "rollback procedures after a bad release," even if the exact words differ.

docs.title: Role of the Vector Database
docs.text:
The vector database stores the numerical vectors produced by the embedding LLM. It is optimized for similarity search, meaning it can quickly find the vectors that are closest to a query vector.

The vector database is responsible for:

  • Storing high-dimensional vectors.
  • Maintaining an ANN index for fast similarity search.
  • Returning the most relevant vector identifiers for a query.
  • Providing similarity scores or distance metrics.
  • Scaling to large corpora without requiring full linear scans.

The vector database is not the system of record for application state. It stores the searchable vector representation, while ship_computer.db stores the relational metadata needed to interpret and govern those vectors.

docs.title: How Spock Uses the Embedding LLM and Vector Database Together
docs.text:
Spock acts as the orchestration layer between the embedding LLM, the vector database, the generative LLM, and ship_computer.db.

The overall process is:

  1. Chunking: Spock splits documents into manageable text chunks.
  2. Embedding: Spock sends each chunk to the embedding LLM.
  3. Indexing: Spock stores the resulting vectors in the vector database.
  4. Mapping: Spock stores the relationship between chunks and vector identifiers in ship_computer.db.
  5. Query Embedding: When a user asks a question, Spock embeds the user prompt.
  6. Similarity Search: Spock queries the vector database with the prompt vector.
  7. Result Resolution: Spock maps returned vector identifiers back to chunks.
  8. Authorization: Spock verifies that the user is allowed to access the retrieved chunks.
  9. Context Assembly: Spock stores and ranks the selected chunks in the context table.
  10. Generation: Spock sends the assembled prompt to the primary generative LLM.
  11. Persistence: Spock stores the response and retrieval metadata in ship_computer.db.

docs.title: Why the Embedding LLM and Vector Database Are Separate from SQLite
docs.text:
SQLite 3 is a relational database. It is well suited for structured data, transactions, joins, and durable application state. It is not optimized for high-dimensional vector similarity search.

The embedding LLM and vector database are therefore used for the semantic search layer, while ship_computer.db remains the authoritative store for:

  • User identity.
  • Session state.
  • Document ownership.
  • Chunk metadata.
  • Retrieval history.
  • Access control.
  • Audit records.
  • Prompt and response persistence.

This separation gives Spock a practical architecture: the vector database provides fast semantic retrieval, the embedding LLM provides semantic representation, and ship_computer.db provides durable, queryable, transactional application state.

docs.title: Long Range Sensors
docs.text: The Long Range Sensors module is responsible for external data capture, web search, and UIEG (Universal Extractor) operations. It provides tools for gathering, processing, and managing external data sources to support knowledge discovery and integration.

docs.title: Components
docs.text: Module Role LongRangeSensors.app Main sensor panel that serves as the central interface for coordinating sensor operations. LongRangeSensors.external_search_panel Web search interface that allows users to perform queries using external search APIs. LongRangeSensors.uieg_capture_panel UIEG capture interface that provides a user-facing control surface for initiating data capture tasks. LongRangeSensors.uieg_crawler Web crawler used by UIEG to automatically gather and scrape content from online sources. LongRangeSensors.uieg_database UIEG persistence layer that stores captured and processed data for later retrieval. LongRangeSensors.uieg_import Module responsible for importing, parsing, and structuring captured content for system ingestion. LongRangeSensors.uieg_preview Preview interface that allows users to review and inspect captured data before promotion. LongRangeSensors.uieg_promote Promotion module that adds approved content to the Knowledge Base for broader access. LongRangeSensors.uieg_repo_fetch Repository fetcher that retrieves data from external repositories and third-party source systems. LongRangeSensors.uieg_status Status service that monitors ongoing UIEG operations and reports their current state. LongRangeSensors.web_search_clients Backend API clients that interface with external search engines and APIs to perform web searches.

docs.title: UIEG Pipeline
docs.text:
1. Capture → Crawl web sources: The UIEG crawler gathers content from online sources, identifies relevant pages or documents, and extracts raw material for downstream processing.
  2. Import → Parse and store documents: Captured data is parsed into structured records and stored in the UIEG database so it can be reviewed later.
  3. Preview → Review captured content: Users inspect extracted content to verify accuracy, relevance, and suitability before promotion.
  4. Promote → Add to knowledge base: Approved content is promoted to the Knowledge Base (KB), making it available for broader retrieval and use by Spock or other consumers.

The pipeline intentionally separates collection from integration so that unverified external data does not directly enter the knowledge graph. This staged approach supports review, correction, and controlled promotion of information before it becomes part of the system's trusted knowledge base.

docs.title: UIEG (Universal Extractor)
docs.text: The Universal Extractor (UIEG) is a core component of the Long Range Sensors module designed to handle the extraction and normalization of data from diverse web sources. It acts as an intermediary layer that standardizes incoming information, making it compatible with the internal knowledge base structure. By automating the extraction process, UIEG reduces manual effort in data ingestion while maintaining high fidelity to the original source content.

docs.title: Data Lifecycle
docs.text:
The sensor module follows a strict data lifecycle to ensure quality and integrity:

  • Ingestion: Raw data is collected via crawlers or APIs.
  • Normalization: Data is parsed and structured during the Import phase.
  • Validation: Human review occurs during the Preview phase.
  • Integration: Verified data is merged into the Knowledge Base during the Promote phase.

This pipeline ensures that only high-quality, relevant, and accurate information contributes to the system's overall knowledge graph.

docs.title: UIEG Naming Note
docs.text: In this documentation, UIEG is used as a project-specific label for the Universal Extractor workflow. It does not refer to a separate external service; rather, it describes the set of components that capture, import, preview, and promote extracted web content into the system's knowledge base.

docs.title: SQLite 3 ship_computer.db
docs.text: ship_computer.db is the SQLite 3 database used by the Spock application as the local system of record for operational state, inquiry history, source metadata, and retrieval context. It supports both Ask AI and Deep Dive workflows by storing the durable data needed to track conversations, preserve citations, manage UIEG pipeline state, and maintain references to embedded content.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The ship_computer.db database provides a persistent, transactional foundation for Spock. It is used to:

  • Store Spock conversations and message history.
  • Record Ask AI inquiries, answers, and retrieved context.
  • Track Deep Dive runs, subqueries, intermediate findings, and final reports.
  • Maintain source metadata for documents, web pages, repositories, and UIEG captures.
  • Store references to chunks, embeddings, and vector DB records.
  • Preserve audit trails for review, debugging, and reproducibility.
  • Support hybrid retrieval by combining relational metadata with lexical search indexes.

In short, ship_computer.db is the authoritative store for what Spock knows about its own operations, while the vector DB is the authoritative store for semantic similarity search over embedded text.

docs.title: Relationship to Spock
docs.text:
Spock uses ship_computer.db as its primary local database for application state. When a user submits an Ask AI question or initiates a Deep Dive inquiry, Spock reads from and writes to this database to maintain context, traceability, and consistency.

The database is especially important because:

  • It allows Spock to resume conversations after restarts.
  • It preserves the exact context used to generate an answer.
  • It enables citation tracking by linking answers to specific chunks and sources.
  • It supports Deep Dive workflows by storing multi-step research state.
  • It provides a stable metadata layer for the vector DB, even if the vector store is external or SQLite-backed.

docs.title: Core Tables
docs.text:
The following table describes the primary table categories used by Spock in ship_computer.db.

Table Purpose spock_conversations Stores top-level conversation records for Ask AI and Deep Dive sessions. spock_messages Stores individual user and assistant messages within a conversation. ask_ai_inquiries Records Ask AI questions, normalized queries, answers, citations, and retrieval metadata. deep_dive_runs Records Deep Dive objectives, status, final reports, and lifecycle timestamps. deep_dive_steps Records individual Deep Dive subqueries, retrieval actions, and intermediate findings. sources Stores source metadata such as URLs, repository identifiers, capture timestamps, and trust levels. documents Stores normalized documents promoted from UIEG or other ingestion paths. chunks Stores text chunks derived from documents for embedding and retrieval. embeddings Stores embedding metadata, model version, dimensionality, and references to vector DB records. vector_index_metadata Tracks vector index names, models, dimensions, metrics, and rebuild state. ui_eg_captures Stores raw capture records from the UIEG pipeline. ui_eg_imports Stores import and parsing results for captured content. ui_eg_previews Stores preview state and review metadata for captured content. ui_eg_promotions Stores promotion records linking approved content to the Knowledge Base. audit_log Stores operational events for debugging, compliance, and traceability.

docs.title: Ask AI Interaction
docs.text:
Ask AI is Spock's direct question-answering mode. It is designed for fast, context-aware responses based on the current conversation and the available knowledge base.

When Spock handles an Ask AI inquiry, it interacts with ship_computer.db in the following way:

  1. Conversation lookup or creation Spock checks whether the current conversation already exists in spock_conversations. If not, it creates a new conversation record.

  2. Message persistence The user's question is stored in spock_messages with metadata such as timestamp, role, and conversation ID.

  3. Query normalization Spock normalizes the question into a canonical form suitable for retrieval. This may include trimming, language normalization, entity extraction, and filter derivation.

  4. Embedding lookup or generation Spock checks whether an embedding for the normalized query already exists in embeddings. If not, it requests the embedding LLM to generate one and stores the resulting metadata in ship_computer.db.

  5. Retrieval context storage After querying the vector DB, Spock stores the retrieved chunk IDs, source IDs, scores, and ranking metadata in ask_ai_inquiries.

  6. Answer generation Spock uses the retrieved context to build a prompt for the answer-generating LLM. The final answer is then stored in ask_ai_inquiries and appended to spock_messages.

  7. Citation preservation The sources and chunks used to support the answer are linked to the inquiry record so that Spock can later explain, audit, or regenerate the response.

This design ensures that Ask AI responses are not only generated in real time but also remain inspectable and reproducible.

docs.title: Deep Dive Interaction
docs.text:
Deep Dive is Spock's extended research mode. It is used when a question requires multi-step investigation, source comparison, or synthesis across multiple documents.

When Spock executes a Deep Dive inquiry, it uses ship_computer.db to maintain a durable research state:

  1. Run creation Spock creates a record in deep_dive_runs containing the objective, status, and lifecycle timestamps.

  2. Research planning Spock decomposes the objective into subquestions or research steps. Each step is stored in deep_dive_steps.

  3. Subquery embedding For each subquery, Spock generates or retrieves an embedding and stores the associated metadata in embeddings.

  4. Retrieval execution Spock queries the vector DB for relevant chunks and stores the retrieved chunk IDs, source IDs, and scores in the corresponding deep_dive_steps record.

  5. Evidence accumulation As Spock gathers evidence, it records intermediate findings, confidence notes, and source references in deep_dive_steps.

  6. Gap detection and follow-up If Spock identifies missing information, it may generate additional subqueries, trigger Long Range Sensors web search, or request UIEG capture of new sources.

  7. Synthesis Once sufficient evidence is collected, Spock synthesizes a final report and stores it in deep_dive_runs.

  8. Audit trail The full sequence of steps, queries, retrieved sources, and final output remains available in ship_computer.db for review and debugging.

This makes Deep Dive a traceable, stateful workflow rather than a single one-shot query.

docs.title: Consistency and Audit
docs.text:
Because Spock depends on both relational state and semantic retrieval, ship_computer.db plays a key role in maintaining consistency:

  • Content hashing prevents duplicate chunks and duplicate embeddings.
  • Embedding versioning ensures that Spock can distinguish vectors generated by different embedding models.
  • Source linkage allows every answer to be traced back to a specific document, chunk, and capture event.
  • Run state tracking allows Deep Dive workflows to be resumed or replayed.
  • Audit logging supports debugging, quality review, and operational monitoring.

If the vector DB is implemented as an external service, ship_computer.db stores the stable identifiers and metadata needed to reconcile Spock's local state with the vector store. If the vector DB is implemented as a SQLite-backed vector extension, ship_computer.db may also host the vector index itself while still serving as the primary metadata and state store.

docs.title: Spock Embedding LLM and Vector DB
docs.text: Spock uses an embedding LLM and a vector DB to convert text into searchable semantic representations. The embedding LLM is responsible for producing dense vector representations of text, while the vector DB is responsible for storing those vectors and retrieving the most relevant ones for a given query.

docs.title: Embedding LLM
docs.text:
The embedding LLM is a specialized model used to transform text into fixed-dimensional numerical vectors. Unlike the answer-generating LLM, the embedding LLM does not produce natural language output. Instead, it produces a vector that captures the semantic meaning of the input text.

Spock uses the embedding LLM for:

  • Embedding Knowledge Base documents.
  • Embedding UIEG-promoted content.
  • Embedding web search results that have been captured and normalized.
  • Embedding user questions in Ask AI.
  • Embedding subqueries in Deep Dive.
  • Embedding repository content and other structured sources.

The embedding LLM is important because it allows Spock to retrieve content based on meaning, not just exact keyword matches.

docs.title: Vector DB
docs.text:
The vector DB is the semantic retrieval layer used by Spock. It stores the vectors produced by the embedding LLM along with the metadata needed to filter, rank, and cite results.

The vector DB is used to:

  • Store high-dimensional vectors for chunks, queries, and subqueries.
  • Perform approximate nearest neighbor search.
  • Retrieve the most semantically relevant chunks for a given query.
  • Apply metadata filters such as source type, date, trust level, and document status.
  • Support hybrid retrieval by combining semantic similarity with lexical search.
  • Maintain index metadata such as model version, dimensionality, and similarity metric.

The vector DB may be implemented as a standalone vector database or as a SQLite-backed vector store. In either case, Spock treats it as the semantic search service and uses ship_computer.db to preserve the relational context around each retrieval.

docs.title: Ask AI Retrieval Flow
docs.text:
The Ask AI flow uses the embedding LLM and vector DB to answer a user question with retrieved context.

  1. Question intake Spock receives the user's question and associates it with the active conversation.

  2. Context assembly Spock loads recent conversation context from ship_computer.db to preserve continuity.

  3. Query embedding Spock sends the normalized question to the embedding LLM and receives a query vector.

  4. Semantic search Spock queries the vector DB for the most similar chunks using the query vector.

  5. Metadata filtering Spock applies filters based on source type, trust level, document status, and other constraints stored in ship_computer.db.

  6. Hybrid ranking Spock may combine vector similarity with lexical search results from ship_computer.db to improve precision.

  7. Prompt construction Spock builds a prompt containing the user question, conversation context, and retrieved chunks.

  8. Answer generation The answer-generating LLM produces a response grounded in the retrieved context.

  9. Result persistence Spock stores the question, answer, retrieved chunks, citations, and retrieval metadata in ship_computer.db.

This flow allows Ask AI to provide fast, grounded answers while preserving a complete record of the evidence used.

docs.title: Deep Dive Retrieval Flow
docs.text:
The Deep Dive flow uses the same embedding and vector retrieval infrastructure, but in a more iterative and stateful way.

  1. Objective decomposition Spock breaks the Deep Dive objective into multiple subquestions or research steps.

  2. Subquery embedding Each subquestion is embedded using the embedding LLM.

  3. Iterative retrieval Spock queries the vector DB for each subquestion and retrieves relevant chunks and sources.

  4. Evidence evaluation Spock evaluates the retrieved evidence for relevance, completeness, and conflicts.

  5. Follow-up retrieval If gaps are detected, Spock generates additional subqueries and performs further vector searches.

  6. External capture if needed If the existing knowledge base is insufficient, Spock may use Long Range Sensors to perform web search or UIEG capture.

  7. Synthesis Spock combines the collected evidence into a structured Deep Dive report.

  8. State persistence The full run, including subqueries, retrieved sources, intermediate findings, and final report, is stored in ship_computer.db.

This makes Deep Dive suitable for complex questions that require comparison, synthesis, and multi-source reasoning.

docs.title: Hybrid Search and Ranking
docs.text:
Spock does not rely on vector search alone. It combines semantic retrieval with relational and lexical signals to improve result quality.

The hybrid retrieval strategy may include:

  • Vector similarity for semantic relevance.
  • Full-text search for exact keyword matches.
  • Metadata filters for source type, date, trust level, and document status.
  • Recency weighting to favor newer content when appropriate.
  • Source confidence weighting to prioritize verified or promoted content.
  • Deduplication to avoid redundant chunks from the same document.
  • Citation grouping to present results by source rather than by isolated fragments.

This approach allows Spock to balance semantic understanding with precise, auditable retrieval.

docs.title: Embedding Lifecycle
docs.text:
The embedding lifecycle connects the Long Range Sensors module, the Knowledge Base, and Spock's retrieval system.

  1. Capture Long Range Sensors captures external content through web search, crawling, or repository fetch.

  2. Import Captured content is parsed and normalized into structured records.

  3. Preview Users review the content for accuracy and relevance.

  4. Promotion Approved content is promoted to the Knowledge Base.

  5. Chunking Promoted documents are split into retrieval-ready chunks.

  6. Embedding Each chunk is sent to the embedding LLM and converted into a vector.

  7. Indexing The vector and associated metadata are stored in the vector DB.

  8. Retrieval Spock uses the vector DB to retrieve relevant chunks for Ask AI and Deep Dive inquiries.

  9. Re-embedding If the embedding model changes, Spock can re-embed affected content and rebuild the vector index.

This lifecycle ensures that content moves from external capture to trusted, searchable knowledge in a controlled and auditable way.
