The adapter abstracts raw SQL operations into structured data access methods, ensuring that schema changes or query optimizations do not require widespread refactoring across the application.

docs.title: Ask AI Inquiries
docs.text:
For "Ask AI" requests, the system performs rapid, context-aware retrieval operations:

  1. Query Parsing & Embedding: The incoming user prompt is tokenized and passed to the embedding LLM, which converts it into a high-dimensional vector representation.
  2. Vector Similarity Search: The database queries the Knowledge Base table to identify relevant text chunks based on cosine similarity or dot product distance against the query vector. Metadata filters may be applied to scope results to specific domains or timeframes.
  3. Context Assembly & Response Generation: Retrieved chunks are ranked, truncated to fit context window limits, and injected into the prompt template. The primary LLM generates a response, which is returned through the MCP protocol. Session state is optionally updated to maintain conversation continuity and track token consumption.

docs.title: Deep Dive Inquiries
docs.text:
For "Deep Dive" requests, the system executes complex, multi-step analytical workflows:

  1. Cross-Table Correlation: The database performs multi-table joins to correlate data across domains, such as linking user session history with analysis logs, system metrics, or external data sources. This enables the agent to trace decision paths and validate findings against historical patterns.
  2. Aggregation & State Persistence: SQL aggregations summarize historical data, calculate trends, and produce derived metrics. Intermediate results and final analysis outputs are persisted to the Analysis Logs and User Sessions tables, ensuring auditability and enabling incremental reasoning across multiple turns.
  3. Transaction Management: All write operations during a Deep Dive session are wrapped in explicit transactions. This ensures atomicity, allowing the system to roll back changes if the analysis fails, encounters validation errors, or exceeds resource thresholds. Read-heavy analytical queries are optimized to avoid holding write locks unnecessarily, preserving system responsiveness.

docs.title: Embedding LLM and Vector Database Integration
docs.text:
The Spock application relies on a tightly coupled architecture for semantic search: an embedding model for vectorization and SQLite as a lightweight, embedded vector database. When a document or knowledge artifact is ingested, it is chunked and passed through the embedding LLM (e.g., text-embedding-3-small, nomic-embed-text, or a local equivalent). The resulting vectors are stored directly in the Knowledge Base table using SQLite's BLOB or REAL array types, often accelerated by extensions like sqlite-vec or application-level vector libraries.

During inference, the same embedding model processes user queries to ensure vector space consistency. SQLite then performs approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) or exact nearest neighbor (NN) searches using distance metrics configured in the schema. This integrated approach eliminates the need for external vector databases like Pinecone, Weaviate, or Milvus, reducing infrastructure complexity, network latency, and operational overhead. By co-locating relational metadata and vector embeddings within a single file, Spock achieves low-latency retrieval, simplified backup procedures, and deterministic state management suitable for conversational AI workflows.

docs.title: Embedding Model Responsibilities
docs.text:
The embedding model is responsible for converting natural language text into numerical vectors that represent semantic meaning. In Spock, this model is used in two critical phases:

  • Ingestion: Knowledge documents, help articles, system notes, or user-provided context are split into manageable chunks. Each chunk is converted into a vector and stored alongside its metadata.
  • Query Time: The user's "Ask AI" or "Deep Dive" prompt is converted into a vector using the same embedding model. This allows the system to compare the query vector against stored knowledge vectors and retrieve semantically relevant content.

Using the same embedding model for both ingestion and querying is essential. If different models are used, their vector spaces may not be compatible, causing poor retrieval quality or meaningless similarity scores.

docs.title: Vector Storage and Search
docs.text:
SQLite does not provide a native vector data type in the core database engine. Therefore, Spock can store embeddings in one of several ways:

  • BLOB Storage: The vector is serialized into a binary blob and stored in a column. The application deserializes the vector and performs similarity calculations in Python or another host language.
  • REAL Array Storage: The vector is stored as a fixed-length sequence of REAL values. This is simpler to inspect but can be less efficient for large-scale search.
  • sqlite-vec or Similar Extension: A vector extension provides optimized storage and nearest-neighbor search directly inside SQLite. This is the preferred approach when the knowledge base grows beyond a few thousand chunks.

For small knowledge bases, exact nearest-neighbor search is acceptable. For larger collections, approximate nearest-neighbor search or hybrid search using full-text search plus vector similarity may improve performance and relevance.

docs.title: Model Consistency and Versioning
docs.text: Because embedding models can change over time, Spock should record the embedding model name, version, and vector dimension alongside each stored vector. This allows the application to detect when a model upgrade requires re-embedding the knowledge base. Without this metadata, the system may silently compare vectors from incompatible models, producing degraded retrieval results.

docs.title: Maintenance and Health
docs.text:
Regular maintenance is required to keep ship_computer.db performant and reliable. Recommended practices include:

  • Enable WAL Mode: Use PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL; to improve concurrent read/write behavior.
  • Set Busy Timeout: Use PRAGMA busy_timeout=5000; or a similar value to reduce transient SQLITE_BUSY errors.
  • Monitor File Growth: Track database size, especially if embeddings are stored locally.
  • Vacuum and Analyze: Periodically run VACUUM and ANALYZE to reclaim space and improve query planning.
  • Validate Integrity: Use PRAGMA integrity_check; during maintenance windows to detect corruption.
  • Back Up the Database File: Because SQLite is file-based, consistent backups can be performed by copying the database file while the application is idle or by using SQLite's online backup API.

docs.title: Database Maintenance
docs.text:
• Vacuuming: Schedule periodic VACUUM operations during low-activity windows to reclaim unused space from deleted or updated records. On large databases, this operation can be resource-intensive and should not run concurrently with critical write operations.
  • Backup Strategy: Maintain regular backups of ship_computer.db. Use a consistent backup method, such as SQLite's Online Backup API or an application-provided export utility, rather than copying the file directly while the application is running, which risks data corruption or incomplete transactions.
  • Integrity Checks: Periodically run integrity checks using PRAGMA integrity_check during maintenance windows to detect file corruption early and validate recovery procedures. Additionally, monitor PRAGMA page_count and PRAGMA freelist_count to track database growth, fragmentation, and storage efficiency over time.

docs.title: SQLite 3 ship_computer.db
docs.text:
ship_computer.db is the local SQLite 3 database used by the Spock application. It serves as the primary structured data store for application state, user data, conversation history, document metadata, retrieval results, and operational logs.

SQLite 3 is an embedded, file-based relational database engine. In the Spock application, it provides:

  • Local persistence: Data is stored in a single database file, making deployment, backup, and recovery straightforward.
  • ACID behavior: Transactions are atomic, consistent, isolated, and durable, which helps protect application state during writes.
  • Multi-reader, single-writer access: Multiple readers can access the database concurrently, while writes are serialized to maintain consistency.
  • Low operational overhead: SQLite does not require a separate database server process, which is useful for local or edge deployments.
  • Structured metadata storage: It stores the canonical text, metadata, relationships, and audit information that support Ask AI and Deep Dive workflows.

The database is not intended to be the primary semantic search index. Semantic search is handled by the vector database, while ship_computer.db remains the source of truth for application data, document content, conversation history, and retrieval metadata.

docs.title: Responsibilities of ship_computer.db
docs.text:
ship_computer.db stores the data required for the Spock application to operate reliably and reproducibly. Typical responsibilities include:

  • Application metadata: schema version, application settings, feature flags, and local configuration.
  • User and session data: user profiles, preferences, permissions, and active session state.
  • Document management: source documents, titles, authors, sources, hashes, timestamps, and content.
  • Chunk management: text chunks derived from documents, chunk ordering, token counts, and metadata.
  • Conversation history: Ask AI and Deep Dive sessions, messages, prompts, responses, and model metadata.
  • Retrieval tracking: which chunks were retrieved for a query, their scores, ranks, and associated vector identifiers.
  • Feedback and evaluation: user ratings, corrections, follow-up questions, and quality metrics.
  • Operational logs: indexing events, embedding model changes, vector database synchronization events, and maintenance actions.

docs.title: Typical Data Model
docs.text:
The exact schema may vary by deployment, but a typical ship_computer.db design includes tables such as the following:

Table Purpose documents Stores source documents, titles, sources, hashes, and timestamps. chunks Stores text chunks derived from documents, including chunk order and metadata. conversations Stores Ask AI and Deep Dive session metadata. messages Stores user questions, assistant responses, model names, token usage, and latency. retrieval_results Stores retrieved chunks, similarity scores, ranks, and vector database identifiers. feedback Stores user ratings, corrections, and qualitative feedback. embedding_jobs Tracks embedding generation, model version, status, and completion time. vector_sync_log Tracks synchronization between SQLite and the vector database. settings Stores application-level and user-level configuration. audit_log Records significant application events for troubleshooting and compliance.

This separation allows Spock to keep human-readable content and application state in SQLite while using the vector database for fast semantic similarity search.

docs.title: Interaction with Spock: Ask AI and Deep Dive
docs.text: The Spock application uses ship_computer.db as the coordination layer for both Ask AI and Deep Dive inquiries. The vector database provides semantic retrieval, while SQLite provides durable context, history, and traceability.

docs.title: Ask AI Workflow
docs.text:
Ask AI is a direct question-and-answer workflow. A user submits a question, and Spock returns a concise, context-aware answer.

The typical Ask AI flow is:

  1. Receive the user question Spock receives the question from the user interface and validates the request.

  2. Create or load the conversation Spock checks whether the question belongs to an existing conversation or starts a new one. It stores the conversation and message metadata in ship_computer.db.

  3. Load relevant context Spock may retrieve recent messages, user preferences, document permissions, and prior retrieval results from SQLite to shape the prompt.

  4. Generate a query embedding Spock sends the question to the embedding model. The embedding model converts the question into a numerical vector that represents its semantic meaning.

  5. Search the vector database Spock queries the vector database for the most similar text chunks. The vector database returns candidate chunks along with similarity scores and metadata.

  6. Filter and rank results Spock applies metadata filters, permission checks, recency rules, and optional reranking to produce a final set of context chunks.

  7. Build the prompt Spock combines the user question, retrieved chunks, metadata, and system instructions into a prompt for the answer-generating model.

  8. Generate the answer The answer-generating model produces a response using the retrieved context.

  9. Store the result Spock writes the answer, retrieved chunks, scores, model metadata, token usage, and latency back to ship_computer.db.

  10. Return the answer Spock returns the answer to the user, optionally including citations or source references.

In this workflow, SQLite is responsible for durable application state, while the vector database is responsible for semantic retrieval.

docs.title: Deep Dive Workflow
docs.text:
Deep Dive is a more complex inquiry workflow. Instead of answering a single question directly, Spock performs iterative research, retrieves multiple sources, compares evidence, and synthesizes a more detailed response.

The typical Deep Dive flow is:

  1. Receive the research request The user submits a broad or complex question that requires deeper analysis.

  2. Create a Deep Dive session Spock creates a session record in ship_computer.db to track the research process.

  3. Decompose the question Spock breaks the request into subquestions, themes, or search intents. For example, a question about system reliability may be decomposed into failure modes, historical incidents, mitigation strategies, and operational recommendations.

  4. Generate embeddings for each subquery Each subquestion is converted into a vector using the embedding model.

  5. Perform multiple vector searches Spock queries the vector database for each subquery, retrieving candidate chunks from the knowledge base.

  6. Deduplicate and merge results Spock removes duplicate chunks, merges overlapping results, and ranks the combined evidence.

  7. Iterate as needed If the initial results are insufficient, Spock may generate follow-up subqueries, refine filters, or search for additional context.

  8. Synthesize the response Spock uses the answer-generating model to produce a structured Deep Dive response, such as a summary, comparison, timeline, or recommendation.

  9. Record the research trail Spock stores the subqueries, retrieved chunks, scores, intermediate reasoning, final answer, and citations in ship_computer.db.

  10. Present the result Spock returns the Deep Dive response to the user, with references to the supporting chunks and sources.

Deep Dive relies more heavily on SQLite because it must preserve the full research trail, including intermediate queries, retrieved evidence, and final synthesis.

docs.title: Embedding LLM and Vector Database
docs.text: The Spock application uses an embedding model, sometimes referred to as an embedding LLM, together with a vector database to support semantic search.

docs.title: What the Embedding Model Does
docs.text:
The embedding model converts text into a numerical vector. Each vector represents the semantic meaning of the text in a high-dimensional space. Text with similar meaning produces vectors that are close together, while unrelated text produces vectors that are farther apart.

For example:

  • A document chunk about “database backup procedures” and a user question about “how to back up the database” should produce similar vectors.
  • A document chunk about “user authentication” and a question about “database backups” should produce less similar vectors.

The embedding model is typically a transformer-based encoder model. It is different from the answer-generating model:

  • Embedding model: converts text into vectors for search and similarity comparison.
  • Answer-generating model: uses retrieved context to produce natural-language responses.

Both models may be local or remote, depending on the deployment. If the embedding model is remote, the text being embedded may leave the local environment. If the model is local, embedding remains on-device.

docs.title: Why Spock Uses Embeddings
docs.text:
Spock uses embeddings because keyword search alone is not sufficient for natural-language questions. Embeddings allow Spock to understand semantic intent, synonyms, paraphrases, and related concepts.

For example, a user may ask:

  • “How do I back up the database?”
  • “What is the recommended backup process?”
  • “Can you explain the database recovery procedure?”

These questions use different wording but have similar intent. Embeddings allow Spock to retrieve relevant chunks even when the exact keywords do not match.

docs.title: How Spock Uses the Embedding Model
docs.text:
Spock uses the embedding model in two main phases:

  1. Indexing phase When documents are added or updated, Spock splits them into chunks, sends each chunk to the embedding model, and stores the resulting vector in the vector database.

  2. Query phase When a user asks a question, Spock sends the question to the same embedding model and uses the resulting vector to search the vector database for similar chunks.

Using the same embedding model for indexing and querying is important. If the model changes, the vector space changes, and previously stored embeddings may no longer be compatible with new query embeddings. In that case, Spock should re-embed the indexed content.

docs.title: Vector Database Role
docs.text:
The vector database stores embeddings and supports fast similarity search. It is optimized for operations such as:

  • Nearest-neighbor search
  • Approximate nearest-neighbor search
  • Cosine similarity, dot product, or Euclidean distance calculations
  • Metadata filtering
  • Batch upserts and deletions
  • Index rebuilding

The vector database is not the primary store for document text or application state. Instead, it stores:

  • The embedding vector
  • A reference to the corresponding chunk or document
  • Metadata used for filtering and ranking
  • Indexing information required for fast search

SQLite remains the source of truth for the actual text, document metadata, conversation history, and retrieval logs.

docs.title: Indexing Pipeline
docs.text:
The indexing pipeline prepares content for semantic search.

  1. Ingest source content Spock receives documents, notes, logs, or other text sources.

  2. Normalize and store content Spock stores the canonical text and metadata in ship_computer.db.

  3. Chunk the content Spock splits the text into manageable chunks. Chunking balances context size, retrieval precision, and model input limits.

  4. Generate embeddings Spock sends each chunk to the embedding model and receives a vector.

  5. Store vector metadata Spock stores the vector in the vector database along with a reference to the chunk ID and relevant metadata.

  6. Record indexing state Spock records the embedding model name, version, dimension, timestamp, and status in ship_computer.db.

This pipeline allows Spock to keep the human-readable content in SQLite while using the vector database for efficient semantic retrieval.

docs.title: Query Pipeline
docs.text:
The query pipeline supports Ask AI and Deep Dive.

  1. Receive the user query Spock receives the question or research request.

  2. Prepare the query Spock may clean, expand, or decompose the query depending on the workflow.

  3. Embed the query Spock sends the query to the embedding model.

  4. Search the vector database Spock requests the most similar vectors from the vector database.

  5. Apply filters Spock filters results by permissions, document type, date range, source, or other metadata.

  6. Rerank results Spock may use a reranker or scoring heuristic to improve result quality.

  7. Assemble context Spock selects the best chunks and formats them for the answer-generating model.

  8. Generate the response Spock produces the final answer or Deep Dive synthesis.

  9. Persist the result Spock stores the query, retrieved chunks, scores, answer, and metadata in ship_computer.db.

docs.title: Consistency Between SQLite and the Vector Database
docs.text:
Because Spock uses two storage systems, it must keep them consistent.

  • SQLite is the source of truth for document text, chunk text, metadata, conversations, and retrieval history.
  • The vector database is a search index for embeddings and similarity lookup.

When content changes, Spock should:

  • Update the canonical text in ship_computer.db.
  • Update or delete the corresponding vector in the vector database.
  • Record the synchronization event in ship_computer.db.
  • Re-embed content if the embedding model changes.

If the vector database becomes unavailable, Spock can fall back to SQLite-based search, such as full-text search or exact matching, if available. This fallback may be less semantically accurate but can preserve basic functionality.

docs.title: Embedding Model Versioning
docs.text:
Embedding models should be versioned because different models produce different vector spaces.

Spock should track:

  • Model name
  • Model version
  • Vector dimension
  • Embedding timestamp
  • Chunk ID
  • Document ID
  • Index status

If Spock upgrades the embedding model, it should rebuild the vector index or maintain separate indexes for different model versions. Mixing embeddings from incompatible models can reduce retrieval quality.

docs.title: Security and Privacy Considerations
docs.text:
Because ship_computer.db may contain sensitive application data, Spock should protect it with appropriate file permissions, encryption at rest, and controlled access.

If the embedding model or vector database is remote, Spock should clearly indicate which data is sent externally. If the deployment requires local-only processing, Spock should use local embedding models and a local vector database.

docs.title: Monitoring and Maintenance
docs.text:
Spock should monitor both SQLite and the vector database to maintain search quality and operational health.

Useful metrics include:

  • ship_computer.db file size
  • SQLite page count and freelist count
  • Number of documents, chunks, and conversations
  • Embedding job success and failure rates
  • Vector database index size
  • Query latency
  • Retrieval hit rate
  • User feedback scores
  • Stale or orphaned vector records

Regular maintenance should include:

  • Backups of ship_computer.db
  • Integrity checks
  • Vacuuming during low-activity windows
  • Reindexing after embedding model changes
  • Cleanup of orphaned vectors
  • Validation of synchronization between SQLite and the vector database

docs.title: Model Selector
docs.text: The Model Selector facilitates the selection of appropriate Large Language Models (LLMs) for specific tasks by evaluating hardware constraints and model specifications. It ensures that chosen models are compatible with the target environment while optimizing for performance, task accuracy, and resource efficiency.

docs.title: Components
docs.text: Module Role model_selector_core Contains the core logic for selecting models based on selection criteria, including filtering algorithms, compatibility checks, and resource estimation. model_selector_panels Provides UI panels for interacting with and selecting models from the registry via a graphical interface. model_pick_policy Defines the policy or ranking mechanism used during model selection to prioritize specific attributes, such as speed versus quality. gemini_openai_models Maintains a registry of available models, including their specifications, capabilities, supported inference engines, and resource requirements.

docs.title: How the Modules Work Together
docs.text:
The Model Selector uses these modules in a coordinated workflow:

  1. Model Discovery — gemini_openai_models provides the catalog of candidate models and their metadata.
  2. Compatibility Filtering — model_selector_core removes models that do not meet hard requirements, such as available VRAM, context length, or inference engine support.
  3. Ranking and Selection — model_pick_policy ranks the remaining candidates according to the desired trade-off between speed, quality, task fit, and resource usage.
  4. User Interaction — model_selector_panels presents the available options and allows users to review or override the selected model when appropriate.

docs.title: Selection Criteria
docs.text:
1. GPU VRAM — The model must fit within the available VRAM of the target hardware. This ensures that the model can be loaded and run without causing memory-related errors or performance degradation.

  2. Note: Memory requirements include both model weights and active context, such as the KV cache. Quantization may reduce this footprint.

  3. Task Match — The model's capabilities should align with the specific requirements of the task. For example, a model designed for language translation may not be suitable for code generation.

  4. Note: Verify capability tags or fine-tuning history to ensure domain-specific proficiency.

  5. Speed — Preference is given to models with lower inference latency when appropriate for the use case. This is particularly important for real-time or interactive applications where response time is critical.

  6. Note: Consider tokens-per-second (TPS), batch size efficiency, and prompt processing overhead when evaluating speed.

  7. Quality — Models are ranked based on their benchmark scores, reflecting overall performance and accuracy. Higher benchmark scores typically indicate better performance on standard evaluation tasks.

  8. Note: Scores may vary based on the specific benchmark suite used, such as MMLU or HumanEval.

docs.title: How Criteria Are Combined
docs.text:
The selector treats some criteria as hard constraints and others as ranking factors:

  • Hard Constraints — Models that fail VRAM, context window, task compatibility, or inference engine requirements are excluded before ranking.
  • Soft Ranking Factors — Remaining models are scored using the active model_pick_policy. Depending on the selected mode, the policy may prioritize lower latency, higher benchmark quality, better task alignment, or a balanced combination of these attributes.

docs.title: Technical Considerations
docs.text:
When using the Model Selector, consider the following technical nuances that affect selection outcomes:

  • Quantization: Models can be loaded in lower precision formats, such as FP8 or INT4, to reduce VRAM usage without significant quality loss. The selector should account for quantized model sizes when checking VRAM limits.
  • Context Window: Ensure the model's maximum context window supports the input length required by the task. Exceeding this limit will result in truncation or errors.
  • Inference Engine Compatibility: Verify that the selected model is compatible with specific hardware accelerators, such as CUDA or ROCm, and software libraries supported by the registry.

docs.title: SQLite 3 ship_computer.db Integration
docs.text: The ship_computer.db file is a local SQLite 3 database used by the Spock application to store structured ship-computer data and to support Ask AI and Deep Dive inquiries. It acts as the system of record for metadata, documents, telemetry, user context, and retrieval results.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The database provides a durable, queryable foundation for the Spock application. It stores the information that Ask AI and Deep Dive need to answer questions, retrieve relevant context, and maintain auditability.

The database is especially useful for:

  • Storing structured records about the ship computer, including configuration, status, logs, and operational data.
  • Maintaining references to documents, knowledge-base entries, and user-generated content.
  • Supporting metadata filtering, such as time range, subsystem, severity, user role, or document type.
  • Providing stable identifiers that can be linked to embeddings in the vector database.
  • Enabling deterministic retrieval, auditing, and debugging of AI responses.

docs.title: Typical Contents
docs.text:
The exact schema may vary by deployment, but a typical ship_computer.db database may include the following categories of data:

Area Description documents Stores source documents, notes, manuals, logs, or knowledge-base entries that can be retrieved by Ask AI or Deep Dive. metadata Stores attributes used for filtering, such as subsystem, timestamp, severity, source, owner, or classification. queries Records user questions, prompts, and request context for auditing and reproducibility. retrieval_results Stores the records returned for a given query, including relevance scores and retrieval metadata. embeddings_index May store local references to vector IDs, embedding model versions, and chunk identifiers. audit_log Tracks model selections, retrieval actions, user overrides, and system events.

docs.title: Relationship to the Vector Database
docs.text:
The SQLite database and the vector database serve complementary roles.

  • SQLite 3 ship_computer.db stores the authoritative structured data, metadata, and references.
  • Vector database stores numerical embeddings and supports semantic similarity search.

A common pattern is to store a stable identifier in both systems. For example, a document chunk in ship_computer.db may have an ID such as doc_1042_chunk_7. The vector database stores the embedding for that chunk and references the same ID. When Spock retrieves a vector match, it can use the ID to load the full text and metadata from SQLite.

This separation allows the system to benefit from:

  • Fast semantic search through the vector database.
  • Reliable structured filtering through SQLite.
  • Easy auditing and debugging because the source records remain in a standard relational database.
  • Independent scaling of vector search and relational data access.

docs.title: Interaction with Spock: Ask AI
docs.text:
Ask AI is intended for direct, focused questions. The Spock application uses ship_computer.db to ground the answer in relevant local data.

A typical Ask AI flow is:

  1. The user submits a question through the Spock interface.
  2. Spock records the question and request context in the database.
  3. The question is converted into an embedding using the selected embedding LLM.
  4. The vector database returns the most semantically similar records.
  5. Spock uses the returned identifiers to load full text and metadata from ship_computer.db.
  6. Optional metadata filters are applied, such as time range, subsystem, document type, or access level.
  7. The retrieved context is assembled into a prompt for the answer LLM.
  8. The LLM generates a response.
  9. Spock stores the response, retrieved sources, model used, and confidence or scoring metadata for auditability.

This approach allows Ask AI to provide concise, evidence-based answers while preserving traceability back to the original records in ship_computer.db.

docs.title: Interaction with Spock: Deep Dive
docs.text:
Deep Dive is intended for broader investigation, where the user needs a more comprehensive understanding of a topic, incident, subsystem, or operational pattern.

Compared with Ask AI, Deep Dive typically uses the database in a more iterative and analytical way:

  • It may retrieve a larger set of related records.
  • It may apply multiple metadata filters.
  • It may group results by subsystem, time, severity, or document type.
  • It may perform follow-up semantic searches based on intermediate findings.
  • It may summarize clusters of related records before generating a final explanation.
  • It may preserve a richer audit trail of the investigation steps.

A typical Deep Dive flow is:

  1. The user requests a detailed analysis or investigation.
  2. Spock creates a Deep Dive session in ship_computer.db.
  3. The initial query is embedded and searched in the vector database.
  4. Spock retrieves candidate records and loads their metadata from SQLite.
  5. The records are grouped, filtered, or ranked using structured criteria.
  6. Spock may issue additional semantic queries to explore related concepts.
  7. The accumulated context is summarized or condensed to fit the answer model's context window.
  8. The LLM produces a structured Deep Dive response.
  9. Spock stores the session, intermediate results, final answer, and source references.

This makes Deep Dive suitable for complex questions that require multiple retrieval passes and structured reasoning over the contents of ship_computer.db.

docs.title: Data Flow
docs.text:
The overall data flow between Spock, SQLite, the embedding LLM, and the vector database is:

  1. Ingestion — Source data is written to ship_computer.db.
  2. Chunking — Long documents or logs are divided into manageable chunks.
  3. Embedding — Each chunk is converted into a vector by the embedding LLM.
  4. Indexing — The vector and its reference ID are stored in the vector database.
  5. Querying — A user question is embedded and searched against the vector index.
  6. Retrieval — Matching IDs are used to load full records from SQLite.
  7. Generation — The answer LLM uses the retrieved context to produce a response.
  8. Audit — The query, retrieved records, model used, and response are stored for review.

docs.title: Consistency and Performance
docs.text:
Because ship_computer.db is a local SQLite 3 database, it is well suited for single-node or embedded deployments. To maintain reliable behavior, the Spock application should consider:

  • WAL mode — Use SQLite Write-Ahead Logging to improve concurrent read performance.
  • Foreign keys — Enforce relationships between documents, metadata, queries, and retrieval results.
  • Indexing — Add indexes on commonly filtered fields, such as timestamp, subsystem, severity, and document type.
  • Versioning — Track embedding model versions so that stale vectors can be detected and rebuilt.
  • Access control — Apply user-level or role-based filtering before records are included in an AI prompt.
  • Backup — Treat ship_computer.db as a critical data store and include it in backup and recovery procedures.

docs.title: Spock Application: Embedding LLM and Vector Database
docs.text: The Spock application uses an embedding LLM and a vector database to convert natural-language questions and stored content into comparable numerical representations. This enables semantic retrieval, allowing the system to find relevant information even when the user's wording does not exactly match the stored text.

docs.title: Role of the Embedding LLM
docs.text:
The embedding LLM is a specialized model that converts text into a fixed-length numerical vector, also called an embedding.

For example:

  • A user question such as "Why did the navigation subsystem report a fault?" is converted into a vector.
  • A stored log entry such as "Navigation fault detected during attitude correction" is also converted into a vector.
  • If the two concepts are semantically related, their vectors will be closer together in vector space.

The embedding LLM does not generate the final answer. Its role is to create a mathematical representation of meaning that can be compared efficiently.

Key responsibilities of the embedding LLM include:

  • Converting user queries into query vectors.
  • Converting documents, logs, notes, and knowledge-base entries into content vectors.
  • Supporting semantic similarity search.
  • Enabling retrieval of relevant context for the answer LLM.

docs.title: Role of the Vector Database
docs.text:
The vector database stores embeddings and supports fast similarity search. It is optimized for answering questions such as:

  • "Which stored records are most similar to this query?"
  • "Which records are closest to this vector?"
  • "Which records match this query within a given similarity threshold?"

The vector database typically stores:

  • The embedding vector.
  • A reference ID linking back to ship_computer.db.
  • Optional metadata for filtering.
  • Index metadata, such as embedding model version and creation timestamp.

The vector database is not a replacement for SQLite. Instead, it provides semantic search, while SQLite provides structured storage, metadata, and authoritative record access.

docs.title: Embedding Pipeline
docs.text:
The embedding pipeline is the process by which text becomes searchable vector data.

A typical pipeline is:

  1. Source Selection — Spock identifies documents, logs, or records that should be indexed.
  2. Chunking — Long text is divided into smaller chunks to improve retrieval precision.
  3. Normalization — Text is cleaned or normalized as needed.
  4. Embedding — The selected embedding LLM converts each chunk into a vector.
  5. Storage — The vector and its reference ID are stored in the vector database.
  6. Metadata Linking — The reference ID is associated with the corresponding record in ship_computer.db.
  7. Version Tracking — The embedding model name and version are recorded so that the index can be rebuilt if the model changes.

docs.title: Ask AI Query Flow
docs.text:
For Ask AI, Spock uses the embedding LLM and vector database to retrieve a small, highly relevant set of context.

The flow is:

  1. The user asks a question.
  2. Spock sends the question to the embedding LLM.
  3. The embedding LLM returns a query vector.
  4. Spock searches the vector database for the closest matching vectors.
  5. The vector database returns a ranked list of reference IDs and similarity scores.
  6. Spock loads the corresponding records from ship_computer.db.
  7. Spock applies metadata filters and access controls.
  8. Spock selects the top records for the answer prompt.
  9. The answer LLM generates a concise response using the retrieved context.
  10. Spock stores the question, retrieved sources, model used, and response.

This flow is optimized for speed and precision. Ask AI typically retrieves a limited number of records to keep the response focused and the prompt size manageable.

docs.title: Deep Dive Query Flow
docs.text:
For Deep Dive, Spock uses the same embedding and vector search foundation but applies a broader retrieval strategy.

The flow is:

  1. The user requests a detailed investigation.
  2. Spock creates a Deep Dive session in ship_computer.db.
  3. The initial query is embedded and searched in the vector database.
  4. Spock retrieves a larger candidate set than it would for Ask AI.
  5. Spock loads metadata from SQLite and applies structured filters.
  6. Spock groups or clusters related records by subsystem, time, severity, or topic.
  7. Spock may generate follow-up queries based on the initial results.
  8. Additional vector searches are performed to expand coverage.
  9. The accumulated context is summarized or condensed.
  10. The answer LLM produces a structured, detailed response.
  11. Spock stores the full investigation trail, including intermediate queries and retrieved records.

This flow is optimized for completeness and context. Deep Dive may perform multiple retrieval passes and use more of the available context window than Ask AI.

docs.title: Indexing and Refresh
docs.text:
The vector index must be maintained over time.

Common maintenance operations include:

  • Initial indexing — Embedding all eligible records when the system is first deployed.
  • Incremental indexing — Embedding new records as they are added to ship_computer.db.
  • Reindexing — Rebuilding the vector index when the embedding model changes.
  • Pruning — Removing vectors for records that have been deleted or declassified.
  • Validation — Checking that vector reference IDs still resolve to valid SQLite records.

Because embeddings are model-specific, Spock should track the embedding model version. If a new embedding model is selected, the system should either rebuild the index or maintain separate indexes for different model versions.

docs.title: Failure Handling and Fallbacks
docs.text:
The Spock application should handle failures gracefully.

Possible failure scenarios include:

  • The embedding LLM is unavailable.
  • The vector database is unreachable.
  • A retrieved reference ID no longer exists in ship_computer.db.
  • The answer LLM exceeds its context window.
  • The selected model does not fit the available hardware.

Recommended fallback behavior includes:

  • Falling back to keyword search or SQLite full-text search if vector search is unavailable.
  • Reducing the number of retrieved records if the prompt is too large.
  • Selecting a smaller or more efficient model through the Model Selector.
  • Logging the failure and presenting a clear status message to the user.
  • Preserving the user's query and partial results for later review.

docs.title: Relationship to Model Selector
docs.text:
The Model Selector supports the Spock application by choosing appropriate models for both embedding and answer generation.

For embedding, the selector may prioritize:

  • Low latency.
  • Small memory footprint.
  • Compatibility with the local inference engine.
  • Sufficient semantic quality for retrieval.

For answer generation, the selector may prioritize:

  • Higher reasoning quality.
  • Larger context window.
  • Better instruction following.
  • Task-specific capability.

This allows Spock to use different models for different stages of the pipeline. For example, a lightweight embedding model may be used for fast vector search, while a larger answer model may be used for generating the final response.

docs.title: SQLite 3 Database (ship_computer.db) Integration
docs.text: The ship_computer.db file serves as the primary relational storage layer for the Spock application, built on SQLite 3. It manages persistent state, user configurations, conversation history, and metadata required for AI-driven features. In Python, the application interfaces with this database using the built-in sqlite3 module, ensuring thread-safe, ACID-compliant operations without requiring a separate database server.

docs.title: Interaction with Ask AI and Deep Dive Inquiries
docs.text:
The database plays a critical role in routing, contextualizing, and persisting user requests:

  • Query Routing & State Management: When a user initiates an "Ask AI" or "Deep Dive" request, the application first queries ship_computer.db for active session states, user preferences, and previously resolved intents. This ensures continuity across multi-turn conversations and prevents redundant processing.
  • Context Caching: For "Ask AI" queries, frequently accessed knowledge snippets, resolved prompts, and system instructions are cached in dedicated tables. This reduces redundant LLM calls, lowers API latency, and accelerates response times for repeated or similar questions.
  • Deep Dive Orchestration: "Deep Dive" inquiries require iterative research, synthesis, and source verification. The database tracks each research step, storing intermediate findings, source URLs, confidence scores, and reasoning chains in structured logs. This allows the application to reconstruct the full inquiry path, support rollback functionality, and maintain audit trails for complex, multi-step queries.
  • Schema Optimization & Concurrency: The database uses indexed foreign keys, prepared statements, and WAL (Write-Ahead Logging) mode to minimize I/O latency. Connection pooling and read-replica routing (where applicable) support concurrent read/write operations during intensive AI processing, preventing database locks during high-throughput inference cycles.

docs.title: Embedding LLM and Vector Database Architecture
docs.text: Spock leverages a dedicated embedding model and a vector database to enable semantic search and context-aware reasoning. This architecture bridges the gap between raw data and the generative LLM, ensuring that responses are grounded in relevant, up-to-date information rather than relying solely on parametric memory.

docs.title: Workflow Overview
docs.text:
1. Text Embedding Generation: When a user submits a query or when new documents are ingested, the application routes the text through a lightweight embedding LLM (e.g., nomic-embed-text, all-MiniLM-L6-v2, or a domain-specific fine-tuned model). This model converts unstructured text into high-dimensional numerical vectors (embeddings) that capture semantic meaning, intent, and contextual relationships rather than exact keyword matches.
  2. Vector Storage & Indexing: The generated embeddings are stored in a vector database (such as ChromaDB, FAISS, or SQLite-VSS). Each vector is paired with metadata (source, timestamp, relevance tags, and chunk boundaries) and indexed using approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) algorithms like HNSW or IVF. This enables sub-millisecond similarity searches even across large, dynamically updating datasets.
  3. Semantic Retrieval for Ask AI: During an "Ask AI" interaction, the user's prompt is embedded and queried against the vector index. The system retrieves the top-k most semantically similar chunks, which are then formatted into a structured context window. This retrieved context is injected into the system prompt before being passed to the primary generative LLM, grounding the response in verified data.
  4. Deep Dive Context Expansion: For "Deep Dive" requests, the vector database performs iterative similarity searches. Initial results seed follow-up queries, allowing the system to traverse related concepts, cross-reference sources, and build a comprehensive knowledge graph. The vector store also supports hybrid search (combining semantic embeddings with keyword/BM25 filtering) to improve precision for technical, code-heavy, or domain-specific terminology.
  5. Feedback Loop & Re-ranking: Retrieved vectors are optionally passed through a cross-encoder re-ranker to refine relevance before context injection. This reduces hallucination risk, filters out low-quality or outdated chunks, and ensures the generative LLM operates on the most accurate and task-aligned information. The re-ranked results are then logged back to ship_computer.db for future caching and audit purposes.

docs.title: Database Architecture
docs.text: The application utilizes a SQLite 3 database file named ship_computer.db to persist critical state information, query history, and model metadata. This lightweight, serverless database ensures portability and low-latency access for the Spock application's core AI functions, specifically Ask AI and Deep Dive inquiries.

docs.title: Design Goals
docs.text:
The database design prioritizes:

  • Local Persistence — Data remains available offline without requiring an external database service or continuous network connectivity.
  • Low-Latency Reads — Frequent lookups of model metadata and session state are optimized for speed through strategic indexing and query caching.
  • Transactional Integrity — Query logs, session updates, and knowledge-base writes are managed within consistent ACID-compliant transaction boundaries to prevent data corruption.
  • Recoverability — Active Deep Dive contexts and intermediate analytical states can be reliably restored after application restarts or unexpected closures.

docs.title: Schema Overview
docs.text:
The ship_computer.db schema is structured to support high-frequency read operations while maintaining strict data integrity for analysis logs. Key tables include:

  • models: Stores registry metadata for available AI models, including configuration paths, quantization profiles, VRAM requirements, context window limits, and inference engine compatibility flags. (Note: Actual model weights are stored externally on disk and referenced by identifier or path.)
  • sessions: Tracks active user sessions, initialization timestamps, expiration policies, and the specific model configurations bound to each session.
  • queries: Logs all Ask AI and Deep Dive inquiries. Records include input prompts, generated responses, associated model identifiers, token counts, and latency metrics for performance monitoring.
  • knowledge_base: Contains structured data, extracted insights, and intermediate reasoning steps generated during Deep Dive sessions to maintain persistent context.

docs.title: Interaction with Spock Application
docs.text:
The Spock application interacts with ship_computer.db through a dedicated ORM layer to ensure type safety, connection pooling, and robust transaction management. The interaction patterns are specifically optimized for the AI inquiry modules:

  1. Ask AI Inquiries:

    • When a user submits an Ask AI query, the system first queries the models table to identify available resources compatible with current hardware constraints and user preferences.
    • Upon completion, the prompt, response, and associated metadata are atomically written to the queries table. This historical log enables the application to track usage patterns, monitor inference latency, and dynamically optimize model selection policies over time.

  2. Deep Dive Inquiries:

    • Deep Dive sessions require multi-step, persistent context. The system writes intermediate analysis results, extracted entities, and reasoning chains to the knowledge_base table to maintain state across iterative steps.
    • Query logs in the queries table are enriched with session identifiers and "Deep Dive" status tags. This allows the application to perform specialized retrieval, filter historical context, and reconstruct the analytical thread during subsequent interactions.

  3. Persistence and Recovery:

    • The database is engineered to survive application restarts and system interruptions. Upon initialization, Spock scans the sessions and knowledge_base tables to reconstruct active contexts. This ensures users can resume Deep Dive sessions seamlessly without re-executing initial analysis steps or losing intermediate findings.

docs.title: Detailed Database Interaction Workflow
docs.text:
To ensure reliability during intensive AI operations, Spock implements a structured data access lifecycle for ship_computer.db:

  • Connection & Concurrency Management: Spock initializes a single, thread-safe SQLite connection at startup. Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) mode is enabled to allow concurrent read operations during heavy write cycles, effectively eliminating database lock contention during active inference.
  • Ask AI Data Flow: User prompts are validated and routed to the selected model. Once the LLM generates a response, the ORM constructs a transaction that inserts the query record, updates session metrics, and commits the transaction. If the inference pipeline fails or times out, the transaction is rolled back to maintain log consistency and prevent orphaned records.
  • Deep Dive Data Flow: Deep Dive operations utilize a state-machine pattern. Each analytical step triggers a database transaction that appends new findings to the knowledge_base table while updating the sessions table with the current step index and checkpoint hash. This granular logging enables precise state reconstruction and allows users to backtrack through the analysis without data loss.
  • Indexing Strategy: Primary keys and foreign keys are strictly enforced. Additional indexes are applied to session_id, model_id, and timestamp columns to accelerate filtering and sorting operations during session recovery and performance analytics.

docs.title: Embedding LLM and Vector Database Integration
docs.text:
To enable semantic understanding and context-aware retrieval, Spock integrates an embedding LLM alongside a vector database layer. This architecture powers the retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline for both Ask AI and Deep Dive inquiries.

The embedding LLM and vector database work together to allow Spock to retrieve relevant information based on meaning rather than exact keyword matching. This is especially important for Ask AI questions that require concise, grounded answers and for Deep Dive sessions that require iterative exploration of related concepts, entities, and prior findings.

docs.title: How Spock Uses the Embedding LLM
docs.text:
The embedding LLM is a specialized model that converts text into numerical vector representations, also called embeddings. Each embedding captures the semantic meaning of the text in a high-dimensional numerical space. Texts with similar meanings produce vectors that are closer together, while unrelated texts produce vectors that are farther apart.

Spock uses the embedding LLM in the following ways:

  • Query Encoding: When a user submits an Ask AI or Deep Dive prompt, Spock sends the prompt to the embedding LLM to generate a query vector.
  • Context Encoding: Relevant documents, knowledge-base entries, extracted insights, and prior Deep Dive findings are also converted into vectors and stored in the vector database.
  • Semantic Matching: Spock compares the query vector against stored vectors to identify the most semantically relevant context.
  • Prompt Augmentation: The retrieved context is inserted into the prompt provided to the generative LLM, improving answer accuracy, relevance, and traceability.
  • Deep Dive Continuity: During Deep Dive sessions, newly generated insights, extracted entities, and intermediate reasoning steps are embedded and stored so that later steps can retrieve earlier context efficiently.

The embedding LLM is distinct from the generative LLM. The generative LLM produces natural-language responses, while the embedding LLM produces numerical representations used for retrieval and similarity search.

docs.title: How Spock Uses the Vector Database
docs.text:
The vector database stores the embeddings produced by the embedding LLM and supports fast similarity search. It allows Spock to retrieve relevant context from large or growing knowledge bases without scanning every record using traditional keyword search.

Spock uses the vector database to:

  • Store embeddings for user documents, knowledge-base entries, Deep Dive findings, and prior query context.
  • Perform similarity searches using metrics such as cosine similarity, dot product, or Euclidean distance.
  • Retrieve the most relevant passages, entities, and reasoning steps for a given prompt.
  • Filter results by session, knowledge-base scope, timestamp, or Deep Dive step.
  • Support iterative retrieval during Deep Dive sessions, where each new question may require access to both original source material and previously generated insights.

The vector database complements ship_computer.db rather than replacing it. SQLite stores relational state, session metadata, query history, and structured knowledge-base records. The vector database stores high-dimensional embeddings and provides semantic search capabilities.

docs.title: Ask AI Semantic Retrieval Workflow
docs.text:
For Ask AI inquiries, Spock uses the embedding LLM and vector database to ground the response in relevant context.

  1. Prompt Reception: The user submits a question or request.
  2. Model Selection: Spock selects an appropriate generative LLM and embedding LLM based on the models table, hardware constraints, and user preferences.
  3. Query Embedding: The prompt is converted into a vector using the embedding LLM.
  4. Vector Search: Spock queries the vector database for the most relevant stored context.
  5. Context Filtering: Results are filtered by session scope, knowledge-base permissions, recency, and relevance score.
  6. Prompt Construction: The retrieved context is combined with the user prompt to form an augmented prompt.
  7. Response Generation: The generative LLM produces the final answer.
  8. Persistence: The prompt, response, retrieved context identifiers, embedding model identifier, vector scores, latency, and token usage are written to the queries table.

This workflow allows Ask AI to provide more accurate and context-aware answers while preserving a complete audit trail of the information used to generate each response.

docs.title: Deep Dive Semantic Retrieval Workflow
docs.text:
Deep Dive inquiries are iterative and stateful. Spock uses the embedding LLM and vector database to maintain semantic continuity across multiple analysis steps.

  1. Session Initialization: Spock creates or resumes a Deep Dive session and records the session state in the sessions table.
  2. Initial Context Retrieval: The initial prompt is embedded, and the vector database is searched for relevant source material and prior findings.
  3. Analysis Step Execution: The generative LLM produces an intermediate analysis, such as extracted entities, hypotheses, comparisons, or reasoning steps.
  4. Insight Embedding: New insights are embedded and stored in the vector database.
  5. Knowledge-Base Update: Structured findings are written to the knowledge_base table, including session identifiers, step indices, and checkpoint hashes.
  6. Iterative Retrieval: For each subsequent Deep Dive step, Spock embeds the new prompt and retrieves both original context and previously generated insights.
  7. State Reconstruction: If the application restarts, Spock uses the sessions, queries, and knowledge_base tables to reconstruct the Deep Dive state and continue the analysis.

This approach allows Deep Dive sessions to build on prior reasoning without requiring the user to repeat earlier steps or manually re-supply context.

docs.title: Embedding and Vector Metadata in ship_computer.db
docs.text:
Although the vector database stores the actual embeddings, ship_computer.db stores the relational metadata needed to manage, trace, and recover semantic retrieval operations.

This metadata may include:

  • Embedding Model Identifiers: The specific embedding LLM used to generate each vector.
  • Vector Store References: Identifiers linking SQLite records to corresponding vectors in the vector database.
  • Retrieval Scores: Similarity scores associated with retrieved context.
  • Session Scope: The session or Deep Dive context to which a vector or retrieved result belongs.
  • Knowledge-Base Links: Relationships between vector records and structured entries in the knowledge_base table.
  • Timestamps: Creation and update times for embeddings and retrieval events.
  • Versioning Information: Model versions, embedding dimensions, and index configurations used to generate or search vectors.

By storing this metadata in ship_computer.db, Spock can maintain a consistent, queryable record of how semantic retrieval was performed, which context influenced each response, and how Deep Dive sessions evolved over time. * Embedding Generation: When a query, document chunk, or knowledge-base entry is processed, the embedding LLM converts textual data into high-dimensional numerical vectors. These vectors capture semantic meaning, allowing the system to match conceptual relevance rather than relying solely on exact keyword matching. In Spock, this step is used for both user prompts and stored knowledge so that Ask AI and Deep Dive requests can be compared against the same semantic space. * Vector Storage & Indexing: Generated embeddings are stored in a dedicated vector database optimized for fast similarity search. Each vector is linked to its source metadata via stable identifiers that reference the knowledge_base and queries tables in ship_computer.db. This hybrid relational-vector approach ensures that semantic search results can be instantly correlated with structured session data, citations, and audit logs. * Semantic Retrieval Workflow: 1. Query Encoding: The user's prompt is passed through the embedding LLM to generate a query vector. 2. Similarity Search: The vector database performs an Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) search to retrieve the most contextually relevant embeddings from the knowledge base. 3. Context Assembly: Retrieved vectors are mapped back to their original text chunks, ranked by cosine similarity or dot-product scores, and injected into the primary LLM's context window alongside the original prompt. 4. Inference & Logging: The LLM generates a response grounded in the retrieved context. The final output, along with the retrieved source references and similarity scores, is logged to ship_computer.db for transparency and future session recovery. * Performance Optimization: To minimize latency, Spock caches frequently accessed embeddings and utilizes batched vector operations. The embedding model runs on the same hardware acceleration stack as the primary inference engine, ensuring efficient resource utilization without requiring external API calls or additional network overhead.

docs.title: SQLite 3 ship_computer.db and Spock Interaction
docs.text:
ship_computer.db is the local SQLite 3 database used by the Spock application to persist application state, user interactions, knowledge-base metadata, and audit information. It is not the primary vector store; instead, it provides the relational context that makes semantic search results traceable, recoverable, and auditable.

Because Spock is a Python and SQLite application, ship_computer.db is typically accessed through Python’s built-in sqlite3 module. SQLite 3 provides a lightweight, file-based, ACID-compliant database that is well suited for local application state, session tracking, and structured logging.

docs.title: Core Tables and Responsibilities
docs.text:
A typical ship_computer.db schema may include tables such as:

Table Purpose sessions Tracks user conversations, session identifiers, timestamps, and conversation state. queries Stores individual user prompts, request type, model settings, and execution metadata. knowledge_base Stores metadata for documents, notes, or knowledge entries available to Spock. chunks Stores text chunks derived from knowledge-base entries, including chunk identifiers and source references. retrieval_results Records which chunks were retrieved for a query, along with similarity scores and ranking information. responses Stores generated answers, response type, model output, and associated citations. deep_dive_runs Tracks multi-step Deep Dive tasks, including objective, status, and intermediate progress. citations Links generated answers to specific source chunks, documents, or knowledge-base entries. audit_logs Records system actions, retrieval events, model calls, and error states for transparency.

These tables allow Spock to maintain a durable record of what the user asked, what information was retrieved, how the answer was generated, and which sources supported the final response.

docs.title: Ask AI Inquiries
docs.text:
For an Ask AI request, Spock uses ship_computer.db to manage a conversational or single-question workflow. The database supports the following steps:

  1. Session Creation or Update Spock creates or updates a session record so that the Ask AI request can be associated with a broader conversation.

  2. Query Recording The user prompt is inserted into the queries table with metadata such as timestamp, request type, model configuration, and any user-provided context.

  3. Knowledge Resolution Spock identifies the relevant knowledge-base entries and text chunks that may be useful for answering the question.

  4. Retrieval Logging The retrieved chunks, similarity scores, and source identifiers are stored in retrieval_results or a similar table.

  5. Response Storage The generated answer is stored in responses, along with citations, confidence indicators, and any follow-up suggestions.

  6. Audit Trail Relevant events are written to audit_logs, allowing Spock to reconstruct the request, verify the sources used, and support future debugging or session recovery.

This workflow allows Spock to answer a question, explain which sources influenced the answer, and restore the conversation later without re-running the full retrieval pipeline.

docs.title: Deep Dive Inquiries
docs.text:
For a Deep Dive request, Spock treats the inquiry as a multi-step research task rather than a single prompt-and-answer exchange. The database supports this workflow by:

  1. Creating a Deep Dive Run A deep_dive_runs record captures the objective, scope, status, and lifecycle of the research task.

  2. Tracking Intermediate Questions Spock may break the Deep Dive into sub-questions, hypotheses, or research steps. Each step can be recorded with its own query metadata.

  3. Storing Evidence Retrieved chunks, documents, and supporting evidence are linked to the Deep Dive run so that the final report can be traced back to specific sources.

  4. Recording Citations Citations are stored in a structured way, allowing Spock to show which sources support each claim or section of the final output.

  5. Persisting the Final Report The synthesized Deep Dive report, assumptions, limitations, and follow-up recommendations are stored for later review.

  6. Supporting Resumability Because the state is persisted in SQLite 3, a long-running Deep Dive can be paused, resumed, or audited after completion.

In both Ask AI and Deep Dive modes, ship_computer.db acts as the source of truth for what the user asked, what Spock retrieved, what it answered, and how the answer can be verified.

docs.title: How Spock Uses the Embedding LLM and Vector Database
docs.text: Spock uses the embedding LLM to translate natural-language content into numerical vectors. These vectors are then stored in a vector database that supports fast similarity search. The primary LLM is responsible for generating natural-language answers, while the embedding LLM is responsible for making content searchable by meaning.

docs.title: Embedding LLM Role
docs.text:
The embedding LLM is used in three main cases:

  • Knowledge Ingestion: When documents, notes, or knowledge-base entries are added, Spock splits them into chunks and generates an embedding for each chunk.
  • Query Processing: When a user submits an Ask AI or Deep Dive prompt, Spock generates an embedding for the prompt.
  • Re-ranking or Filtering: In some workflows, Spock may generate additional embeddings for sub-questions, candidate summaries, or evidence fragments to improve retrieval precision.

The embedding model does not generate the final user-facing answer. It produces vectors that allow Spock to find semantically related content before the primary LLM composes a response.

docs.title: Vector Database Role
docs.text:
The vector database stores the generated embeddings and provides similarity search. For each vector, Spock stores or references metadata such as:

  • Source document or knowledge-base entry identifier
  • Chunk identifier
  • Session or query identifier
  • Timestamp
  • Content type
  • Access permissions or scope, if applicable

When Spock needs context, it sends the query vector to the vector database and requests the nearest neighbors. The vector database returns the most relevant vectors and their associated metadata. Spock then uses those metadata identifiers to retrieve the original text chunks from ship_computer.db or the local document store.

docs.title: End-to-End Retrieval and Answering
docs.text:
1. The user submits an Ask AI or Deep Dive request.
  2. Spock records the request in ship_computer.db.
  3. The embedding LLM converts the request into a vector.
  4. The vector database searches for similar knowledge-base vectors.
  5. Spock retrieves the corresponding text chunks and metadata.
  6. The primary LLM receives the user prompt plus the retrieved context.
  7. The primary LLM generates a grounded answer.
  8. Spock stores the answer, citations, similarity scores, and execution metadata in ship_computer.db.

This design separates semantic search from answer generation. The embedding LLM and vector database make it possible to find relevant information by meaning, while SQLite 3 provides durable, queryable records of the conversation, sources, and audit trail.

docs.title: Navigation Station
docs.text: The Navigation Station serves as Spock's initialization wizard. It automates the hardware bring-up process by detecting connected components, configuring the software environment, and launching necessary servers to ensure the system is ready for operation.

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
Module Role NavigationStation.app Main application entry point that coordinates the initialization workflow NavigationStation.steps.configure Configuration step — sets up runtime settings, environment options, and required data structures NavigationStation.steps.hardware Hardware detection step — identifies connected hardware components and validates their availability NavigationStation.steps.launch Server launch step — starts required servers and services needed for operation NavigationStation.steps.status Status verification step — checks the status of launched services, hardware, and overall system readiness

Note: These modules represent distinct phases that execute sequentially during the initialization workflow. The NavigationApp class coordinates this sequence, collects results from each phase, and reports whether the system is ready for use.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text: To use the Navigation Station, you can either import and run the NavigationApp class in Python or execute it via the command line interface (CLI). Ensure your development environment is configured correctly before proceeding.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before running the Navigation Station, verify that:

  1. Python Environment: A virtual environment, for example .venv, is active or explicitly referenced by the interpreter path.
  2. Dependencies: All required Python packages are installed within that environment.
  3. OS Compatibility: Command paths and executable names may vary depending on your operating system. See the CLI usage examples below.

docs.title: Python Usage
docs.text:
from NavigationStation.app import NavigationApp

app = NavigationApp()
app.run()

This snippet instantiates the NavigationApp class and triggers the initialization sequence defined in the components above. Execution typically proceeds through hardware detection, configuration, server launch, and status verification.

docs.title: CLI Usage
docs.text:
If you prefer using the command line, you can run the Navigation Station using the following command:

.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m spock_bringup_menu

This command assumes that a Python virtual environment is located at .venv. The -m flag tells Python to execute spock_bringup_menu as a module entry point, which ultimately invokes the same initialization workflow used by NavigationApp.

Note: This example uses Windows PowerShell syntax, indicated by the backslash path separator. If you are on Linux or macOS, use the appropriate path separator and interpreter location. For example:

.venv/bin/python -m spock_bringup_menu

You may also activate your virtual environment first if your shell setup requires it.

docs.title: SQLite 3 Database: ship_computer.db
docs.text:
ship_computer.db is the local SQLite 3 database used by the Spock application to persist operational state, configuration data, hardware inventory, and AI-assisted inquiry records. It provides a lightweight, file-based relational store that is well suited to a single-node ship computer deployment where offline operation, low overhead, and transactional integrity are important.

The database is not primarily used to store large vector embeddings. Instead, it stores structured metadata, session history, configuration state, and references to content that may be indexed in a separate vector database.

docs.title: Purpose of ship_computer.db
docs.text:
The ship_computer.db database supports several core responsibilities:

  • System state tracking: Stores the results of hardware detection, service launch, and readiness checks performed by the Navigation Station.
  • Configuration persistence: Preserves runtime settings, environment options, and user-selected preferences.
  • Ask AI support: Records user questions, assistant responses, retrieved context, citations, and session history.
  • Deep Dive support: Stores multi-step investigation records, evidence items, intermediate findings, and final generated reports.
  • Auditability: Provides a durable record of what the system detected, launched, queried, and generated.

docs.title: Relationship to the Spock Application
docs.text:
The Spock application interacts with ship_computer.db through Python’s SQLite support, either directly using the sqlite3 module or through an ORM or data-access layer. The database acts as the system of record for structured application data.

For example:

  • The Navigation Station may write hardware detection results and service status into the database.
  • Ask AI may read configuration and document metadata, then write the user’s question and the generated answer.
  • Deep Dive may create a session record, store each investigation step, and persist the final report.

This separation allows Spock to keep structured data in SQLite while using a vector database for semantic search over unstructured text.

docs.title: Representative Schema
docs.text:
The exact schema may vary by deployment, but a representative ship_computer.db schema includes the following data domains:

Table Purpose system_info Stores system identification, version, build, and deployment metadata hardware_components Stores detected hardware components, status, and validation results configuration Stores runtime settings, environment options, and user preferences services Stores launched services, expected state, and observed state documents Stores metadata for documents available to Ask AI and Deep Dive document_chunks Stores chunk-level metadata and references to vector database records ask_ai_sessions Stores Ask AI conversation sessions ask_ai_messages Stores individual user and assistant messages within an Ask AI session ask_ai_citations Stores source references used to support an Ask AI answer deep_dive_sessions Stores Deep Dive investigation sessions deep_dive_steps Stores individual steps, queries, findings, and evidence within a Deep Dive session deep_dive_reports Stores final generated Deep Dive reports and summaries

docs.title: How ship_computer.db Supports Ask AI
docs.text:
Ask AI is the conversational query interface where a user asks a natural-language question and Spock returns an answer grounded in available system data, documents, or operational context.

The database supports Ask AI in the following ways:

  1. Session management
  2. Each Ask AI conversation is associated with a session record.

  3. The session may store the user, timestamp, model settings, and active context.

  4. Message persistence

  5. User questions and assistant responses are stored as messages.

  6. This allows Spock to maintain conversational context and support follow-up questions.

  7. Retrieval metadata

  8. When Ask AI retrieves relevant content, the database can store which documents or chunks were considered.

  9. This supports transparency and debugging.

  10. Citation tracking

  11. If the answer is grounded in specific sources, the database can store citation records.

  12. Citations may include document identifiers, chunk identifiers, page numbers, or vector database record identifiers.

  13. Configuration lookup

  14. Ask AI may read configuration values from the database, such as enabled data sources, retrieval limits, or model preferences.

A typical Ask AI data flow is:

  1. The user submits a question.
  2. Spock creates or updates an Ask AI session record.
  3. Spock stores the user message.
  4. Spock retrieves relevant context from the vector database and/or structured data.
  5. Spock generates an answer using the retrieved context.
  6. Spock stores the assistant response.
  7. Spock stores citations, retrieval metadata, and any relevant provenance information.

docs.title: How ship_computer.db Supports Deep Dive
docs.text:
Deep Dive is a more investigative workflow than Ask AI. Instead of returning a single answer, Deep Dive may perform multiple retrieval steps, analyze related evidence, compare findings, and produce a structured report.

The database supports Deep Dive by storing the full investigation lifecycle:

  1. Session creation
  2. A Deep Dive session is created when the user starts an investigation.

  3. The session stores the initial objective, scope, and relevant constraints.

  4. Step tracking

  5. Each Deep Dive step is stored as a separate record.

  6. A step may represent a sub-question, a retrieval action, an analysis action, or a synthesis action.

  7. Evidence collection

  8. Relevant documents, chunks, logs, or structured records are associated with the session.

  9. The database stores references to the evidence rather than duplicating large content.

  10. Finding persistence

  11. Intermediate findings, hypotheses, or summaries can be stored for later review.

  12. This allows the application to resume or continue an investigation.

  13. Report generation

  14. The final Deep Dive report is stored in the database.
  15. The report may include an executive summary, supporting evidence, citations, and confidence notes.

A typical Deep Dive data flow is:

  1. The user defines an investigation objective.
  2. Spock creates a Deep Dive session.
  3. Spock breaks the objective into sub-questions or analysis steps.
  4. For each step, Spock retrieves relevant content using the vector database and/or structured queries.
  5. Spock stores the step, retrieved evidence, and intermediate findings.
  6. Spock synthesizes the findings into a final report.
  7. Spock stores the final report and associated citations.

docs.title: Division of Responsibility Between SQLite and the Vector Database
docs.text:
The SQLite database and the vector database serve different purposes.

Concern ship_computer.db Vector Database Data type Structured relational data High-dimensional semantic vectors Primary use State, sessions, configuration, citations, reports Semantic similarity search Query style SQL queries Vector similarity queries Content stored Metadata and references Embeddings and associated text chunks Typical operations Insert, update, select, join Index, search, filter, rank

In practice, Spock may use SQLite to store the identity of a document chunk and the vector database to store the embedding for that chunk. When a user asks a question, Spock can search the vector database for semantically similar chunks and then use SQLite to retrieve metadata, citations, and session context.

docs.title: Embedding LLM and Vector Database
docs.text: Spock uses an embedding LLM and a vector database to enable semantic search over natural-language content. This allows Ask AI and Deep Dive to find relevant information based on meaning rather than only exact keyword matches.

docs.title: Role of the Embedding LLM
docs.text:
An embedding LLM is a language model that converts text into a numerical vector, also called an embedding. Each vector represents the semantic meaning of the text in a high-dimensional space.

For example:

  • “What is the status of the navigation system?”
  • “Is the nav system operational?”
  • “Check navigation readiness.”

These phrases may not share many exact keywords, but an embedding model can represent them as vectors that are close to one another because they express a similar intent.
