The embedding LLM is not the same as the answer-generation LLM. Its role is to produce vectors for search, not to generate natural-language responses.

docs.title: How Embeddings Are Created
docs.text:
The embedding process generally follows these steps:

  1. Text preparation
  2. Documents, logs, or other content are split into manageable chunks.

  3. Chunking helps preserve context while keeping embeddings focused.

  4. Embedding generation

  5. Each chunk is passed to the embedding LLM.

  6. The model returns a fixed-length vector.

  7. Normalization

  8. The vector may be normalized to improve similarity calculations.

  9. Storage

  10. The vector is stored in the vector database.
  11. Metadata, such as document ID, chunk ID, source, and timestamp, is stored alongside the vector.

docs.title: Role of the Vector Database
docs.text:
The vector database stores embeddings and supports similarity search. It allows Spock to answer questions such as:

  • “Which content is most relevant to this user question?”
  • “Which chunks are semantically closest to this Deep Dive sub-question?”
  • “Which evidence items support this finding?”

The vector database typically supports:

  • Cosine similarity
  • Dot product similarity
  • Euclidean distance
  • Metadata filtering
  • Top-k retrieval
  • Batch indexing

docs.title: Ask AI Retrieval Pipeline
docs.text:
When a user submits an Ask AI question, Spock uses the embedding LLM and vector database as part of the retrieval pipeline.

  1. Query embedding

  2. The user’s question is converted into a vector using the same embedding model used for the indexed content.

  3. Vector search

  4. Spock queries the vector database for the most similar content chunks.

  5. The search may return the top-k results, where k is a configurable number.

  6. Metadata filtering

  7. Spock may filter results by document type, source, time range, access level, or other metadata.

  8. Reranking

  9. The retrieved chunks may be reranked using additional signals, such as keyword overlap, recency, or relevance scores.

  10. Context assembly

  11. The selected chunks are assembled into a prompt context for the answer-generation model.

  12. Answer generation

  13. The answer-generation LLM produces a response grounded in the retrieved context.

  14. Persistence

  15. The question, answer, retrieved chunks, and citations are stored in ship_computer.db.

docs.title: Deep Dive Retrieval Pipeline
docs.text:
Deep Dive uses the same embedding and vector search capabilities, but applies them iteratively across multiple investigation steps.

  1. Objective decomposition

  2. Spock breaks the user’s investigation objective into sub-questions or analysis tasks.

  3. Step-specific embedding

  4. Each sub-question is converted into an embedding vector.

  5. Targeted retrieval

  6. Spock searches the vector database for content relevant to that specific step.

  7. Evidence accumulation

  8. Retrieved chunks are stored as evidence in the Deep Dive session.

  9. Cross-step synthesis

  10. Spock compares findings across steps and identifies patterns, conflicts, or gaps.

  11. Report generation

  12. Spock generates a structured report using the accumulated evidence.

  13. Session persistence

  14. The full Deep Dive session, including steps, evidence, and final report, is stored in ship_computer.db.

docs.title: Why Both SQLite and a Vector Database Are Needed
docs.text:
SQLite provides reliable structured storage for application state and inquiry history. The vector database provides semantic search over unstructured text.

Together, they allow Spock to:

  • Maintain durable session and configuration data.
  • Search content by meaning rather than only keywords.
  • Ground Ask AI answers in relevant evidence.
  • Support Deep Dive investigations with multi-step retrieval and synthesis.
  • Preserve citations and provenance for generated responses.

docs.title: Database Architecture and Data Interaction
docs.text: The Spock application relies on a persistent data layer to maintain state between sessions and support advanced analytical features. This architecture is centered around the SQLite 3 database engine, specifically utilizing the ship_computer.db file for local storage.

docs.title: SQLite 3 Overview
docs.text:
• Engine: SQLite 3 serves as the primary relational database management system (RDBMS). It is a serverless, zero-configuration, transactional SQL database engine that operates directly on a single file.
  • Storage Location: The database resides in a single file named ship_computer.db, typically located within the application's data directory or another path defined by deployment configuration.
  • Initialization: The schema for this database is created and initialized during the NavigationStation.steps.configure phase of the initialization workflow. This process includes table creation, index generation, and insertion of any required seed data needed by subsequent operational steps.
  • Concurrency & Safety: SQLite handles concurrent read operations efficiently and can be configured to use write-ahead logging (WAL) mode to improve data integrity and reduce lock contention during frequent application updates.

docs.title: ship_computer.db Schema and Operational Role
docs.text:
While the exact table definitions are managed dynamically during configuration, ship_computer.db logically organizes data into three primary domains:

  1. Session & Context Management: Tracks active user sessions, conversation history, prompt templates, and AI response metadata. This enables stateful interactions without relying on external session stores.
  2. Knowledge & Reference Data: Stores curated documents, system prompts, user preferences, and configuration overrides that the AI references during generation.
  3. Analytics & Task State: Maintains records for long-running computational jobs, intermediate results, data lineage, and execution logs.

The application layer interacts with ship_computer.db through parameterized SQL queries and an ORM/DAO abstraction layer. All write operations are wrapped in transactions to guarantee ACID compliance, while read-heavy operations leverage indexed columns for fast retrieval.

In practice, ship_computer.db acts as the system of record for structured application state. It stores the information Spock needs to understand what the user is asking, where the relevant data came from, which session the request belongs to, and how previous operations were executed. This makes the database essential for both conversational continuity and reproducible analytical workflows.

docs.title: Interaction with Ask AI
docs.text:
The "Ask AI" feature utilizes ship_computer.db as a critical component of a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) workflow. The application layer queries relevant context from the database, then supplies that context to the LLM prompt. This ensures responses reflect stored preferences, prior interactions, and curated knowledge snippets without requiring the model itself to maintain persistent memory.

  • Context Storage: The database stores user preferences, historical query logs, and indexed knowledge-base snippets. When a user submits a prompt, the application retrieves the most relevant historical context and system guidelines to construct a structured prompt.
  • Session Management: Active sessions are tracked within the database using unique session identifiers. Follow-up questions automatically reference earlier context, maintaining conversational continuity and reducing redundant prompt engineering.
  • Asynchronous Logging & State Updates: While the LLM generates responses in real time, the application updates ship_computer.db asynchronously. This logs interactions, updates session state, and preserves conversation history for future reference without blocking the user interface.
  • Prompt Assembly Pipeline: Retrieved relational data is merged with vector search results and formatted into a structured prompt template before being sent to the inference engine.

For Ask AI, ship_computer.db provides the structured foundation for the request. It determines which session the prompt belongs to, which user preferences should influence the answer, which documents or knowledge entries are eligible for retrieval, and which prior messages should be included in the context window. The database does not generate the answer itself; instead, it supplies the trusted, queryable context that makes the generated response more accurate, personalized, and consistent.

docs.title: Interaction with Deep Dive
docs.text:
The "Deep Dive" feature leverages the database for complex data analysis, result caching, lineage tracking, and long-running task recovery.

  • Analytical Result Caching: Intermediate results from computationally intensive queries are serialized and cached in the database. When similar analytical work is requested, the system checks for valid cached results before re-executing pipelines, significantly reducing latency and resource consumption.
  • Metadata & Lineage Tracking: The schema includes tables that record query parameters, data transformation steps, model versions, and result provenance. This supports full reproducibility and auditability of "Deep Dive" sessions.
  • State Persistence & Recovery: Unlike ephemeral server memory, critical state for long-running Deep Dive tasks is persisted in ship_computer.db. If the application restarts or encounters a transient failure, the system can resume analysis from the last checkpoint without data loss.
  • Query Optimization: Frequently accessed analytical datasets are materialized as views or indexed tables, allowing the application to execute complex joins and aggregations efficiently.

In Deep Dive workflows, ship_computer.db is especially important because analytical tasks are often multi-step, resource-intensive, and time-sensitive. The database allows Spock to track the lifecycle of each analysis, preserve intermediate outputs, and reconstruct the exact sequence of operations that produced a result. This is critical for debugging, auditing, and resuming work after interruptions.

docs.title: Embedding LLM and Vector Database Integration
docs.text:
While ship_computer.db handles relational data, session state, and metadata, Spock employs a dedicated Embedding LLM and Vector Database to power semantic search and high-dimensional similarity matching. This hybrid architecture ensures both precise relational filtering and contextual semantic retrieval.

The Embedding LLM and Vector Database are separate from the generative LLM that produces natural-language answers. Their purpose is not to answer questions directly, but to transform text into numerical representations that can be compared by meaning rather than exact keyword match.

docs.title: Embedding LLM Responsibilities
docs.text:
The Embedding LLM converts textual content into dense vector representations, commonly called embeddings. These vectors capture semantic meaning, allowing Spock to identify related concepts even when the wording differs.

For example, the phrases:

  • "show me recent anomalies"
  • "find unusual behavior from the last week"
  • "what looked abnormal recently?"

may not share many exact keywords, but their embeddings can be close in vector space because they express similar intent.

Spock uses the Embedding LLM in several ways:

  • Query Embedding: When a user submits an Ask AI or Deep Dive request, the application converts the user's prompt into an embedding vector.
  • Document Embedding: Knowledge-base entries, reference documents, system notes, and analytical summaries are embedded during ingestion or indexing.
  • Semantic Matching: The application compares the query embedding against stored embeddings to find the most semantically relevant content.
  • Context Selection: The most relevant embedded items are retrieved and used to enrich the prompt sent to the generative LLM.

This allows Spock to understand intent, topic, and context more effectively than keyword-only search.

docs.title: Vector Database Responsibilities
docs.text:
The Vector Database stores the high-dimensional embeddings produced by the Embedding LLM. It is optimized for similarity search, meaning it can quickly identify which stored vectors are closest to a given query vector.

The Vector Database typically stores:

  • Embedding Vectors: Numeric representations of text content.
  • Document Metadata: Identifiers, source references, timestamps, permissions, and content type.
  • Chunk References: Pointers to the specific text segment that was embedded.
  • Index Structures: Approximate nearest neighbor indexes that enable fast similarity search over large collections.

The Vector Database is not a replacement for ship_computer.db. Instead, it complements it. The relational database stores structured facts, session state, and operational metadata, while the vector database stores semantic representations used for meaning-based retrieval.

docs.title: How Spock Uses the Embedding LLM and Vector Database in Ask AI
docs.text:
In Ask AI, the Embedding LLM and Vector Database support semantic retrieval of relevant context before the generative LLM produces a response.

A typical Ask AI flow works as follows:

  1. Prompt Intake: The user submits a question or request.
  2. Session Lookup: Spock identifies the active session in ship_computer.db and retrieves prior conversation context.
  3. Query Embedding: The Embedding LLM converts the user's prompt into a vector representation.
  4. Vector Search: Spock queries the Vector Database for the most semantically similar knowledge entries, documents, or prior responses.
  5. Relational Filtering: Spock uses ship_computer.db to filter results based on session ownership, permissions, recency, document status, and user preferences.
  6. Context Ranking: The application combines vector similarity scores with relational metadata to rank the most useful context.
  7. Prompt Assembly: The selected context is inserted into a structured prompt template.
  8. Generation: The generative LLM produces the final answer using the assembled context.
  9. Persistence: The question, retrieved context, generated answer, and metadata are stored back in ship_computer.db.

This approach allows Ask AI to answer questions using both semantic understanding and structured application state. The vector database helps Spock find relevant meaning, while the relational database ensures the response is grounded in the correct session, permissions, and historical context.

docs.title: How Spock Uses the Embedding LLM and Vector Database in Deep Dive
docs.text:
In Deep Dive, the Embedding LLM and Vector Database help Spock locate relevant analytical context, prior results, and related data sources before executing or resuming complex analysis.

A typical Deep Dive flow works as follows:

  1. Analysis Request: The user requests a detailed investigation or analytical task.
  2. Task Initialization: Spock creates or resumes a task record in ship_computer.db.
  3. Semantic Discovery: The Embedding LLM converts the analysis request into a vector.
  4. Vector Retrieval: The Vector Database returns related analytical summaries, prior Deep Dive results, reference documents, or data descriptions.
  5. Structured Validation: Spock checks ship_computer.db to confirm that the retrieved items are valid, accessible, and relevant to the current task.
  6. Pipeline Planning: The application uses the retrieved context to determine which datasets, transformations, or cached results should be used.
  7. Execution & Checkpointing: As the analysis progresses, intermediate results and checkpoints are written to ship_computer.db.
  8. Result Enrichment: Final results may be summarized, indexed, and embedded so future Deep Dive requests can retrieve them semantically.

This makes Deep Dive more efficient because Spock can reuse prior analytical work, discover related data sources, and avoid repeating expensive computations when semantically similar results already exist.

docs.title: Hybrid Search and Ranking
docs.text:
Spock does not rely on vector search alone. Instead, it uses a hybrid retrieval strategy that combines semantic similarity with structured relational constraints.

The application may combine:

  • Vector Similarity: Measures how closely the meaning of the query matches stored content.
  • Keyword Matching: Captures exact terms, identifiers, or technical names that may be important.
  • SQL Filters: Enforces session, permission, recency, status, and source constraints.
  • Metadata Scoring: Prioritizes results based on document type, confidence, freshness, or user preference.

This hybrid approach improves accuracy because semantic search can find conceptually related content, while relational filtering ensures that only valid and authorized data is used.

docs.title: Indexing and Synchronization
docs.text:
For the Embedding LLM and Vector Database to be useful, Spock must maintain an indexing pipeline that keeps semantic content synchronized with relational metadata.

The pipeline generally includes:

  1. Ingestion: New documents, summaries, preferences, or analytical results are received.
  2. Chunking: Long content is divided into meaningful segments suitable for embedding.
  3. Embedding: Each chunk is converted into a vector by the Embedding LLM.
  4. Storage: The vector and associated metadata are written to the Vector Database.
  5. Relational Sync: The corresponding metadata, source identifiers, and access controls are stored in ship_computer.db.
  6. Invalidation: When content is deleted, updated, or deauthorized, Spock removes or marks the corresponding vector entries as stale.

This synchronization is important because the Vector Database may contain semantically relevant content that is no longer valid, accessible, or current. ship_computer.db provides the authoritative relational state used to validate and filter vector search results.

docs.title: Failure Handling and Fallback Behavior
docs.text:
Because the Embedding LLM and Vector Database are external dependencies, Spock should be designed to degrade gracefully if they are unavailable.

Possible fallback behaviors include:

  • Keyword-Only Search: If vector search is unavailable, Spock can fall back to SQL-based keyword search over indexed text fields.
  • Cached Context: Previously retrieved context may be reused if it is still valid according to ship_computer.db.
  • Reduced Personalization: If session or preference data cannot be retrieved, Spock can still answer using general knowledge, but with less contextual accuracy.
  • Task Delay: For Deep Dive workflows, semantic discovery may be deferred until the vector service is available, while structured task state remains recoverable from ship_computer.db.

This layered design ensures that the core application remains functional even when semantic retrieval is temporarily degraded.

docs.title: Security and Privacy Considerations
docs.text:
Embeddings are numerical representations of text and are not directly human-readable, but they can still reveal semantic relationships if accessed improperly. For this reason, Spock should treat vector data with the same care as the source text.

Security controls may include:

  • Access Control: Vector search results are filtered using permissions stored in ship_computer.db.
  • Session Isolation: User-specific context is not exposed across sessions.
  • Metadata Protection: Sensitive metadata is not embedded unnecessarily.
  • Audit Logging: Retrieval and generation events are recorded in the relational database for review.
  • Data Lifecycle Management: Stale, deleted, or unauthorized content is removed from both the vector index and relational stores.

docs.title: Summary of the Hybrid Data Architecture
docs.text:
The Spock data architecture is intentionally hybrid:

  • ship_computer.db provides structured, transactional, and authoritative application state.
  • The Embedding LLM converts text into semantic vector representations.
  • The Vector Database enables fast meaning-based retrieval over large collections of content.
  • The Generative LLM produces natural-language responses using the retrieved context.

Together, these components allow Spock to support Ask AI and Deep Dive with both conversational continuity and analytical depth. The relational database ensures correctness, state, and auditability, while the embedding and vector layers enable semantic understanding and intelligent context discovery.

docs.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation Architecture
docs.text:
• Embedding Generation: When documents, knowledge snippets, or user queries are ingested, the application passes them through a lightweight Embedding LLM, such as a fine-tuned transformer model. This model converts text into fixed-dimensional numerical vectors that capture semantic meaning, tone, and contextual relationships.

  • Vector Storage & Indexing: Generated embeddings are stored in a specialized Vector Database optimized for high-dimensional data. The vector DB maintains an approximate nearest neighbor, or ANN, index, such as HNSW or IVF-PQ, to enable millisecond-scale similarity searches across large collections of vectors.

  • Hybrid Retrieval Workflow:

  • A user query is first embedded using the same embedding model used for document ingestion.
  • The vector DB performs a similarity search to retrieve the top-K semantically relevant chunks.
  • These results are cross-referenced with ship_computer.db to apply relational filters, such as user permissions, session context, document metadata, or recency constraints.

  • The filtered and ranked results are injected into the LLM prompt alongside system instructions.

  • Synchronization & Consistency: The application maintains a mapping table in ship_computer.db that links relational record IDs to their corresponding vector embeddings. This ensures that updates, deletions, or version changes in the relational database are accurately reflected in the vector index, preventing stale or orphaned embeddings.

  • Performance Optimization: Embedding generation is batched and cached to avoid redundant model inference. The vector DB operates in memory for low-latency similarity queries, while ship_computer.db handles durable storage and transactional integrity. This separation of concerns allows Spock to scale efficiently under concurrent Ask AI and Deep Dive workloads.

docs.title: SQLite 3 ship_computer.db
docs.text:
ship_computer.db is the durable relational database used by the Spock application. It is implemented with SQLite 3 and serves as the system of record for structured application state, user context, permissions, document metadata, retrieval mappings, and audit information.

Unlike the vector database, ship_computer.db is not primarily used for semantic similarity search. Instead, it provides the relational context needed to make retrieval results safe, accurate, and relevant to the current user, session, and application mode.

docs.title: Primary Responsibilities
docs.text:
ship_computer.db is responsible for:

  • Storing user accounts, roles, and permission scopes.
  • Tracking active sessions and conversation state.
  • Managing document, chunk, and knowledge-base metadata.
  • Linking relational records to vector embeddings.
  • Supporting Ask AI and Deep Dive workflows.
  • Enforcing access control before content is sent to the LLM.
  • Recording query history, citations, and audit events.
  • Maintaining consistency between relational data and vector data.

docs.title: Core Table Concepts
docs.text:
The database may include tables such as:

  • users
  • Stores user identity, role, and access level.
  • sessions
  • Tracks active Ask AI or Deep Dive sessions.
  • documents
  • Stores source documents, file paths, titles, owners, and status.
  • chunks
  • Stores text fragments derived from documents.
  • embeddings_map
  • Maps chunk or document IDs to vector IDs in the vector database.
  • permissions
  • Defines which users or roles can access specific documents or knowledge areas.
  • query_log
  • Records user queries, retrieval results, and response metadata.
  • deep_dive_state
  • Stores intermediate context, selected sources, and investigation state for Deep Dive.
  • audit_events
  • Records access, deletion, permission changes, and other sensitive operations.

docs.title: Relationship to the Vector Database
docs.text:
The vector database stores numerical embeddings and performs semantic similarity search. ship_computer.db stores the meaning, ownership, and lifecycle of the content behind those embeddings.

For example, a vector search may return a chunk that is semantically similar to a user query. Before that chunk is used in an LLM prompt, Spock checks ship_computer.db to confirm that:

  • The user is allowed to access the chunk.
  • The chunk belongs to an active document.
  • The document has not been deleted or revoked.
  • The chunk is not marked as deprecated.
  • The chunk is relevant to the current session or Deep Dive context.
  • The chunk should be included based on recency, priority, or source type.

This hybrid approach combines semantic relevance from the vector database with business rules and access control from SQLite.

docs.title: Ask AI Interaction
docs.text: Ask AI is the conversational question-answering mode in Spock. It is designed for direct user questions that require grounded answers from available knowledge sources.

docs.title: Ask AI Workflow
docs.text:
1. The user submits a question through the Spock interface.
  2. The application records the session and query in ship_computer.db.
  3. The query is sent to the Embedding LLM to generate a query vector.
  4. The vector database searches for the most semantically similar chunks.
  5. Spock retrieves the corresponding relational metadata from ship_computer.db.
  6. The application filters results based on permissions, document status, and session context.
  7. The remaining chunks are ranked and formatted into a prompt.
  8. The LLM generates an answer using the retrieved context.
  9. The answer, citations, and query metadata are stored back in ship_computer.db.

docs.title: Why ship_computer.db Is Required for Ask AI
docs.text:
Ask AI cannot rely on vector similarity alone. A semantically relevant chunk may still be inaccessible, outdated, or inappropriate for the current user.

ship_computer.db ensures that Ask AI answers are:

  • Permission-aware.
  • Session-aware.
  • Source-aware.
  • Audit-ready.
  • Consistent with the current state of the knowledge base.

docs.title: Deep Dive Interaction
docs.text: Deep Dive is the investigative mode in Spock. It is designed for multi-step exploration, where the application may perform repeated retrieval, compare sources, build context, and maintain a working investigation state.

docs.title: Deep Dive Workflow
docs.text:
1. The user starts a Deep Dive session.
  2. Spock creates or resumes a session record in ship_computer.db.
  3. The user provides a topic, question, or investigation goal.
  4. The application performs one or more vector similarity searches.
  5. Each retrieval result is validated against relational metadata in ship_computer.db.
  6. Relevant chunks are added to the Deep Dive context.
  7. The application may perform follow-up searches based on newly discovered concepts.
  8. The LLM synthesizes findings, identifies gaps, and proposes next steps.
  9. The session state, selected sources, and intermediate conclusions are persisted in ship_computer.db.

docs.title: Deep Dive State Management
docs.text:
Deep Dive requires more persistent state than Ask AI. ship_computer.db may store:

  • The original investigation goal.
  • Previously retrieved chunks.
  • Chunks selected for the current context.
  • Chunks excluded due to permissions or low relevance.
  • Intermediate summaries.
  • Follow-up questions generated by the application.
  • Source citations.
  • User feedback on retrieved results.

This allows Deep Dive to resume later, continue from a previous point, or branch into related investigations without losing context.

docs.title: Embedding LLM and Vector Database Workflow
docs.text: The Embedding LLM and vector database work together to enable semantic retrieval. The Embedding LLM converts text into numerical vectors, while the vector database stores those vectors and finds the most similar ones to a query.

docs.title: Embedding LLM Role
docs.text:
The Embedding LLM is responsible for transforming natural language into a numerical representation that can be compared mathematically.

It is used for:

  • Document chunks.
  • Knowledge snippets.
  • User queries.
  • Deep Dive follow-up prompts.
  • Cached or precomputed semantic representations.

A good embedding model should preserve semantic relationships so that similar concepts produce vectors that are close together in vector space.

docs.title: Vector Database Role
docs.text:
The vector database is responsible for:

  • Storing embeddings.
  • Maintaining an ANN index.
  • Performing fast similarity search.
  • Returning the top-K most relevant vectors.
  • Supporting metadata filtering where applicable.

The vector database is optimized for speed and scale. It is not the primary source of truth for permissions, document lifecycle, or application state.

docs.title: Hybrid Retrieval in Spock
docs.text:
Spock uses a hybrid retrieval model because neither semantic search nor relational filtering alone is sufficient.

The vector database answers the question:

What content is semantically similar to the user's request?

ship_computer.db answers the question:

Is this content allowed, current, relevant, and appropriate for this user and session?

Together, they produce retrieval results that are both semantically relevant and operationally safe.

docs.title: Consistency and Data Lifecycle
docs.text: Because Spock uses both a relational database and a vector database, the application must keep the two stores consistent.

docs.title: Embedding Mapping
docs.text:
Each chunk or document in ship_computer.db should have a corresponding vector ID in the vector database. This mapping allows Spock to:

  • Locate the vector for a given chunk.
  • Delete the vector when a chunk is removed.
  • Replace the vector when a chunk is updated.
  • Rebuild indexes after bulk changes.
  • Audit which vector records belong to which relational records.

docs.title: Update Handling
docs.text:
When a document or chunk is updated, Spock should:

  1. Update the relational record in ship_computer.db.
  2. Generate a new embedding for the updated text.
  3. Replace or insert the new vector in the vector database.
  4. Update the mapping table.
  5. Record the change in the audit log.

docs.title: Deletion Handling
docs.text:
When a document or chunk is deleted, Spock should:

  1. Mark or remove the relational record in ship_computer.db.
  2. Remove or tombstone the corresponding vector in the vector database.
  3. Update the mapping table.
  4. Ensure the deleted content is no longer returned in Ask AI or Deep Dive results.

docs.title: Permission Changes
docs.text: When permissions change, Spock does not necessarily need to regenerate embeddings. Instead, it updates the relational permission records in ship_computer.db. Future retrieval results are filtered using the updated permissions before being sent to the LLM.

docs.title: Performance and Scalability
docs.text:
The architecture separates semantic search from relational governance.

  • The vector database provides fast similarity search.
  • The Embedding LLM provides semantic encoding.
  • ship_computer.db provides durable, transactional, and permission-aware state.
  • The Python application coordinates retrieval, filtering, prompt construction, and persistence.

This design allows Spock to handle concurrent Ask AI and Deep Dive workloads while maintaining accurate, auditable, and permission-safe responses.

docs.title: Ship Computer Database
docs.text: The ship_computer.db SQLite 3 database serves as the persistent storage layer for the Spock application. It stores structured data required by the Ask AI and Deep Dive features, including inquiry metadata, query history, retrieval logs, session state, and audit information. The database integrates with the RAG API Server to ensure that user questions are answered using relevant context from the knowledge base, while maintaining a reliable, queryable record of all requests and system actions.

docs.title: Components
docs.text: Module Role ship_computer.db SQLite 3 database file that stores structured metadata, user inquiries, retrieval logs, session state, and application state required by Ask AI and Deep Dive workflows. spock_rag_adapter.bridge_host Adapter and host layer that connects client or UI requests to the RAG pipeline. It routes incoming requests to the appropriate handler, validates input, and returns responses in a standardized format. spock_rag_adapter.embedding_corpus Manages the document embedding pipeline, converting raw text into numerical representations, or embeddings. These vectors are used for semantic similarity calculations during retrieval. spock_rag_adapter.rag_host Contains the core RAG server logic, including query processing, context retrieval from the indexed corpus, response generation or assembly, and coordination with the SQLite database and vector store.

docs.title: Endpoints
docs.text:
The following endpoints are provided by the RAG API Server. They operate on data managed through ship_computer.db and the associated vector store.

Method Path Description POST /index Indexes documents into the vector store, enabling efficient semantic search. Used to add or update documents in the knowledge base. POST /query Queries the knowledge base using a natural language question. The system retrieves relevant documents and generates an answer based on the retrieved context. GET /health Performs a health check to verify that the API server is running and its core components are functioning correctly. POST /db/initialize Initializes the SQLite database schema, creating the tables required for Ask AI and Deep Dive inquiries.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
To fully understand the functionality described above, it is helpful to define the underlying technical terms:

  • SQLite 3: A lightweight, serverless, and self-contained relational database engine that stores all data in a single file (ship_computer.db). It supports ACID properties—Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability—ensuring data integrity during concurrent operations and Ask AI query processing.
  • Vector Store: A specialized storage mechanism optimized for storing and retrieving high-dimensional embeddings. It enables fast similarity searches by calculating distances between query vectors and document vectors, identifying contextually relevant content regardless of exact keyword matches.
  • Semantic Search: A retrieval methodology that prioritizes meaning over lexical matching. By leveraging embeddings and vector similarity metrics, it identifies documents that are conceptually aligned with a user's query, even when terminology differs.
  • Ask AI Inquiries: User requests processed through the RAG pipeline. The ship_computer.db database logs metadata for each inquiry, including timestamps, user identifiers, confidence scores, and response status, enabling audit trails, debugging, and performance analytics.
  • Deep Dive Analysis: An advanced feature that allows users to explore topics with greater granularity. It triggers iterative database queries to retrieve related documents, cross-reference findings within the knowledge base, and assemble comprehensive, multi-faceted responses.

docs.title: Database Architecture & Application Interaction
docs.text:
The ship_computer.db file acts as the relational backbone for the Spock application, specifically designed to support the operational and audit requirements of Ask AI and Deep Dive workflows. Unlike the vector store, which handles unstructured semantic data, SQLite 3 manages structured relational data through a normalized schema optimized for fast reads and writes.

For Ask AI inquiries, the database records a unique inquiry ID, timestamp, user session context, and the raw query string. As the RAG pipeline processes the request, intermediate results—such as retrieved document IDs, similarity scores, and LLM response tokens—are logged. This creates a complete audit trail that allows administrators to trace how a specific answer was constructed, verify retrieval accuracy, and monitor system latency.

For Deep Dive inquiries, the database handles more complex state management. Deep Dive sessions often involve multi-turn interactions and iterative context expansion. The SQLite database stores session state, tracks which documents have already been presented to the user, and logs cross-referencing operations. This prevents redundant retrievals, maintains conversation continuity, and ensures that expanded context is properly versioned and linked back to the original inquiry. All interactions are transactionally safe, leveraging SQLite's journaling mechanisms to prevent data corruption during high-throughput query processing.

docs.title: Embedding LLM and Vector Store Workflow
docs.text:
The Spock application uses an embedding LLM and a vector store together to perform semantic retrieval. In this context, the embedding LLM is the model responsible for converting text into numerical vector representations. It is distinct from any answer-generation LLM that may later use the retrieved context to compose a response.

When documents are added to the knowledge base, the Spock application processes them through the embedding pipeline. The document text is split into manageable chunks, and each chunk is passed to the embedding LLM. The embedding LLM produces a high-dimensional vector that represents the semantic meaning of that chunk. These vectors, along with associated metadata such as document ID, chunk ID, source, and timestamp, are stored in the vector store.

When a user submits an Ask AI or Deep Dive question, the Spock application sends the user's query to the embedding LLM. The embedding LLM converts the query into a vector using the same embedding space as the indexed documents. The vector store then performs a similarity search, comparing the query vector against the stored document vectors. The most similar vectors are returned, typically as a ranked set of top-k results.

The vector store is optimized for this type of search. It can quickly identify semantically related content even when the user's wording does not exactly match the wording in the source documents. For example, a query about “power loss during docking” may retrieve documents that discuss “energy interruption during berthing” because their embeddings are close in vector space.

The retrieved chunks are then used by the RAG pipeline as context. The Spock application may pass these chunks to an answer-generation model, or it may assemble a response directly from the retrieved content. In either case, the vector store provides the relevant semantic context, while the SQLite database records the structured details of the request, retrieval, and response.

docs.title: SQLite 3 Interaction Details
docs.text:
The ship_computer.db database is the authoritative structured record for Spock application activity. It does not replace the vector store; instead, it complements it by storing the relational and audit data needed to understand, debug, and manage Ask AI and Deep Dive behavior.

The database typically tracks the following categories of information:

  • Inquiry records: Each Ask AI or Deep Dive request is assigned a unique identifier. The database stores the user or session context, the original question, the request timestamp, and the final response status.
  • Retrieval logs: For each query, the database records the documents or chunks returned by the vector store, their similarity scores, and the order in which they were retrieved. This allows administrators to inspect whether the correct context was selected.
  • Session state: Deep Dive workflows may span multiple turns. The database stores the current state of the session, including which topics have been explored, which documents have already been shown, and which follow-up questions have been generated.
  • Response artifacts: The database may store the final answer, the model or pipeline version used, token counts, confidence indicators, and any errors that occurred during processing.
  • Audit events: Important system actions, such as indexing jobs, schema initialization, failed queries, or manual corrections, are recorded to support operational review and compliance.

During an Ask AI request, the Spock application uses SQLite 3 in a transactional workflow. First, it creates or updates an inquiry record. Next, it sends the query to the embedding LLM and vector store. After the vector store returns relevant chunks, the application logs the retrieval results. Finally, it stores the generated or assembled response and commits the transaction. If any step fails, the transaction can be rolled back, preventing partial or inconsistent records from being written.

During a Deep Dive request, the database plays a larger role. The application may create a session record, then perform multiple retrieval passes as the user explores the topic. Each pass is linked to the session and to the original inquiry. The database tracks which documents have already been used, which new documents were retrieved, and how the context expanded over time. This enables the Spock application to avoid repeating the same results, maintain a coherent narrative, and provide users with progressively deeper analysis.

The separation between SQLite 3 and the vector store is intentional. The vector store is optimized for fast semantic similarity search over high-dimensional embeddings. SQLite 3 is optimized for reliable structured queries, joins, filtering, and transactional integrity. Together, they allow Spock to answer questions using meaningful context while preserving a durable, inspectable record of every interaction.

docs.title: Embedding LLM & Vector Database Integration
docs.text:
The Spock application relies on a dedicated embedding LLM and a vector database to power its semantic retrieval capabilities. The embedding LLM is a specialized neural network model trained to map text into a high-dimensional vector space. When a document is ingested via the /index endpoint, the spock_rag_adapter.embedding_corpus module passes the text through this model, generating a fixed-length numerical array (the embedding) that captures the semantic meaning, context, and intent of the content.

These embeddings are stored in the vector database alongside lightweight metadata (for example, document source, chunk ID, and indexing timestamp). When a user submits a query through Ask AI or Deep Dive, the same embedding LLM processes the question to generate a query vector. The vector database then performs a nearest-neighbor search, calculating similarity metrics (such as cosine similarity or Euclidean distance) between the query vector and the stored document vectors.

This integration decouples semantic understanding from keyword matching. The embedding LLM ensures that conceptually related content is retrieved even when the vocabulary differs, while the vector database provides low-latency retrieval at scale. The top-ranked results are returned to the rag_host, which formats them into a context window for the generative LLM. This pipeline ensures that responses are grounded in indexed, semantically relevant knowledge-base content rather than relying solely on the LLM's pre-trained parameters.

docs.title: Detailed Explanation: How Spock Uses the Embedding LLM and Vector Database
docs.text:
The Spock application uses two distinct AI components for retrieval-augmented generation:

  • Embedding LLM: Converts text into numerical vectors that represent semantic meaning.
  • Generative LLM: Produces natural-language answers using the retrieved context.

The vector database is not responsible for generating answers. It is a search index that stores embeddings and supports fast similarity search. The embedding LLM is responsible for turning text into a form that the vector database can compare.

docs.title: Indexing Path
docs.text:
When Spock indexes content, it follows a retrieval-oriented workflow:

  1. A document or text payload is submitted through the /index endpoint.
  2. The spock_rag_adapter.embedding_corpus module prepares the text for embedding.
  3. The text is split into manageable chunks so that retrieval can return precise, relevant passages rather than entire documents.
  4. Each chunk is passed through the embedding LLM.
  5. The resulting embedding vector is stored in the vector database with metadata such as source, chunk identifier, and timestamp.
  6. Indexing activity is recorded in ship_computer.db for auditability and operational tracking.

This process creates a searchable semantic index. The vector database stores the numerical representations, while ship_computer.db stores the durable operational record of what was indexed and when.

docs.title: Query Path
docs.text:
When a user submits an Ask AI or Deep Dive inquiry, Spock uses the same embedding model to convert the user's question into a query vector. The vector database then searches for stored embeddings that are closest to that query vector.

The retrieval process works as follows:

  1. The user's question is received by the Spock application.
  2. The question is converted into an embedding vector using the embedding LLM.
  3. The vector database performs a similarity search against the indexed embeddings.
  4. The most relevant document chunks are returned with similarity scores.
  5. The rag_host selects the strongest results and assembles them into a context window.
  6. The generative LLM uses that context to produce a grounded response.
  7. The inquiry, retrieval results, response, and audit data are persisted in ship_computer.db.

This design allows Spock to answer questions using indexed knowledge rather than relying only on the generative LLM's internal training data.

docs.title: Ask AI vs. Deep Dive
docs.text:
Both Ask AI and Deep Dive use the same core embedding and vector-search pipeline, but they differ in depth and audit behavior.

Mode Typical Behavior Ask AI Performs a focused retrieval pass and returns a concise, context-grounded answer. Deep Dive Performs a more extensive retrieval and analysis workflow, potentially using multiple retrieval passes, broader context, and more detailed audit logging.

In both cases, the embedding LLM provides semantic matching, the vector database provides fast retrieval, and ship_computer.db provides the durable record of the inquiry and its supporting evidence.

docs.title: Data Flow
docs.text:
A typical request moves through the system as follows:

  1. A client or user interface sends a request to spock_rag_adapter.bridge_host.
  2. For indexing operations, raw text is processed by spock_rag_adapter.embedding_corpus, converted into embeddings via the embedding LLM, and stored in the vector store. Corresponding metadata and indexing logs are recorded in ship_computer.db.
  3. For query operations, the user's question is converted into an embedding. The vector store performs a similarity search to retrieve the most relevant document chunks.
  4. The retrieved context is passed to the generative LLM to assemble a response. Inquiry details, retrieval results, timestamps, similarity scores, and audit logs are persistently stored in ship_computer.db for compliance, debugging, and performance analysis.

docs.title: SQLite 3 ship_computer.db and Spock Inquiry Integration
docs.text:
ship_computer.db is a SQLite 3 database file used as the durable operational store for the Spock application. It is separate from the vector database. The vector database is optimized for high-dimensional similarity search, while SQLite is optimized for durable, transactional, queryable records.

For Ask AI and Deep Dive inquiries, ship_computer.db serves as the system of record for:

  • Inquiry lifecycle state
  • User prompts and system responses
  • Retrieval evidence and similarity scores
  • Indexing activity
  • Audit events
  • Performance and debugging data

This separation is important because the vector database is best suited for fast semantic search, while SQLite provides a reliable place to store the business and audit context around each request.

docs.title: Role in Ask AI and Deep Dive
docs.text:
When an Ask AI or Deep Dive request is received, the Spock application uses ship_computer.db to track the full lifecycle of the inquiry.

For Ask AI, the database typically records:

  • The user's question
  • The inquiry mode
  • The retrieval results used to answer the question
  • The final generated response
  • Timestamps and latency information
  • Any errors or status changes

For Deep Dive, the database records the same core information but may also capture a more detailed event trail, such as:

  • Multiple retrieval passes
  • Intermediate analysis steps
  • Expanded context selections
  • Additional audit events
  • More detailed performance metrics

This makes ship_computer.db especially useful for compliance, troubleshooting, and post-hoc review of how Spock arrived at a particular answer.

docs.title: Representative Schema
docs.text:
The following schema is representative of the data the application needs to persist for Ask AI and Deep Dive workflows:

CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS inquiries (
    id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    mode TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (mode IN ('ask_ai', 'deep_dive')),
    session_id TEXT,
    user_id TEXT,
    prompt TEXT NOT NULL,
    status TEXT NOT NULL,
    created_at TEXT NOT NULL,
    completed_at TEXT,
    response TEXT,
    model TEXT,
    retrieval_count INTEGER,
    latency_ms INTEGER
);

CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS retrieval_results (
    id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    inquiry_id TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES inquiries(id),
    rank INTEGER NOT NULL,
    chunk_id TEXT,
    source TEXT,
    similarity_score REAL,
    retrieved_at TEXT NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS inquiry_events (
    id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    inquiry_id TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES inquiries(id),
    event_type TEXT NOT NULL,
    payload TEXT,
    created_at TEXT NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS index_jobs (
    id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    source TEXT,
    status TEXT NOT NULL,
    chunk_count INTEGER,
    created_at TEXT NOT NULL,
    completed_at TEXT
);

docs.title: Interaction Sequence
docs.text:
The interaction between Spock, the vector database, and ship_computer.db typically follows this sequence:

  1. spock_rag_adapter.bridge_host receives an Ask AI or Deep Dive request.
  2. An inquiry record is created in ship_computer.db.
  3. spock_rag_adapter.embedding_corpus converts the user's question into an embedding vector.
  4. The vector database performs a similarity search and returns the most relevant chunks.
  5. The retrieval results are written to ship_computer.db.
  6. rag_host assembles the retrieved context and calls the generative LLM.
  7. The final response is stored in ship_computer.db.
  8. For Deep Dive, additional events and retrieval passes may be recorded as the workflow progresses.

docs.title: Why SQLite Is Used
docs.text:
SQLite is a practical choice for this role because it provides:

  • Local, file-based storage with minimal operational overhead
  • Strong transactional behavior for reliable writes
  • Easy backup and inspection
  • SQL-based querying for audit and debugging
  • A simple deployment model that fits well with a Python application

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
To start the RAG API server using a Windows PowerShell virtual environment:

.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m _start_rag_api

Alternatively, you can start the server directly using the following Python code:

from rag_api_server import app
import uvicorn

uvicorn.run(app, host="0.0.0.0", port=8080)

This launches the FastAPI server on port 8080, making the RAG API available for use. The first command assumes that a virtual environment exists at .venv in the current directory. The second snippet requires uvicorn to be installed in your Python environment. For local development, you may prefer binding to 127.0.0.1 instead of 0.0.0.0 if the server does not need to accept connections from other network interfaces.

docs.title: Database Management
docs.text:
To manage ship_computer.db directly:

  1. Initialize: Call the /db/initialize endpoint to ensure the database schema matches the application requirements.
  2. Backup: Copy the ship_computer.db file to a secure location before making significant changes. If possible, stop the API server or disable active writes while copying the file to prevent file locking or corruption.
  3. Inspect: Use SQLite command-line tools to inspect the database structure and contents:
sqlite3 ship_computer.db ".tables"
sqlite3 ship_computer.db "SELECT * FROM inquiries LIMIT 10;"

docs.title: Science Station
docs.text:
The Science Station serves as the central interface for wiki querying and ship's log access, enabling efficient data retrieval and historical record review within the system.

Module Role ScienceStation.app Main science panel. Manages the primary user interface and core application logic. ScienceStation.ships_logs Ship's log viewer. Dedicated component for browsing, filtering, and displaying historical ship logs. ScienceStation.wiki_run Wiki agent runner. Agent module responsible for executing queries against external wiki databases.

The Science Station relies on a local SQLite 3 database file named ship_computer.db to persist critical data and facilitate high-speed retrieval.

docs.title: SQLite 3 Database Architecture (ship_computer.db)
docs.text:
The ship_computer.db file functions as the persistent data layer for the Spock application, ensuring fast, reliable access to structured records and AI interaction metadata.

  • Schema & Data Storage: The database contains normalized tables for ship logs, wiki query caches, session history, and embedding metadata. Primary keys and foreign keys enforce referential integrity, while indexed columns (e.g., timestamps, query hashes, log IDs) optimize read performance.
  • Ask AI Interaction: When a user initiates an "Ask AI" request, the application first queries ship_computer.db for cached responses or relevant contextual snippets. If a cache miss occurs, the request is routed to the external LLM. Upon completion, the response, along with metadata (timestamp, confidence score, and associated vector IDs), is written to the database. This caching layer reduces redundant API calls and accelerates repeat queries.
  • Deep Dive Interaction: The "Deep Dive" feature leverages the database to perform cross-referential analysis. It executes parameterized SQL queries against the ship's log tables to extract historical entries matching specific keywords, dates, or event types. These results are then joined with cached wiki data and stored as structured analysis reports. The database's ACID compliance guarantees that concurrent Deep Dive operations do not corrupt log integrity or produce inconsistent reads.
  • Maintenance & Performance: The database is configured with WAL (Write-Ahead Logging) mode to support concurrent read/write operations without locking. Periodic vacuuming and index rebuilding are handled automatically by the application to prevent fragmentation and maintain sub-second query latency.

docs.title: Embedding LLM and Vector Database Workflow
docs.text:
The Spock application employs a hybrid AI architecture that separates semantic retrieval from content generation. This is achieved through a dedicated embedding model, a local vector database, and a generative LLM.

  • Text Embedding Process: Unstructured data (ship logs, wiki articles, and user queries) is passed through a lightweight embedding model. This model converts text into high-dimensional numerical vectors that mathematically represent semantic meaning, rather than relying on exact keyword matches.
  • Vector Database Indexing: Generated vectors are stored in a local vector database optimized for approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search. The vector DB maintains an index that allows the application to rapidly compare incoming query vectors against thousands of stored document vectors, retrieving the most semantically relevant chunks in milliseconds.
  • Query Resolution Pipeline:
  • Ingestion & Embedding: User input is transformed into a query vector.
  • Similarity Search: The vector DB performs a cosine similarity or dot-product search, returning the top-k most relevant log entries and wiki excerpts.
  • Context Assembly: Retrieved chunks are formatted into a structured prompt context, preserving source attribution and metadata.
  • LLM Generation: The generative LLM receives the original query alongside the assembled context and produces a synthesized, fact-grounded response.
  • State & Traceability: While the vector database handles semantic matching, ship_computer.db tracks query history, user preferences, and embedding versioning. This separation ensures that AI interactions remain auditable, reproducible, and independent of external network dependencies.

On Windows PowerShell, use the local .venv Python environment to run the following command:

.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m spock_wiki_adapter

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before running the Science Station, confirm that the following environment requirements are met:

  1. Python Environment: Create and activate a Python virtual environment (.venv). This isolates project dependencies from the system Python installation and helps prevent dependency conflicts.
  2. Path Configuration: The command paths shown below are specific to Windows PowerShell environments. Run the script from a terminal that matches the documented file structure, for example .venv\Scripts\python.exe.

docs.title: Virtual environment setup (Windows)
docs.text:
If you need to create or refresh the virtual environment in PowerShell:

python -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1

Then install project dependencies if a requirements file is present:

pip install -r requirements.txt

This step ensures that spock_wiki_adapter and its required packages are available inside the isolated environment.

docs.title: Path notes
docs.text:
• On Windows PowerShell, use backslashes (\) in relative paths.
  • The interpreter path .venv\Scripts\python.exe points to the Python executable inside the project virtual environment.
  • If you activate the virtual environment first, you can usually run python -m spock_wiki_adapter instead of using the full interpreter path.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
To start the Science Station, run the following command in PowerShell:

.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m spock_wiki_adapter

This command invokes the spock_wiki_adapter module, which serves as the entry point for initializing the Science Station application. The -m flag tells Python to execute a package or module by name rather than running a standalone script file.

Ensure that the Python virtual environment (.venv) is properly set up and activated before running this command to avoid dependency errors. If you are not using an activated shell, use the full path shown above so PowerShell resolves the correct interpreter.

docs.title: Cross-platform note
docs.text:
On macOS or Linux shells, the equivalent command typically uses forward slashes:

.venv/bin/python -m spock_wiki_adapter

Use this form only if your project structure and virtual environment layout match that platform convention.

docs.title: SQLite 3 ship_computer.db
docs.text: ship_computer.db is the local SQLite 3 database used by the Spock application as the primary structured store for Science Station content. It is a single-file database, which makes it easy to bundle, inspect, and version alongside the application without requiring a separate database server.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The database provides durable, queryable storage for the information that Ask AI and Deep Dive need to ground their responses. It typically stores:

  • Wiki or article records, including titles, slugs, source URLs, and revision metadata.
  • Chunked text segments that can be retrieved as context for language-model prompts.
  • Metadata used for filtering, such as tags, categories, dates, authorship, and content type.
  • Conversation history, user questions, generated answers, and citation references.
  • Retrieval caches or query logs that help improve performance and auditability.
  • Foreign-key relationships that allow Deep Dive to traverse related records.

docs.title: Typical contents
docs.text:
A representative schema may include tables such as:

CREATE TABLE wiki_pages (
    id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    slug TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    title TEXT NOT NULL,
    source_url TEXT,
    created_at TEXT,
    updated_at TEXT
);

CREATE TABLE wiki_chunks (
    id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    page_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES wiki_pages(id),
    chunk_index INTEGER NOT NULL,
    content TEXT NOT NULL,
    token_count INTEGER,
    embedding_id TEXT
);

CREATE TABLE conversations (
    id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id TEXT,
    created_at TEXT,
    mode TEXT CHECK (mode IN ('ask_ai', 'deep_dive'))
);

CREATE TABLE messages (
    id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    conversation_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES conversations(id),
    role TEXT NOT NULL,
    content TEXT NOT NULL,
    created_at TEXT
);

CREATE TABLE citations (
    id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    message_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES messages(id),
    chunk_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES wiki_chunks(id),
    relevance_score REAL
);

The exact schema may vary, but the important architectural point is that SQLite holds the authoritative text, metadata, and relational links, while the vector database holds the numeric embeddings used for semantic search.

docs.title: How Spock interacts with the database
docs.text:
The spock_wiki_adapter module acts as the bridge between the Spock application and ship_computer.db. During startup, it typically:

  1. Opens the SQLite database file.
  2. Validates or migrates the schema.
  3. Loads configuration for Ask AI and Deep Dive.
  4. Exposes repository functions for reading pages, chunks, conversations, and citations.
  5. Coordinates with the embedding service and vector database when semantic retrieval is required.

For Ask AI, Spock uses the database mainly to fetch precise context after semantic search has identified relevant chunks. For Deep Dive, Spock uses the database more extensively to filter, join, paginate, and trace relationships across multiple records.

docs.title: Ask AI interaction
docs.text:
Ask AI is a retrieval-augmented question-answering feature. A typical flow is:

  1. The user submits a question.
  2. Spock stores the question in the conversations and messages tables.
  3. The embedding model converts the question into a vector.
  4. The vector database returns the most semantically similar chunks.
  5. Spock uses the returned chunk identifiers to load the full text and metadata from ship_computer.db.
  6. The prompt builder combines the question, retrieved context, and citation metadata.
  7. The answer-generating language model produces a response.
  8. Spock stores the answer and the citations used to support it.

This design keeps the answer grounded in the local wiki content and makes it possible to show users which records informed the response.

docs.title: Deep Dive interaction
docs.text:
Deep Dive is a longer, multi-step investigation mode. It uses the same core components as Ask AI, but with a broader and more structured retrieval strategy.

Compared with Ask AI, Deep Dive may:

  • Run multiple embedding queries to cover different aspects of the user's request.
  • Apply structured filters from SQLite, such as date range, category, source type, or tag.
  • Follow foreign-key relationships to find related pages, chunks, or entities.
  • Build an evidence set from several retrieval passes.
  • Store intermediate steps, plans, and citations so the user can review the reasoning path.
  • Use cached results from ship_computer.db to avoid repeated expensive retrieval or embedding calls.

In this mode, SQLite is not merely a lookup table. It is the relational backbone that lets Spock move from "find similar text" to "assemble a coherent, citable investigation."

docs.title: What the embedding LLM does
docs.text:
The embedding LLM, or embedding model, converts text into a numeric vector. Each vector represents the semantic meaning of the text in a high-dimensional space. Text with similar meaning is placed closer together in that space.

This is different from the answer-generating language model. The embedding model does not write the final response. Its job is to make text searchable by meaning rather than by exact keyword match.

docs.title: How Spock uses the embedding model
docs.text: Spock uses the embedding model in two main phases.

docs.title: Indexing phase
docs.text:
When wiki content is added or updated:

  1. Spock splits the content into manageable chunks.
  2. Each chunk is stored in ship_computer.db.
  3. The embedding model converts each chunk into a vector.
  4. The vector is stored in the vector database.
  5. A link between the chunk and its vector is maintained, often through an embedding_id or similar identifier.

docs.title: Query phase
docs.text:
When a user asks a question:

  1. Spock embeds the user's question using the same embedding model.
  2. The vector database searches for the nearest vectors.
  3. The top matching chunk identifiers are returned.
  4. Spock retrieves the corresponding text and metadata from ship_computer.db.
  5. The retrieved context is used to build the prompt for the answer-generating model.

Using the same embedding model for indexing and querying is important because it ensures that both content and questions are represented in the same semantic space.

docs.title: Role of the vector database
docs.text:
The vector database stores the numeric embeddings and provides fast similarity search. It is optimized for approximate nearest-neighbor queries, which are well suited to semantic search over large text collections.

The vector database complements SQLite:

Component Primary responsibility SQLite ship_computer.db Authoritative text, metadata, relationships, conversation history, and citations Vector database Semantic similarity search over embedded text chunks Embedding model Converts text into vectors for both indexing and querying Answer-generating model Produces the final user-facing response from the retrieved context

docs.title: Ask AI versus Deep Dive
docs.text:
Ask AI typically performs a single semantic search pass. It embeds the question, retrieves a small number of relevant chunks, and asks the language model to answer directly from that context.

Deep Dive performs a more complex retrieval process. It may combine semantic search with structured database queries, repeated retrieval, relationship traversal, and evidence aggregation. The result is a more detailed response that can cite multiple sources and explain how the evidence was assembled.

docs.title: Why both SQLite and a vector database are needed
docs.text:
Keyword search and semantic search solve different problems. SQLite can answer questions such as:

  • Which chunks belong to a specific page?
  • Which records were updated within a date range?
  • Which chunks are tagged with a particular category?
  • Which previous messages cited a given source?

The vector database can answer questions such as:

  • Which chunks are semantically similar to this question?
  • Which passages discuss a concept even if they do not use the exact same words?
  • Which content is conceptually related to the user's request?

By combining both, Spock can retrieve relevant content efficiently while preserving the structured context needed for accurate, citable, and auditable responses.

docs.title: Database Architecture: ship_computer.db
docs.text: This section describes the architecture of the primary data store for the Spock application. The database is implemented with SQLite 3 and stored as a local file named ship_computer.db. It provides persistent storage for session state, query history, knowledge-graph data, and user context used by the Ask AI and Deep Dive modules.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
ship_computer.db is initialized at application startup and remains available while the application runs. Unlike in-memory caches or temporary API responses, this database retains durable information that must survive restarts:

  • Session state: Active and completed Ask AI and Deep Dive sessions.
  • Query history: User inputs and model responses used to reconstruct conversation context.
  • Knowledge graph data: Entities and relationships extracted during Deep Dive analysis.
  • User context: Profile-specific preferences, including settings such as WarpCore.theme.

All database access is routed through a repository layer. This architectural pattern keeps SQL logic separate from application features, makes behavior easier to test, and reduces the risk of inconsistent writes or SQL injection vulnerabilities.

docs.title: Schema Design
docs.text:
The schema is optimized for local read-heavy workloads with periodic writes during session creation, response logging, and Deep Dive extraction. The core tables are:

Table Name Purpose Primary Key Notes sessions Tracks Ask AI and Deep Dive sessions. session_id Stores timestamps, status, and the associated user profile. query_logs Maintains a history of text inputs and model responses. log_id Supports retrieval of recent interactions for context reconstruction. knowledge_graph Stores entities and relationships extracted during Deep Dive analysis. entity_id Enables relationship mapping across analyzed topics. user_context Persists user-specific configuration for AI inquiries. profile_id Linked to the settings store for theme and preference management, including WarpCore.theme.

The tables are intentionally simple so that common operations—creating a session, appending a query log entry, reading recent context, and persisting extracted entities—remain fast and easy to reason about. Indexes are applied to foreign keys and frequently queried columns, such as session_id, profile_id, and timestamp, to ensure fast lookups during active conversations.

docs.title: Interaction with Spock Application
docs.text: The Spock application interacts with ship_computer.db through a dedicated repository layer that abstracts raw SQL queries. This prevents API endpoints or UI components from accessing the database directly, improving security, maintainability, and testability.

docs.title: Ask AI Integration
docs.text:
When a user submits an inquiry through the Ask AI module, the following data flow occurs:

  1. Session Initialization: The application checks for an active session tied to the current profile. If none exists, the repository inserts a new record into sessions with a unique session_id, timestamp, and initial status (active).
  2. Context Assembly: The repository queries user_context for profile-specific preferences and fetches the most recent N entries from query_logs scoped to the current session_id. This historical data is serialized into a structured prompt template.
  3. Inference and Logging: The assembled prompt is sent to the LLM. Upon receiving a response, the repository inserts both the user query and the model response into query_logs within a single transaction, preserving chronological order and token usage metadata.
  4. State Synchronization: The UI updates in real time via WebSocket or polling, reflecting the new message while the database remains the source of truth for session continuity.

docs.title: Deep Dive Integration
docs.text:
The Deep Dive module performs more intensive, multi-step analysis:

  1. Graph Construction: As the AI analyzes a topic, it extracts named entities, concepts, and semantic relationships. The repository batches these extractions and writes them to knowledge_graph, linking them to the parent session_id.
  2. Entity Persistence and Deduplication: Before insertion, the repository checks for existing entities to prevent duplication. Relationships are stored as directed edges, enabling traversal and visualization across analyzed material.
  3. Context Reuse and Cross-Referencing: Persisted graph data can be queried by Ask AI or other features when relevant context is needed. For example, if a user asks a follow-up question referencing a previously analyzed entity, the repository retrieves related graph nodes and injects them into the prompt context.
  4. Session Finalization: Once analysis completes, the sessions record status updates to completed, and a summary index is generated for faster future retrieval.

docs.title: SQLite 3 Runtime Behavior
docs.text:
ship_computer.db is an embedded SQLite 3 database file, so it does not require a separate database server process. The Spock application opens the file through the repository layer and uses SQLite 3 for local, file-based persistence.

SQLite 3 is well suited to this use case because it supports concurrent readers and a single writer, which matches the Spock workload: many reads for context reconstruction and UI state, with writes during session creation, response logging, and Deep Dive extraction. The repository layer uses short transactions to keep writes consistent and to reduce the chance of lock contention.

The database file is the durable source of truth for relational data. In-memory caches, WebSocket state, and temporary prompt buffers may improve responsiveness, but they are not relied upon for persistence. If the application restarts, Spock can reconstruct the active conversation, user preferences, and Deep Dive graph from ship_computer.db.

docs.title: Embedding LLM and Vector Database
docs.text:
Spock uses an embedding LLM and a vector database to add semantic retrieval to the Ask AI and Deep Dive workflows. The embedding LLM is not the same model that generates final answers. Its role is to convert text into dense numeric vectors, also called embeddings, that represent meaning rather than exact keyword matches.

The vector database stores those embeddings together with metadata. It allows Spock to find semantically similar passages, entities, or concepts quickly. ship_computer.db remains the primary record store for sessions, query logs, user context, and knowledge-graph metadata, while the vector database acts as a retrieval accelerator for semantic search.

docs.title: Embedding LLM Responsibilities
docs.text:
The embedding LLM is used to create vector representations for:

  • User questions submitted through Ask AI.
  • Recent conversation turns used to preserve context.
  • Source passages or documents analyzed during Deep Dive.
  • Extracted entities, concepts, and relationship descriptions.
  • Candidate summaries or evidence snippets that may be injected into a prompt.

Each embedding is associated with metadata such as profile_id, session_id, entity_id, source location, timestamp, and embedding model version. This metadata allows Spock to scope retrieval to the correct user, session, and analysis context.

docs.title: Vector Database Responsibilities
docs.text:
The vector database stores:

  • The numeric embedding vector.
  • The original text or a reference to the text.
  • Metadata used for filtering and tracing.
  • Similarity index structures that support fast nearest-neighbor search.

Spock typically uses cosine similarity or another vector similarity metric to rank candidate results. The vector database is not a replacement for ship_computer.db; it complements the relational store by enabling semantic matching across large amounts of text and extracted concepts.

docs.title: Ask AI Semantic Retrieval Flow
docs.text:
For an Ask AI inquiry, Spock uses the embedding LLM and vector database in the following way:

  1. Query Embedding: The user's question, and optionally the most recent conversation turns, are sent to the embedding LLM to produce a query vector.
  2. Semantic Retrieval: Spock searches the vector database for the most similar stored passages, entities, or Deep Dive artifacts. Results are filtered by the current profile_id and, when appropriate, the active session_id.
  3. Context Assembly: The repository layer combines the retrieved semantic context with data from ship_computer.db, including recent query_logs, user_context preferences, and relevant knowledge_graph nodes.
  4. Prompt Construction: The combined context is serialized into a structured prompt for the answer-generating LLM.
  5. Response Logging: After the LLM responds, Spock logs the user query, model response, retrieved vector identifiers, and token usage metadata in query_logs. This allows future sessions to trace which semantic evidence influenced the answer.

This approach allows Ask AI to answer questions using both explicit conversation history and semantically related material that may not share exact keywords with the user's question.

docs.title: Deep Dive Semantic Analysis Flow
docs.text:
Deep Dive uses the embedding LLM and vector database to make multi-step analysis more coherent:

  1. Passage Chunking: The input material is divided into meaningful chunks, such as paragraphs, sections, or extracted statements.
  2. Embedding Generation: Each chunk, entity, and relationship description is converted into an embedding by the embedding LLM.
  3. Semantic Clustering: Spock uses vector similarity to group related concepts, detect near-duplicate entities, and identify recurring themes.
  4. Relationship Enrichment: Similarity scores help rank candidate relationships and suggest connections that may not be obvious from keyword matching alone.
  5. Graph Persistence: The repository layer stores the resulting entities and relationships in knowledge_graph, while the vector database retains the embeddings and retrieval metadata.
  6. Cross-Session Reuse: Future Ask AI or Deep Dive requests can retrieve related vectors and graph nodes, allowing Spock to build on previously analyzed material.

docs.title: Coordination Between SQLite and the Vector Store
docs.text:
The repository layer coordinates the two storage systems:

  • ship_computer.db stores durable relational records, including session identifiers, query history, user preferences, and knowledge-graph edges.
  • The vector database stores embeddings and similarity search indexes.
  • Vector records reference relational identifiers such as session_id, profile_id, and entity_id, so Spock can trace semantic results back to the authoritative database records.
  • If vector retrieval is unavailable, Spock can fall back to SQLite-based context reconstruction, recent query history, and keyword or graph-based lookup.

This separation keeps the relational database simple and reliable while giving Spock the semantic retrieval capability needed for natural-language Ask AI and Deep Dive experiences.

docs.title: Embedding LLM and Vector Database Integration
docs.text:
While ship_computer.db manages structured relational data, the Spock application leverages an embedding LLM and a vector database to enable semantic search and high-dimensional context retrieval.
